CAUTI: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection, usually E. coli.
CBD: Common bile duct, carrying bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
CBG: Capillary blood glucose, the bedside finger-prick reading.
CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy: a talking therapy that changes unhelpful thoughts and behaviours.
CCB: Calcium channel blocker (e.g. amlodipine); first-line for age 55 or over or Black patients.
CCBs: Calcium channel blockers such as amlodipine; can reduce intestinal motility.
CCU: Coronary care unit: ward with continuous cardiac monitoring.
CD20: Surface protein on B cells targeted by rituximab.
CD21: Complement receptor 2 on B cells; the entry receptor for EBV.
CD4: Surface marker on T-helper cells that HIV uses to enter cells.
CD4 count: Number of helper T cells; below 200 cells/µL defines AIDS.
CD8+: Marker of cytotoxic T cells that kill virus-infected cells.
CEA: Carcinoembryonic antigen; tumour marker used to monitor colorectal cancer treatment.
CFS: Chronic fatigue syndrome: disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise for at least 3 months, not explained by another condition.
CFTR: Cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator, an epithelial chloride channel.
CG109: NICE guideline on transient loss of consciousness ('blackouts') in people over 16.
CGM: Continuous glucose monitoring with a sensor under the skin.
CGRP: Calcitonin gene-related peptide: a neuropeptide driving neurogenic inflammation and vasodilation in migraine.
CGRP inhibitor: A drug that blocks calcitonin gene-related peptide, a key driver of migraine pain.
CHA2DS2-VASc: Score estimating stroke risk in AF to decide anticoagulation.
CHARTS: Mnemonic for upper lobe fibrosis: coal, histiocytosis/HP, ankylosing spondylitis, radiation, TB, silicosis/sarcoid.
CHOCOLATE: Mnemonic for migraine triggers: chocolate, hangovers, orgasms, cheese/caffeine, oral contraceptives, lie-ins, alcohol, travel, exercise.
CIN: Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia: pre-cancerous change graded I to III.
CIS: Carcinoma in situ: flat, high-grade, non-invasive cancer of the lining.
CK: Creatine kinase: a muscle enzyme that is very high in rhabdomyolysis.
CK-MB: A heart-specific creatine kinase enzyme that falls quickly after MI, making it useful for spotting reinfarction.
CKD: Chronic kidney disease: kidney damage or reduced function lasting 3 months or more.
CKD-mineral bone disease: Bone and mineral problems in CKD: abnormal calcium, phosphate, PTH and vitamin D, fractures and calcification.
CLL: Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, a common cause of warm AIHA.
CML: Chronic myeloid leukaemia: defined by the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22); massive splenomegaly.
CMPA: Cow's milk protein allergy: an immune reaction to the proteins in cow's milk.
CMT1A: The commonest Charcot-Marie-Tooth subtype, caused by PMP22 gene duplication.
CMV retinitis: Cytomegalovirus infection of the retina causing floaters and visual loss when CD4 is below 50.
CN V: The trigeminal nerve, the fifth cranial nerve.
CN VII: The facial nerve: moves the face and carries taste, tear, saliva and stapedius fibres.
CNS: Central nervous system: the brain and spinal cord.
CNS bleed: Bleeding inside the brain or spinal cord.
CNS depression: Slowing of brain function, causing drowsiness, reduced consciousness and slowed breathing.
CNS dysfunction: Brain not working properly, such as confusion, seizures or reduced consciousness.
CNS lesion: A damaged or abnormal area in the brain or spinal cord, such as a tumour or abscess.
CO2: Carbon dioxide; breathing it off removes acid and raises blood pH.
CO2 retainer: A patient with chronically raised pCO2 who risks worsening with uncontrolled oxygen.
CO2 retention: Build-up of carbon dioxide in the blood.
COCP: Combined oral contraceptive pill; its oestrogen raises clotting risk.
COMT inhibitor: Drug such as entacapone that slows peripheral levodopa breakdown and prolongs each dose.
COPD: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; the most important cause of respiratory acidosis.
COPD exacerbation: A flare of COPD with worse breathlessness, cough and sputum.
COX-1: Cyclooxygenase-1: enzyme that makes thromboxane in platelets and protective prostaglandins in the stomach.
COX-2: Inducible cyclooxygenase involved in inflammation; also blocked by aspirin.
CPAP: Continuous positive airway pressure via a tight mask; keeps alveoli open in pulmonary oedema.
CPP: Cerebral perfusion pressure: MAP minus ICP; the pressure driving blood through the brain.
CPPD: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, the umbrella term that includes pseudogout.
CPR: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation: chest compressions and rescue breaths.
CRAB: HyperCalcaemia, Renal impairment, Anaemia, Bone lesions: myeloma end-organ damage.
CRB-65: CURB-65 without the urea, used in the community where blood results are not available.
CRP: C-reactive protein; a blood marker of inflammation used to guide antibiotics in acute cough.
CRT: Cardiac resynchronisation therapy: a biventricular pacemaker that makes both ventricles contract together.
CRT-D: A CRT device that is also an implantable defibrillator.
CSF: Cerebrospinal fluid, which surrounds the brain and spinal cord.
CSF diversion: Draining CSF away, for example with an external drain or shunt, to relieve hydrocephalus.
CSF protein: Protein level in the spinal fluid; raised with normal cell count in GBS.
CT: Computed tomography: cross-sectional X-ray imaging used to find and stage cancer.
CT CAP: CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, used to find a primary tumour or other spread.
CT KUB: Non-contrast CT of kidneys, ureters and bladder; the standard test for stones.
CT abdomen: A cross-sectional X-ray scan of the abdomen.
CT abdomen and pelvis: Cross-sectional scan showing the site and cause of the obstruction.
CT angiogram: CT scan with IV contrast showing the aorta's size, shape and leaks; used to plan EVAR.
CT angiography: CT scan with IV contrast that maps the arteries and shows blockages or aneurysms.
CT aortic angiogram: Contrast CT timed for the aorta; the gold-standard test, showing the false lumen.
CT chest: Computed tomography scan giving cross-sectional images of the chest.
CT colonography: CT 'virtual colonoscopy' after bowel preparation and gas insufflation.
CT coronary angiography: CT scan with contrast showing coronary narrowing; first-line test for stable angina.
CT head: CT scan of the brain, done before LP if raised ICP is suspected.
CT perfusion: A CT scan showing blood flow in the brain, used to find salvageable tissue.
CT pulmonary angiography: A CT scan with contrast in the lung arteries, used to look for clots.
CT sinuses: A CT scan of the facial sinuses, used in severe, recurrent or complicated disease.
CT urogram: CT with contrast timed to show the kidneys, ureters and bladder lining.
CT with contrast: CT scan after injecting dye to show blood vessels and inflamed tissue more clearly.
CT-guided: Using CT images to steer a needle or drain into the right place.
CT-guided biopsy: Needle biopsy of a lung lesion using CT to guide it; used for peripheral masses.
CTCA: CT coronary angiography: first-line non-invasive scan of the coronary arteries.
CTD: Connective tissue disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis, SLE or scleroderma.
CTEPH: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, caused by unresolved pulmonary emboli.
CTPA: CT pulmonary angiogram; timed for the pulmonary arteries to look for PE, not dissection.
CURB-65: Pneumonia severity score: confusion, urea over 7, RR 30 or more, low BP, age 65 or over.
CYP2C19: Liver enzyme that activates clopidogrel; inhibited by omeprazole and esomeprazole.
CYP2E1: Cytochrome P450 enzyme induced by chronic drinking; metabolises alcohol and makes free radicals.
CYP450: Liver enzyme family that breaks down many drugs, including warfarin.
CYP450 inducer: Drug that speeds up CYP450, lowering levels of drugs like warfarin.
CYP450 inducers: Drugs such as rifampicin and carbamazepine that speed up liver breakdown of other drugs.
CYP450 inhibitor: Drug that slows CYP450, raising levels of drugs like warfarin.
Cachexia: Severe wasting of muscle and fat from chronic illness.
Caecal: Relating to the caecum, the first pouch of the large bowel in the right iliac fossa.
Caecal volvulus: Volvulus of a mobile caecum; gives right iliac fossa pain and a small bowel obstruction picture.
Caeruloplasmin: Copper-carrying protein; low in Wilson's disease.
Caffeine: A stimulant found in coffee, tea and energy drinks that worsens essential tremor.
Café-au-lait spots: Flat, light-brown skin patches; many of them suggest neurofibromatosis type 1.
Calcification: Build-up of calcium deposits that stiffen tissue such as valve leaflets.
Calcified: Hardened by deposits of calcium salts; shows white on X-ray.
Calcineurin inhibitor: Drug that blocks T-cell activation; used topically in eczema to avoid steroid side effects.
Calcipotriol: Topical vitamin D analogue that slows keratinocyte growth.
Calcitriol: The active form of vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D), made in the kidney.
Calcium: Blood calcium level, checked because hypercalcaemia causes constipation.
Calcium carbonate: A calcium supplement and antacid that reduces levothyroxine absorption.
Calcium channel blocker: A drug that blocks calcium entry into muscle cells, relaxing artery walls.
Calcium gluconate: IV calcium given to stabilise the heart muscle in severe hyperkalaemia; it does not lower potassium.
Calcium influx: Calcium entering a cell, which in smooth muscle triggers contraction.
Calcium phosphate: A radiopaque stone type made of calcium and phosphate.
Calcium pyrophosphate: The calcium salt that forms the rhomboid crystals of pseudogout.
Calcium supplements: Tablets of calcium to replace dietary calcium lost when dairy is cut out.
Caldicott Guardian: A senior NHS person responsible for protecting patient information and approving its use.
Calf: The back of the lower leg.
Callus: Thickened skin over a pressure point; a warning sign of ulcer risk in a neuropathic foot.
Calorie deficit: Eating fewer calories than the body uses, leading to weight loss.
Cameron ulcers: Linear erosions in a hiatus hernia at the diaphragmatic pinch, causing occult bleeding.
Campylobacter: Commonest UK bacterial cause of bloody diarrhoea, often from undercooked chicken.
Campylobacter jejuni: Gut bacterium whose infection commonly triggers GBS.
Cancer work-up: Tests to find the type and spread of a suspected cancer.
Cancer-associated thrombosis: A blood clot caused by an active cancer making the blood clot more easily.
Candesartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker used as second-line migraine prophylaxis.
Candida albicans: The commonest Candida yeast; normal flora of mouth, gut and vagina.
Candidiasis: Infection caused by Candida yeasts, usually Candida albicans.
Cannon A waves: Large JVP waves when the atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.
Capacity: The ability to make a specific decision at a specific time, judged by the four-stage test.
Capillary: Finger-prick sample used at the bedside for glucose and ketone measurements.
Capillary blood gas: Blood gas test on a small sample from a finger or heel prick.
Capillary blood ketones: Ketone level measured from a finger-prick blood sample with a bedside meter.
Capillary leak: Fluid escaping from damaged small vessels into tissues, causing oedema and low circulating volume.
Capillary occlusion: Blockage of the smallest blood vessels.
Capillary permeability: How easily fluid and proteins leak out through the walls of the smallest blood vessels.
Caplan syndrome: Rheumatoid lung nodules in people exposed to coal, silica or asbestos dust.
Capnography: Continuous measurement and waveform of exhaled CO2; confirms the tube is in the trachea.
Capsule: The fibrous wall that forms around a mature abscess.
Caput medusae: Dilated veins radiating from the umbilicus, a sign of portal hypertension.
Carbamazepine: A second-line AED for focal seizures; an enzyme inducer that weakens hormonal contraception.
Carbidopa: Peripheral DOPA decarboxylase inhibitor given with levodopa.
Carbimazole: Antithyroid drug that blocks hormone synthesis; used for hyperthyroidism, never for hypothyroidism.
Carbonic acid: H2CO3, formed when CO2 dissolves in water; splits into H+ and bicarbonate.
Carcinoma: Cancer arising from epithelial cells, such as breast or lung.
Carcinoma in situ: High-grade cancer cells confined to the lining, not yet invasive.
Cardiac MRI: Magnetic resonance scan of the heart; the gold-standard test for myocarditis.
Cardiac action potential: The electrical cycle of a heart muscle cell during each beat.
Cardiac arrest: Sudden cessation of cardiac output, so circulation stops.
Cardiac cirrhosis: Liver scarring from long-term venous congestion in right heart failure.
Cardiac conduction: The spread of electrical impulses through the heart that triggers each beat.
Cardiac embolism: A clot formed in the heart that travels and lodges in an artery.
Cardiac failure: The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
Cardiac membrane: The membrane of heart muscle cells, made unstable by high potassium.
Cardiac monitoring: Continuous ECG display to catch arrhythmias early.
Cardiac output: Heart rate multiplied by stroke volume: blood pumped per minute.
Cardiac resynchronisation therapy: A pacemaker pacing both ventricles so they contract together.
Cardiac sarcoidosis: Granulomas in the heart causing heart block, arrhythmias or heart failure.
Cardiac syncope: Fainting caused by a heart problem such as an arrhythmia; more dangerous than vasovagal.
Cardiac tamponade: Blood or fluid in the pericardium compressing the heart and stopping it filling.
Cardioembolic: Caused by a clot that travels from the heart.
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lungs from raised pressure in an overloaded or failing heart.
Cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor perfusion because the heart cannot pump enough.
Cardiology: Branch of medicine dealing with the heart.
Cardiomegaly: An enlarged heart shadow on CXR: cardiothoracic ratio above 0.5 on a PA film.
Cardiomyopathy: Heart muscle disease; iron causes restrictive or dilated forms.
Cardioprotective aspirin: Low-dose aspirin taken to prevent heart attacks and strokes.
Cardiothoracic surgery: Surgery on the heart and chest.
Cardiotoxic: Damaging to the heart or its rhythm.
Cardiotoxicity: Drug damage to the heart muscle, such as heart failure from trastuzumab.
Cardiotropic: Having a tendency to infect heart tissue.
Cardiovascular collapse: Sudden failure of the circulation with very low blood pressure and loss of consciousness.
Cardiovascular disease: Disease of the heart and blood vessels, such as heart attack and stroke.
Cardiovascular risk: The chance of having a heart attack or stroke over a given time, often 10 years.
Carers: Family or friends who look after the patient and can tell staff what they would want.
Carney complex: Rare inherited syndrome of adrenal nodules, skin pigmentation and heart myxomas.
Carotid: The main arteries in the neck supplying the head.
Carotid artery dissection: A tear in the carotid artery wall that can cause stroke, often in young people.
Carotid atherosclerosis: Fatty plaque in the carotid artery that can shed emboli to the eye or brain.
Carotid disease: Narrowing of the carotid arteries by atherosclerosis.
Carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove plaque from the carotid artery to reduce stroke risk.
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: Syncope from pressure on the neck (shaving, tight collar), usually in older people.
Carotid sinus massage: Pressing over the carotid sinus in the neck to stimulate the vagus nerve and slow the heart.
Carotids: The carotid arteries in the neck.
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve at the wrist causing tingling in the thumb, index and middle fingers.
Carpometacarpal joint: Joint between wrist bones and hand bones; the first one is at the base of the thumb.
Carrier: A person with one faulty copy who is usually unaffected but can pass it on.
Cartilage: Firm connective tissue that supports the walls of the larger airways.
Carvallo's sign: A right-sided murmur that gets louder on inspiration.
Carvedilol: Non-selective beta-blocker with alpha-blocking action, used to prevent first variceal bleeds.
Casal's necklace: Hyperpigmented band of dermatitis around the neck in pellagra.
Cascade screening: Testing relatives of someone with an inherited condition.
Cascade testing: Testing the relatives of someone with an inherited condition such as FH.
Caseating: With central cheesy necrosis; typical of TB granulomas.
Cast immobilisation: A limb held still in a plaster cast, a risk factor for DVT.
Catabolic: Breaking down body tissues for energy, causing weight loss.
Catch-up vaccination: Giving missed vaccine doses to people who were not fully immunised.
Catecholamines: Adrenaline and noradrenaline; cortisol keeps blood vessels responsive to them.
Catheter: A tube passed into the bladder to drain urine.
Catheter intervention: Removing or breaking up a clot using a tube passed through the blood vessels.
Catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
Cauda equina: The bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord, resembling a horse's tail.
Cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots causing saddle anaesthesia, retention and LMN leg signs.
Causative medication: The drug responsible for causing the symptom.
Causative organism: The microbe responsible for an infection.
Cavitation: A hollow, air-filled space forming inside an area of lung destroyed by infection, typical of S. aureus or Klebsiella.
Cavity: An air-filled hole in the lung where tissue has died and drained.
Cefalexin: Oral cephalosporin used for UTI in late pregnancy and complicated UTI.
Cefotaxime: A third-generation cephalosporin used in infants and with amoxicillin in Listeria risk groups.
Ceftriaxone: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used IV to treat SBP.
Cefuroxime: IV cephalosporin used for pyelonephritis in pregnancy.
Ceiling of care: The agreed upper limit of treatment escalation for a patient.
Celecoxib: A COX-2 selective NSAID with less stomach irritation.
Cell count: The number of white cells, especially neutrophils, in a fluid sample.
Cell lines: The separate families of blood cells: red cells, white cells and platelets.
Cell lysis: Cells bursting open, releasing their contents such as purines.
Cell turnover: How fast cells divide and die.
Cell wall: The rigid outer layer of bacteria; atypical organisms lack a typical one, so beta-lactams do not work.
Cell-mediated: An immune response driven by T cells rather than antibodies; delayed in onset.
Cell-mediated immunity: T-cell driven immunity that controls fungi, viruses and intracellular organisms.
Cellulitis: Acute bacterial infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, usually of one lower leg.
Centor: Short for the Centor criteria, the sore throat score used to decide antibiotics.
Centor criteria: Four-point score (exudate, tender anterior nodes, fever over 38°C, no cough) estimating the chance of Group A strep.
Central: Within the brain and spinal cord.
Central cause: A cause inside the brain or brainstem rather than in the nerve itself.
Central chest pain: Pain in the middle of the chest, behind the breastbone.
Central clearing: Paler centre to a lesion with a red edge.
Central sensitisation: The spinal cord and brain become over-responsive to pain signals, so pain is felt more easily.
Central sleep apnoea: Pauses in breathing because the brain stops sending the signal to breathe, usually without loud snoring.
Central venous catheter: A line placed in a large central vein for drugs, nutrition or monitoring.
Central vertigo: Vertigo from the brainstem or cerebellum, e.g. stroke; often with neurological signs.
Central zone: The part of the prostate surrounding the ejaculatory ducts; rarely the site of cancer.
Centrilobular necrosis: Death of liver cells around the central veins (zone 3), the pattern of paracetamol injury.
Cephalosporin: A class of beta-lactam antibiotics, such as ceftriaxone.
Cerebellar signs: Signs of cerebellum damage: ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech.
Cerebellar stroke: Infarction of the cerebellum; a dangerous central cause of vertigo with ataxia.
Cerebellar syndrome: Signs of cerebellar damage: ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus, slurred speech, dysdiadochokinesia.
Cerebellum: The part of the brain at the back that coordinates balance and movement.
Cerebral blood volume: The amount of blood held in the brain's vessels at any time.
Cerebral cortex: The outer layer of grey matter of the brain.
Cerebral glucose metabolism: The brain's use of glucose for energy, which needs thiamine.
Cerebral hypoperfusion: Not enough blood flow reaching the brain.
Cerebral hypoxia: Lack of oxygen to the brain, causing injury within minutes.
Cerebral ischaemia: Not enough blood flow to the brain, which can lead to infarction.
Cerebral lupus: Neuropsychiatric lupus: brain involvement causing psychosis, seizures, severe headache or confusion.
Cerebral oedema: Brain swelling, a rare but deadly DKA complication in children, linked to rapid osmotic shifts during treatment.
Cerebral perfusion: Blood flow to the brain; consciousness is lost when it falls too low.
Cerebral vasculature: The blood vessels of the brain.
Cerebritis: Early, poorly defined inflammation of brain tissue before an abscess capsule forms.
Cervical: Relating to the neck part of the spine, C1 to C7.
Cervical cord compression: Pressure on the spinal cord in the neck, causing limb weakness and sensory loss.
Cervical lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes in the neck.
Cervical spine: The neck vertebrae; injury is a concern after trauma, so the neck is not tilted.
Charcot foot: Neuropathic joint destruction: a warm, swollen foot that collapses into deformity.
Charcot neuroarthropathy: Progressive destruction of foot bones and joints in a foot without protective sensation.
Charcot's triad: RUQ pain, jaundice and fever: the classic presentation of cholangitis.
Charcot-Marie-Tooth: Autosomal dominant inherited neuropathy with distal weakness and foot drop.
Chelation: Using a drug that binds a metal so it can be excreted.
Chemical peritonitis: Peritoneal inflammation caused by spilled acid and gut contents before infection sets in.
Chemotherapy: Drugs that kill rapidly dividing cancer cells.
Chest X-ray: Plain X-ray of the chest, used here to look for pneumonia.
Chest drain: A tube placed through the chest wall to drain fluid, pus or air from the pleural space.
Chest examination: Inspecting, palpating, percussing and listening to the chest.
Chest leads: The six ECG electrodes V1 to V6 placed across the chest.
Chest physiotherapy: Breathing and positioning techniques to help clear sputum from the lungs.
Chest wall: The ribs, muscles and tissues of the chest under the breast.
Chickenpox: Primary infection with varicella zoster virus, giving an itchy vesicular rash.
Child-Pugh score: Severity score using bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites and encephalopathy, graded A to C.
Childbearing age: The years a woman can become pregnant, roughly from puberty to menopause.
Chills: Feeling cold and shivery, often as a temperature rises.
Chlamydia: The commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK.
Chlamydia psittaci: Atypical bacterium caught from birds, causing psittacosis.
Chlamydia trachomatis: Sexually transmitted organism that can cause neonatal conjunctivitis.
Chloramphenicol: Topical broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotic; first choice for bacterial conjunctivitis.
Chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to cover alcohol withdrawal.
Chloride channel: A membrane protein that lets chloride ions move across cells; draws water into mucus.
Chloride influx: Movement of negative chloride ions into a neuron, making it less likely to fire.
Chlorphenamine: A sedating H1 antihistamine; supportive only in anaphylaxis.
Cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts, usually behind an obstruction.
Cholecalciferol: Vitamin D3, used to correct vitamin D deficiency.
Cholecystectomy: Surgical removal of the gallbladder, offered after recovery to prevent recurrence.
Cholecystitis: Inflammation of the gallbladder from an impacted stone, with pain and fever but usually no jaundice.
Choledocholithiasis: Gallstones in the common bile duct.
Cholestasis: Reduced bile flow, causing raised conjugated bilirubin, ALP and GGT.
Cholestatic: Pattern of liver blood tests showing blocked bile flow, mainly raised ALP and GGT.
Cholesterol: A fatty molecule used in cell membranes and hormones; carried in blood by lipoproteins.
Cholinergic: Relating to acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter for attention and memory.
Cholinergic crisis: Weakness, sweating, salivation and diarrhoea from too much acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.
Chondrocalcinosis: Calcium deposits visible in joint cartilage on X-ray, typical of pseudogout.
Chromaffin cells: Catecholamine-producing cells of the adrenal medulla, the origin of phaeochromocytoma.
Chromosome 16: The chromosome carrying the PKD1 gene, the main gene in adult polycystic kidney disease.
Chronic alcohol use: Long-term heavy drinking, which shrinks the brain and stretches bridging veins.
Chronic arthritis: Joint inflammation persisting beyond about six months.
Chronic bronchitis: Chronic airway inflammation with mucus hypersecretion and productive cough.
Chronic carriage: Long-term persistence of a virus in the body.
Chronic cough: A cough lasting more than 8 weeks.
Chronic destructive joint disease: Long-term damage to joints visible on X-ray as erosions and deformity.
Chronic discoid lupus erythematosus: Skin-limited lupus causing red, scaly, scarring plaques in sun-exposed areas.
Chronic fissure: A fissure lasting more than a week, often with a sentinel tag.
Chronic gastritis: Long-standing inflammation of the stomach lining.
Chronic haemolytic anaemia: Long-standing anaemia caused by ongoing early destruction of red cells.
Chronic hyperglycaemia: Blood glucose that stays too high over months to years, damaging nerves and small vessels.
Chronic hypoxia: Long-term low oxygen levels in the body's tissues.
Chronic inflammation: Long-lasting immune activity that damages tissue over time.
Chronic kidney disease: Long-term reduction in kidney function lasting over 3 months.
Chronic limb ischaemia: Long-standing reduced blood supply to a limb, usually from atherosclerosis.
Chronic liver disease: Long-term liver damage lasting over six months, often leading to cirrhosis.
Chronic osteomyelitis: Long-standing bone infection with dead bone, often needing surgery.
Chronic pain disorder: A condition causing pain that persists or recurs for months or longer.
Chronic respiratory failure: Long-term inability of the lungs to keep blood oxygen or carbon dioxide normal.
Chronic skin changes: Long-standing damage such as eczema, ulcers or fungal infection that weakens the skin barrier.
Chronic spontaneous urticaria: Chronic urticaria with no external trigger, often driven by autoantibodies against mast cells.
Chronic stress: Long-lasting activation of the body's stress response, which harms health over time.
Chronic thromboembolic disease: Lung arteries left permanently narrowed by old clots that never dissolved.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hyperte: Pulmonary hypertension from unresolved clots scarring and blocking the pulmonary arteries.
Chronic tophaceous gout: Long-standing gout with tophi and joint damage from years of high urate.
Chronic urticaria: Recurrent wheals on most days for 6 weeks or more, usually with no identifiable trigger.
Chronic viral hepatitis: Long-term liver infection with hepatitis B or C virus.
Chrysotile: White, curly serpentine asbestos; less carcinogenic than amphiboles.
Chvostek's sign: Twitching of the face when the facial nerve is tapped in front of the ear.
Ciclosporin: An immunosuppressant used after transplant; causes gum overgrowth, excess hair and nephrotoxicity.
Cilia: Tiny hair-like projections on lining cells that beat to move mucus.
Ciliary muscle: The muscle in the ciliary body that changes lens shape for focusing.
Ciliary spasm: Painful contraction of the ciliary muscle in an inflamed eye.
Ciprofloxacin: Oral fluoroquinolone antibiotic that covers Pseudomonas.
Circinate balanitis: Painless lesions on the glans or prepuce of the penis in reactive arthritis.
Circle of Willis: The ring of arteries at the base of the brain linking carotid and vertebrobasilar circulations.
Circulating volume: The amount of blood in the vessels, which keeps organs perfused.
Circulation: Movement of blood around the body.
Circulatory dysfunction: Failure to maintain adequate blood pressure and organ perfusion.
Circumferentially: Growing all the way around the bowel wall.
Circumflex: Branch of the left coronary artery supplying the lateral wall.
Cirrhosis: End-stage scarring of the liver with nodules, causing portal hypertension and liver failure.
Cisplatin: Platinum chemotherapy used for advanced or metastatic bladder cancer.
Citalopram: An SSRI antidepressant known to prolong the QT interval.
Citrullinated proteins: Proteins in which arginine has been converted to citrulline; targets of anti-CCP.
Cl: Chloride, a main negative ion in blood.
Clarithromycin: A macrolide antibiotic used when a patient is penicillin allergic.
Class II compression stockings: Medium-pressure stockings worn after healing to stop venous ulcers recurring.
Class III antiarrhythmic: Drug that blocks potassium channels, prolonging action potential and refractory period.
Claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking a set distance, relieved by rest.
Claudication distance: How far a patient can walk before claudication pain starts.
Clean-contaminated: An operation entering the gut, airway or urinary tract under controlled conditions, such as appendicectomy.
Clindamycin: Antibiotic for penicillin allergy; carries a high risk of C. difficile diarrhoea.
Clinical Activity Score: Seven-point score of pain, redness and swelling; 3 or more means active thyroid eye disease.
Clinical assessment: Diagnosis made from history, examination and mental state, without a confirmatory test.
Clinical diagnosis: A diagnosis made from history and examination without needing tests.
Clinical ethics: Applying ethical principles to real decisions about individual patients' care.
Clinically significant: Enough to matter for treatment or vision.
Clobetasol propionate: A very potent topical corticosteroid; avoid on the face and in children.
Clobetasone butyrate: A moderate-potency topical corticosteroid (0.05%); not to be confused with clobetasol.
Clonal: All descended from one original abnormal cell.
Clonic: The rhythmic jerking phase of a seizure.
Clonic phase: The rhythmic jerking part of a seizure.
Clopidogrel: P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet given with aspirin in ACS.
Close contact: Being near an infected person, close enough to breathe their droplets or touch shared surfaces.
Close contacts: People with prolonged close exposure, such as household members, in the week before illness.
Closed fracture: A break where the skin is intact.
Closed-loop obstruction: Obstruction where a segment of bowel is blocked at both ends, so pressure rises fast.
Clostridioides difficile: Spore-forming anaerobe that causes diarrhoea and colitis after antibiotics.
Clostridium perfringens: Anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod that causes gas gangrene.
Clot: A solid plug of platelets and fibrin that stops bleeding.
Clot evacuation: Surgical removal of a blood clot.
Clot retention: Inability to pass urine because blood clots block the bladder outlet.
Clotrimazole: Topical or vaginal azole antifungal; the pessary is used in pregnancy.
Clotting: The process by which blood turns from liquid to a gel to stop bleeding.
Clotting factor: A blood protein that helps form a clot.
Clotting factors: Blood proteins that work in sequence to form a fibrin clot.
Clotting profile: A set of blood tests (PT, APTT, fibrinogen) showing how well the blood clots.
Clubbing: Loss of the nail-bed angle and bulbous fingertips, seen in asbestosis and lung cancer.
Clumsy-hand dysarthria: A lacunar syndrome of slurred speech with a clumsy hand.
Cluster headache: Severe unilateral headache around the eye lasting 15 minutes to 3 hours, with a red watery eye.
Cluster of grapes: Groups of cystic dilated bronchi on HRCT in severe bronchiectasis.
Co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin plus clavulanic acid; first-line IV antibiotic for cholangitis.
Co-codamol: Combination tablet of codeine (an opioid) and paracetamol; 30/500 means 30 mg codeine and 500 mg paracetamol.
Co-infection: Infection with two strains or germs at the same time.
Co-prescribe: Prescribe one drug alongside another, often to protect against side effects.
Co-trimoxazole: Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole; treats and prevents PCP.
Coagulase: Enzyme that clots plasma; separates Staph. aureus (positive) from Staph. epidermidis (negative).
Coagulase-negative staphylococci: Skin staphylococci such as S. epidermidis that colonise lines and form biofilms.
Coagulation cascade: Chain of clotting factor reactions ending in fibrin formation.
Coagulation factors: Plasma proteins that work in sequence to form a fibrin clot.
Coagulation profile: Tests of clotting: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and D-dimer.
Coagulation screen: Blood tests of clotting: PT, APTT, fibrinogen and platelet count.
Coagulopathy: Impaired blood clotting causing a bleeding tendency.
Coal worker's pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from coal dust in miners, with upper zone nodules and fibrosis.
Coal workers' pneumoconiosis: Lung scarring from inhaling coal dust over many years.
Coalesce: To merge together into one mass.
Coarctation: A congenital narrowing of the aorta causing radio-femoral delay and upper limb hypertension.
Coarctation of the aorta: Congenital narrowing of the aorta causing arm hypertension and weak, delayed femoral pulses.
Coarse crackles: Loud, low-pitched crackles heard with a stethoscope, from secretions in the airways.
Cobblestone papillae: Large bumps on the inner eyelid seen in allergic conjunctivitis.
Cocaine: Stimulant drug that causes coronary vasospasm and raises MI risk.
Coccobacilli: Short, oval rod-shaped bacteria between cocci and rods in shape.
Coccobacillus: A bacterium shaped between a sphere and a rod, such as Haemophilus influenzae.
Cochlear blood flow: Blood supply to the cochlea; betahistine is thought to increase it.
Cochlear duct: The fluid-filled tube in the cochlea containing the hearing hair cells.
Cockcroft-Gault: A formula using age, sex, weight and creatinine to estimate creatinine clearance for drug dosing.
Codeine: A weak opioid painkiller; in overuse headache it is withdrawn gradually.
Coeliac disease: Gluten-sensitive enteropathy that can cause functional hyposplenism.
Cofactor: A helper molecule an enzyme needs to work.
Coffee bean sign: AXR appearance of sigmoid volvulus: a huge dilated loop with a central dividing line.
Cognition: Mental processes such as thinking, memory, attention and understanding.
Cognitive: Relating to thinking, such as worrying thoughts.
Cognitive impairment: Problems with memory, thinking or attention.
Cognitive reserve: The brain's ability to cope with insults before function declines.
Cognitive stimulation therapy: Group activities and exercises that keep memory and thinking active in mild to moderate dementia.
Cogwheel rigidity: Jerky, ratchet-like resistance to passive movement from rigidity plus tremor.
Colchicine: Anti-inflammatory drug for acute gout that blocks microtubules; causes diarrhoea and vomiting.
Cold agglutinins: Antibodies that clump red cells at low temperatures, produced in Mycoplasma infection.
Cold compress: A cool, damp cloth held on the eye to ease swelling and discomfort.
Cold intolerance: Feeling cold easily when others are comfortable.
Cold sore: Recurrent HSV blisters on or around the lip.
Cold water immersion: Placing the body in cold water: the fastest way to cool a heat stroke patient.
Colecalciferol: Vitamin D3 supplement used for bone protection.
Colicky: Pain that comes and goes in waves.
Colicky pain: Pain that comes and goes in waves, typical of a blocked hollow organ.
Collagen: A strong structural protein in the aortic wall that resists rupture.
Collagenous matrix: A scaffold of collagen fibres, here the scar tissue replacing normal marrow.
Collapse: Sudden loss of postural tone, often with loss of consciousness.
Collapsing FSGS: An aggressive form of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis where glomerular capillaries collapse; typical of HIVAN.
Collapsing pulse: A pulse that rises fast then falls away abruptly; also called water hammer pulse, typical of AR.
Collateral circulation: Alternative small vessels that bypass a gradually narrowing artery.
Collateral veins: Extra veins that open up to carry blood around a blockage.
Collateral vessels: Small alternative arteries that grow around a blockage.
Collection: A pocket of fluid or pus within tissues or a body space.
Colles' fracture: Dorsally displaced fracture of the distal radius after a fall on an outstretched hand.
Colonic mucosal cells: The cells lining the inside of the colon.
Colonic pH: The acidity of the contents of the large bowel.
Colonic transit: The movement of stool through the colon.
Colonisation: Bacteria living and multiplying on or in tissue, which may lead to infection.
Colonises: Lives on a body surface without necessarily causing disease.
Colonoscopy: Camera test looking inside the whole colon.
Colorectal: Relating to the colon and rectum.
Colorectal cancer: Cancer of the colon or rectum; can bleed slowly and cause iron deficiency.
Colorectal carcinoma: Cancer of the colon or rectum.
Colour blindness: Difficulty telling colours apart; with ethambutol, red-green first.
Colour desaturation: Colours, especially red, look faded in one eye; an early sign of optic nerve disease.
Colour vision: Ability to tell colours apart; an early loss signals optic nerve damage.
Columnar: Tall, column-shaped lining cells typical of the gut above the dentate line.
Columnar metaplasia: Replacement of normal squamous lining with tall, stomach-like columnar cells.
Coma: Deep unconsciousness from which the patient cannot be roused.
Combination inhaler: One inhaler containing two drugs, such as a steroid and a long-acting bronchodilator.
Combined oral contraceptive pill: Oestrogen plus progestogen pill; contraindicated in migraine with aura because of stroke risk.
Commissural fusion: Leaflets stuck together at their edges, narrowing the valve; typical of rheumatic MS.
Commissure: The junction where two valve leaflets meet.
Commissurotomy: Splitting the fused edges (commissures) of valve leaflets to widen the valve.
Common cold: A mild viral URTI of the nose and throat, usually rhinovirus.
Common femoral artery: Main artery of the leg in the groin, continuing from the external iliac artery.
Common fibular: Another name for the common peroneal nerve, which wraps around the fibular head.
Common pathway: The final shared part of the clotting cascade, from factor X to fibrin.
Common peroneal nerve: Nerve winding round the fibular neck; injury causes foot drop.
Communicate: Express the decision by any means: speech, writing, signs or blinking.
Community circulation: How widely a virus is spreading among the public at the time.
Community-acquired pneumonia: Pneumonia caught outside hospital, most often from Strep. pneumoniae.
Comorbid: Existing at the same time as another condition.
Comorbidities: Other medical conditions a patient has at the same time.
Comorbidity: Another long-term illness the patient also has, e.g. diabetes or heart failure.
Compartment syndrome: Raised pressure in a muscle compartment that cuts off its blood supply.
Compatibility: Whether donor blood can be safely given to a recipient without an immune reaction.
Compensated: Cirrhosis with no ascites, bleeding, jaundice or encephalopathy.
Compensated respiratory acidosis: Raised CO2 with normal pH because the kidneys have raised bicarbonate.
Compensation: The body adjusting one thing (here, pushing out CSF and venous blood) to offset another.
Compensatory: A response that makes up for a loss or change elsewhere in the body.
Competitive inhibition: A drug binds the enzyme's active site, blocking the normal substrate.
Competitively block: Occupy a receptor so the natural chemical, here histamine, cannot bind.
Complement: Blood proteins that, once activated by antibody, damage cell membranes.
Complement-mediated lysis: Killing of a cell when complement proteins punch holes in its membrane.
Complementary: Working in different ways that add to each other.
Complete facial paralysis: Total loss of movement on one side of the face.
Complete heart block: Third-degree block: atria and ventricles beat independently.
Complex partial seizures: Older name for focal seizures with impaired awareness.
Compliance: How easily the lungs stretch; low in fibrosis.
Complicated UTI: UTI in men, pregnancy, abnormal urinary tract, catheters or systemic illness.
Compression: Squeezing of the nerve, here by swelling inside a tight canal.
Compression duplex USS: Leg ultrasound that checks if veins squash and blood flows; a vein that will not compress contains clot.
Compression symptoms: Symptoms caused by an enlarging mass pressing on nearby structures, e.g. hoarseness or difficulty swallowing.
Compression-to-ventilation ratio: The number of chest compressions given for each set of rescue breaths.
Compressive goitre: A goitre big enough to press on the windpipe or gullet.
Compressive optic neuropathy: Optic nerve damage from swollen orbital contents pressing on it; sight-threatening.
Compulsivity: Repeating behaviours driven by an urge that is hard to resist.
Concentric: Rings sharing the same centre, like a target.
Concentric hypertrophy: Even thickening of the ventricular wall with a small cavity, from pressure overload.
Concordant: All three parts of triple assessment agree.
Conduction: The spread of the electrical signal through the heart.
Conduction aphasia: Inability to repeat words, from an arcuate fasciculus lesion.
Conduction block: Failure of signals to pass a damaged segment of nerve, while the axon remains intact.
Conduction disease: Damage to the heart's electrical pathways, causing heart block.
Conduction tissue: Specialised heart muscle that carries the electrical signal, including the AV node.
Confidentiality: The duty to keep patient information private unless a recognised exception applies.
Confirmatory assay: A second, different test used to confirm a positive screening result.
Confirmatory test: A more definite test used after a positive screen to make the diagnosis.
Confusion: Muddled thinking and poor attention, here from poor brain perfusion.
Confusion screen: Blood tests to find reversible causes of confusion, such as thyroid, B12, calcium and glucose.
Congenital: Present at or acquired around birth.
Congenital heart block: Complete heart block present at birth, from maternal anti-Ro/La damaging the fetal AV node.
Congenital heart disease: Heart structural abnormalities present from birth.
Coning: Herniation of the brainstem through the foramen magnum due to raised pressure, which can be fatal.
Conjugate eye movements: Both eyes moving together in the same direction.
Conjugated bilirubin: Water-soluble bilirubin processed by the liver; appears in urine when bile is blocked.
Conjugation: Joining a molecule to another, such as glutathione, to make it harmless and excretable.
Conjunctiva: Thin membrane covering the white of the eye and the inside of the eyelids.
Conjunctival: Relating to the conjunctiva, the thin membrane covering the white of the eye.
Conjunctival injection: Redness of the conjunctiva from dilated blood vessels.
Conjunctival pallor: Pale lining of the lower eyelid, a bedside sign of anaemia.
Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of the conjunctiva, causing a red eye with discharge and irritation.
Conn's syndrome: Primary hyperaldosteronism: high sodium, low potassium and hypertension; the opposite of Addison's.
Connective tissue: Supporting fibrous tissue that holds the breast together.
Connective tissue disorder: Inherited or acquired disease of the structural proteins that support tissues, such as collagen or fibrillin.
Conservative: Managed without drugs or surgery, using lifestyle changes.
Conservative management: Non-surgical treatment such as diet, laxatives and creams.
Conservatively: Without active procedures, by monitoring and modifying risk factors.
Consolidation: Lung where the air spaces have filled with fluid, pus or cells, so it looks solid and white on X-ray.
Constipation: Infrequent or hard stools; a common hidden cause of delirium in older inpatients.
Constitutional symptoms: Whole-body symptoms such as fever, weight loss, night sweats and fatigue.
Constitutively active: Switched on all the time, without the normal signal.
Constricting pain: A tight, squeezing or band-like pain.
Constrictive pericarditis: Stiff, scarred pericardium restricting heart filling, raising venous pressure and causing ascites.
Constructional apraxia: Inability to copy or draw shapes, such as interlocking pentagons, despite normal strength.
Contact allergies: Reactions to substances touching the skin, such as latex or cosmetics.
Contact lenses: Lenses worn on the eye; they raise the risk of keratitis and must be left out during infection.
Contact screening: Testing people who have been in close contact with an infected person.
Contact sports: Sports with body contact or impact, such as rugby or boxing, which risk abdominal trauma.
Contact tracing: Finding and testing people exposed to an infectious patient.
Contaminated: An operation with gross spillage or acute inflammation, such as a perforated appendix.
Contiguous: Spreading to the next adjacent node group in order.
Contiguous spread: Spread of infection directly from a neighbouring infected structure.
Contiguously: By direct spread into neighbouring tissue.
Contraception: Methods to prevent pregnancy; enzyme-inducing AEDs make hormonal pills less effective.
Contraceptive diaphragm: A dome-shaped barrier placed over the cervix, which raises UTI risk.
Contracted bladder: A small, scarred bladder that holds little urine.
Contractility: How forcefully the heart muscle squeezes with each beat.
Contraindicated: Should not be used because it could cause harm in that patient.
Contraindication: A reason not to give a treatment because it may cause harm.
Contraindications: Reasons a treatment should not be given.
Contralateral: On the opposite side of the body to the lesion.
Contrast: A dye injected before a scan so areas with leaky blood vessels show up brightly.
Contrast agents: Dyes given for scans to make structures stand out; some are toxic to the kidneys.
Contrast imaging: Scans taken after injecting dye so areas with leaky vessels show up brightly.
Contrast-enhanced: Imaging using an injected dye to make vessels show up clearly.
Contrast-enhanced CT: CT scan taken after an iodine dye is injected, so leaky or inflamed tissue lights up.
Controlled oxygen: Oxygen given at a set, limited dose to avoid worsening CO2 retention.
Conus medullaris: The tapered lower end of the spinal cord, at about the L1 vertebra.
Conus medullaris syndrome: Compression of the tapered end of the cord at L1, giving mixed upper and lower motor neurone signs.
Conventional DMARD: A traditional small-molecule disease-modifying drug such as methotrexate, as opposed to a biologic.
Convulsions: Involuntary jerking movements; brief ones can occur in faints as well as seizures.
Convulsive status epilepticus: A tonic-clonic seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery between.
Coombs test: Another name for the direct antiglobulin test.
Cor pulmonale: Right heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
Core biopsy: Wider needle sample of tissue for histology.
Core needle biopsy: A wide needle takes a tissue core for histology and receptor testing.
Core symptoms: The key features needed for diagnosis: low mood, loss of interest and reduced energy.
Cornea: The clear front window of the eye.
Corneal exposure: Drying of the cornea because the lids do not cover it properly.
Corneal reflex: Blinking when the cornea is touched; tests V1 sensation and CN VII.
Corneal ulceration: A breach in the corneal surface that can scar and threaten sight.
Coronary angiogram: Invasive X-ray of the coronaries with contrast via a catheter; the gold standard.
Coronary angiography: X-ray of the coronary arteries using dye injected through a catheter.
Coronary arteries: The arteries on the heart's surface that supply the heart muscle.
Coronary artery disease: Narrowing of the coronary arteries by atheroma.
Coronary artery territory: The area of heart muscle supplied by one coronary artery.
Coronary blood flow: Blood flow through the arteries supplying the heart muscle.
Coronary flow reserve: How much coronary blood flow can rise above resting levels when demand increases.
Coronary ostia: The openings of the coronary arteries in the aortic root.
Coronary perfusion: Blood flow through the coronary arteries to the heart muscle.
Coronavirus: A family of viruses causing colds and COVID-19.
Corrigan's sign: Visible bounding pulsation of the carotid arteries in aortic regurgitation.
Cortex: Outer layer of the brain; the motor cortex sends movement commands to muscles.
Cortical: Relating to the hard outer shell of bone.
Cortical atrophy: Shrinking of the outer grey matter of the brain.
Cortical blindness: Loss of vision due to damage to the visual cortex, with normal eyes.
Cortical destruction: Erosion of the hard outer bone layer, visible on X-ray later in infection.
Cortical innervation: Nerve supply coming from the cerebral cortex.
Cortical neurons: Nerve cells in the outer grey matter of the brain.
Cortical spreading depression: A slow wave of neuronal depolarisation then suppressed activity across the cortex; the cause of aura.
Corticospinal tract: The main motor pathway running from the cortex down the spinal cord to the motor neurones.
Corticosteroids: Steroid hormones and drugs that suppress inflammation and the immune response.
Cortisol: Main glucocorticoid; maintains blood pressure, glucose and the stress response.
Coryza: Inflammation of the nasal lining causing a runny, blocked nose and sneezing.
Costochondritis: Inflammation where ribs join the sternum; reduces chest expansion in AS.
Costophrenic angle: The angle where the diaphragm meets the chest wall on CXR; blunted by an effusion.
Costovertebral angle: Angle between the 12th rib and the spine, over the kidney.
Cottage cheese: Describes the thick, white, lumpy discharge typical of vaginal thrush.
Cough suppressant: A medicine that reduces the urge to cough.
Court order: An instruction from a court, which can legally require disclosure of patient information.
Courvoisier's law: In jaundice, a palpable non-tender gallbladder is unlikely to be due to gallstones.
Courvoisier's sign: Painless palpable gallbladder with jaundice, suggesting malignancy not stones.
Covid-19: Illness caused by the SARS-CoV-2 coronavirus, ranging from a cold to severe pneumonia.
Cow's milk protein allergy: Immune reaction in infants to cow's milk proteins, either IgE or non-IgE mediated.
Coxiella burnetii: Organism causing Q fever in farmers and abattoir workers; a culture-negative cause.
Coxsackie: An enterovirus that commonly causes viral pericarditis and myocarditis.
Coxsackievirus: An enterovirus that causes hand, foot and mouth disease.
Coxsackievirus A16: Enterovirus causing hand, foot and mouth disease.
Coxsackievirus B: Enterovirus that is the most common cause of viral myocarditis.
Coxsackieviruses: Enteroviruses causing meningitis, hand, foot and mouth disease and myocarditis.
CrCl: Creatinine clearance, an estimate of kidney function.
Crack cocaine: A smoked form of cocaine that constricts vessels and can cause ulcers.
Crackles: Short popping sounds on inspiration as fluid-filled small airways and alveoli open.
Craggy: Rough and irregular to feel, typical of cancer.
Cramps: Painful squeezing spasms of the gut muscle.
Cranial: Relating to the skull or head.
Cranial cavity: The space inside the skull that holds the brain.
Cranial nerve: One of 12 nerve pairs that leave the brain directly, numbered I to XII.
Cranial nerve nuclei: Clusters of nerve cells in the brainstem from which cranial nerves arise.
Cranial nerve palsy: Weakness or paralysis of a muscle supplied by one of the twelve cranial nerves.
Cranial nerves: The 12 pairs of nerves arising directly from the brain and brainstem.
Cranial vault: The bony box of the skull that holds the brain.
Creatine kinase: Muscle enzyme that rises when muscle fibres are damaged.
Creatinine: A muscle breakdown product cleared by the kidneys; a rising level means falling kidney function.
Creatinine clearance: The volume of blood cleared of creatinine per minute, used as an estimate of kidney filtration.
Creon: Pancreatic enzyme replacement capsules taken with meals.
Crepitations: Crackles heard with a stethoscope; coarse in bronchiectasis, fine in fibrosis.
Crepitus: Crackling felt under the skin from gas in the tissues.
Crescendo-decrescendo: A murmur that builds up then fades, typical of outflow obstruction.
Critical care: Intensive care unit support for organ failure.
Critical limb ischaemia: Severe chronic ischaemia with rest pain, ulcers or gangrene.
Critical mass: Enough myocardium depolarised together to stop chaotic activity.
Critical stenosis: A narrowing tight enough to threaten blood flow even at rest.
Critical volume: The point where the brain can no longer compensate for added volume and ICP shoots up.
Crocidolite: Blue asbestos, an amphibole and the most carcinogenic type.
Crohn's: Crohn's disease: a chronic inflammatory bowel disease that can cause diarrhoea.
Crohn's disease: Inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the gut, including the anus.
Cross-links: When one allergen binds two neighbouring IgE molecules at once, triggering the mast cell to release its contents.
Cross-reactivity: An allergy to one drug causing reactions to a chemically similar drug, e.g. penicillins and cephalosporins.
Cross-talk: Signals jumping between neighbouring nerve fibres that have lost insulation.
Crossmatch: Testing donor blood against the patient's blood so units are ready for transfusion.
Croup: Viral laryngotracheobronchitis in young children causing a barking cough and stridor.
Crusting: Dried discharge on the lashes, especially on waking.
Crusts: Dried scabs that form as blisters break and heal; once all lesions crust, chickenpox is no longer infectious.
Crutch impingement: Pressure on the radial nerve in the armpit from leaning on crutches.
Cryptococcal meningitis: Fungal meningitis from Cryptococcus neoformans, usually when CD4 is below 50.
Cryptococcus: A fungus (Cryptococcus neoformans) inhaled from soil and bird droppings that can spread to the meninges in immunosuppression.
Cryptococcus neoformans: Encapsulated yeast causing meningitis in immunocompromised patients.
Cryptoglandular: Arising from the anal glands that open into the anal crypts at the dentate line.
Cryptosporidiosis: Parasitic infection causing chronic watery diarrhoea in advanced HIV.
Crystal arthropathy: Joint disease caused by crystals depositing in and around the joint, mainly gout and pseudogout.
Crystalloid: Clear salt-based IV fluid such as 0.9% sodium chloride.
Crystals: Urate or calcium pyrophosphate crystals in joint fluid, which point to gout or pseudogout.
Culture: Growing bacteria from a sample in the lab to identify them and their antibiotic sensitivities.
Culture negative: No organism grows when the sample is cultured in the laboratory.
Culture-negative endocarditis: Endocarditis with negative blood cultures, from prior antibiotics or hard-to-grow organisms.
Cultures: Samples grown in the lab to identify bacteria, here from the patient and the blood bag.
Cupula: A jelly-like flap in each canal that bends with fluid movement to signal rotation.
Curschmann spirals: Spiral mucus plugs from small airways seen in asthmatic sputum or histology.
Cushing's disease: Cushing's syndrome caused specifically by an ACTH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
Cushing's syndrome: Clinical state caused by prolonged excess cortisol from any source.
Cushing's triad: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing from brainstem compression; a late sign.
Cutaneous allodynia: Pain from normally painless touch on the skin, such as brushing hair.
Cutaneous manifestation: A sign of a disease seen in the skin.
Cutaneous oedema: Swelling of the skin from trapped fluid.
Cutaneous vasculitis: Inflammation of small blood vessels in the skin, causing purpura or ulcers.
Cyanocobalamin: A form of vitamin B12 used as a supplement.
Cyanosis: Bluish skin or lips from low blood oxygen.
Cyanotic congenital heart disease: Heart defects present from birth that shunt deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, such as tetralogy of Fallot.
Cyclopentolate: Anticholinergic eye drop that dilates the pupil and relaxes the ciliary muscle, easing uveitis pain.
Cyclophosphamide: Chemotherapy drug whose metabolite (acrolein) irritates the bladder and raises cancer risk.
Cycloplegic: Drug that paralyses the ciliary muscle, relieving spasm.
Cystic airspaces: Abnormal round air-filled spaces with walls.
Cystic fibrosis: Autosomal recessive CFTR defect causing thick secretions in lungs, pancreas and gut.
Cystine: Amino acid forming stones in a genetic condition (cystinuria).
Cystitis: Infection or inflammation of the bladder; lower UTI.
Cystoscopy: Looking inside the bladder with a camera through the urethra.
Cytochrome P450: A family of enzymes; azoles block the fungal version needed to make ergosterol.
Cytogenetics: Study of chromosomes in cancer cells to find translocations that guide prognosis and treatment.
Cytokine: Signalling protein from immune cells; TNF-alpha and IL-6 drive sepsis.
Cytokine storm: Excessive release of inflammatory signalling proteins that damages tissues throughout the body.
Cytokines: Inflammatory signalling proteins released during infection or surgery.
Cytologically: Judged by looking at cells under a microscope.
Cytology: Looking at cells under the microscope; often non-diagnostic for mesothelioma in pleural fluid.
Cytopathic: Directly damaging or killing the cells a virus infects.
Cytopenia: A low count of any one blood cell type.
Cytopenias: Low counts of one or more blood cell types.
Cytoplasm: The inside of a cell outside the nucleus.
Cytotoxic: Toxic to cells, directly damaging or killing them.
Cytotoxic T-cells: CD8+ white cells that kill virus-infected cells.
Cytotoxic oedema: Swelling of brain cells themselves from energy failure, as in stroke; steroids do not help it.
D-dimer: Fibrin breakdown product; raised in clotting and often in Covid-19.
D2 antagonist: A drug that blocks dopamine D2 receptors, reducing nausea and vomiting.
DAA: Direct-acting antiviral; drugs that block hepatitis C proteins and cure most patients.
DAMN: Drugs to stop in AKI: Diuretics, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, Metformin, NSAIDs.
DANISH: Mnemonic for cerebellar signs: dysdiadochokinesia, ataxia, nystagmus, intention tremor, slurred speech, hypotonia.
DAPT: Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, usually continued for 12 months after ACS.
DAS28: Disease Activity Score using 28 joints, ESR/CRP and patient score; remission is under 2.6.
DAT: Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test, which detects antibody or complement on red cells.
DCIS: Ductal carcinoma in situ: malignant duct cells with an intact basement membrane, often seen as microcalcification.
DCM: Dilated cardiomyopathy: dilated, poorly contracting ventricle causing heart failure.
DCT: Distal convoluted tubule of the nephron.
DEXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry: a scan measuring bone mineral density.
DH: Dermatitis herpetiformis: the itchy blistering skin manifestation of coeliac disease.
DHFR: Dihydrofolate reductase, the enzyme blocked by methotrexate.
DHT: Dihydrotestosterone: a potent androgen made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase; drives prostate growth.
DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting that uses up platelets and clotting factors.
DIP: Distal interphalangeal joint, the finger joint nearest the fingertip.
DKA: Diabetic ketoacidosis: hyperglycaemia, ketones and metabolic acidosis from insulin deficiency.
DLB: Dementia with Lewy bodies: fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
DLCO: Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide; reduced in emphysema.
DMT: Disease-modifying therapy: a drug that reduces relapse rate in MS.
DNA synthesis: Making new DNA, required every time a cell divides.
DOAC: Direct oral anticoagulant, such as apixaban, used to prevent clots in AF.
DOACs: Direct oral anticoagulants: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban and dabigatran.
DPP-4 inhibitor: Gliptin (e.g. sitagliptin) that prolongs incretin action; weight neutral.
DR ABCDE: Danger, Response, Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure: structured emergency assessment.
DRAGON score: Predicts 3-month outcome after thrombolysis with alteplase.
DRE: Digital rectal examination: feeling the prostate through the rectal wall.
DSM-5: The American Psychiatric Association's manual of diagnostic criteria for mental disorders.
DVLA: The UK driving licence agency; after successful angioplasty for ACS the patient should not drive for 1 week.
DVT: Deep vein thrombosis: clot in a deep vein causing a warm, swollen leg.
DVT prophylaxis: Measures to prevent leg vein clots, such as compression stockings or low-dose heparin.
DWI: Diffusion-weighted MRI, the most sensitive scan for acute infarction, which shows as bright.
DXA: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry; the scan that measures bone density for osteoporosis.
DaTSCAN: SPECT scan of dopamine transporters in the striatum; reduced in Parkinson's.
DaTscan: A SPECT scan of dopamine transporter uptake; reduced in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's.
Dabigatran: A DOAC that directly inhibits thrombin; reversed with idarucizumab.
Dactylitis: Swelling of a whole finger or toe ('sausage digit'), typical of psoriatic arthritis.
Dalrymple's sign: Upper lid retraction so white sclera shows above the iris in straight-ahead gaze.
Dangling: Hanging the leg over the bed edge so gravity improves blood flow to the foot.
Dapagliflozin: SGLT2 inhibitor that slows CKD progression; can cause genital candidiasis.
Dapsone: An antibiotic used for leprosy and some skin diseases; a strong oxidant.
Darbepoetin alfa: A long-acting synthetic erythropoietin given by subcutaneous injection.
Darifenacin: An antimuscarinic drug that relaxes the bladder to reduce urgency and frequency.
Daytime sleepiness: Falling asleep or struggling to stay awake in the day, the main driving risk in OSA.
De Musset's sign: Head nodding with each heartbeat in aortic regurgitation.
De Quervain's tenosynovitis: Inflammation of thumb tendons at the wrist, causing radial wrist pain; a differential for thumb base OA.
De Quervain's thyroiditis: Painful post-viral thyroid inflammation that leaks hormone; self-resolving.
Dead space: Airway or lung that is ventilated but takes no part in gas exchange.
Debilitating: Severely weakening, so normal activity becomes very hard.
Debridement: Surgical removal of dead or infected tissue.
Decision-making capacity: Ability to understand, retain, weigh up information and communicate a decision (Mental Capacity Act 2005).
Decision-specific: Capacity applies to one decision; a person may decide some things but not others.
Decompensated: When the body can no longer cope with a disease and organs start to fail.
Decompensated cirrhosis: Cirrhosis with failing liver function: ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding.
Decompensated liver disease: Cirrhosis with complications such as jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy or bleeding varices.
Decompensates: Stops coping, so the compensation fails and symptoms appear.
Decompensation: When chronic liver disease tips into failure: ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding.
Decompresses: Releases pressure by draining the fluid.
Decompression: Releasing trapped gas and fluid from obstructed bowel to reduce pressure.
Decompression surgery: An operation to relieve pressure on a trapped nerve.
Decompressive hemicraniectomy: Removing part of the skull to relieve pressure from a swollen infarct.
Decongestant: A drug that narrows nasal blood vessels to unblock the nose.
Decontamination: Removing or binding a poison so less is absorbed.
Decreased PaCO2: Lower than normal carbon dioxide in arterial blood, from overbreathing.
Decreased breath sounds: Quieter breath sounds, heard over fluid, collapse or air.
Decremental response: Progressive fall in muscle response with repeated nerve stimulation, typical of myasthenia.
Deep SSI: Infection extending into the fascia and muscle beneath the incision.
Deep bleeding: Bleeding into joints and muscles rather than the skin surface.
Deep fascia: Tough connective tissue sheet wrapping muscles, beneath the fat; infection spreads fast along it.
Deep femoral artery: Branch of the femoral artery (profunda femoris) supplying the thigh muscles.
Deep tendon reflexes: Muscle jerks on tapping a tendon, such as the ankle or knee jerk.
Deep vein: A large vein running deep in the muscles, as opposed to the superficial veins under the skin.
Deeper dermis: The lower dermis; swelling here, with subcutaneous tissue, gives angioedema.
Defecatory mechanism: The coordinated muscle actions needed to pass stool.
Defective mineralisation: Failure to lay calcium and phosphate crystals into the bone matrix, leaving it soft.
Defective virus: A virus that cannot replicate or form particles without help from another virus.
Defibrillation: An unsynchronised shock that depolarises the myocardium to stop VF or pVT.
Defibrillator: A machine that reads the heart rhythm and delivers an electric shock.
Definitive: Final and targeted, rather than a best guess.
Definitive thyroid treatment: Permanent treatment of Graves': radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy.
Definitive treatment: Treatment that removes the cause for good, such as radioiodine or surgery.
Degeneration: Gradual breakdown and loss of function of a tissue.
Degenerative calcification: Age-related calcium deposition stiffening the aortic valve; the commonest UK cause of AS.
Degenerative mitral valve disease: Wear-and-tear or myxomatous change of the mitral valve; the commonest UK cause of MR.
Degenerative spine disease: Age-related wear of the discs and joints of the spine.
Degradation: Breakdown of a structure or molecule.
Degranulation: Release of stored chemicals, such as histamine, from mast cell or basophil granules.
Dehydrated: Short of body water, for example from not drinking.
Dehydration: Too little water in the body.
Delayed hypersensitivity: A Type IV reaction appearing hours to days after exposure, driven by T cells.
Delineate: To show the exact outline and position of something.
Delirium: Acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and cognition caused by an underlying illness or drug.
Delirium tremens: Severe alcohol withdrawal with confusion, tremor and hallucinations.
Delta wave: A slurred upstroke of the QRS from early ventricular activation via an accessory pathway.
Deltoid: The large shoulder muscle that lifts the arm, supplied by the axillary nerve.
Delusions: Fixed false beliefs held despite clear evidence against them.
Demand-supply mismatch: When the heart needs more oxygen than the narrowed arteries can deliver.
Demarcated: Having a clear edge; poorly demarcated means the border fades out.
Dementia: Gradual, progressive decline in memory and thinking over months to years.
Demyelinating plaques: Areas of myelin loss in the brain or spinal cord, typical of MS.
Demyelination: Damage to the myelin sheath that insulates nerve fibres.
Denatured haemoglobin: Haemoglobin damaged by oxidation so it clumps together.
Dendritic ulcer: Branching corneal ulcer seen with fluorescein; the sign of HSV keratitis.
Denosumab: Monoclonal antibody against RANKL, injected under the skin every 6 months.
Dense breast tissue: Breast with more glandular tissue, common in younger women, which hides lesions on mammograms.
Dense breasts: Breasts with more glandular than fatty tissue, which makes mammograms harder to read.
Dental infection: Infection of a tooth or gum, such as a dental abscess, which can spread to nearby structures.
Dentate line: The wavy line in the anal canal marking the junction of hindgut and ectoderm-derived epithelium.
Deoxygenated: Having given up its oxygen, as in tissues and small veins.
Dependence: Compulsion to drink with withdrawal symptoms on stopping.
Dependent position: The lowest point when lying down, where loose debris settles by gravity.
Dependent zones: The lowest parts of the lung in the patient's position, where inhaled material settles by gravity.
Depigmentation: Loss of skin colour, here from steroid inhibition of melanocytes.
Depolarisation: A change in a cell's electrical charge that fires a nerve signal.
Depolarise: Make the cell membrane's charge less negative so the cell fires.
Depolarising neuromuscular blockers: Paralysing drugs used in anaesthesia that work by persistently stimulating acetylcholine receptors.
Deposits: Clumps of cancer cells that have settled and grown in a new site.
Depressants: Substances such as alcohol or benzodiazepines that dampen nervous system activity.
Depression: Persistent low mood and loss of interest, common alongside IBS.
Dermal: Relating to the dermis, the deeper layer of the skin.
Dermal swelling: Fluid collecting within the skin layer, raising a wheal.
Dermatitis: Inflammation of the skin; here small pustules or spots.
Dermatology: The medical specialty of skin disease.
Dermatomal: Following the area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve root.
Dermatomes: Areas of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve.
Dermis: The layer of skin under the epidermis, containing vessels, nerves and lymphatics.
Dermo-epidermal junction: Boundary between the epidermis and the dermis below it.
Dermographism: Wheals raised along lines where the skin has been stroked or scratched.
Descending aorta: Part of the aorta running down through the chest and abdomen after the arch.
Descending inhibitory control: Signals from the brain that calm spinal reflexes; their loss causes spasticity and brisk reflexes.
Desferrioxamine: Injected iron chelator used when venesection is unsuitable.
Desmopressin: Synthetic vasopressin analogue that releases stored vWF and raises factor VIII; for mild haemophilia A.
Detemir: Long-acting basal insulin (Levemir), continued during DKA treatment to prevent rebound ketosis.
Detoxification: The liver's removal of toxins such as ammonia and drugs from the blood.
Detrusor: The smooth muscle wall of the bladder; invasion makes a tumour muscle-invasive.
Detrusor overactivity: Involuntary detrusor contractions during bladder filling, seen on urodynamics.
Developmental delay: A child reaching milestones such as walking or talking later than expected.
Deviated septum: A nasal septum bent to one side, narrowing one nostril.
Dexamethasone: Potent corticosteroid that rapidly reduces vasogenic oedema around brain tumours.
Dextrocardia: Heart on the right side of the chest.
Diabetes: Condition of raised blood glucose from lack of or resistance to insulin.
Diabetes mellitus: Raised blood glucose from lack of insulin or insulin resistance.
Diabetic foot infection: Infection of a diabetic foot ulcer or tissues; limb-threatening and needs urgent assessment.
Diabetic ketosis: Raised glucose and ketones without acidosis; treated with subcutaneous insulin and fluids rather than the DKA protocol.
Diabetic nephropathy: Kidney damage from long-standing diabetes; the leading cause of CKD.
Diabetic neuropathy: Nerve damage from diabetes, typically glove-and-stocking sensory loss.
Diabetic retinopathy: Damage to the retinal blood vessels caused by long-standing diabetes.
Diagnosis of exclusion: A diagnosis made once other possible causes have been ruled out.
Diagnostic and therapeutic: Able both to find the problem and to treat it in the same procedure.
Diagnostic tap: A small-volume paracentesis to send fluid for cell count, albumin and culture.
Diagnostic triad: Three findings that together make the diagnosis.
Dialysis: Artificial removal of waste and fluid from the blood when the kidneys fail.
Diameter: Width of a vessel measured straight across.
Diaphoresis: Heavy sweating, often a sign of autonomic activation.
Diaphragm: Dome-shaped muscle separating chest from abdomen; the main breathing muscle.
Diaphragmatic hiatus: The opening in the diaphragm through which the oesophagus passes.
Diaphragmatic irritation: Blood or inflammation touching the diaphragm, which refers pain to the shoulder tip via the phrenic nerve.
Diaphysis: The shaft of a long bone.
Diarrhoea: Loose or watery stools passed more often than normal.
Diastole: The relaxation phase of the heartbeat.
Diastolic: During diastole, when the ventricles relax and fill.
Diastolic dysfunction: Impaired relaxation and filling of the ventricle, the mechanism of HFpEF.
Diastolic filling: The ventricle filling with blood while it relaxes.
Diastolic filling time: The time the heart relaxes and fills; the coronary arteries fill mainly then.
Diastolic murmur: Abnormal heart sound heard between S2 and S1, while the heart relaxes.
Diclofenac: An NSAID given IM as first-line analgesia for renal colic.
Dietary fibre: Indigestible plant material that bulks and softens stool.
Differential: Another condition that could explain the same symptoms.
Differentials: Other conditions that could explain the same symptoms.
Differentiated: How closely cells resemble their normal mature form; poorly differentiated cancers are more aggressive.
Differentiation: The process of an immature cell maturing into its final form.
Diffuse: Spread over a wide area rather than in one spot.
Diffuse alveolar damage: Widespread injury to the air sacs, the tissue pattern seen in ARDS.
Diffusion distance: How far gases must travel between alveolar air and blood.
Diffusion-weighted MRI: An MRI sequence that shows a new ischaemic infarct as bright within minutes.
Digital stimulation: Using a gloved finger in the rectum to trigger bowel emptying.
Digoxin: Cardiac glycoside used as second-line AF rate control.
Dihydrofolate reductase: The enzyme that makes tetrahydrofolate for DNA synthesis; inhibited by methotrexate.
Dihydropyridine: Calcium channel blocker that mainly dilates vessels (amlodipine, felodipine, nifedipine).
Dihydrotestosterone: A more potent form of testosterone that drives prostate growth.
Dilatation: Widening of a hollow organ such as the colon.
Dilated bile ducts: Bile ducts widened by pressure behind a blockage.
Dilated cardiomyopathy: Enlarged, weak left ventricle with poor pumping; a chronic result of myocarditis.
Dilated pupils: Pupils wider than normal, seen with serotonergic or stimulant drugs such as MDMA.
Dilation: Widening of a vessel beyond its normal diameter.
Diltiazem: Rate-limiting CCB used for angina when beta-blockers are contraindicated.
Dilutional hyponatraemia: Low sodium caused by too much water in the body, not by sodium loss.
Dimples of Venus: Skin dimples over the posterior superior iliac spines, the landmark for Schober's test.
Diphtheria: Rare toxin-producing infection with a grey adherent throat membrane, in unvaccinated people.
Diplococci: Bacteria seen in pairs of round cells on microscopy.
Diplopia: Double vision; a red flag in vertigo.
Direct access: GPs can book an endoscopy themselves without first referring to a specialist.
Direct inoculation: Bacteria introduced straight into tissue by injury, surgery or an adjacent ulcer.
Direct pathway: Basal ganglia route that facilitates wanted movement; driven by dopamine.
Direct thrombin inhibitor: A drug that binds and blocks thrombin itself.
Direct visualisation: Looking at the bowel lining directly with a camera.
Disc prolapse: The soft centre of an intervertebral disc bulging through its outer ring onto nerves.
Disc space: The gap between two vertebrae occupied by an intervertebral disc.
Discharge: Fluid coming from the eye; watery, sticky or purulent.
Discharge criteria: Conditions a patient must meet before it is safe to send them home.
Discharging sinus: A tract from infected tissue to the skin that leaks pus.
Disclose: To share patient information with another person or organisation.
Discoid rash: Red, scaly, sometimes scarring plaques on sun-exposed skin; the main feature of discoid lupus.
Disease-modifying: A treatment that changes the course of the disease, not just symptoms.
Disinhibition: Loss of social restraint: rude, impulsive or inappropriate behaviour.
Disorientation: Not knowing the time, place or person.
Dissection flap: The torn inner layer of the aorta seen on imaging, separating true and false lumens.
Disseminated gonococcal infection: Gonorrhoea that has spread through the blood to joints, tendons and skin.
Dissemination in time and space: Lesions occurring at different times and in different parts of the CNS; required to diagnose MS.
Distal: Further from the origin, here away from the heart.
Distal airways: The smallest airways furthest from the trachea, near the alveoli.
Distal convoluted tubule: The part of the nephron after the loop of Henle, where thiazides act.
Distal joints: Joints far from the trunk, such as toes, ankles and fingers.
Distal nephron: The distal tubule and collecting duct, where aldosterone acts.
Distal phalanx: The tip bone of a finger or toe.
Distal propagation: Extension of a clot further downstream along the vessel.
Distal radius: The wrist end of the radius, a common fragility fracture site.
Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy: The commonest diabetic neuropathy: both sides, starting in the feet and spreading upwards.
Distal tibia: The lower end of the shin bone, near the ankle.
Distended abdomen: A swollen, bloated tummy; here from air pumped into the stomach.
Distension: Swelling of the abdomen from gas or fluid.
Distributive shock: Low blood pressure from widespread vasodilation, as in anaphylaxis and sepsis.
Diuretic: A drug that increases urine output to remove excess fluid.
Diuretics: Drugs that increase urine output, such as furosemide.
Diurnal: Following a daily rhythm; cortisol peaks in the morning and falls at night.
Diurnal cortisol variation: The normal daily rhythm of cortisol, highest in the morning and lowest at midnight.
Diurnal variation: Change in a measurement across the day, such as peak flow lower in the morning.
Diverticulitis: Inflammation of colonic diverticula, usually in the sigmoid colon, causing LIF pain.
Dix-Hallpike: A test that turns the head 45° and lies the patient back quickly to provoke BPPV.
Dizziness: Feeling light-headed or unsteady, a common alpha-blocker side effect.
DoLS: Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards: legal checks needed before restricting the freedom of someone who lacks capacity.
Dobutamine: An IV inotrope that strengthens heart contraction.
Docetaxel: A taxane chemotherapy drug that stops cell division; the D in FEC-D.
Dolutegravir: An integrase inhibitor used in first-line HIV regimens.
Dominant S wave: A QRS that is mainly downward, as in V1 in LBBB.
Dominant hemisphere: The side of the brain that controls language, the left in most people.
Domperidone: Antiemetic dopamine antagonist that does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
Donepezil: Cholinesterase inhibitor used in Alzheimer's dementia.
Donor: The person who gave the blood.
