Dopamine: A neurotransmitter involved in movement, reward and arousal.
Dopamine agonists: Drugs that stimulate dopamine receptors directly, such as ropinirole and rotigotine.
Dopamine antagonist: A drug that blocks dopamine receptors, used to stop nausea and vomiting.
Dopamine antagonists: Drugs that block dopamine receptors, such as haloperidol.
Dopamine transporter: Protein on dopamine neurons that recycles dopamine; reduced on DaTSCAN when neurons are lost.
Dopaminergic neurons: Nerve cells that make and release dopamine.
Doppler: Handheld ultrasound probe used to hear arterial flow and measure ankle pressure.
Doppler ultrasonography: Ultrasound that shows blood flow in vessels.
Doppler ultrasound: Ultrasound that uses frequency shift to show and measure blood flow.
Dormant: Alive but inactive and not multiplying.
Dorsal columns: Spinal cord tracts carrying vibration and position sense.
Dorsum of foot: The top surface of the foot.
Double sickening: Getting better from a cold and then worse again, suggesting secondary bacterial infection.
Double-strand break: A break across both strands of DNA, repaired by BRCA-dependent pathways.
Double-stranded DNA: Genetic material made of two paired strands; herpesviruses carry their genome this way.
Double-stranded DNA virus: A virus whose genome is two-stranded DNA, like all herpesviruses.
Down syndrome: Trisomy 21; the extra amyloid precursor gene causes early-onset Alzheimer's.
Downregulate: To reduce the number or response of receptors after continuous stimulation.
Downregulates: Turns down the activity or number of a system or receptor.
Downregulation: A cell reducing the number or sensitivity of its receptors after prolonged stimulation.
Doxazosin: An alpha-1 blocker used for resistant hypertension and enlarged prostate.
Doxycycline: Tetracycline antibiotic; avoided in pregnancy and young children.
Drainage: Removing fluid, here from the pleural space, using a needle or tube.
Dressler's syndrome: Autoimmune pericarditis weeks after MI, with chest pain, fever and widespread ST elevation.
Drop attack: A sudden fall from loss of muscle tone without warning or loss of consciousness.
Droperidol: Dopamine-blocking antiemetic and sedative that worsens Parkinson's.
Drug holiday: A planned break from a bisphosphonate after 3 to 5 years of treatment.
Drug overdose: Taking more of a drug than the body can safely handle.
Drug-induced lupus: Lupus-like illness caused by drugs such as isoniazid or hydralazine, sparing kidneys and brain, resolving on stopping them.
Drug-induced parkinsonism: Parkinson-like signs caused by dopamine-blocking drugs, usually symmetrical.
Dry cough: A cough that brings up no sputum.
Dry mouth: Reduced saliva, from involvement of CN VII fibres to the salivary glands.
Dry mucous membranes: A dry mouth and tongue, a sign of fluid loss.
Dry tap: A failed marrow aspirate because the marrow is fibrosed; classic of myelofibrosis.
Dual antiplatelet therapy: Aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor, continued for 12 months after MI.
Duct: A small tube in the breast that carries milk to the nipple.
Duct ectasia: Widening of the ducts behind the nipple, causing discharge in older women.
Ducts: The tubes that carry milk from the lobules to the nipple.
Duke criteria: Major and minor criteria combining cultures, echo and clinical signs to diagnose endocarditis.
Duke's: Colorectal cancer staging A to D based on wall invasion, nodes and metastases.
Dullness: A flat, non-resonant percussion note over lung that is solid or has fluid around it.
Duloxetine: An SNRI antidepressant used for neuropathic pain, especially when amitriptyline is contraindicated.
Duodenal: Relating to the duodenum, the first part of the small intestine.
Duodenal biopsy: A small tissue sample taken from the duodenum during endoscopy.
Duodenal ulceration: Ulcers in the first part of the small bowel.
Duplex ultrasound: Ultrasound combining images and Doppler flow; first-line imaging for PAD.
Dupuytren's contracture: Thickening of the palmar fascia causing fixed flexion of the ring and little fingers.
Dural puncture: A needle breaching the dura, as in spinal anaesthesia or lumbar puncture.
Dust mites: Tiny bugs in house dust whose droppings are a common allergen.
Duty of care: The legal obligation to act in the patient's interest and avoid causing them harm.
Duty of confidentiality: A doctor's obligation to keep information about a patient private unless an exception applies.
Dysarthria: Slurred speech from weak or uncoordinated speech muscles.
Dyscrasia: An abnormal state of blood cells; plasma cell dyscrasias include MGUS and myeloma.
Dysdiadochokinesia: Inability to perform rapid alternating movements; a cerebellar sign.
Dyskinesia: Involuntary movements, such as chewing or writhing, seen in anti-NMDA encephalitis.
Dyslipidaemia: Abnormal blood lipids, such as high triglycerides and low HDL.
Dyspepsia: Indigestion: upper abdominal discomfort, often after eating.
Dysplastic: Abnormal in shape and maturation; a sign of disordered cell development.
Dyspnoea on exertion: Breathlessness brought on by physical activity.
Dysregulated: Out of control; the immune response becomes excessive and harms the body's own organs.
Dysregulation: Abnormal control of a system, so it is over- or under-active.
Dystonia: Sustained muscle contraction causing twisting or abnormal postures.
Dysuria: Pain or burning on passing urine.
Déjà vu: A strong feeling of having lived a moment before; a temporal lobe aura.
E. coli: Escherichia coli, a Gram-negative gut bacterium and common cause of cholangitis.
E. coli O157: A toxin-producing E. coli causing bloody diarrhoea and haemolytic uraemic syndrome.
EASL: European Association for the Study of the Liver.
EATL: Enteropathy-associated T-cell lymphoma: a non-Hodgkin lymphoma of the small bowel complicating coeliac disease.
EBV: Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever.
EBV serology: Blood tests for antibodies to EBV antigens such as VCA IgM; gold standard.
ECG: Electrocardiogram: a recording of the heart's electrical activity from electrodes on the skin.
ECM: Extracellular matrix: the collagen and protein scaffold between cells, excessive in fibrosis.
ECMO: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation: a machine that pumps and oxygenates blood outside the body, also rewarming it.
ECT: Electroconvulsive therapy: a controlled seizure under anaesthesia for severe or resistant depression.
EEG: Electroencephalogram: records the brain's electrical activity through scalp electrodes.
EF: Ejection fraction: the share of ventricular blood ejected per beat.
EIA: Enzyme immunoassay: a lab test detecting an antigen or antibody.
ELISA: Lab antibody test, used here to screen for HIV.
EMA: Anti-endomysial antibodies: a blood test for coeliac disease.
EMG: Electromyography: recording muscle electrical activity to detect denervation.
ENT referral: Sending the patient to an ear, nose and throat specialist.
ENaC: Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct, increased by aldosterone.
EOMs: Extraocular muscles, the six muscles that move each eye.
EPAP: Expiratory positive airway pressure on BiPAP; it holds alveoli open.
EPO: Erythropoietin, the kidney hormone that drives red cell production; given by injection in CKD anaemia.
ER: Oestrogen receptor; ER-positive tumours respond to hormone therapy.
ERCP: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography: endoscope into the bile duct to diagnose and remove stones.
ESC/ERS: European Society of Cardiology and European Respiratory Society, who publish the pulmonary hypertension guidelines.
ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate, a non-specific marker of inflammation.
ESRD: End-stage renal disease: kidney failure needing dialysis or transplant.
ESWL: Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy: shock waves from outside the body break up the stone.
ET tube: Endotracheal tube: a tube passed through the mouth into the trachea to ventilate the lungs.
EUA: Examination under anaesthesia: the surgeon examines and probes the anal canal while the patient is asleep.
EUGOGO: European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy, which sets management principles for thyroid eye disease.
EUS: Endoscopic ultrasound: ultrasound probe on an endoscope to stage local depth and nodes.
EVAR: Endovascular aneurysm repair: a stent graft placed through the femoral arteries.
EVLA: Endovenous laser ablation: heat from a laser fibre closes the vein.
Early afterdepolarisations: Abnormal depolarisations during repolarisation that trigger torsades.
Early diastolic murmur: A soft blowing murmur just after S2; loudest at the left sternal edge in aortic regurgitation.
Early intervention: Treatment started at an early stage to stop progression.
Early invasive management: Doing coronary angiography and treating blockages within days rather than with drugs alone.
Early morning specimen: The first urine passed after waking, most concentrated and best for ACR.
Early satiety: Feeling full after eating only a little, here from a large spleen pressing on the stomach.
Early-onset: Starting at a younger age than usual, here before 65.
Easy bruising: Bruises appearing after minor or no injury.
Ebstein's anomaly: Heart defect of the tricuspid valve linked to lithium in pregnancy.
Eccentric hypertrophy: Ventricular dilation with wall growth, from volume overload.
Echo: Echocardiogram: ultrasound scan of the heart.
Echo 8: Echovirus type 8, an enterovirus that can cause pericarditis.
Echocardiogram: Ultrasound of the heart; estimates pulmonary pressure and shows the right ventricle.
Echocardiography: Ultrasound imaging of the heart showing valves, chambers and blood flow.
Echoviruses: Enteroviruses that commonly cause viral meningitis.
Ectopic: Arising in an abnormal place, here nerve impulses starting along a damaged nerve.
Ectopic ACTH syndrome: Cushing's caused by a tumour outside the pituitary, often lung, that makes ACTH.
Ectopic pacemaker: A group of heart cells outside the sinus node that starts firing impulses.
Eczema: Chronic itchy, dry, inflamed skin condition, common in atopic people.
Eczema coxsackium: Coxsackievirus infection of eczematous skin; mimics eczema herpeticum but does not respond to aciclovir.
Eczema herpeticum: Widespread HSV-1 infection of eczematous skin with fever; a dermatological emergency.
Edrophonium: Very short-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used in the historic Tensilon test.
Effacement: Flattening of podocyte foot processes, seen on electron microscopy.
Effective arterial underfilling: Arteries feel underfilled despite total body fluid overload, triggering salt and water retention.
Effective circulating volume: The part of the blood volume that actually fills the arteries and perfuses organs.
Efferent: Carrying signals away from the central nervous system to a muscle or gland.
Efferent arteriolar tone: How constricted the vessel leaving the glomerulus is; constriction keeps filtration pressure up.
Efferent arteriole: The small artery leaving the glomerulus; its tone keeps filtration pressure up.
Effusion: Excess fluid inside a joint, causing swelling.
Ejaculation: Release of semen, which can temporarily raise PSA.
Ejection fraction: The percentage of blood in the left ventricle pumped out with each beat; normal is above 50%.
Ejection systolic murmur: A crescendo-decrescendo murmur in systole, as in aortic stenosis.
Elastic recoil: The lung's natural tendency to spring back, which drives expiration.
Elastin: A stretchy protein in the aortic media that lets it recoil.
Elective caesarean section: A planned surgical delivery before labour starts.
Elective splenectomy: A planned, non-emergency operation to remove the spleen.
Electric-shock-like: Sudden, sharp, stabbing pain like an electric shock.
Electrical alternans: QRS height alternating beat to beat as the heart swings in a large effusion.
Electrical axis: The overall direction of the heart's electrical activity seen on ECG.
Electrolyte: A salt in the blood such as sodium or potassium.
Electrolyte imbalance: Abnormal blood levels of salts such as potassium, magnesium or calcium.
Electrolyte loss: Salts such as sodium and potassium lost in the urine along with water.
Electrolytes: Salts in the blood such as sodium and potassium.
Elevate the legs: Raising the legs above the heart to push blood back to the central circulation.
Elevation: Raising the affected limb above heart level to reduce swelling.
Eligible population: The group of people a screening programme is offered to.
Elimination: Removal of a drug or toxin from the body.
Embolectomy: Surgical removal of an embolus, usually with a balloon catheter.
Embolic stroke: A stroke caused by a clot or debris travelling to a brain artery.
Embolisation: The process of a clot or debris travelling in the blood and blocking a distant vessel.
Embolise: When a clot breaks off and travels to block a vessel elsewhere.
Embolism: Blockage of a blood vessel by material, such as a clot, that has travelled from elsewhere in the circulation.
Embolus: A clot or other material carried in the blood that blocks a distant artery.
Embryo sign: AXR appearance of caecal volvulus: a comma-shaped dilated loop arising from the right lower quadrant.
Embryogenesis: Development of the embryo in early pregnancy.
Emergency surgery: An unplanned operation done urgently, with less time to optimise the patient.
Emollient: A moisturiser that softens skin and restores the barrier.
Empagliflozin: An SGLT2 inhibitor: makes the kidneys pass glucose and salt.
Emphysema: Permanent destruction of alveolar walls, causing air trapping and poor gas exchange.
Emphysematous pyelonephritis: Necrotising kidney infection with gas in the tissue, mainly in diabetics.
Empiric: Started before the organism is known, aimed at the likeliest cause.
Empirical: Treatment started on the most likely cause before test results confirm it.
Empirical antibiotics: Antibiotics started before culture results, based on the likely organism.
Empirically: Treated on the most likely cause before test results confirm it.
Empyema: Pus in the pleural space, usually from an infected effusion next to a pneumonia.
Emtricitabine: An NRTI often paired with tenofovir as the cART backbone.
Enalapril: An ACE inhibitor used for high blood pressure and heart failure.
Encapsulated: Surrounded by a capsule that separates it from neighbouring tissue.
Encapsulated bacteria: Bacteria with a polysaccharide capsule that resists phagocytosis unless coated by antibody.
Encephalitis: Inflammation of the brain tissue itself, usually viral or autoimmune.
Encephalomyelitis: Inflammation of both the brain and the spinal cord.
Encephalopathy: Diffuse brain dysfunction causing confusion or reduced consciousness.
End-inspiratory: Occurring at the end of breathing in.
End-organ damage: Damage to the brain, heart, kidneys or eyes caused by high blood pressure.
End-organ ischaemia: Organ damage from poor blood supply.
End-stage: The final, irreversible stage of organ failure.
End-stage disease: The final, most severe stage of a disease, here kidney failure.
End-stage renal failure: Kidney function too low to sustain life without dialysis or transplant.
End-tidal CO2: The CO2 level at the end of each breath out; absent if the tube is in the oesophagus.
Endemic area: A region where a disease is constantly present in the population.
Endocardial surface: The smooth inner lining of the heart chambers and valves.
Endocarditis: Infection of the heart valves that can throw infected emboli into the bloodstream.
Endocardium: The thin inner lining of the heart chambers and valves.
Endocrine: Glands releasing hormones into the blood, such as pancreatic insulin.
Endocrinologist: A specialist doctor in hormone conditions such as diabetes.
Endogenous: Coming from the patient's own body, such as their skin or gut flora.
Endoleak: Persistent blood flow into the aneurysm sac outside an EVAR stent graft.
Endolymph: The fluid inside the semicircular canals.
Endolymphatic hydrops: Excess endolymph in the inner ear, the mechanism of Ménière's disease.
Endometrial: Relating to the lining of the womb.
Endomyocardial biopsy: Sample of heart muscle taken via a catheter; investigation of choice in fulminant myocarditis.
Endoscopic: Done through a camera passed into the gut.
Endoscopic stenting: Placing a mesh tube through a blocked segment using an endoscope to keep it open.
Endoscopic ultrasound: Ultrasound performed from a probe on an endoscope inside the gut.
Endoscopy: A camera passed into the gut, here to look for and band oesophageal varices.
Endothelial: Relating to the cells lining blood vessels.
Endothelial injury: Damage to the inner lining of blood vessels, which encourages clotting.
Endothelin: A powerful vessel-narrowing chemical released by the lining of blood vessels.
Endothelin receptor antagonist: Drug, such as bosentan, that blocks the vasoconstrictor endothelin in PAH.
Endothelium: The single cell layer lining blood vessels; damaged by cytokines in sepsis.
Endotoxin: A toxic component of the outer wall of Gram-negative bacteria.
Endotracheal aspirate: Secretions sucked from the breathing tube of a ventilated patient and sent for culture.
Endotracheal tube: A breathing tube passed into the trachea for mechanical ventilation.
Endovascular: Treatment from inside the vessel through a catheter.
Energy metabolism: How cells convert food into usable energy, mainly in mitochondria.
Engorgement: Overfull, swollen, painful breasts from milk building up.
Enoxaparin: A low molecular weight heparin used for thromboprophylaxis.
Entacapone: COMT inhibitor added to levodopa for wearing-off.
Entamoeba histolytica: A parasite causing amoebic dysentery and liver abscess, acquired through travel.
Enteric organisms: Bacteria that normally live in the gut.
Enterococcus: Gut organism causing endocarditis after GI or GU procedures.
Enterovirus: Group of viruses including Coxsackie, spread by the faecal-oral and respiratory routes.
Enteroviruses: Viruses such as coxsackie and echovirus, the commonest cause of viral meningitis.
Enthesis: The point where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone.
Enthesitis: Inflammation where tendons or ligaments insert into bone, such as the Achilles insertion.
Entrapment: Squeezing of a nerve as it passes through a tight space.
Entrapment neuropathy: A nerve squeezed at a narrow point, such as the median nerve in carpal tunnel syndrome.
Envelope: Outer lipid coat of a virus.
Enzyme function: How well the body's protein catalysts work; they slow down in the cold and break down in heat.
Enzyme inducer: A drug that speeds liver metabolism of other drugs, lowering their levels, such as carbamazepine.
Eosinophil count: The number of eosinophils in the blood; raised levels suggest steroid-responsive disease.
Eosinophilic asthma: A type of asthma driven by eosinophils that responds well to steroids.
Eosinophilic infiltration: Eosinophils moving into and building up in a tissue such as the airway wall.
Eosinophilic inflammation: Airway inflammation driven by eosinophils, typical of allergic asthma and responsive to steroids.
Eosinophilic nucleoli: Pink-staining nucleoli, prominent in Reed-Sternberg cells.
Eosinophils: White cells that drive allergic airway inflammation; raised in eosinophilic asthma.
Epaderm: A brand of greasy emollient ointment.
Ephaptic transmission: Abnormal 'cross-talk' where an impulse in one bare fibre triggers impulses in its neighbour.
Epidemics: Sudden rises in cases of a disease within a population.
Epidemiological: Relating to the patterns and causes of disease in populations.
Epidermal: Relating to the epidermis, the outer layer of skin.
Epidermis: The outer layer of the skin, made mostly of keratinocytes.
Epidermoid cysts: Benign skin cysts filled with keratin.
Epididymis: The coiled tube on the back of the testis where sperm mature and are stored.
Epididymitis: Inflammation of the epididymis, behind the testis.
Epidural abscess: A collection of pus in the epidural space that can compress the cord; risk in IVDU.
Epidural analgesia: Pain relief given through a catheter into the epidural space, for example in labour.
Epidural haematoma: Bleeding into the epidural space, linked to anticoagulants or dural puncture.
Epidural space: The space between the vertebrae and the dura, containing fat and veins.
Epigastric: Relating to the upper central abdomen; a rising epigastric feeling is a classic temporal lobe aura.
Epiglottitis: Infection of the epiglottis causing drooling, stridor and airway risk.
Epilepsy: A tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, usually diagnosed after two or more.
Epileptic activity: Abnormal, synchronised firing of brain neurones that causes a seizure.
Epiphysis: The end of a long bone, beyond the growth plate.
Epirubicin: An anthracycline chemotherapy drug; the E in FEC-D.
Episcleritis: Inflammation of the episclera; gritty, red, not painful.
Epithelial: Relating to the lining or glandular cells of an organ.
Epithelial cells: Cells that line surfaces and ducts; most breast cancers start in the duct lining.
Epithelialise: Become lined with epithelium, which makes a tract permanent.
Epithelioid cells: Activated macrophages that look like epithelial cells, forming granulomas.
Epithelium: The layer of cells lining a surface, here the inside of the airways.
Eplerenone: An aldosterone antagonist (MRA) with fewer hormonal side effects than spironolactone.
Epley manoeuvre: A series of head positions that uses gravity to move otoconia back into the utricle.
Epoprostenol: A prostacyclin given by continuous infusion to dilate pulmonary arteries in severe PAH.
Epstein-Barr virus: A gamma-herpesvirus spread by saliva that causes glandular fever.
Epworth: Short for the Epworth Sleepiness Score, a 0 to 24 questionnaire on daytime sleepiness.
Epworth Sleepiness Score: Questionnaire scoring the chance of dozing in eight situations, 0 to 24; 16 or more is severe.
Epworth score: Questionnaire scoring daytime sleepiness; used when OSA is suspected.
Eradication therapy: Combined antibiotics and a PPI given to clear H. pylori.
Erb's palsy: C5/C6 brachial plexus injury giving the waiter's tip posture.
Erect CXR: A chest X-ray taken sitting or standing so free gas rises under the diaphragm.
Erect chest X-ray: Chest film taken with the patient upright so free gas rises under the diaphragm.
Erectile dysfunction: Inability to achieve or keep an erection; an autonomic feature of diabetes.
Ergocalciferol: Vitamin D2, used to correct vitamin D deficiency.
Ergosterol: The sterol in fungal cell membranes, equivalent to cholesterol in human cells.
Eron classification: Grades cellulitis severity from Class I (well, no comorbidity) to Class IV (sepsis or necrotising fasciitis).
Erosion: A bite-shaped area of bone lost at a joint margin, seen on X-ray.
Erosions: Shallow breaks in the skin surface.
Eruptive xanthomas: Crops of small yellow papules on buttocks or limbs, seen with very high triglycerides.
Erysipelas: Superficial form of cellulitis of the upper dermis with a sharp, raised edge.
Erythema: Redness of the skin from increased blood flow.
Erythema multiforme: Hypersensitivity rash with target lesions on the hands and feet, most often triggered by HSV-1.
Erythema nodosum: Painful, red, raised nodules, usually on the shins.
Erythematous: Red, from increased blood flow due to inflammation.
Erythematous halo: A ring of red, inflamed skin around a spot or blister.
Erythrasma: Corynebacterium skin-fold infection; brown scaly patches that fluoresce coral red under Wood's lamp.
Erythroid: Relating to the red cell line.
Erythroid precursors: Immature cells in the marrow that develop into red cells.
Erythroid progenitors: Early marrow cells that develop into red blood cells.
Erythromycin: Macrolide antibiotic; the choice for penicillin-allergic pregnant women.
Erythropoiesis: Production of red blood cells in the bone marrow.
Erythropoietin: A kidney hormone that tells the bone marrow to make red cells.
Erythrovirus: An older name for the genus containing parvovirus B19.
Escalate: Seek senior or specialist help because the patient is not improving or is seriously ill.
Escalation: Calling for more senior help or moving to a higher level of care when a patient worsens.
Escherichia coli: A Gram-negative gut bacterium; the most likely organism in cholecystitis.
Essential hypertension: High blood pressure with no identifiable cause; 90-95% of cases.
Essential tremor: Familial, symmetrical postural and action tremor without bradykinesia.
EtCO2: End-tidal carbon dioxide; a sudden rise during CPR suggests ROSC.
Etanercept: Fusion protein that binds and neutralises TNF-alpha.
Ethambutol: An anti-tuberculosis antibiotic that reduces urate excretion and can trigger gout.
Ethmoid sinus: Small air cells between the eyes, separated from the orbit by very thin bone.
Ethosuximide: A T-type calcium channel blocker, first line for absence seizures.
Etoposide: A chemotherapy drug that blocks the enzyme topoisomerase II; part of BEP.
Euglycaemic DKA: DKA with near-normal glucose, classically caused by SGLT2 inhibitor drugs.
Eustachian tube: The tube linking the middle ear to the back of the nose.
Evacuation: Surgical removal of a collection, such as a blood clot.
Evaporation: Loss of the tear film to the air when the eye stays open.
Everted umbilicus: Belly button pushed outwards by raised intra-abdominal pressure.
Ewing's sarcoma: A malignant bone tumour of children and young adults, with an onion-skin periosteal reaction.
Exacerbation: An acute worsening of symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation.
Excess tearing: Watering eye, often because tears no longer drain properly as the lid is weak.
Excisional lymph node biopsy: Surgical removal of a whole node for histology; gold standard for lymphoma.
Exclusively breastfed: An infant fed only breast milk, with no formula or solids.
Excoriation: A scratch mark where the skin surface has been scraped off.
Excoriations: Scratch marks on the skin from persistent itching.
Excrete: Get rid of from the body; humans have no active way to excrete iron.
Excretion: Removal of waste from the body, here by the kidneys into urine.
Exercise tolerance: How much physical activity someone can do before symptoms stop them.
Exertional dyspnoea: Breathlessness brought on by physical effort.
Exertional syncope: Fainting during effort because cardiac output cannot rise to meet demand.
Exocrine: Glands releasing secretions into ducts, such as pancreatic digestive enzymes.
Exogenous: Coming from outside the patient, such as theatre staff, instruments or the environment.
Exogenous steroids: Steroid medicines given from outside the body, which can suppress the adrenals.
Exophthalmos: Proptosis due to thyroid eye disease; the eye bulges forward.
Exotoxin: A toxin secreted by bacteria into the surroundings.
Expansile: Pushes the examiner's fingers apart, not just up, suggesting an aneurysm rather than a transmitted pulse.
Expiratory: Happening when breathing out; expiratory wheeze points to lower airway narrowing.
Exploratory laparotomy: Opening the abdomen surgically to find and treat a problem.
Exposure keratopathy: Damage to the cornea from drying because the lids cannot cover it properly.
Expressive aphasia: Difficulty producing speech while understanding is kept (Broca's aphasia).
Expressive dysphasia: Difficulty producing speech despite knowing what to say.
Extensively hydrolysed formula: Infant formula with milk proteins broken into small fragments, first line for CMPA.
Extensor plantars: An upgoing big toe on stroking the sole (Babinski sign), showing an upper motor neurone lesion.
Extensor surfaces: The outer side of joints, such as the backs of elbows and fronts of knees.
External beam radiotherapy: Radiation aimed at a tumour from a machine outside the body.
External carotid: The branch of the carotid artery that supplies the face, scalp and nose.
External iliac artery: Pelvic artery that becomes the common femoral artery as it passes under the inguinal ligament.
External opening: The hole of a fistula on the skin near the anus, where discharge appears.
Extra-articular: Features occurring outside the joints, such as eye, skin or tendon involvement.
Extra-lymphatic: Outside the lymph nodes and lymphatic organs.
Extradural: Outside the dura: between the skull and the dura mater.
Extranodal: Outside the lymph nodes, e.g. gut, bone marrow or skin.
Extraocular muscles: The six muscles that move each eye.
Extrapulmonary TB: TB outside the lungs, such as lymph nodes, bone, gut or meninges.
Extrapyramidal: Movement side effects of dopamine blockade: stiffness, tremor, slowness.
Extrapyramidal side effects: Drug-induced movement problems such as dystonia, more likely in young women on dopamine antagonists.
Extravascular haemolysis: Red cell destruction outside blood vessels, mainly by spleen and liver macrophages.
Extreme hyperglycaemia: Very high blood glucose, typically over 30 mmol/L in HHS.
Extrinsic allergic alveolitis: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: immune reaction to inhaled organic antigens such as mouldy hay or bird proteins.
Extrinsic pathway: Clotting cascade arm triggered by tissue factor and factor VII, measured by PT.
Exudate: Protein-rich pleural fluid from inflammation or malignancy (protein above 30 g/L or by Light's criteria).
Exudates: Yellow deposits of leaked lipid and protein in the retina.
Exudative pleural effusion: Protein-rich fluid around the lung caused by inflammation or malignancy.
Eye ointment: Thick lubricant applied to the eye, usually at night.
Eyelid cleansers: Gentle wipes or solutions to clean allergens and debris from the lids.
Ezetimibe: Blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption; first add-on when a statin is not enough.
F8: Gene on the X chromosome encoding factor VIII.
F9: Gene on the X chromosome encoding factor IX.
FAP: Familial adenomatous polyposis: APC mutation causing hundreds of colonic polyps and near-certain cancer.
FBC: Full blood count: haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
FCU: Flexor carpi ulnaris: ulnar-supplied wrist flexor; loss makes the wrist deviate radially.
FEC-D: Chemotherapy: fluorouracil, epirubicin, cyclophosphamide, then docetaxel.
FEU: Fibrinogen-equivalent units, a unit used to report D-dimer.
FEV1/FVC: The ratio of FEV1 to FVC; below 0.7 means airflow obstruction.
FFP: Fresh frozen plasma: contains clotting factors, given for coagulopathy with active bleeding.
FFP3: A high-filtration respirator mask worn by staff caring for infectious TB.
FIT: Faecal immunochemical test, detecting hidden blood in stool to screen for bowel cancer.
FLOT: Chemotherapy of 5-FU, leucovorin, oxaliplatin and docetaxel given around gastric cancer surgery.
FN: False negative: test negative but disease present.
FNA: Fine needle aspiration: drawing fluid or cells out with a thin needle.
FODMAP: Fermentable, poorly absorbed carbohydrates that draw in water and produce gas.
FOLFIRINOX: Combination chemotherapy (folinic acid, fluorouracil, irinotecan, oxaliplatin) for advanced pancreatic cancer.
FP: False positive: a positive test in someone without the disease.
FRAX: Online tool giving the 10-year probability of a hip or major osteoporotic fracture.
FRIII: Fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion: weight-based IV insulin (0.1 units/kg/hour) used to clear ketones in DKA.
FSGS: Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, a cause of nephrotic syndrome.
FSH: Follicle-stimulating hormone; pituitary hormone controlling sperm and egg development.
FVC: Forced vital capacity: total air blown out after a full breath in.
Facial diplegia: Weakness of both sides of the face.
Facial droop: Sagging of one side of the face from muscle weakness.
Facial nerve palsy: Weakness of the muscles of one side of the face due to facial nerve damage.
Facial pain: Pain over the cheeks, forehead or between the eyes, from pressure in blocked sinuses.
Facial plethora: A red, flushed face from too many red blood cells.
Factor IX: A clotting factor of the intrinsic pathway; missing in haemophilia B. Also called Christmas factor.
Factor IX assay: Blood test measuring factor IX activity; confirms haemophilia B.
Factor V Leiden: Inherited mutation making blood more likely to clot.
Factor VIII: A clotting factor of the intrinsic pathway; missing in haemophilia A.
Factor VIII assay: Blood test measuring factor VIII activity; confirms haemophilia A and grades severity.
Factor X: Clotting factor activated by IXa plus VIIIa; it converts prothrombin to thrombin.
Factor Xa: Activated factor X, which converts prothrombin into thrombin.
Factor replacement: Giving the missing clotting factor into a vein.
Faecal calprotectin: A stool marker of bowel inflammation, raised in inflammatory bowel disease.
Faecal impaction: Hard stool stuck in the rectum, often from opiates and immobility.
Faecal incontinence: Loss of control of the bowels.
Faecal mass: The bulk of stool in the bowel.
Faecal peritonitis: Infection of the peritoneum from bowel contents after a perforation.
Faget sign: Relative bradycardia with fever; classic in typhoid.
Failure to thrive: Older term for a child not gaining weight or growing as expected.
Falls: Unintended drops to the ground; a key risk with sudden vertigo, especially in older people.
Falls prevention: Measures that cut the chance of falling, such as removing hazards, reviewing drugs and improving balance.
False localising sign: A sign caused by raised pressure in general, not by a lesion at that site, such as a 6th nerve palsy.
False lumen: A new channel of blood inside the aortic wall, created when blood splits the layers.
False positive: A test result that says positive when the condition is not actually present.
Faltering growth: Weight gain slower than expected, crossing down centile lines.
Famciclovir: Alternative oral antiviral for herpes infections.
Familial: Running in families because of an inherited gene change.
Familial hypercholesterolaemia: Inherited, usually autosomal dominant, LDL receptor defect causing very high LDL from birth.
Familial risk: Increased risk of disease because of affected family members, suggesting an inherited cause.
Family history: Illness in blood relatives, suggesting an inherited cause.
Farmer's lung: Hypersensitivity pneumonitis from fungal spores in mouldy hay.
Fascia: A sheet of tough connective tissue wrapping muscles and organs.
Fascial compartment: Group of muscles enclosed by tough fascia that cannot stretch when they swell.
Fascial layers: The sheets of fascia separating fat and muscle.
Fascial planes: Gaps between fascial layers that infection tracks along.
Fasciotomy: Cutting the fascia to relieve compartment syndrome.
Fastidious: Hard to grow in the lab because it needs special conditions.
Fasting plasma glucose: Blood glucose measured after at least 8 hours without food.
Fat necrosis: Hard benign lump after trauma or surgery that can mimic cancer.
Fat redistribution: Movement of body fat to the trunk, face and back of neck.
Fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E and K, absorbed with fat.
Fatigability: Weakness that gets worse with repeated use and recovers with rest.
Fatigable: Weakness that worsens with repeated or sustained use and recovers with rest.
Fatigue: Extreme tiredness or lack of energy not relieved by rest.
Fava beans: Broad beans; they contain oxidants that trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Fc portion: The tail end of an antibody that binds immune cells and complement.
Fc receptor: A receptor on immune cells that grips the tail end of an antibody, holding IgE on mast cells.
FcεRI: High-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells; a target of autoantibodies in chronic urticaria.
FeNO: Fractional exhaled nitric oxide: a breath test that measures eosinophilic airway inflammation.
FeNa: Fractional excretion of sodium: the share of filtered sodium passed in urine; above 1% suggests ATN.
Febrile non-haemolytic reaction: Common, mild fever and chills during transfusion caused by cytokines from donor white cells.
Febuxostat: Second-line xanthine oxidase inhibitor used if allopurinol is not tolerated.
Felodipine: Long-acting dihydropyridine CCB; preferred add-on to a beta-blocker in angina.
Felty's syndrome: Rheumatoid arthritis with splenomegaly and neutropenia.
Femoral branch: The branch of the genitofemoral nerve supplying skin of the upper inner thigh; the sensory limb of the cremasteric reflex.
Femoral head: The ball at the top of the thigh bone that sits in the hip socket.
Femoral-popliteal: The arterial segment from the femoral artery in the thigh to the popliteal artery behind the knee.
Fermentable carbohydrates: Sugars and fibres that gut bacteria break down, producing gas.
Ferric carboxymaltose: Intravenous iron preparation that replaces iron stores quickly.
Ferritin: Protein that stores iron; its blood level reflects iron stores but rises with inflammation.
Ferroportin: Iron exporter on gut and macrophage cells that releases iron into the blood.
Ferrous fumarate: Oral iron tablet, first-line treatment for iron deficiency anaemia.
Ferrous sulphate: Oral iron tablet that reduces levothyroxine absorption if taken together.
Festination: Short, quickening steps as if chasing the centre of gravity.
Fetal: Relating to the developing baby in the womb.
Fetal bradycardia: An abnormally slow heart rate in the unborn baby.
Fetal haemoglobin: HbF: two alpha and two gamma chains; it does not sickle.
Fetus: The unborn baby; delivery removes the obstetric trigger.
FeverPAIN: An alternative sore throat score: fever, purulence, fast attendance, inflamed tonsils, no cough or coryza.
Fexofenadine: Non-sedating H1 antihistamine used first line for urticaria.
Fibrillin-1: A connective tissue protein that supports elastic fibres; defective in Marfan's syndrome.
Fibrin: Protein mesh that strengthens a platelet plug into a stable clot.
Fibrinogen: A clotting protein that is used up and falls in DIC.
Fibrinogen replacement: Giving fibrinogen, usually as cryoprecipitate, when levels are low.
FibroScan: Transient elastography: an ultrasound-based measure of liver stiffness, first-line for assessing fibrosis.
Fibroadenoma: Benign smooth, very mobile lump in young women.
Fibroblast: A cell that makes collagen and other scar tissue proteins.
Fibrocystic change: Benign hormone-related lumpiness and cysts in the breast.
Fibrogenesis: The laying down of scar tissue (collagen) in an injured organ.
Fibromuscular stroma: The fibrous and smooth muscle tissue that supports the prostate.
Fibronodular opacification: Areas of scarring and small nodules seen as white shadows on a chest X-ray.
Fibroscan: An ultrasound-based test that measures liver stiffness to stage fibrosis.
Fibrosis: Scarring with collagen deposition that stiffens an organ.
Fibrotic septa: Bands of scar tissue that divide the liver into nodules.
Fibrous capsule: A wall of scar-like connective tissue that forms around a mature abscess.
Fibrous sac: A tough bag of connective tissue, here the pericardium wrapping the heart.
Fibrous tissue: Connective tissue rich in collagen that gives structure.
Fibrovascular proliferation: Growth of scar tissue with new vessels that can pull on and detach the retina.
Fibular head: The top of the fibula, just below the outside of the knee.
Fidaxomicin: Oral macrocyclic antibiotic for recurrent C. difficile; lower recurrence than vancomycin.
Field change: Carcinogen damage across a whole lining, so new tumours can arise anywhere in it.
Fifth disease: Another name for erythema infectiosum (slapped cheek), caused by parvovirus B19.
Filaggrin: A skin protein that helps build the stratum corneum barrier; mutated in many with eczema.
Filling pressures: The pressures in the heart chambers as they fill with blood.
Filtration gradient: The pressure difference that drives fluid out of the glomerular capillaries into the tubule.
Fine needle aspiration: Thin needle draws out cyst fluid or cells; confirms and treats a cyst.
Fine tremor: A small, fast shake, best seen in the outstretched hands.
Finger-prick sample: A drop of capillary blood taken by pricking the fingertip.
First web space: The skin between the big toe and second toe.
First-degree heart block: PR interval longer than 200 ms with every P wave conducted.
Fistula: An abnormal tract connecting two epithelial surfaces, here the anal canal and the perianal skin.
Fistula-in-ano: Another name for an anal fistula.
Fistulotomy: Laying the fistula tract open so it heals from the base.
Fixed dilated pupil: A large pupil that does not constrict to light, a sign of third nerve compression.
Fixed flexion: A joint stuck bent that cannot be straightened.
Fixed obstruction: Airway narrowing that does not improve with a bronchodilator.
Fixed-rate: A set insulin dose per hour based on body weight, not adjusted to each glucose reading.
Flank: The side of the body between the ribs and the hip.
Flank masses: Lumps felt in the sides of the abdomen; bilateral ones suggest enlarged polycystic kidneys.
Flank pain: Pain in the side of the body between the ribs and hip, over the kidney.
Flapping tremor: Asterixis: a coarse flap of outstretched hands, seen with CO2 retention.
Flare: A sudden return or worsening of symptoms.
Flare-ups: Periods when symptoms suddenly get worse.
Flash pulmonary oedema: Sudden fluid in the lungs, classically recurrent in renal artery stenosis.
Flatus: Wind passed from the back passage.
Flatus tube: A soft rectal tube left in after decompression to let gas escape and stop re-twisting.
Flexible cystoscopy: Cystoscopy with a bendable scope under local anaesthetic; the gold-standard diagnostic test.
Flexural: In the skin creases on the bending side of joints, such as inner elbows and backs of knees.
Flexures: Skin creases such as the inside of the elbow and back of the knee.
Floaters: Moving specks or strands in the vision from debris or blood in the vitreous.
Flora: The mix of microbes normally living at a body site.
Flow cytometry: Laser test that identifies cells by surface markers; first-line for CLL.
Flu-like illness: Fever, aches, tiredness and headache resembling influenza, often a viral prodrome.
Flu-like symptoms: Fever, aches, chills and tiredness similar to influenza.
Flucloxacillin: A penicillin resistant to staphylococcal beta-lactamase; first choice for S. aureus.
Fluconazole: Oral azole antifungal; 150 mg single dose treats vaginal thrush.
Fluctuance: A boggy, fluid-filled feel on palpation, suggesting a pus collection.
Fluctuant: Feels like fluid under pressure when pressed.
Fluctuating: Varying over hours, with better and worse periods.
Flucytosine: Antifungal combined with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis.
Fluid bolus: A quick set volume of IV fluid (e.g. 500 mL) given to test and treat low blood pressure.
Fluid challenge: A rapid IV fluid bolus, usually 250 to 500 mL, given to see whether perfusion and urine output improve.
Fluid congestion: Build-up of fluid in tissues and vessels because blood backs up behind a failing heart.
Fluid overload: Too much fluid in the body, causing swelling, breathlessness and crackles in the lungs.
Fluid overloaded: Having too much fluid in the body, causing swelling, breathlessness and raised JVP.
Fluid protein: Amount of protein in pleural fluid; high levels suggest an exudate.
Fluid resuscitation: Giving IV fluids quickly to restore circulating volume and blood pressure.
Fluid thrill: A tap on one flank felt as a wave on the other, seen in large-volume ascites.
Fluid-resuscitated: Given enough IV fluid to restore circulating volume.
Flumazenil: Benzodiazepine receptor antagonist; can trigger seizures, so used with caution.
Fluorescein: Orange dye that stains damaged corneal epithelium green under blue light.
Fluorescein angiography: Dye injected into a vein and photographed in the retina to show leaking, blocked or new vessels.
Fluorouracil: A chemotherapy drug that blocks DNA synthesis; the F in FEC-D.
Flushing: Sudden reddening and warmth of the skin.
Fluticasone: A corticosteroid used as a nasal spray for allergic rhinitis.
Fluticasone-azelastine: Combined steroid and antihistamine nasal spray for rhinitis not controlled by a steroid spray.
Foam cell: Macrophage stuffed with oxidised LDL; the building block of a fatty streak.
Foam moulding: Industrial shaping of foam products, a source of isocyanate exposure.
Foamy urine: Frothy urine caused by large amounts of protein in it.
Focal: Starting in one area of one hemisphere of the brain.
Focal aware: A focal seizure where the person stays aware throughout.
Focal chest findings: Signs in one part of the lung, such as crackles or bronchial breathing, suggesting pneumonia.
Focal crackles: Crackles heard in one area of the chest.
Focal demyelination: Loss of the myelin sheath at one spot along a nerve.
Focal impaired-awareness: A focal seizure where awareness is lost and the person cannot recall it.
Focal neuro signs: Deficits pointing to one specific area of the brain, such as one-sided weakness or speech loss.
Focal neurological deficit: Loss of function in one part of the nervous system, such as weakness of one limb.
Focal neurological deficits: Loss of function in a specific body part from damage to one brain area.
Focal neurological signs: Signs pointing to damage in one area of the nervous system, such as one-sided weakness.
Focal neurology: Neurological signs affecting one area, such as weakness of one limb.
Focal neuropathy: Neuropathy affecting one nerve or one area, rather than a widespread pattern.
Focal signs: Neurological signs pointing to damage in one specific part of the brain, such as one-sided weakness.
Folate: A B vitamin needed for DNA synthesis, found in leafy greens.
Folate antagonist: A drug that blocks the use of folate, which cells need to make DNA.
Folate cycle: The chain of reactions recycling folate forms to supply building blocks for DNA.
Folic acid: B vitamin taken before and in early pregnancy to reduce neural tube defects.
Follicular cell: The thyroid cell that makes thyroid hormone.
Fondaparinux: Factor Xa inhibitor anticoagulant used in NSTEMI.
Food allergies: Immune reactions to foods such as milk, egg or peanut.
Foot drop: Inability to lift the front of the foot, from common peroneal nerve damage.
Foot processes: The finger-like extensions of podocytes that wrap the capillaries and form the filtration slits.
Foot ulcer: An open sore on the foot, common in diabetes from nerve damage and poor circulation.
Foot ulcers: Open sores on the foot that heal poorly, often over pressure points in a numb foot.
Foramen magnum: The large hole at the base of the skull through which the brainstem joins the spinal cord.
Forced vital capacity: The most air a person can breathe out forcefully after a full breath in.
Foreign body: An object that should not be there, such as food or a toy in the airway.
Foreign body sensation: Feeling that something is stuck in the eye.
Formal notification: Officially reporting a suspected case to public health using the set form.
Formoterol: A LABA with a fast onset, so it can be used as a reliever with ICS.
Fosfomycin: Alternative oral antibiotic for uncomplicated lower UTI.
Foul breath: Bad-smelling breath, from anaerobic infection or pus.
Foul-smelling sputum: Bad-smelling phlegm, typical of anaerobic infection such as a lung abscess.
Four-stage test: Can the patient understand, retain, weigh up the information and communicate a decision?
Fournier's gangrene: Necrotising fasciitis of the scrotum, perineum or vulva.
Fractional excretion of sodium: The percentage of filtered sodium that ends up in urine.
Fractionated metanephrines: Separate measurements of metanephrine and normetanephrine, here collected in urine over 24 hours.
Fracture risk: The chance of breaking a bone, usually expressed over the next 10 years.
Fragility fracture: A fracture from a fall from standing height or less.
Fragmented sleep: Sleep broken up by many brief awakenings, so it is not restful.
Frailty: Reduced physical reserve in older people, so small stresses such as cold or infection cause big decline.
Framingham: An older cardiovascular risk score, an alternative to QRISK3.
Fraser guidelines: Criteria for giving contraception advice to under-16s without parental consent.
Free IgE: IgE circulating unbound in the blood, available to attach to mast cells.
Free T4: Unbound thyroxine in the blood, the active measured thyroid hormone level.
Free air under the diaphragm: Gas seen beneath the diaphragm on erect chest X-ray, meaning a gut perforation.
Free fatty acids: Fatty acids released from stored fat by lipolysis; the liver turns them into ketones.
Free haemoglobin: Haemoglobin released into plasma when red cells burst inside vessels.
Free wall rupture: Tear through the ventricle wall after MI causing cardiac tamponade.
Frequency: Passing urine more often than normal.
Friction rub: Scratchy sound heard as inflamed pericardial layers rub together.
Frontal bossing: Prominent forehead from marrow expansion in the skull bones.
Frontal lobe: Brain lobe at the front, controlling movement, behaviour and personality.
Frontal lobes: The front parts of the brain, controlling personality, behaviour, planning and movement.
Frontal sinus: Sinus in the forehead bone above the eyebrows.
Frontotemporal atrophy: Shrinking of the frontal and temporal lobes, seen in FTD.
Frontotemporal dementia: Dementia of the frontal and temporal lobes, with early personality change and preserved memory.
Fructose: A sugar made from sorbitol in the polyol pathway.
Full blood count: A blood test measuring haemoglobin, white cells and platelets.
Full house: Renal biopsy staining positive for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3 and C1q, characteristic of lupus nephritis.
Full-term: Born at 37 weeks of pregnancy or later.
Fulminant hepatic failure: Sudden, severe liver failure with encephalopathy in someone without previous liver disease.
Fulminant myocarditis: Severe, rapidly progressive myocarditis with overt heart failure or shock.
Functional TR: TR from a dilated right ventricle stretching a structurally normal valve.
Functional asplenia: A spleen that is present but no longer works.
Functional bowel disorders: Gut symptoms with no structural cause, such as irritable bowel syndrome.
Functional distress: Upset and disruption to daily life, work and sleep caused by symptoms.
Functional hyposplenism: A spleen that is present but does not work, as in sickle cell or coeliac disease.
Functional imaging: Tests showing whether a narrowing causes ischaemia: stress echo, cardiac MRI, perfusion scan.
Functional impairment: Difficulty carrying out normal roles such as work, study or self-care.
Functional incontinence: Leakage with a normal bladder because the person cannot reach the toilet in time.
Functional obstruction: Blockage caused by bowel that cannot relax, without a physical blockage.
Fundal: Relating to the fundus, the back of the eye seen through the pupil.
Fundoplication: Surgery wrapping the top of the stomach around the lower oesophagus to stop reflux.
Fundoscopy: Looking at the back of the eye with an ophthalmoscope to see the retina and optic disc.
Fundus: The inside back surface of the eye, including retina, optic disc and macula.
Fungal: Caused by a fungus, such as Candida.
Fungal spores: Tiny reproductive particles released by moulds, easily inhaled.
Furosemide: A loop diuretic that removes excess fluid.
Fusidic acid: Topical antibiotic safe throughout pregnancy; second line for bacterial conjunctivitis.
Fusion gene: A hybrid gene formed when pieces of two genes are joined.
Fusion protein: A protein made from two genes joined by a translocation.
G-protein: Signalling protein that passes a hormone's message inside the cell.
G6PD: Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase, an enzyme making NADPH to protect red cells from oxidation.
G6PD deficiency: Inherited enzyme deficiency in which some drugs trigger haemolysis of red cells.
GABA-A: The main inhibitory brain receptor; benzodiazepines boost its chloride current.
GABA-A receptor: Chloride channel receptor enhanced by benzodiazepines; downregulates with long-term use.
GAD: Generalised anxiety disorder: excessive, uncontrollable worry about many things for at least 6 months.
GAD-7: Seven-question score of anxiety severity; 15 or more is severe.
GAGs: Glycosaminoglycans, water-attracting sugar chains that cause tissue swelling.
GBM: Glomerular basement membrane; the filter layer between capillary and Bowman's space.
GBS: Guillain-Barré syndrome: post-infectious ascending areflexic weakness.
GCA: Giant cell arteritis: large-vessel vasculitis in older people causing headache and sudden visual loss.
GCS: Glasgow Coma Scale, a 3 to 15 score of eye, verbal and motor responses.
GDH: Glutamate dehydrogenase: a screening stool test for C. difficile, confirmed with a toxin test.
GFR: Glomerular filtration rate: how much blood the kidneys filter per minute.
GGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase; rises with ALP in cholestasis.
GH: Growth hormone, made by somatotroph cells of the anterior pituitary.
GI: Gastrointestinal: the gut from mouth to anus.
GI TB: Tuberculosis of the gut, usually the ileocaecal region.
GI bleed: Bleeding anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract.
GI bleeding: Bleeding into the gut, presenting as haematemesis or melaena.
GI/GU surgery: Operations on the gut (gastrointestinal) or urinary and genital (genitourinary) tract.
GINA: Global Initiative for Asthma, an international asthma guideline group.
GLP-1: Glucagon-like peptide-1, a gut incretin hormone that boosts insulin and reduces appetite.
GLP-1 mimetic: Injected GLP-1 receptor agonist (e.g. semaglutide) used for weight loss and diabetes.
GLP-1 receptor agonist: Injectable drug (e.g. semaglutide) that boosts insulin release and causes weight loss.
GMC: General Medical Council, which sets UK doctors' professional standards on consent and confidentiality.
GNAS: Gene for a G-protein that relays the PTH signal; mutations cause PTH resistance.
GNAS mutation: A change in the gene for a G-protein that passes on the PTH signal inside cells.
GOJ: Gastro-oesophageal junction, where the oesophagus joins the stomach.
GOLD: Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease, an international COPD guideline group.
GORD: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease: symptoms or damage from stomach contents flowing back into the oesophagus.
GPA: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis, an ANCA-positive small-vessel vasculitis that can cause scleritis.
GRACE score: A risk score estimating death after ACS; in NSTEMI a value above 3% means angiography within 72 hours.
GTCS: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure: stiffening then rhythmic jerking with loss of consciousness.
GTN: Glyceryl trinitrate, a nitrate that dilates veins and coronary arteries to relieve ischaemic pain; avoid if systolic BP under 90.
GUM: Genitourinary medicine: the specialty managing sexual health and HIV.
Gabapentin: An anticonvulsant used for neuropathic pain.
Gabapentinoid: Drug class including gabapentin and pregabalin that calms overactive nerve signalling.
Gadolinium: A contrast agent used in MRI that can harm kidneys.
Gadolinium-enhancing: Lights up after gadolinium contrast, showing a new, active lesion with a leaky blood-brain barrier.
Gain-of-function: A mutation making a protein do something new and harmful, rather than stop working.
Gait disturbance: An abnormal way of walking, such as unsteadiness or shuffling.
Galactocele: Milk-filled cyst in a woman who has recently stopped breastfeeding.
Galantamine: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor used for mild to moderate Alzheimer's.
Gallop: A heart rhythm with an extra sound, like a galloping horse.
Gallstones: Hard deposits of cholesterol or pigment that form in the gallbladder.
Gamma chains: The globin chains of fetal haemoglobin, which replace beta chains before birth.
Gamma-haemolytic: Bacteria that do not break down red cells on blood agar.
Ganciclovir: Antiviral used intravenously for CMV retinitis.
Ganglia: Clusters of nerve cell bodies outside the brain and spinal cord.
Gangrene: Death of tissue from lost blood supply; black and shrunken.
Gangrenous: Dead and decaying tissue, often black, from lost blood supply or infection.
Gardner's: FAP variant with osteomas, epidermoid cysts, lipomas and supernumerary teeth.
Gas exchange: Movement of oxygen into, and carbon dioxide out of, the blood in the alveoli.
Gas trapping: Air left stuck in the lungs at the end of breathing out because airways close early.
Gastric carcinoma: Stomach cancer; pernicious anaemia raises the risk.
Gastric contents: Food, fluid and acid from the stomach.
Gastric emptying: The rate food leaves the stomach for the small intestine.
Gastric fundus: The dome-shaped upper part of the stomach, above the oesophageal entry.
Gastric mucosa: The inner lining of the stomach.
Gastric reflux: Stomach contents coming back up the oesophagus.
Gastroduodenal anastomosis: A surgical join between the remaining stomach and the duodenum.
Gastroenteritis: Infection of the stomach and bowel causing vomiting and diarrhoea.
Gastroenterology: The hospital specialty dealing with the gut and liver.
Gastrointestinal (GI): Relating to the stomach and intestines.
Gastroparesis: Delayed stomach emptying without blockage, causing early fullness, bloating and vomiting.
Gastroscopy: A camera passed through the mouth to view the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
Gastrostomy: Feeding tube placed through the abdominal wall into the stomach.
Gender: Whether the patient is male or female; DEXA reference values are adjusted for it.
General Surgery: The surgical specialty covering the abdomen and bowel, including colorectal problems.
General anaesthesia: Drug-induced unconsciousness, used to stop refractory status epilepticus.
Generalised abdominal tenderness: Pain on pressing anywhere across the abdomen rather than in one spot.
Generalised seizure: Abnormal electrical activity spreading across both sides of the brain.
Generalised tonic-clonic: A seizure involving both hemispheres: loss of consciousness, stiffening, then rhythmic jerking.
Genetic predisposition: An inherited tendency to develop a disease.
Genetic testing: Testing DNA for a disease-causing variant, here HFE mutations.
Genetically susceptible: Carrying genes that raise the risk of a disease.
Genital branch: The branch of the genitofemoral nerve that supplies the cremaster muscle; the motor limb of the cremasteric reflex.
Genital herpes: HSV infection of the genitals, causing painful ulcers; usually HSV-2.
Genital secretions: Fluids from the genital tract, which carry virus during an outbreak.
Genitourinary (GU): Relating to the genital and urinary organs.
Genome integration: A virus inserting its genetic material into the host cell's DNA.
Genotoxic: Damaging to DNA, causing mutations that can lead to cancer.
Gentamicin: An aminoglycoside antibiotic that is toxic to kidney tubules.
Germ cell: A cell that develops into sperm or eggs.
Germ-cell cancer: Cancer of the cells that make sperm or eggs, such as testicular teratoma.
Germinal centre: Part of a lymph node follicle where B cells mature; origin of Reed-Sternberg cells.
Germinate: When a dormant spore turns back into an active, multiplying bacterium.
Germline: Present in every cell from birth, so it can be inherited.
Gestation: The length of pregnancy, counted in weeks.
Giant cell arteritis: Granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries that can cause sudden blindness.
Giant cell tumour: A usually benign but locally aggressive bone tumour near joints, with a soap bubble X-ray look.
Giant cells: Large cells with many nuclei, formed by fused macrophages in granulomas.
Giant platelets: Abnormally large platelets on a blood film, typical of ET.
Giardia: Protozoan parasite from contaminated water causing watery diarrhoea, bloating and malabsorption.
Giardia lamblia: Protozoan parasite from untreated water causing malabsorption.
Giardiasis: Infection of the small bowel with the parasite Giardia lamblia.
Gillick competence: A child under 16 can consent to treatment if they fully understand what is involved.
Gingival hypertrophy: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of ciclosporin.
Glandular architecture: The normal arrangement of glands within a tissue.
Glandular epithelium: The lining cells of the breast ducts and lobules.
Glandular fever: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by Epstein-Barr virus.
Glandular tissue: The milk-producing lobules and ducts of the breast.
Glasgow-Blatchford score: Risk score for upper GI bleeding using urea, Hb, BP, pulse and other features.
Glasgow-Imrie: The Modified Glasgow severity score for pancreatitis, done at 48 hours; 3 or more is severe.
Glass test: Pressing a glass on a rash; if it stays visible it is non-blanching.
Gleason X: Gleason score that cannot be determined from the sample.
Gleason score: Sum of the two commonest histological patterns (each 1 to 5); 8 to 10 is high grade.
Glial: Relating to support cells of the nervous system.
Glioblastoma: The most aggressive primary brain tumour in adults, usually a single irregular ring-enhancing mass.
Global memory loss: Patchy loss across all kinds of memory, often with 'don't know' answers.
Global systolic dysfunction: The whole ventricle contracts poorly, not just one coronary territory.
Globin: The protein chains of haemoglobin; adults mostly have two alpha and two beta.
Glomerular: To do with the glomeruli, the filtering units of the kidney.
Glomerular filtration barrier: The three-layer filter of the glomerulus: endothelium, basement membrane and podocytes.
Glomerular hyperfiltration: Abnormally high filtration per glomerulus; the earliest change in diabetic kidneys.
Glomerulonephritis: Inflammation of the glomeruli, often causing blood and protein in the urine.
Glomerulosclerosis: Scarring of the kidney glomeruli, a cause of CKD in hypertension.
Glomerulus: The tiny knot of capillaries in each nephron that filters blood to make urine.
Glossitis: Smooth, red, sore tongue from loss of papillae; seen in iron, B12 and folate deficiency.
Glove and stocking: Sensory loss in the hands and feet, like wearing gloves and socks; typical of length-dependent neuropathy.
Glucagon: Hormone used to treat beta-blocker overdose bradycardia by raising cAMP.
Glucocorticoid: A steroid hormone such as cortisol or prednisolone.
Glucocorticoid replacement: Giving steroid tablets to replace missing cortisol.
Glucocorticoids: Steroid drugs such as prednisolone; long-term use thins bone.
Glucogel: A glucose gel squeezed into the cheek (buccal) for conscious patients who cannot self-treat.
Glucose homeostasis: Keeping blood glucose stable; the failing liver cannot, so hypoglycaemia occurs.
Glucose metabolism: Breakdown of glucose to release energy (ATP) in cells.
Glucose-dependent insulin secretion: Insulin released only when glucose is high, so GLP-1 drugs rarely cause hypoglycaemia alone.
Glutamate: The main excitatory neurotransmitter; too much damages neurones.
Glutathione: Antioxidant that protects red cells from oxidative damage.
Glycation: Glucose sticking to proteins without an enzyme, as in HbA1c and AGEs.
Glycosaminoglycans: Water-attracting molecules made by fibroblasts that cause tissue swelling.
Glycosuria: Glucose in the urine, which occurs once blood glucose exceeds the kidney's reabsorption threshold.
Glycosylation: Attachment of glucose to proteins such as haemoglobin; longer-lived red cells collect more.
GnRH agonist: Drug that first stimulates, then switches off, the pituitary's GnRH receptors.
Goitre: Enlargement of the thyroid gland, seen as a neck swelling.
Gold standard: The most accurate test available for confirming a diagnosis.
Gonococcal arthritis: Joint infection from disseminated gonorrhoea, often after migratory joint pains and skin lesions.
Gonococcus: Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in newborns it causes severe purulent conjunctivitis.
Gonorrhoea: Sexually transmitted infection caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.
Goodsall's rule: Predicts the internal fistula opening: posterior external openings curve to the posterior midline, anterior ones run straight.
Gout: Inflammatory arthritis caused by monosodium urate crystals forming when blood urate is high.
Gram stain: Stain that shows bacteria in fluid; negative in reactive arthritis joint fluid.
Gram-negative: Bacteria with a thin cell wall and outer membrane that stain pink, such as Klebsiella and Pseudomonas.
Gram-negative diplococci: Paired bean-shaped bacteria that stain pink; classic for Neisseria.
Gram-negative rod: Rod-shaped bacterium staining pink on Gram stain.
Gram-positive: Bacteria with a thick cell wall that stains purple with Gram stain.
Gram-positive diplococci: Paired purple-staining cocci on Gram stain, typical of pneumococcus.
Granuloma: A compact cluster of activated macrophages and other immune cells walling off an antigen.
Granulomatous: Inflammation forming clusters of macrophages and immune cells.
Granulomatous infection: An infection the body walls off with granulomas, clusters of macrophages and lymphocytes.
Granulomatous inflammation: Inflammation forming granulomas: clusters of macrophages walling off a trigger.
Graves' disease: Autoimmune hyperthyroidism; linked to coeliac disease.
Graves' orbitopathy: Another name for thyroid eye disease.
Gravity: The downward pull used by the Epley manoeuvre to move otoconia.
Greater petrosal nerve: Branch of CN VII supplying the tear (lacrimal) gland.
Green Book: UK guidance on immunisation against infectious disease.
Green-top Guideline: An evidence-based clinical guideline published by the RCOG.
Grey baby syndrome: Circulatory collapse in neonates who cannot metabolise chloramphenicol.
Grey matter: Brain tissue made mostly of neuron cell bodies.
Grey-white matter junction: The boundary between the cortex and the underlying white matter, where metastases typically lodge.
Grittiness: A feeling like sand in the eye, typical of viral conjunctivitis.
Gritty eyes: A sandy, foreign-body feeling from a dry ocular surface.
Groin: The crease where the thigh meets the abdomen.
Ground-glass: Hazy increased lung density on CT through which vessels are still visible.
Group 2: Vocational driving licence (lorries and buses) with stricter medical standards.
Group A Streptococcus: Streptococcus pyogenes; the commonest cause of type 2 necrotising fasciitis.
Group A strep: Streptococcus pyogenes; causes scarlet fever, tonsillitis and severe invasive infections.
Group B Streptococcus: The commonest cause of neonatal meningitis, passed from mother at birth.
Group CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy delivered to several patients together.
Group O: Blood with no A or B antigens, so O red cells can be given to anyone.
Guarding: Reflex tensing of the abdominal wall muscles when the inflamed area is pressed.
Guedel: Another name for an oropharyngeal airway.
Guillain-Barré syndrome: Immune-mediated ascending paralysis with lost reflexes, often after Campylobacter.
Gum hyperplasia: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of long-term phenytoin.
Gum hypertrophy: Overgrowth of the gums, a side effect of calcium channel blockers.
Gut hormones: Hormones released by the gut after eating that affect insulin and appetite, such as GLP-1 and PYY.
Gut motility: Movement of food along the gut by muscle contraction.
Guttate psoriasis: Many small drop-shaped plaques appearing 2 to 4 weeks after a streptococcal infection.
GvHD: Graft-versus-host disease: donor immune cells attacking the recipient's tissues.
Gynaecological: Relating to the female reproductive organs.
Gynaecomastia: Breast tissue enlargement in men, from reduced oestrogen breakdown in liver disease.
H+/K+ ATPase: The proton pump on parietal cells that secretes stomach acid.
H. influenzae: Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative coccobacillus linked with COPD exacerbations.
H. pylori: Helicobacter pylori: curved Gram-negative bacterium causing gastritis, ulcers and gastric cancer.
H1 agonist: A drug that stimulates histamine H1 receptors.
H1 receptor: Histamine receptor on vessels and nerves that drives vasodilation, leak and itch.
H1 receptor antagonist: An antihistamine that blocks histamine's H1 receptor, easing itch and redness.
H2 receptor antagonist: Drug such as famotidine that blocks histamine-driven acid secretion.
H2RA: Short for H2 receptor antagonist, e.g. famotidine, which reduces acid by blocking histamine receptors.
H3 antagonist: A drug that blocks histamine H3 receptors, increasing histamine release.
HACEK: Group of fastidious gram-negative organisms that cause culture-negative endocarditis.
HAP: Hospital-acquired pneumonia: pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after admission.
HAS: Human albumin solution, given IV to support circulating volume in paracentesis and SBP.
HAV: Hepatitis A virus, a faeco-orally spread RNA virus causing acute hepatitis only.
HBIG: Hepatitis B immunoglobulin: ready-made antibodies given for immediate protection after exposure.
HBPM: Home blood pressure monitoring: the patient measures their own BP at home, an alternative to ABPM.
HBV: Hepatitis B virus, a blood-borne DNA virus that can cause chronic infection.
HBV DNA: Viral load of hepatitis B in the blood.
HBeAg: Hepatitis B e antigen; marks active replication and high infectivity.
HBsAg: Hepatitis B surface antigen; positive means current infection.
HCC: Hepatocellular carcinoma: primary liver cancer arising in cirrhosis, screened with ultrasound and AFP.
HCO3: Bicarbonate, the main blood buffer; low levels mean metabolic acidosis.
HCO3-: Bicarbonate, the main blood buffer base; normal 22–26 mmol/L.
HCV: Hepatitis C virus, a blood-borne RNA virus that is often chronic and silent.
HCV RNA: The genetic material of hepatitis C; detecting it means active infection.
HDL: High-density lipoprotein; carries cholesterol back to the liver, protecting against atherosclerosis.
HDU: High dependency unit: a step between the ward and ICU.
HDV: Hepatitis D (delta) virus, a defective virus that needs hepatitis B to survive.
HER2: Growth factor receptor; overexpression gives aggressive cancer treatable with trastuzumab.
HEV: Hepatitis E virus, a faeco-orally spread virus that is dangerous in late pregnancy.
HFE: Gene regulating hepcidin; mutations cause hereditary haemochromatosis.
HFpEF: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (above 50%): the ventricle is stiff and fills poorly.
HFrEF: Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction: the ventricle cannot squeeze properly.
HHS: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: very high glucose and dehydration without significant ketosis, typically type 2.
HHT: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia: autosomal dominant fragile vascular malformations causing recurrent bleeds.
HHV-6: Human herpesvirus 6, the cause of roseola infantum.
HHV-8: Human herpesvirus 8, the cause of Kaposi's sarcoma.
HIT: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia: immune platelet fall 5 to 14 days after heparin, with clots.
HIV: Human immunodeficiency virus, which weakens the immune system.
HIV RNA PCR: A test that amplifies and counts HIV genetic material in the blood to give the viral load.
HIVAN: HIV-associated nephropathy: collapsing FSGS causing nephrotic syndrome.
HLA-B27: A class I HLA gene variant strongly linked to ankylosing spondylitis and other seronegative spondyloarthropathies.
HLA-DQ2: The main genetic susceptibility allele for coeliac disease.
HLA-DQ8: The second genetic susceptibility allele for coeliac disease.
HLA-DR3: Immune gene type linked to several autoimmune diseases, including Hashimoto's and type 1 diabetes.
HLA-DR4: HLA class II gene variant linked to RA and anti-CCP positivity.
HLA-DR5: An immune gene variant linked to Hashimoto's.
HLA-matched: A donor whose tissue type matches the recipient, lowering rejection risk in transplant.
HMG-CoA reductase: Rate-limiting enzyme in liver cholesterol synthesis; the target of statins.
HNF-1 alpha: Transcription factor gene whose mutation causes MODY 3.
HNPCC: Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer; another name for Lynch syndrome.
HOCM: Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy: inherited asymmetric septal thickening causing diastolic dysfunction.
HPA axis: Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis: CRH, then ACTH, then cortisol, with negative feedback.
HPT: Health protection team: the local UKHSA team that receives notifications and organises contact tracing.
HPV: Human papillomavirus, a sexually transmitted virus; persistent high-risk types cause CIN and cervical cancer.
HRCT: High-resolution CT, used to show lung fibrosis and pleural disease in detail.
HRT: Hormone replacement therapy; oestrogen-containing HRT raises clotting risk.
HSV: Herpes simplex virus; HSV-1 reactivation is the leading theory for Bell's palsy.
HSV-1: Herpes simplex virus type 1, the cause of cold sores and eczema herpeticum.
HSV-2: Herpes simplex virus type 2: classically causes genital herpes; latent in the sacral ganglia.
HUS: Haemolytic uraemic syndrome: haemolytic anaemia, low platelets and kidney injury.
Haem: The iron-containing ring in haemoglobin that binds oxygen.
Haem synthesis: The chain of reactions that builds haem; it needs iron.
Haemarthrosis: Bleeding into a joint, causing a hot, swollen, painful joint with reduced movement.
Haematinics: B12, folate and iron studies, checked because deficiencies can cause reversible cognitive decline.
Haematocrit: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells; raised in polycythaemia.
Haematogenous dissemination: Spread of infection through the bloodstream.
Haematogenous spread: Spread of infection or cancer through the bloodstream.
Haematological malignancy: Cancer of blood cells or bone marrow, such as leukaemia or lymphoma.
Haematology: The medical specialty dealing with blood and clotting disorders.
Haematoma: A collection of blood outside vessels, e.g. deep in a muscle.
Haematoma evacuation: Surgically removing a collection of blood to relieve pressure on the brain.
Haematoma expansion: Growth of a bleed after it starts, worsening pressure on the brain.
Haematopoiesis: The production of blood cells from stem cells in the bone marrow.
Haematopoietic stem cell: A marrow stem cell that can make every type of blood cell.
Haematopoietic stem cells: Marrow stem cells that give rise to all blood cell lines.
Haematuria: Blood in the urine, either visible or found only on testing.
Haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload causing liver disease, diabetes, bronze skin and pseudogout.
Haemodialysis: Filtering the blood through a machine, usually three times a week.
Haemodynamic: Relating to blood flow and blood pressure.
Haemodynamic instability: Low blood pressure and fast pulse showing poor circulation.
Haemodynamically unstable: Circulation is failing: low blood pressure, fast heart rate or poor organ perfusion.
Haemofiltration: A form of renal replacement therapy that filters blood continuously, often on ICU.
Haemoglobin: The iron-containing protein in red cells that carries oxygen.
Haemoglobin electrophoresis: Test that separates and measures each haemoglobin type; gold standard for haemoglobinopathies.
Haemoglobinisation: Filling a developing red cell with haemoglobin.
Haemoglobinopathies: Inherited disorders of haemoglobin structure (e.g. sickle cell) or synthesis (thalassaemia).
Haemoglobinuria: Free haemoglobin in the urine, making it dark red or brown.
Haemolysis: Premature destruction of red blood cells.
Haemolysis screen: Blood tests (Hb, LDH, bilirubin, haptoglobin, film, DAT) that look for red cell breakdown.
Haemolytic: Relating to the destruction of red blood cells.
Haemolytic anaemia: Anaemia from early red cell destruction: raised reticulocytes, bilirubin and LDH.
Haemolytic anaemias: Anaemias caused by red cells being destroyed faster than normal, e.g. sickle cell disease.
Haemopericardium: Blood in the pericardial sac, e.g. after trauma or cardiac surgery.
Haemophilia: An inherited lack of a clotting factor causing prolonged bleeding.
Haemophilia A: X-linked recessive deficiency of clotting factor VIII; the commonest haemophilia.
Haemophilia B: X-linked recessive deficiency of clotting factor IX (Christmas disease).
Haemophilic arthropathy: Chronic joint damage from repeated bleeds into the same joint.
Haemophilus: Haemophilus influenzae, a common bacterial cause of conjunctivitis, especially in children.
Haemophilus influenzae: Gram-negative coccobacillus; the commonest organism in bronchiectasis exacerbations.
Haemorrhagic necrosis: Tissue death with bleeding; why HSV encephalitis can put red cells in the CSF.
Haemorrhagic stroke: Stroke caused by bleeding into or around the brain.
Haemorrhoidal plexus: The network of veins in the anal cushions.
Haemorrhoids: Swollen vascular cushions in the anal canal that can bleed painlessly.
Haemosiderin: Iron pigment staining the skin brown in venous disease.
Haemosiderosis: Iron deposition in tissues, here from repeated transfusions.
Haemostasis: The body's process of stopping bleeding.
Haemostatic balance: The balance between clotting and bleeding in the blood.
Haldane effect: Oxygen binding to haemoglobin releases CO2, raising blood CO2.
Half-life: The time for the level of a substance in the body to halve.
Hallmark: The most characteristic feature of a condition.
Hallucinations: Seeing or hearing things that are not there.
Haloperidol: Typical antipsychotic (dopamine antagonist) used in low dose for agitated delirium.
Hammer toe: Toe deformity with a flexed PIP joint.
Hand-foot syndrome: Painful swelling of the hands and feet from bone infarction in young children; another name for dactylitis.
Hand-to-mouth: Faecal-oral spread from contaminated hands, typical of enteroviruses.
Handheld Doppler: A bedside probe that turns arterial blood flow into sound.
Haptoglobin: Plasma protein that binds free haemoglobin; it falls in intravascular haemolysis.
Harmful alcohol intake: Drinking that is already causing physical or mental harm.
Hartmann's: Short for Hartmann's procedure: sigmoid resection with an end colostomy.
Hartmann's procedure: Sigmoid colectomy with end colostomy and closed rectal stump; used in emergencies.
Hashimoto's: Autoimmune thyroiditis causing hypothyroidism; linked to coeliac disease.
Hashimoto's disease: Autoimmune thyroiditis, the commonest cause of hypothyroidism.
Hashimoto's thyroiditis: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid causing hypothyroidism.
Hashitoxicosis: Brief hyperthyroid phase early in Hashimoto's as damaged follicles release stored hormone.
Hay fever: Seasonal allergic rhinitis caused by pollen, giving sneezing, itchy eyes and a runny nose.
Hb: Haemoglobin, measured in g/L on a full blood count.
HbA: Normal adult haemoglobin: two alpha and two beta chains.
HbA1c: Glycated haemoglobin, showing average glucose over about 3 months; 48 mmol/mol or above means diabetes.
HbA2: Minor adult haemoglobin (two alpha, two delta chains); above 3.5% suggests beta-thalassaemia trait.
HbBart's: Haemoglobin made of four gamma chains, seen when all four alpha genes are deleted.
HbF: Fetal haemoglobin (two alpha, two gamma chains); it does not sickle.
HbS: Sickle haemoglobin, from a point mutation in beta-globin; it polymerises when deoxygenated.
HbSS: Two copies of the sickle gene: sickle cell disease.
Head impulse test: A bedside test for vestibular nerve function in continuous vertigo.
Head injury: Any blow to the head; in haemophilia assume a bleed inside the skull.
Head tilt-chin lift: The standard manoeuvre to open the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin.
Head trauma: Injury to the head, which can dislodge otoconia.
Head tremor: Rhythmic nodding or shaking of the head, also called titubation.
Headache diary: A record of attacks, triggers and painkiller use that supports the diagnosis.
Health-economic: Relating to the costs and benefits of health interventions.
Hearing loss: Reduced ability to hear; absent in BPPV.
Heart block: Delayed or failed conduction from atria to ventricles.
