Heart failure: The heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
Heartburn: A burning feeling behind the breastbone caused by acid reflux.
Heat dissipation: Getting rid of body heat, mainly by sweating and widening skin blood vessels.
Heat intolerance: Feeling uncomfortably hot in conditions others find normal.
Heavy menstrual periods: Excess menstrual blood loss, also called menorrhagia.
Heberden's nodes: Hard bony swellings of the DIP joints in osteoarthritis.
Heerfordt syndrome: Sarcoid with uveitis, parotid swelling, fever and facial nerve palsy.
Heinz bodies: Clumps of denatured haemoglobin inside red cells, seen in G6PD deficiency.
Hemi-diaphragm: The left or right half of the diaphragm as seen on a chest X-ray.
Hemiballismus: Violent flinging movements of one side, from a contralateral subthalamic nucleus lesion.
Hemiparesis: Weakness of one side of the body.
Hemispheres: The left and right halves of the brain.
Henna: A plant dye for skin and hair; an oxidant that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Heparin: Anticoagulant that potentiates antithrombin III; given IV immediately in acute limb ischaemia.
Hepatic abscess: A collection of pus within the liver.
Hepatic congestion: Blood backing up in the liver because of high venous pressure.
Hepatic encephalopathy: Confusion and drowsiness from toxins such as ammonia that a failing liver cannot clear.
Hepatic flap: Another name for asterixis: a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands.
Hepatic injury: Liver damage, shown by raised liver enzymes or bilirubin.
Hepatic stellate cells: Liver cells that store vitamin A and, when activated by injury, become collagen-producing myofibroblasts.
Hepatic vein: Veins that drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava.
Hepatitis B: A blood-borne virus infecting the liver that can pass from mother to baby.
Hepatitis B reactivation: Flare of dormant hepatitis B when the immune system is suppressed, e.g. by rituximab.
Hepatitis C: A blood-borne virus that causes chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis.
Hepatitis screen: Blood tests for hepatitis B and C infection.
Hepatocellular: Relating to the liver cells themselves.
Hepatocellular carcinoma: Primary liver cancer, which cirrhosis greatly increases the risk of.
Hepatocyte: The main functional cell of the liver.
Hepatocytes: The main working cells of the liver.
Hepatojugular reflux: A sustained rise in JVP when pressing on the liver.
Hepatomegaly: Enlarged liver, felt below the right costal margin.
Hepatorenal syndrome: Kidney failure caused by severe liver disease and splanchnic vasodilation.
Hepatosplenomegaly: Enlargement of both liver and spleen.
Hepatotoxicity: Damage to the liver caused by a drug or chemical.
Hepcidin: Liver hormone that reduces iron absorption by degrading ferroportin.
Herceptin: Brand name for trastuzumab, the anti-HER2 antibody.
Hereditary: Passed down through families in the genes.
Hereditary angioedema: Inherited C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency causing swelling without hives; does not respond well to adrenaline.
Hereditary haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload that deposits iron in the liver, heart and pancreas.
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia: An inherited condition causing fragile, dilated blood vessels that bleed easily, especially in the nose.
Hereditary spherocytosis: Inherited red cell membrane defect making cells spherical and fragile; autosomal dominant.
Hernia reduction: Pushing herniated tissue back to its normal position.
Herniation: Brain tissue being pushed across rigid structures inside the skull by raised pressure, which can be fatal.
Heroin: An opioid drug; overdose slows breathing.
Herpes encephalitis: HSV infection of the brain, typically the temporal lobes; causes fever, confusion and seizures.
Herpes labialis: Cold sores on the lips, which can flare during Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia.
Herpes simplex: A virus causing cold sores and genital ulcers.
Herpes simplex keratitis: HSV infection of the cornea causing a painful red eye and a dendritic ulcer.
Herpes simplex virus: A common virus that lies dormant in nerves and can reactivate; HSV-1 is the leading cause of viral encephalitis.
Herpesvirus: A family of DNA viruses that stay in the body for life after first infection, including VZV and herpes simplex.
Hertel exophthalmometer: Instrument that measures how far each eye protrudes.
Hertel exophthalmometry: Measurement of how far the cornea sits in front of the lateral orbital rim.
Hertoghe sign: Loss of the outer (lateral) third of the eyebrows, a sign of hypothyroidism.
Hesitancy: Delay in starting the urine stream.
Hesselbach's triangle: Weak area of the posterior inguinal wall bounded by inferior epigastric vessels, rectus and inguinal ligament.
Heterogeneous: Made up of many different types.
Heterophile antibody test: Blood test for non-specific antibodies made in EBV infection that clump animal red cells; the monospot is one.
Heterozygous: Carrying one faulty copy and one normal copy of a gene.
Hib: Haemophilus influenzae type b, and the vaccine against it.
High altitude: Low oxygen at height drives overbreathing and respiratory alkalosis.
High anterior resection: Removal of the sigmoid colon and upper rectum with a join.
High-dependency setting: A unit with closer monitoring than a ward but less than ICU (HDU).
High-flow oxygen: Oxygen given at a high rate, e.g. 15 L/min through a non-rebreathe mask.
High-grade: Cancer cells that look very abnormal and tend to behave aggressively.
High-intensity statin: A statin dose expected to cut LDL by over 40%, such as atorvastatin 80mg.
High-output cardiac failure: Heart failure where the heart cannot meet a very high demand for output.
High-output heart failure: Failure because the body demands too much output (thyrotoxicosis, pregnancy, anaemia), not because the heart is damaged.
High-resolution CT: A CT scan with thin slices that shows fine detail.
Higher cortical dysfunction: Problems such as aphasia, neglect or apraxia that point to cortex damage.
Highly active RRMS: Relapsing-remitting MS with frequent, disabling relapses despite or before treatment.
Hilar: Relating to the lung root, where the bronchi, vessels and lymph nodes enter.
Hip abduction: Moving the leg out to the side, away from the midline.
Hip adduction: Bringing the leg in towards the midline.
Hip flexion: Lifting the thigh forwards at the hip.
Hip fracture: A break at the top of the femur, usually after a fall; carries high morbidity and mortality.
Hip replacement: Surgery replacing the femoral head and socket with an artificial joint.
Hippocampal: Relating to the hippocampus, the memory-forming structure deep in the temporal lobe.
Hippocampal atrophy: Shrinkage of the memory centres of the medial temporal lobe, typical of Alzheimer's.
Hippocampus: A brain structure important for memory and mood regulation.
Hirschsprung's disease: Congenital absence of ganglion cells in the distal bowel causing functional obstruction.
Hirsutism: Excess male-pattern hair growth, a side effect of phenytoin.
Histamine: Mediator released by mast cells that causes itch, vasodilation, leaky vessels and smooth muscle contraction.
Histamine analogue: A drug with a similar structure to histamine that acts on its receptors.
Histamine control: A positive control drop in skin prick testing that should always produce a wheal.
Histiocytosis: A rare disorder where histiocytes (immune cells) build up and damage tissues, including lung.
Histological: Relating to the microscopic structure of tissue, as seen on biopsy.
Histology: Examining tissue under the microscope to make a definitive diagnosis.
Histone: A protein around which DNA is wound inside the nucleus.
Hoarse voice: A rough, croaky voice, here a sign of swelling around the larynx.
Hoarseness: A rough, weak or croaky voice, often from a problem with the vocal cords or their nerve.
Hodgkin lymphoma: Lymphoma with Reed-Sternberg cells, often in young adults, spreading node to node.
Hodgkin's: Hodgkin lymphoma; these patients are at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD.
Hodgkin's lymphoma: A lymph node cancer containing Reed-Sternberg cells.
Hoffmann's sign: Thumb flexion when the middle finger tip is flicked, a UMN sign.
Hoist transfer: Moving a person with a mechanical lift; even this can break fragile bone.
Holter: Portable ECG recording over 24 hours or longer.
Holter monitor: Portable ECG recording over 24 or 48 hours to catch intermittent arrhythmias.
Homologous recombination: Accurate repair of DNA double-strand breaks using the sister chromatid as a template.
Homonymous hemianopia: Loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes, from a lesion behind the optic chiasm.
Homozygous: Having two identical faulty copies of a gene, one from each parent.
Honeycombing: Clustered cystic airspaces with thick fibrotic walls on HRCT: end-stage fibrosis.
Hoover's sign: Test for functional leg weakness using involuntary hip extension when the other leg flexes.
Horizontal fissure: The line separating the right upper and middle lung lobes, seen on chest X-ray.
Horizontal nystagmus: Involuntary side-to-side jerking movements of the eyes.
Hormonal contraception: Contraceptives containing oestrogen and/or progestogen, such as the combined pill.
Hormonal fluctuation: Rising and falling levels of hormones such as oestrogen, which can trigger migraine.
Horner's: Ptosis, small pupil and reduced sweating from sympathetic chain damage.
Horner's syndrome: Ipsilateral miosis, ptosis and anhidrosis from damage to the sympathetic chain.
Horseshoe kidney: Congenitally fused kidneys lying across the aorta, which complicates open repair.
Hospital-acquired pneumonia: Pneumonia starting 48 hours or more after hospital admission.
Hospitalisation: Being admitted to and staying in hospital.
Hospitalised: Admitted to hospital as an inpatient.
Host defences: The body's natural protections against infection.
Host immune response: The body's own defence that clears the infection.
Hostile abdomen: An abdomen with dense adhesions or previous surgery that makes open repair risky.
Hot flushes: Sudden feelings of heat and sweating, a side effect of tamoxifen.
Hot potato voice: A muffled voice, as if speaking with a hot potato in the mouth, typical of quinsy.
House-Brackmann: Grading scale for facial nerve function, from I (normal) to VI (complete paralysis).
Howell-Jolly bodies: Nuclear fragments in red cells seen on the blood film when the spleen is not working.
Human Albumin Solution: Purified human albumin given IV to hold fluid in the circulation, e.g. in severe burns.
Human albumin solution: Intravenous albumin used to protect circulation and kidneys in liver patients.
Humeral head: The ball at the top of the upper arm bone that forms the shoulder joint.
Humeral shaft: The long middle part of the upper arm bone.
Humoral immunity: Immunity carried out by antibodies made by B cells.
Hutchinson's sign: Shingles vesicles on the tip of the nose, warning of eye involvement.
Hydralazine: Vasodilator antihypertensive and a classic cause of drug-induced lupus.
Hydrocephalus: Build-up of CSF in the ventricles of the brain, raising intracranial pressure.
Hydrochloric acid: HCl, the acid made by the stomach lining.
Hydrochlorothiazide: A thiazide diuretic that lowers urinary calcium to prevent stones.
Hydrocortisone: Synthetic cortisol; the glucocorticoid replacement in Addison's.
Hydrocortisone 1%: A mild-potency topical corticosteroid, safe for the face and flexures.
Hydrogen ion: H+, the particle that makes a solution acidic.
Hydrolysis: Breaking a molecule apart using water, as lipase does to triglycerides.
Hydromol: A brand of emollient ointment or cream.
Hydronephrosis: Swelling of the kidney's collecting system from blocked urine flow.
Hydrops fetalis: Severe fluid build-up in a fetus from heart failure due to profound anaemia.
Hydrostatic pressure: Pushing pressure of fluid within vessels that drives it out into tissues.
Hydroxocobalamin: The form of vitamin B12 given by intramuscular injection in the UK.
Hydroxyapatite: The calcium phosphate mineral that makes bone hard.
Hydroxychloroquine: Mild DMARD that can cause bull's eye retinopathy, needing annual eye checks.
Hydroxyurea: Oral drug that raises HbF and reduces sickle crises (also called hydroxycarbamide).
Hyperaemia: Increased blood flow to a tissue, a sign of inflammation.
Hyperaemic: Red and engorged with extra blood flow.
Hypercalcaemia: Raised blood calcium; causes thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion.
Hypercalcaemia of malignancy: High calcium from cancer, through bone destruction or PTHrP release.
Hypercalcaemic crisis: Dangerously high calcium causing confusion, vomiting, dehydration and arrhythmia; needs urgent treatment.
Hypercalciuria: Too much calcium in the urine.
Hypercapnia: A raised carbon dioxide level in the blood from under-breathing.
Hypercellular: A marrow packed with cells; seen in MDS and leukaemia despite low blood counts.
Hypercoagulability: An increased tendency of the blood to clot.
Hypercoagulable: More likely than normal to form blood clots.
Hyperdense: Appearing brighter or whiter than surrounding tissue on CT.
Hyperdense artery sign: A bright artery on non-contrast CT showing thrombus within it.
Hyperdiploidy: Extra chromosomes in leukaemic cells; a good prognostic sign in ALL.
Hyperfiltration: Abnormally high filtration by remaining nephrons, which damages them over time.
Hyperinflation: Over-expanded lungs from trapped air, giving a barrel chest and flat diaphragms.
Hyperintensity: An area appearing brighter than surrounding tissue on MRI.
Hyperkalaemia: A high blood potassium level, dangerous because it can cause fatal arrhythmias.
Hyperlipidaemia: Raised fats such as cholesterol in the blood.
Hyperlucent: Appearing darker than normal on X-ray because there is more air and less tissue.
Hypernatraemic dehydration: Dehydration with high sodium because more water than salt has been lost.
Hyperosmolar: Having too many dissolved particles in the blood.
Hyperparathyroidism: Overactive parathyroid glands causing high calcium; associated with pseudogout.
Hyperphosphataemia: High blood phosphate because failing kidneys cannot excrete it.
Hyperphosphorylated: Carrying too many phosphate groups, which makes tau clump into tangles.
Hyperpigmentation: Darkening of the skin, e.g. palmar creases, scars and gums, from high ACTH.
Hyperpigmented skin: Darker skin, here from iron deposits.
Hyperplasia: Enlargement of an organ due to an increased number of cells.
Hyperplastic: Showing an increased number of normal cells.
Hyperpolarisation: Making a neuron's inside more negative so it is less likely to fire.
Hyperreflexia: Exaggerated, brisk tendon reflexes: an upper motor neurone sign.
Hypersegmented neutrophils: Neutrophils with six or more nuclear lobes; a sign of megaloblastic anaemia.
Hypersensitivity: An exaggerated or inappropriate immune response that damages the body's own tissues.
Hypersensitivity pneumonitis: Another name for extrinsic allergic alveolitis.
Hypersomnia: Sleeping excessively long or feeling very sleepy during the day.
Hypersplenism: An enlarged, congested spleen trapping blood cells, causing low platelets or pancytopenia.
Hypersynchronous: Many neurons firing together at the same moment, abnormally.
Hypertensive nephrosclerosis: Scarring of the kidney's small vessels from long-standing high blood pressure.
Hypertensive retinopathy: Damage to the retinal blood vessels caused by high blood pressure.
Hyperthyroidism: Thyrotoxicosis caused by the thyroid gland overproducing hormone.
Hypertonic saline: Concentrated salt solution, nebulised to draw water into mucus and loosen it.
Hypertrichosis: Excess hair growth, a side effect of ciclosporin.
Hypertrophy: Enlargement of a muscle because each cell grows bigger.
Hyperuricaemia: A raised level of uric acid (urate) in the blood.
Hyperventilating: Breathing faster or deeper than needed, which blows off CO2 and lowers PCO2.
Hyperventilation: Breathing faster or deeper than needed; on a ventilator it lowers CO2 to shrink cerebral blood volume.
Hyperviscosity: Abnormally thick blood that flows sluggishly, causing headache, visual upset and clots.
Hypoactive delirium: Delirium with drowsiness and withdrawal; easily missed.
Hypoalbuminaemia: Low blood albumin, from poor liver synthesis or malnutrition.
Hypoallergenic: Unlikely to trigger an allergic reaction.
Hypoallergenic formula: Infant milk with proteins broken down or replaced so it is unlikely to trigger allergy.
Hypocalcaemia: Low blood calcium; overbreathing lowers ionised calcium, causing tingling and cramps.
Hypocellular: A marrow with too few blood-forming cells, replaced by fat; typical of aplastic anaemia.
Hypochromic: Red cells paler than normal because they contain less haemoglobin.
Hypodense: Darker than normal brain on CT, as with oedema or many tumours.
Hypoechoic: Darker than surrounding tissue on ultrasound; typical of fluid or pus.
Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism: Low sex hormones because the pituitary makes too little LH and FSH.
Hypokalaemia: Low blood potassium; the commonest DKA complication, causing small T waves, prolonged PR and arrhythmias.
Hypomimia: Reduced facial expression, a mask-like face.
Hypomotile: Moving less than normal; here, a sluggish gut.
Hypoparathyroidism: Low parathyroid hormone, causing low calcium; a risk of thyroidectomy.
Hypoperfused: Receiving less blood flow than it needs.
Hypoperfusion: Not enough blood flow to deliver oxygen to tissues.
Hypopituitarism: Failure of the pituitary to make one or more hormones, including ACTH.
Hypopnoea: A partial reduction in airflow during sleep with a drop in oxygen saturation or an arousal.
Hypopyon: A layer of pus (white cells) in the anterior chamber of the eye.
Hyposegmented: A neutrophil nucleus with fewer lobes than normal.
Hyposplenism: Poor splenic function, raising the risk of infection by encapsulated bacteria.
Hypotension: Low blood pressure; in DKA it means severe dehydration and calls for a fluid bolus.
Hypothalamic: To do with the hypothalamus, the brain region that controls hormones such as ADH.
Hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid; a reversible cause of raised cholesterol.
Hypoventilation: Breathing too little air per minute to clear carbon dioxide.
Hypovolaemia: Low circulating blood volume, for example from bleeding.
Hypovolaemic shock: Dangerously low blood pressure and poor perfusion from loss of blood or fluid volume.
Hypoxaemia: Low oxygen level in arterial blood.
Hypoxaemic respiratory failure: Low blood oxygen (type 1 respiratory failure) from the lungs not oxygenating blood.
Hypoxanthine: A purine breakdown product turned into xanthine by xanthine oxidase.
Hypoxia: Low oxygen delivery to the tissues.
Hypoxic: Having low oxygen levels in the blood or tissues.
Hypoxic brain injury: Brain damage from lack of oxygen, starting within minutes of arrest.
Hypoxic drive: Breathing stimulated by low oxygen rather than high CO2.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction: Constriction of pulmonary arterioles in response to low alveolar oxygen.
Hz: Hertz: cycles per second, used to describe tremor frequency.
IBD: Inflammatory bowel disease: ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease.
IBS: Irritable bowel syndrome: functional bowel disorder with no inflammation or bleeding.
IBS-M: IBS with mixed constipation and diarrhoea.
IBS-SSS: IBS Symptom Severity Score, out of 500.
ICA: Internal carotid artery, the main artery to the front of the brain.
ICD: Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator; shocks VT or VF automatically.
ICD-10: The previous WHO classification; depression needs 2 of 3 core symptoms plus 2 others.
ICD-11: The WHO's current International Classification of Diseases, used for diagnostic criteria.
ICH: Intracranial haemorrhage: bleeding inside the skull.
ICP: Intracranial pressure: the pressure inside the skull.
ICP monitoring: A pressure sensor (bolt) placed in or on the brain on ICU to measure ICP continuously.
ICS: Inhaled corticosteroid, such as budesonide or beclometasone; a preventer.
ICU: Intensive care unit, where all dissection patients go for continuous BP monitoring.
IDC: Invasive ductal carcinoma, the most common breast cancer.
IGF-1: Insulin-like growth factor 1, made by the liver in response to GH; the acromegaly screening test.
IGF-1 receptor: Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor, which may also be stimulated in thyroid eye disease.
IGRA: Interferon-gamma release assay: a blood test for TB exposure, not affected by BCG.
IHD: Ischaemic heart disease: angina and myocardial infarction from coronary atherosclerosis.
IIH: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised brain pressure without a mass, causing headache and papilloedema.
IL-1: Interleukin-1, a pro-inflammatory cytokine causing fever and joint inflammation.
IL-12: Interleukin-12, a cytokine that drives Th1 responses; shares the p40 subunit with IL-23.
IL-17 inhibitor: A biologic that blocks interleukin-17, a key inflammatory signal in AS.
IL-1β: Interleukin-1 beta, a cytokine that drives the inflammation of a gout attack.
IL-23: Cytokine that sustains IL-17 producing T cells; the IL-17/IL-23 axis.
IL-6: Interleukin-6, an inflammatory cytokine central to the cytokine storm.
ILD: Interstitial lung disease: disorders that inflame or scar the lung interstitium.
IM adrenaline: Adrenaline injected into muscle, the anterolateral thigh, as first-line anaphylaxis treatment.
IMA: Inferior mesenteric artery: supplies the hindgut from the distal transverse colon to the upper rectum.
IMCA: Independent mental capacity advocate, appointed for serious decisions when a person lacking capacity has no one to consult.
INO: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: failed adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the other on lateral gaze.
INR: International normalised ratio: measures clotting time; raised when the liver cannot make clotting factors.
IOP: Intraocular pressure; normal is about 10 to 21 mmHg.
IPAP: Inspiratory positive airway pressure on BiPAP; it boosts each breath to blow off CO2.
IPF: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: progressive scarring of the lung with no identifiable cause.
IPSS: International Prostate Symptom Score: a 0 to 35 questionnaire grading LUTS severity.
IRIS: Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome: worsening of a hidden infection as immunity recovers on cART.
IRMA: Intraretinal microvascular abnormality: abnormal shunt vessels within the retina in severe NPDR.
ISMN: Isosorbide mononitrate: a long-acting nitrate tablet.
ITP: Immune thrombocytopenia: antibodies destroy platelets; clotting times are normal.
ITU: Intensive therapy unit, for patients needing organ support.
IU: International units, used to dose vitamin D.
IUS: Intrauterine system (e.g. Mirena), the contraception of choice with enzyme-inducing AEDs.
IV: Intravenous: given directly into a vein.
IV adrenaline infusion: Continuous adrenaline into a vein, used only by experts for refractory anaphylaxis.
IV antibiotics: Antibiotics given directly into a vein for serious infections.
IV contrast: Dye given into a vein so vessels and organs show up on CT.
IV corticosteroids: Steroids by drip, such as methylprednisolone, to damp orbital inflammation.
IV drug injection: Injecting drugs into a vein, which can introduce skin bacteria into the blood.
IV drug use: Injecting drugs into veins; a risk factor for deep soft-tissue infection.
IV fluid bolus: A quick infusion of fluid into a vein to raise blood pressure.
IV fluids: Fluids given directly into a vein.
IV glucose: Glucose solution given into a vein, used when the patient cannot take sugar by mouth.
IV immunoglobulin: Pooled donor antibodies given into a vein that dampen the autoimmune attack.
IV iron: Iron given into a vein, which raises iron stores faster than tablets.
IVIG: Intravenous immunoglobulin: pooled antibodies that dampen the autoimmune attack in crisis.
IVIg: Intravenous immunoglobulin, pooled antibodies used to dampen autoimmune disease.
Ibuprofen: An NSAID; first-line simple analgesic for tension-type headache.
Idiopathic PAH: Pulmonary arterial hypertension with no identifiable cause; rare, often young women.
Idiopathic interstitial pneumonia: A group of lung-scarring or inflammatory diseases of unknown cause; IPF is the main one.
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension: Raised intracranial pressure without a mass, usually in young overweight women; a key migraine differential.
IgA: Immunoglobulin A: the antibody class measured in coeliac blood tests; IgA deficiency gives a false negative.
IgA deficiency: Low or absent IgA, commoner in coeliac disease, causing false-negative IgA antibody tests.
IgA nephropathy: Glomerulonephritis with IgA deposits, typically visible haematuria after a sore throat.
IgE: Immunoglobulin E, the antibody that binds mast cells and drives immediate allergic reactions.
IgE-mediated: An immediate allergic reaction driven by IgE antibodies and mast cells.
IgG: Immunoglobulin G, the main antibody class; markedly raised in autoimmune hepatitis.
IgM: Immunoglobulin M; characteristically raised in primary biliary cholangitis.
Ileocaecal resection: Removal of the terminal ileum and caecum.
Ileocolic anastomosis: Surgical join between the ileum and the colon after a right hemicolectomy.
Ileostomy: An opening of the ileum onto the abdominal wall, often after bowel resection.
Iliac: The pelvic arteries; disease here causes buttock claudication.
Ilio-femoral bypass: A graft from the iliac artery to the femoral artery.
Imatinib: Tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting BCR-ABL; first-line in CML.
Immature cells: Young blood cells that are normally kept in the marrow until they mature.
Immobilisation: Keeping a broken bone still, for example with a cast or sling.
Immobility: Being unable to move around much, which slows the gut.
Immune clearance: Removal of organisms by white cells and antibodies.
Immune complex: Antibody bound to antigen that deposits in tissues and triggers inflammation.
Immune evasion: A germ's ability to escape recognition by existing antibodies.
Immune function: The body's ability to fight infection.
Immune response: The body's defence reaction against infection.
Immune suppression: Weakening of the immune system, here a short-lived effect of measles infection.
Immune tolerance: The immune system's normal ability not to attack the body's own molecules.
Immune-complex-mediated: Damage from antibody-antigen clumps depositing in tissues (type III hypersensitivity).
Immune-mediated: Caused by the body's own immune system, such as antibodies.
Immunisation status: Record of which vaccines a patient has had.
Immunity: Protection against an infection, from past infection or vaccination, shown by IgG antibodies.
Immunocompromised: Having a weakened immune system, for example from HIV, chemotherapy or steroids.
Immunodeficiency: A weakened immune system, inherited or acquired, raising infection risk.
Immunofluorescence: Biopsy technique using fluorescent antibodies to show which immune proteins are deposited in tissue.
Immunogenic: Able to provoke an immune response.
Immunogenicity: How strongly something provokes an immune response.
Immunoglobulin: Antibodies; given intravenously (IVIg) as pooled donor antibodies to modulate the immune system.
Immunoglobulins: Antibodies (IgG, IgA, IgM); low levels suggest immunodeficiency as a cause.
Immunological phenomena: Duke minor criteria from immune complexes, such as Osler's nodes or Roth spots.
Immunology: Blood tests of the immune system, such as immunoglobulin levels and autoantibodies.
Immunomodulation: Altering or damping the immune response, how DMTs work.
Immunomodulatory: Altering or calming the immune response.
Immunosuppressant: A drug that dampens the immune system.
Immunosuppressants: Drugs that dampen the immune system, such as methotrexate.
Immunosuppressed: Having a weakened immune system that cannot destroy donor white cells.
Immunosuppression: Drugs that dampen the immune system; used in aplastic anaemia to stop stem cell destruction.
Immunosuppressive therapy: Drugs that damp down the immune system, such as steroids or biologics.
Immunosuppressives: Drugs that dampen the immune system, such as azathioprine.
Immunotherapy: Treatment that stimulates the immune system to attack cancer cells.
Impaired consciousness: Reduced alertness, from drowsiness to coma.
Impairment: Reduced ability to function normally in work, relationships or daily activities.
Implant: A man-made device placed in the body.
Impotence: Inability to achieve or keep an erection.
Impulse control disorders: Compulsive gambling, shopping, eating or hypersexuality, mostly from dopamine agonists.
Imrie: Surgeon who co-developed the Glasgow severity score for pancreatitis.
In-situ: Forming in its original place, here a clot forming within the brain artery itself.
Inadequate sample: A sample that cannot be read reliably, so must be repeated.
Inappropriately normal: A normal value that should be low given the situation, so still abnormal.
Inattention: Inability to focus or sustain attention; core feature of delirium.
Incidental: Found by chance while looking for something else.
Incidental finding: Something discovered by chance while testing for another reason.
Incidentally: Found by chance while testing for something else.
Incision: The surgical cut through the skin.
Incision and drainage: Cutting open an abscess to let the pus out.
Incompetent valve: A valve that does not close fully, so blood leaks backwards.
Incomplete emptying: The feeling that the bladder is not empty after passing urine.
Incomplete evacuation: The feeling that the bowel has not emptied fully after opening.
Incretin: Gut hormone released after eating that boosts glucose-dependent insulin secretion.
Incubation: Time from catching an infection to developing symptoms.
Indapamide: Thiazide-like diuretic added when BP stays high despite a maximised ACE inhibitor or ARB.
India ink: CSF stain that shows the capsule of Cryptococcus.
Indicator condition: An illness that should prompt an HIV test, such as TB, shingles in the young or lymphoma.
Indigestion: Discomfort in the upper abdomen after eating.
Indinavir: HIV protease inhibitor linked to radiolucent stones.
Indirect pathway: Basal ganglia route that inhibits unwanted movement; dopamine normally restrains it.
Indomethacin: A potent NSAID often used for gout.
Induction chemotherapy: First intensive phase of chemotherapy aiming to put leukaemia into remission.
Induration: Firm, thickened tissue caused by inflammation.
Indwelling lines: Catheters left in a vein for a long time.
Indwelling pleural catheter: A tunnelled tube left in the chest so a recurrent effusion can be drained at home.
Ineffective erythropoiesis: Red cell precursors die in the marrow before they mature.
Infarction: Tissue death caused by loss of its blood supply.
Infarcts: Areas of tissue death caused by loss of blood supply.
Infection: Invasion by germs; the commonest trigger of HHS.
Infection control: Measures such as isolation, hand hygiene and PPE to stop spread.
Infection prevention: Measures to stop infection spreading between patients.
Infection screen: Tests looking for infection, such as urine and blood cultures, CRP and chest X-ray.
Infectious mononucleosis: Glandular fever: EBV infection with sore throat, posterior nodes, fatigue and splenomegaly.
Infective endocarditis: Infection of the inner lining of the heart, usually a valve, forming vegetations.
Infective trigger: An infection that sets off a longer-lasting illness.
Infectivity: How easily an infected person passes the virus on.
Inferior MI: Infarction of the inferior wall, seen as ST elevation in II, III and aVF.
Inferior frontal gyrus: A fold of the frontal lobe containing Broca's area, which produces speech.
Inferior leads: ECG leads II, III and aVF, which look at the bottom of the heart.
Inferior rectus: Eye muscle that pulls the eye down; often enlarged in TED, so upgaze is restricted.
Infertility: Inability to conceive after a year of regular unprotected sex.
Infiltrate: Hazy shadowing on chest X-ray from fluid, cells or inflammation in the lung.
Infiltrates: Spreads diffusely through tissue rather than forming a lump.
Infiltrative: Describes diseases where abnormal material builds up in and damages an organ.
Inflammasome: A protein complex inside immune cells that switches on IL-1β release.
Inflammation: The body's response to injury or infection, causing swelling and redness.
Inflammatory: Driven by the immune response, causing redness, heat and swelling.
Inflammatory arthritides: Arthritis driven by the immune system, such as rheumatoid or psoriatic arthritis.
Inflammatory breast cancer: Aggressive cancer in dermal lymphatics causing a red, swollen breast; staged T4.
Inflammatory cascade: A chain of immune signals that amplifies inflammation.
Inflammatory cells: White blood cells, such as eosinophils and neutrophils, drawn in to a site of inflammation.
Inflammatory disease: A condition driven by ongoing inflammation, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.
Inflammatory exudate: Protein-rich fluid with white cells that leaks from inflamed vessels into tissue.
Inflammatory infiltrate: A crowd of immune cells within a tissue.
Inflammatory markers: Blood tests that rise with inflammation or infection, such as CRP, white cell count and ESR.
Inflammatory mediators: Chemicals such as cytokines that drive inflammation and vessel leak.
Inflammatory stiffness: Stiffness worst after rest and in the morning that eases with movement.
Inflation pressure: The pressure the ventilator uses to push air into the lungs; high in near-fatal asthma due to narrow airways.
Infliximab: Chimeric monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha, given by infusion.
Influenza: The flu virus, causing fever, aches and cough.
Infra-red photocoagulation: Infra-red light used to scar and shrink small internal haemorrhoids.
Infrarenal: Below the level of the renal arteries; where most AAAs arise.
Infraspinatus: Rotator cuff muscle that turns the arm outwards.
Infusion: A drug or fluid given continuously into a vein over a set time.
Inguinal ligament: The ligament in the groin; the external iliac artery becomes the femoral artery beneath it.
Inhaled corticosteroid: A steroid inhaler used in asthma and COPD, such as beclometasone; it can cause oral thrush.
Inhaled steroids: Corticosteroids breathed into the lungs to reduce airway inflammation in asthma.
Inherited bleeding disorder: A bleeding tendency passed on in the genes.
Initiation: The period when a drug is first started.
Inner ear: The fluid-filled part of the ear containing the cochlea (hearing) and the balance organs.
Innervation: The nerve supply to a part of the body.
Innocuous stimuli: Normally harmless sensations, such as light touch or a breeze.
Inotropes: Drugs such as dobutamine and milrinone that increase the force of heart contraction.
Inpatients: Patients admitted to a hospital ward.
Insect bite: A sting or bite that can trigger a local or systemic allergic reaction.
Insensate: Unable to feel pain or touch.
Insidious onset: Symptoms that start gradually and subtly rather than suddenly.
Insomnia: Difficulty getting to sleep or staying asleep.
Inspiratory: Happening when breathing in; inspiratory stridor points to upper airway narrowing.
Inspiratory crackles: Crackling sounds heard on breathing in, from airways opening or secretions.
Inspiratory muscle training: Exercises against resistance to strengthen the breathing-in muscles.
Inspiratory stridor: High-pitched noise on breathing in, caused by narrowing of the upper airway.
Instrumentation: Passing instruments such as a catheter or cystoscope into the urinary tract.
Insulation: Material used to stop heat loss; older lagging often contained asbestos.
Insulin: The hormone that lets cells take up glucose and switches off ketone production.
Insulin deficiency: Too little insulin, from beta-cell loss (absolute) or failure to keep up with demand (relative).
Insulin pump: A device that delivers insulin continuously under the skin.
Insulin resistance: Reduced response of tissues to insulin, so more insulin is needed to control glucose.
Insulin secretion: Release of insulin from pancreatic beta cells.
Integrase inhibitor: Drug such as dolutegravir that stops viral DNA joining the host genome.
Intellect: The ability to think, reason and understand.
Intent: How determined a person is to act on suicidal thoughts.
Intention tremor: A tremor that gets worse as the hand approaches a target, a cerebellar sign.
Intercostal space: The gap between two ribs, used as a landmark for ECG electrode placement.
Intercurrent illness: A new illness happening on top of an existing condition.
Interferon beta: Injected first-line disease-modifying therapy that reduces MS relapses.
Interim anticoagulation: Starting a blood thinner while waiting for a scan to confirm or exclude a clot.
Interleukin: A signalling protein (cytokine) that immune cells use to talk to each other.
Interlocking pentagons: Two overlapping five-sided shapes the patient copies to test visuospatial skills.
Intermediate risk: A FRAX fracture risk high enough to need a DEXA scan before deciding on treatment.
Intermittent: Coming and going rather than constant.
Intermittent claudication: Cramping leg pain on walking a predictable distance, relieved by rest.
Intermittent flow: Urine flow that stops and starts.
Intermittent hypoxia: Repeated short drops in blood oxygen, as happens with each apnoea.
Intermittently: Coming and going rather than continuous.
Internal capsule: A tight bundle of motor and sensory fibres deep in the brain; small infarcts here give pure weakness.
Internal carotid: The branch of the carotid artery that supplies the brain and eyes.
Internal opening: The hole of a fistula inside the anal canal, usually at the dentate line.
Internal rotation: The limb turned inwards towards the midline.
Internalisation: The cell pulling receptors from its surface inside, reducing the number available.
Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: Eye movement sign from an MLF lesion: affected eye cannot adduct, the other eye has nystagmus.
Intersphincteric: The space between the internal and external anal sphincters.
Interstitial: Affecting the tissue between the alveoli rather than filling the air spaces themselves.
Interstitial fibrosis: Scarring of the tissue between the air sacs, making the lungs stiff.
Interstitial infiltrates: Shadowing from disease in the tissue between the air sacs.
Interstitial lung disease: A group of conditions that scar and stiffen the tissue between the air sacs of the lungs.
Interstitial lung fibrosis: Scarring of the tissue between the alveoli that stiffens the lungs.
Interstitium: The tissue between the alveoli and capillaries where gas exchange happens.
Intertrigo: Inflammation of skin folds from friction and moisture, often infected by Candida.
Intestinal absorption: Uptake of nutrients such as calcium and phosphate from the gut into the blood.
Intestinal calcium absorption: Uptake of calcium from food in the gut.
Intestinal motility: Movement of the gut wall that pushes contents along.
Intima: The innermost lining layer of an artery wall.
Intimal fibrosis: Scarring of the inner lining of an artery, narrowing it.
Intoxication: Poisoning by a substance, such as lithium or salicylate, that dialysis can remove.
Intra-abdominal abscess: A pocket of pus inside the abdomen, for example after bowel surgery.
Intra-abdominal pressure: Pressure inside the abdomen, raised by straining, pregnancy and obesity.
Intra-articular: Injected directly into the joint space.
Intracellular organism: A microbe that lives and multiplies inside host cells.
Intracerebral haemorrhage: Bleeding into the brain tissue itself.
Intracranial haemorrhage: Bleeding inside the skull; the most dangerous complication of haemophilia.
Intraductal papilloma: Benign wart-like duct growth causing clear or bloody nipple discharge.
Intraepidermal: Within the epidermis, the outer skin layer.
Intraglomerular hypertension: Abnormally high pressure inside the glomerulus, which damages the filter over time.
Intraglomerular pressure: The pressure inside the glomerulus that drives filtration; too high damages it.
Intrahepatic vascular resistance: Resistance to blood flow through the liver, raised by scarring.
Intramedullary nail: A metal rod inserted down the marrow cavity of a long bone to fix a fracture.
Intramuscular: Given by injection into a muscle.
Intranasal: Given into the nose, usually as a spray.
Intranasal corticosteroid: A steroid nasal spray that reduces nasal inflammation over days.
Intraosseous: Drug access through a needle into bone marrow.
Intrapericardial pressure: The pressure inside the pericardial sac around the heart.
Intrapulmonary nodules: Small round lesions within the lung tissue.
Intrathoracic pressure: The pressure inside the chest cavity, which falls when you breathe in.
Intratubular pressure: Pressure inside the kidney tubules, which rises when urine flow is blocked.
Intravascular haemolysis: Red cells bursting inside the blood vessels, releasing free haemoglobin.
Intravesical: Given directly into the bladder through a catheter.
Intravesical chemotherapy: Chemotherapy instilled directly into the bladder through a catheter.
Intravitreal: Injected directly into the vitreous of the eye.
Intrinsic: AKI caused by damage within the kidney itself, such as ATN or glomerulonephritis.
Intrinsic factor: Stomach protein needed to absorb vitamin B12 in the terminal ileum.
Intrinsic factor antibodies: Autoantibodies against intrinsic factor; the most specific test for pernicious anaemia.
Intrinsic hand muscles: Small muscles inside the hand that control fine finger movements.
Intrinsic pathway: Clotting cascade arm involving factors XII, XI, IX and VIII, measured by APTT.
Intubation: Passing a tube into the trachea so a machine can ventilate the lungs.
Invasive ductal carcinoma: Breast cancer from duct cells that has breached the basement membrane; the most common type.
Invasive lobular carcinoma: Invasive cancer of lobular cells that is often missed on mammogram.
Inverted T wave: A T wave pointing downwards on the ECG, a sign of ischaemia.
Investment: In anatomy, how far a covering layer wraps around a structure.
Involucrum: A sheath of new reactive bone that forms around a sequestrum.
Iodine: The element the thyroid needs to make T3 and T4.
Iodine allergy: Reaction to iodine-based contrast dye used in CT scans.
Iodine deficiency: Too little dietary iodine, which the thyroid needs to make hormone.
Ipratropium: A short-acting muscarinic antagonist bronchodilator, nebulised in acute asthma.
Ipsilateral: On the same side as the lesion.
Iris: The coloured ring of muscle that controls the size of the pupil.
Iris sphincter: The ring muscle of the iris that constricts the pupil.
Iron absorption: Uptake of dietary iron through the duodenum into the blood.
Iron chelating agent: A drug that binds iron so it can be excreted.
Iron chelation: Drug treatment that binds excess iron so it can be excreted.
Iron deficiency: Too little iron in the body to make normal amounts of haemoglobin.
Iron deficiency anaemia: Low haemoglobin with small red cells from lack of iron.
Iron overload: Too much total body iron, deposited in organs and causing damage.
Iron studies: Blood tests of iron status: serum iron, ferritin, transferrin and transferrin saturation.
Iron tablets: Oral iron supplements, a common cause of constipation and dark stools.
Iron-deficiency anaemia: Low haemoglobin from lack of iron, often from slow blood loss.
Irreducible: Cannot be pushed back or made smaller.
Irregular mass: A lump with an uneven, poorly defined edge, a feature of cancer.
Irregular pupil: A misshapen pupil, often from the iris sticking to the lens in uveitis.
Irregular respirations: Abnormal, uneven breathing pattern from brainstem compression.
Irregularly irregular: No pattern to the beat intervals at all; typical of AF.
Irreversible: Cannot be undone; dead tissue does not recover.
Irritability: Being easily annoyed or quick to anger.
Irritants: Substances that damage skin directly, such as soaps and detergents.
Ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, leading to damage and death if not reversed.
Ischaemic ECG changes: ST or T wave changes showing the heart muscle is short of blood.
Ischaemic heart disease: Reduced blood supply to the heart muscle from narrowed coronary arteries.
Ischaemic stroke: Stroke caused by a blocked artery to the brain.
Ischaemic time: How long a tissue has been without an adequate blood supply.
Ischiorectal: The fat-filled space beside the anal canal, between the levator ani and the ischium.
Ishak staging: A biopsy score of how much fibrosis is present in the liver.
Ishihara: Colour vision test using plates of coloured dots containing hidden numbers.
Islet: Clusters of hormone-making cells in the pancreas, including the insulin-making beta cells.
Isocyanates: Chemicals in spray paints and foams; the commonest cause of occupational asthma.
Isoelectric line: The flat baseline of the ECG between waves.
Isolation: Nursing an infectious patient in a side room to stop spread.
Isoniazid: Anti-tuberculosis antibiotic that can trigger drug-induced lupus.
Isoprenaline: Beta-agonist infusion used for bradycardia when atropine fails.
Isosorbide mononitrate: Long-acting oral nitrate; needs asymmetric dosing to avoid tolerance.
Isotope uptake: How much of a radioactive tracer the thyroid takes up on a scan, showing how active it is.
Ivabradine: Drug slowing the sinus node to reduce heart rate; a third-line angina add-on.
J: Joules: the unit of energy for a defibrillator shock.
J wave: A hump at the junction of the QRS and ST segment, classic in hypothermia.
JAK-STAT: A cell signalling pathway that tells marrow cells to grow.
JAK2: A signalling enzyme; the V617F mutation switches it permanently on.
JAK2 V617F: The point mutation in JAK2 found in most PV and many ET and PMF cases.
JBDS: Joint British Diabetes Societies, who publish the UK HHS and DKA guidelines.
JCVI: Joint Committee on Vaccination and Immunisation, which advises the UK on vaccines.
JJ stent: Tube from kidney to bladder placed via cystoscopy to bypass an obstruction.
JME: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: morning jerks, absences and GTCS in teenagers.
JVP: Jugular venous pressure; a raised JVP shows high right-sided filling pressure.
Jacksonian march: Clonic jerking that spreads up a limb, from a frontal motor cortex focus.
Janeway lesions: Painless red macules on the palms or soles caused by septic emboli.
Jaundice: Yellow skin and eyes from raised bilirubin.
Jaw claudication: Jaw pain on chewing due to reduced blood flow to the jaw muscles; specific for GCA.
Jaw thrust: Lifting the jaw forward from behind its angles to open the airway without moving the neck.
Jejunal: Relating to the jejunum, the middle part of the small bowel.
Jobe's: Empty can test of supraspinatus strength.
Jod-Basedow effect: Iodine excess triggering uncontrolled hormone synthesis, causing hyperthyroidism.
Joint aspiration: Drawing fluid out of a joint with a needle for analysis.
Joint damage: Wear and destruction of cartilage and bone from repeated bleeds.
Joint insult: Any earlier damage to a joint, such as a fracture or ligament tear.
Joint protection: Rest, splinting and physiotherapy to stop a bleeding joint being damaged.
Joint space: The gap between bones on X-ray, filled by cartilage; it narrows when cartilage is lost.
Joint space narrowing: Loss of the gap between bones on X-ray, reflecting cartilage loss.
Justice: Fair allocation of resources and equal treatment of patients.
Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy: A generalised epilepsy of adolescence with morning myoclonic jerks, absences and tonic-clonic seizures.
Juxta-articular erosions: Bone erosions at the joint margins; the hallmark X-ray sign of RA.
K-ATP channel: ATP-sensitive potassium channel on beta cells; closing it triggers insulin release.
KCl: Potassium chloride, added to IV fluids to replace potassium.
KDIGO: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes; international guideline body for kidney disease.
KRAS: Oncogene mutated midway through the adenoma-carcinoma sequence.
Kaposi's sarcoma: HHV-8 driven tumour of endothelial cells causing purple skin and mucosal lesions.
Kartagener syndrome: Primary ciliary dyskinesia with situs inversus.
Kayser-Fleischer rings: Copper-brown rings at the edge of the cornea in Wilson's disease.
Kehr's sign: Left shoulder-tip pain from blood irritating the diaphragm, a sign of splenic rupture.
Keratinocyte: The main cell type of the epidermis.
Keratitis: Inflammation or infection of the cornea; sight-threatening, especially in contact lens wearers.
Keratoderma blenorrhagica: Waxy yellow-brown thickened lesions on the soles or palms, fairly specific to reactive arthritis.
Kerley B lines: Short horizontal lines at the lung edges on CXR, caused by fluid in the interlobular septa.
Kernig's sign: Pain and resistance when extending the knee with the hip flexed.
Ketamine cystitis: Bladder damage from chronic ketamine use: thick wall, small contracted bladder.
Ketogenesis: Making ketones from fatty acids in the liver.
Ketogenic diet: A high-fat, very low-carbohydrate diet that can reduce seizures in some patients.
Ketonaemia: Ketones in the blood; above 3 mmol/L is one of the DKA diagnostic criteria.
Ketone bodies: Acidic fuels (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate, acetone) the liver makes from fatty acids when insulin is lacking.
Ketones: Acidic fuel molecules made by the liver from fatty acids when cells cannot use glucose.
Ketosis: Raised ketones in the body from fat breakdown when insulin is lacking.
Kidney stones: Hard deposits, often calcium, that form in the kidney and can cause severe flank pain.
Kidney transplant: Surgery placing a donor kidney into a patient with end-stage kidney failure; the definitive treatment.
Kiesselbach's plexus: A network of superficial arteries on the anterior septum from internal and external carotid branches.
Killip: A bedside classification of heart failure severity after MI, from no crackles (I) to cardiogenic shock (IV).
Kimmelstiel-Wilson lesions: Rounded nodules of nodular glomerulosclerosis; the classic biopsy finding of advanced diabetic nephropathy.
King's College Criteria: Criteria used to decide which patients with acute liver failure need urgent transplant.
Klebsiella: A Gram-negative bacterium that causes urinary and other infections.
Klebsiella pneumoniae: Encapsulated Gram-negative rod causing pneumonia and sepsis.
Klumpke's palsy: C8/T1 brachial plexus injury paralysing the small hand muscles, possibly with Horner's.
Knee dislocation: Displacement of the tibia from the femur, often damaging nerves and arteries.
Knee extension: Straightening the knee, done by the quadriceps.
Kocher's criteria: Four-point score (non-weight bearing, fever, WCC, ESR) estimating septic arthritis risk in a limping child.
Koebner phenomenon: New lesions appearing at sites of skin trauma such as scratches or scars.
Koilonychia: Thin, spoon-shaped nails seen in iron deficiency.
Koplik spots: Tiny white spots on a red base inside the cheeks, seen early in measles.
Korsakoff syndrome: Chronic memory loss with confabulation after untreated thiamine deficiency.
Korsakoff's: Short for Korsakoff's syndrome: chronic amnesia and confabulation after untreated Wernicke's.
Korsakoff's syndrome: Chronic, largely irreversible amnesia with confabulation following untreated Wernicke's encephalopathy.
Krukenberg tumour: Metastasis to the ovaries, usually bilateral, classically from signet ring gastric cancer.
Kupffer cell: Resident macrophage of the liver sinusoids.
Kussmaul breathing: Deep, laboured breathing that blows off CO2 to compensate for metabolic acidosis.
Kussmaul's sign: A paradoxical rise in JVP on inspiration.
Kyphosis: Forward curvature of the upper spine, often from vertebral compression fractures.
L1: The first lumbar vertebra, roughly where the spinal cord ends in adults.
L5 root lesion: Damage to the fifth lumbar nerve root, causing weak inversion and eversion plus foot drop.
LA: Left atrium, the chamber receiving blood from the lungs before it passes to the left ventricle.
LABA: Long-acting beta-2 agonist, such as formoterol or salmeterol.
LACI: Lacunar infarct: small deep perforating artery stroke causing pure motor or sensory loss without cortical signs.
LAD: Left anterior descending artery, supplying the anterior wall and most of the septum.
LAMA: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist, such as tiotropium.
LBBB: Left bundle branch block: delayed conduction in the left ventricle giving broad QRS; new LBBB with chest pain is treated as STEMI.
LCIS: Lobular carcinoma in situ: non-invasive lobular cells, usually found by chance.
LDH: Lactate dehydrogenase, an enzyme released by damaged cells; a Glasgow criterion if above 600.
LDL: Low-density lipoprotein; carries cholesterol to tissues and deposits it in artery walls.
LDL receptor: Liver cell receptor that removes LDL from the blood; defective in FH.
LFTs: Liver function tests, including bilirubin, ALP, ALT and γGT.
LGE: Late gadolinium enhancement: MRI marker of scar or inflammation in the myocardium.
LH: Luteinising hormone; pituitary hormone driving testosterone production.
LIF: Left iliac fossa: the lower left area of the abdomen.
LLETZ: Large loop excision of the transformation zone, the treatment for CIN II.
LMN: Lower motor neurone: from the brainstem nucleus to the muscle; lesions weaken the whole half of the face.
LMN lesion: Lower motor neurone lesion: damage to the nerve itself, so the forehead is also weak.
LMWH: Low molecular weight heparin, such as dalteparin or enoxaparin; given by injection.
LPA: Lasting power of attorney, which can give a named person authority over health decisions.
LRTI: Lower respiratory tract infection: infection of the bronchi or lung tissue below the larynx.
LTOT: Long-term oxygen therapy for at least 15 hours a day in chronic hypoxaemia.
LTRA: Leukotriene receptor antagonist, such as montelukast.
LUQ: Left upper quadrant of the abdomen, where the spleen lies.
LUTS: Lower urinary tract symptoms: voiding problems (weak stream, hesitancy) and storage problems (frequency, urgency, nocturia).
LV: Left ventricle, the main pumping chamber that ejects blood into the aorta.
LV aneurysm: Thinned, bulging scarred ventricle wall weeks after MI, with persistent ST elevation.
LV dysfunction: Impaired pumping of the left ventricle.
LVEF: Left ventricular ejection fraction: the percentage of blood pumped out with each beat.
LVH: Left ventricular hypertrophy: thickening of the left ventricle wall.
LVP: Large-volume paracentesis: draining several litres of ascites through a needle.
Lab confirmation: Proof of the infection by a laboratory test.
Labetalol: An IV alpha and beta-blocker used first to lower heart rate and BP in dissection.
Labyrinthitis: Inflammation of the labyrinth: continuous vertigo with hearing loss.
Laceration: A tear or cut in tissue.
Lacosamide: Antiepileptic that slowly inactivates sodium channels; second-line for focal seizures.
Lacrimal gland: Gland above the outer eye that makes tears.
Lactate: A product of anaerobic metabolism; its level reflects how much tissue is ischaemic.
Lactational: Related to breastfeeding or milk production.
Lactic: Relating to lactic acid, produced when cells cannot use oxygen to make energy.
Lactulose: Osmotic laxative that reduces ammonia absorption, used for hepatic encephalopathy.
Lacunar: A small deep infarct from occlusion of a perforating artery, often from hypertension.
Lacy: A net-like, reticular pattern of rash, as seen on the limbs after slapped cheek.
Lagger: A worker who wraps pipes and boilers with insulation, historically asbestos.
Lagophthalmos: Inability to close the eyelids fully.
Lambert-Eaton: Lambert-Eaton syndrome: presynaptic calcium channel antibodies, often with small cell lung cancer; strength improves with effort.
Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: Anti-VGCC antibody syndrome: proximal leg weakness that improves with exertion, linked to small cell.
Lamina papyracea: The paper-thin bone between the ethmoid sinus and the orbit.
Lamivudine: An NRTI used in HIV and hepatitis B.
Lamotrigine: A sodium channel blocking AED, preferred in pregnancy; can cause a serious rash.
Lanosterol 14α-demethylase: Fungal CYP450 enzyme making ergosterol; the target of azoles.
Lanz incision: A transverse right iliac fossa incision used for open appendicectomy.
Laparotomy: Open abdominal surgery through a large incision.
Laplace's law: Wall tension is proportional to pressure times radius, so wider aneurysms are under more tension.
Large artery occlusion: Blockage of a major brain artery such as the proximal MCA or ICA.
Large bowel obstruction: Blockage of the colon causing distension, vomiting, constipation and no flatus.
Large-joint arthropathy: Joint disease affecting big joints such as knees and hips.
Large-volume paracentesis: Draining several litres of ascites to relieve tense distension, given with albumin cover.
Laryngeal: Relating to the larynx, the voice box.
Laryngeal TB: TB of the larynx, highly infectious.
Laryngeal mask airway: A supraglottic airway that sits over the larynx; quick to insert but does not protect against aspiration.
Laryngeal muscles: Muscles of the voice box that control the vocal cords and voice.
Laryngeal obstruction: Narrowing or blockage at the voice box, causing stridor.
Laryngotracheal: Relating to the larynx and trachea.
Laryngotracheobronchitis: Inflammation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi: the formal name for croup.
Larynx: The voice box, at the top of the trachea.
Lasting power of attorney: A legal document letting a chosen person make health or financial decisions if the patient loses capacity.
Latchkey incontinence: Urge leakage triggered by arriving home and putting the key in the door.
Late gadolinium enhancement: Bright areas on cardiac MRI after contrast showing scar or inflammation.
Late menopause: Periods stopping later than usual, giving more years of oestrogen exposure.
Late-onset asthma: Asthma that starts in adulthood rather than childhood.
Latency: The time between exposure and disease appearing; decades for asbestos.
Latency period: The time between exposure to a cause and the disease appearing.
Latent: Present but dormant, not causing symptoms.
Latent TB: Dormant TB infection without symptoms, which can reactivate when immunity is suppressed.
Latent stage: An early phase when disease is present but causes no symptoms.
Lateral chest wall: The side of the chest, under the armpit.
Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh: A purely sensory nerve supplying skin over the outer thigh.
Lateral fissure: A fissure at the side of the anus, such as 3 o'clock, needing investigation.
Lateral gaze: Looking to one side, moving both eyes horizontally.
Lateral lumbar flexion: Side-bending of the lower spine; reduced early in AS.
Lateral rectus palsy: Weakness of the eye muscle that turns the eye outwards (sixth nerve), causing a squint and double vision.
Latex: Natural rubber used in gloves and catheters, a common cause of contact allergy.
Laxative: A drug that helps the bowels open.
Laxatives: Drugs that soften stool or speed bowel movement.
Lead poisoning: Toxicity from lead exposure; it blocks haem synthesis and can cause sideroblastic anaemia.
Leads II, III, aVF: The ECG leads that look at the inferior (bottom) wall of the heart.
Leaflet: One of the flaps of a heart valve.
Least restrictive option: Under the MCA, the choice that limits the person's rights and freedom the least.
Leflunomide: DMARD that can raise blood pressure; teratogenic.
Left atrial appendage: A pouch off the left atrium where clots form in AF.
Left atrium: The heart chamber that receives oxygenated blood from the lungs.
Left bundle branch block: Delayed conduction down the left bundle, producing broad QRS complexes; new LBBB can mean acute MI.
Left heart failure: The left ventricle cannot pump well, so pressure backs up into the lungs.
Left lateral tilt: Tilting a pregnant patient about 15° to the left to relieve aortocaval compression.
Left sternal edge: The area just left of the breastbone where aortic regurgitation is best heard.
Left upper sternal border: The area just left of the upper breastbone (pulmonary area).
Left ventricle: The thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta.
Legal requirement: A duty set by law, such as reporting notifiable diseases, that overrides confidentiality.
Legionella: Legionella pneumophila: atypical bacterium spread through water systems such as air conditioning.
Legislation: Laws passed by government; here the Health Protection Regulations.
Length-dependent: Damage that affects the longest nerves first, so the feet before the hands.
Lens capsule: The thin clear membrane surrounding the lens of the eye.
Leprosy: A chronic Mycobacterium leprae infection of skin and nerves.
Leptin: Fat-derived satiety hormone; obese people become resistant to its effect.
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: Rare X-linked recessive disorder of purine metabolism causing high urate, gout, self-injury and developmental delay.
Letrozole: Aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal ER-positive breast cancer.
Leucocyte esterase: Enzyme from white cells detected on a dipstick; marker of pyuria.
Leucopenia: A low total white cell count (alternative spelling of leukopenia).
Leucoplakia: A white patch on a mucous membrane, such as the inside of the mouth.
Leukaemia: Cancer of white blood cells that starts in the bone marrow.
Leukocyte adhesion molecules: Surface proteins (such as alpha-4 integrin) that let white cells stick to and cross vessel walls.
Leukocyte esterase: An enzyme released by white cells, detected on dipstick as a sign of pyuria.
Leukoerythroblastic: Blood film with immature white and red cells, from marrow infiltration or stress.
Leukopenia: A low total white cell count.
Leukoplakia: A white oral patch that cannot be scraped off; potentially premalignant.
Leukostasis: Very high blast counts clogging small vessels, causing headache, visual change and breathlessness.
Leukotrienes: Lipid mediators from mast cells that cause prolonged bronchoconstriction and vascular leak.
Levator ani: The sheet of pelvic floor muscle that supports the rectum and other pelvic organs.
Levetiracetam: Anti-epileptic drug commonly used for seizures caused by brain tumours.
Levodopa: Dopamine precursor that crosses the blood-brain barrier; the most effective Parkinson's drug.
Levothyroxine: Synthetic T4 tablet, first-line replacement treatment for hypothyroidism.
Lewy bodies: Clumps of misfolded alpha-synuclein protein inside neurons.
Lewy body dementia: Dementia with fluctuating cognition, visual hallucinations and parkinsonism.
Lhermitte's sign: Electric shock sensation down the spine or limbs on neck flexion; a cervical cord lesion.
Licence: A driving licence; Group 1 for cars and motorbikes, Group 2 for lorries and buses.
Lichenification: Thickened, leathery skin with exaggerated markings from chronic scratching.
Lid hygiene: Gently cleaning the eyelids and lashes with clean water and cotton wool.
Lid lag: The upper lid is slow to follow the eye down; can occur in any thyrotoxicosis.
Lid retraction: The eyelid sits higher than normal, exposing sclera above the iris.
Lidocaine: Antiarrhythmic used as an alternative to amiodarone in refractory VF.
Life expectancy: How long a person is expected to live.
Lifestyle: Changes to daily habits such as meals, fluids, sleep and exercise.
Lifestyle modification: Changes such as stopping smoking, exercise and diet to slow disease.
Ligament: A tough band joining bone to bone that stabilises a joint.
Ligation: Tying off a blood vessel to stop bleeding.
Light touch: Sensation tested with cotton wool, carried by large sensory nerve fibres.
Lilliputian: Hallucinations of small people or animals, classic in Lewy body dementia.
Limb buds: The early swellings in the embryo that grow into arms and legs.
Limb ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a limb, threatening tissue survival.
Limb leads: ECG electrodes placed on the arms and legs.
Limb weakness: Weakness in an arm or leg, pointing to a central lesion.
Limb-threatening: Severe enough that the limb could be lost, e.g. from poor arterial supply.
Limbic encephalitis: Autoimmune inflammation of the limbic system causing memory loss and seizures.
Limbic system: Brain structures including the amygdala that process emotion and fear.
Limping: Walking unevenly to avoid putting weight on a painful leg.
Line sepsis: Bloodstream infection arising from a central venous catheter.
Liothyronine: Synthetic T3; faster acting and not first-line for hypothyroidism.
Lipase: Enzyme that breaks down dietary triglycerides so fat can be absorbed.
Lipid peroxidation: Free-radical damage to fats in cell membranes, injuring hepatocytes.
Lipid profile: Blood test measuring total cholesterol, LDL, HDL and triglycerides.
Lipid specialist: A doctor in a lipid clinic who manages inherited and resistant lipid disorders.
Lipids: Blood fats such as cholesterol and triglycerides.
Lipiduria: Fat in the urine, seen as fatty casts or oval fat bodies.
Lipodermatosclerosis: Chronic hardening and brown-red discolouration of lower-leg skin from venous disease.
Lipolysis: Breakdown of stored fat into free fatty acids and glycerol, switched on when insulin is absent.
Lipomas: Benign fatty lumps under the skin.
Lipooligosaccharide: The meningococcal endotoxin that triggers DIC and shock.
Lipoprotein: A particle of protein and fat that carries lipids through the blood, such as LDL or HDL.
Lipoprotein lipase: Enzyme on vessel walls that breaks down triglyceride-rich lipoproteins.
Liraglutide: Daily GLP-1 mimetic used for weight loss and type 2 diabetes.
Lisinopril: An ACE inhibitor used to lower blood pressure and protect the kidneys.
Listeria: A bacterium causing meningitis in over-60s, pregnancy and immunosuppression; needs amoxicillin.
Listeria monocytogenes: A Gram-positive rod spread by soft cheese and unpasteurised milk.
Lithium: Mood stabiliser for bipolar disorder that can cause hypothyroidism and goitre.
Little's area: The anterior-inferior nasal septum where Kiesselbach's plexus lies; source of most nosebleeds.
Live vaccine: A vaccine containing a weakened living organism, unsafe in immunosuppression.
Liver architecture: The normal organised arrangement of liver cells, vessels and bile ducts.
Liver biopsy: Taking liver tissue for histology; the gold standard for cirrhosis, contraindicated if INR above 1.5.
Liver disease: Damaged liver makes fewer clotting factors, so bleeding is harder to stop.
Liver failure: Loss of the liver's ability to make proteins, clear toxins and process bilirubin.
Liver transplant: Surgical replacement of a failing liver with a donor liver.
Liver ultrasound: Imaging of the liver with sound waves to look at size, texture and blood flow.
Lobar: In one of the brain's lobes near the surface, rather than deep.
Lobar pneumonia: Pneumonia filling one whole lobe of a lung, classically caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Lobectomy: Surgery to remove one lobe of a lung.
Lobule: A milk-producing unit of the breast.
Lobules: The milk-producing glands of the breast.
Local anaesthetic: A drug, such as lidocaine, that numbs a small area.
Locally advanced: Cancer that has grown into nearby tissue or nodes but not spread distantly.
Locked-in syndrome: Basilar artery occlusion causing quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.
LogMAR: Visual acuity scale where 0.0 is normal and higher numbers mean worse vision.
Loin: The side of the back between the ribs and the hip.
Loin pain: Pain in the flank between the ribs and hip, often from the kidney.
Long QT: QTc above 440 ms in men or 460 ms in women; risks torsades.
Long bone: A bone longer than it is wide, such as the femur, tibia or humerus.
Long-acting bronchodilators: Inhalers such as LABAs and LAMAs that keep the airways open for about 12 to 24 hours.
Long-acting insulin: Background (basal) insulin that works for about 24 hours; continued during DKA treatment.
Long-haul travel: A long flight or journey, usually over 4 hours, causing prolonged sitting.
Long-segment lesion: A narrowing that extends over a long length of artery.
Long-term oxygen therapy: Oxygen for at least 15 hours a day for chronic hypoxia, which slows pulmonary hypertension in COPD.
Loop diuretics: Strong diuretics such as furosemide that act on the loop of Henle to remove fluid.
Looser's zones: Pseudofractures: radiolucent transverse bands with sclerotic edges, often at the hip.
Loratadine: A non-sedating oral antihistamine; first line for mild allergic rhinitis.
Lorazepam: Benzodiazepine used for sedation when antipsychotics must be avoided, and for rapid tranquillisation.
Losartan: An angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB), used when ACE inhibitors cause cough.
Loss of consciousness: Being unresponsive and unaware of surroundings.
Loss-of-function: A mutation that stops a gene's protein working.
Loss-of-function mutation: A gene change that stops the protein working properly.
Loud P2: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, suggesting pulmonary hypertension.
Low birth weight: A baby weighing under 2.5 kg at birth.
Low salt diet: Cutting dietary sodium, thought to reduce endolymph volume.
Low sats: Low oxygen saturation on pulse oximetry.
Low voltage complexes: Small QRS complexes on the ECG, seen with myocardial oedema or effusion.
Low-dose IV insulin: A small, steady insulin infusion, used in HHS only after fluids.
Low-dose aspirin: 75 to 150mg aspirin daily, used in pregnancy to lower pre-eclampsia risk.
Low-grade dyskaryosis: Mildly abnormal cervical cells that may progress and need colposcopy.
Low-grade inflammation: Mild but long-lasting inflammation throughout the body.
Low-impact fall: A fall from standing height or less.
Low-impact trauma: A force that would not normally break bone, such as a fall from standing.
Low-voltage QRS: Small QRS complexes on the ECG, here because over-inflated lungs insulate the heart.
Low-volume urine: Passing small amounts of urine as the kidneys conserve water.
Lower left sternal edge: The area just left of the lower breastbone, where tricuspid murmurs are best heard.
Lower lobes: The bottom sections of each lung.
Lower motor neurone: The nerve running from the anterior horn of the cord out to the muscle.
Lower respiratory tract: The airways below the larynx: trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli.
Lower third: The bottom part of the oesophagus, nearest the stomach.
Lubricant: A gel applied before opening the bowels to ease passage of stool.
Lubricating drops: Eye drops that moisten and soothe the eye surface.
Lubricating eye drops: Artificial tears that protect a dry or exposed cornea.
Lucozade: A glucose drink used as oral fast-acting glucose.
Lugano staging: Lymphoma staging system (stages 1 to 4) based on the diaphragm and organ spread; replaced Ann Arbor.
Lumbar: Relating to the lower back part of the spine, L1 to L5.
Lumbar puncture: Needle sampling of CSF from the lower back; dangerous when a mass lesion raises intracranial pressure.
Lumbar vertebrae: The five bones of the lower back.
Lumbosacral nerve roots: The nerve roots leaving the lower spine (lumbar and sacral) that supply the legs, bladder and bowel.
Lumbosacral roots: The nerve roots from the lower spine and sacrum that supply the legs, bladder and bowel.
Lumen: The open channel inside a blood vessel.
Luminal: Relating to the lumen, the inside space of a tube.
Lumpectomy: Breast-conserving removal of a tumour with a clear margin.
Lung abscess: A pus-filled cavity inside the lung, often after aspiration, seen as a cavity with a fluid level.
Lung bases: The bottom parts of the lungs.
Lung cancer: Cancer arising in the lung, a common cause of hypercalcaemia.
Lung function: How well the lungs move air, usually measured by spirometry such as FEV1.
Lung function tests: Breathing tests measuring lung volumes, airflow and gas transfer.
Lung parenchyma: The functional gas-exchanging tissue of the lung.
Lung transplantation: Surgical replacement of one or both diseased lungs with donor lungs.
Lung volume reduction surgery: Removing hyperinflated emphysematous lung to improve mechanics.
Lupus: Systemic lupus erythematosus: an autoimmune disease that can attack the kidneys, skin, joints and blood.
Lupus nephritis: Immune-complex glomerulonephritis in SLE causing proteinuria, haematuria, hypertension and rising creatinine.
Lupus pernio: Purple, indurated rash on the nose and cheeks in sarcoidosis; not related to SLE.
Luteal phase: Second half of the menstrual cycle, after ovulation, when progesterone is high.
Lyme disease: Tick-borne Borrelia infection that can cause facial palsy, sometimes bilateral.
Lymph node biopsy: Removing a lymph node or part of one to examine under the microscope.
Lymph nodes: Small filters along lymph vessels that trap cells and microbes and can harbour cancer spread.
Lymphadenopathy: Enlarged lymph nodes, such as in the axilla.
Lymphangitis: Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, seen as red streaks tracking towards lymph nodes.
Lymphatic: Relating to lymph vessels and nodes.
Lymphatic channels: Thin vessels that drain tissue fluid towards lymph nodes.
Lymphatic drainage: Removal of tissue fluid by the lymphatic vessels.
Lymphatic spread: Cancer cells travelling through lymph vessels to lymph nodes.
Lymphatic system: The network of lymph vessels, nodes, spleen and thymus that drains tissue fluid and hosts immune cells.
Lymphoblasts: Immature lymphoid blasts, seen in ALL.
Lymphocyte: A white blood cell (T-cell or B-cell) of the adaptive immune system.
Lymphocyte-depleted: Rarest Hodgkin subtype with the worst prognosis; older or HIV patients.
Lymphocyte-predominant: Hodgkin subtype with the best prognosis, often found early.
Lymphocytes: White blood cells (T and B cells) that dominate in viral and autoimmune inflammation.
Lymphocytosis: Raised lymphocyte count; in CSF, suggests a viral or autoimmune cause.
Lymphoedema: Swelling from damaged lymph drainage, often of the arm after axillary surgery.
Lymphoid organ: An organ of the immune system such as the spleen or thymus.
Lymphoid tissue: Tissue made of immune cells, such as lymph nodes and Peyer's patches, that responds to infection.
Lymphoma: Cancer of lymphocytes arising in lymph nodes or other lymphatic tissue.
Lymphomatous infiltration: Invasion of tissue by lymphoma-like or lymphoid cells.
Lymphopenia: Low lymphocyte count, a common blood finding in active SLE.
Lymphoproliferative malignancy: A cancer of lymphocytes, such as CLL or lymphoma.
Lynch syndrome: Autosomal dominant mismatch repair defect causing early right-sided colorectal and endometrial cancers.
Lytic: Bone-destroying; lytic lesions are areas where bone has been eaten away.
Lytic lesion: An area where bone has been destroyed, appearing as a dark hole on X-ray.
Löfgren's syndrome: Acute sarcoidosis with fever, BHL, erythema nodosum and polyarthralgia; good prognosis.
M cells: Specialised epithelial cells over Peyer's patches that sample gut contents; S. typhi enters through them.
M protein: Another name for the paraprotein band on electrophoresis.
M1: Screening grade for maculopathy needing referral, such as exudates near the fovea.
M3 receptor: Muscarinic receptor on the detrusor that mediates bladder contraction.
MAHA: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia: red cells sheared in small damaged vessels.
MAO-B inhibitor: Drug such as selegiline or rasagiline that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
MAP: Mean arterial pressure; the target in shock is usually 65 mmHg or above.
MART: Maintenance and reliever therapy: one ICS/formoterol inhaler used regularly and as needed.
MCA: Mental Capacity Act 2005, the framework for adults who lack capacity.
MCA stroke: Stroke in the middle cerebral artery territory, which can impair swallowing.
MCH: Mean cell haemoglobin, the average amount of haemoglobin per red cell; low in iron deficiency.
MCP: Metacarpophalangeal joint, the knuckle joint; typical in rheumatoid arthritis.
MCP joints: Metacarpophalangeal joints: the knuckles where fingers meet the hand.
MCV: Mean cell volume; a raised MCV (macrocytosis) is common with heavy alcohol use.
MDF: Maddrey's discriminant function, the severity score that guides steroid use.
MDMA: Ecstasy: a stimulant drug that can cause hyperthermia and serotonin toxicity.
MDRD: An eGFR equation using creatinine, age, gender and ethnicity.
MDS: Myelodysplastic syndrome: a clonal marrow disorder with ineffective, dysplastic blood cell production.
MDT: Multidisciplinary team meeting that plans cancer treatment.
ME/CFS: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome; the name used in the NICE guideline.
MELD: Model for End-Stage Liver Disease: score from bilirubin, INR and creatinine to prioritise transplant.
MEN 1: Inherited syndrome of parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
MEN 2: Inherited syndrome of medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and (2A) hyperparathyroidism.
MEN type 1: Inherited syndrome of parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
MEN1: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1: parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumours.
MEN2: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2: inherited syndrome with phaeochromocytoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma.
MEN2A: Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2A: medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and parathyroid disease.
METAVIR: Histological staging system for liver fibrosis, F0 (none) to F4 (cirrhosis).
MGUS: Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance: a small paraprotein without CRAB that can progress.
MI: Myocardial infarction: death of heart muscle from prolonged ischaemia.
MIS: Memory Impairment Screen, a short test of delayed recall.
MLF: Medial longitudinal fasciculus: brainstem tract linking the CN VI and CN III nuclei for conjugate gaze.
MLH1: DNA mismatch repair gene mutated in Lynch syndrome.
MMF: Mycophenolate mofetil, an immunosuppressant used in lupus nephritis.
MMR: The measles, mumps and rubella vaccine.
MMSE: Mini-Mental State Examination, a longer cognitive test used in dementia.
MND: Motor neurone disease: progressive degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons.
MODS: Multi-organ dysfunction syndrome: failure of two or more organ systems, usually from systemic inflammation such as sepsis.
MODY: Maturity-onset diabetes of the young: single-gene diabetes before 25, often treated with sulfonylureas.
MONA: Old mnemonic for immediate ACS care: morphine, oxygen, nitrates, aspirin; oxygen now only if saturations below 94%.
MPN: Myeloproliferative neoplasm: a clonal marrow disorder overproducing one or more blood cell lines.
MPO: Myeloperoxidase: enzyme in myeloid granules; positive staining marks myeloid blasts.
MPT: Melphalan, prednisolone and thalidomide; a regimen for older patients.
MR angiography: MRI of the arteries with contrast, giving anatomical detail.
MRA: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone, eplerenone); blocks aldosterone.
MRC: Medical Research Council 0 to 5 scale for muscle power.
MRC grade: Muscle power scale from 0 (no movement) to 5 (normal power).
MRCP: MRI of the bile and pancreatic ducts; the most accurate non-invasive biliary imaging.
MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging; used in atypical cases to exclude central or structural lesions.
MRI brain: A detailed scan of the brain using magnets, used here to exclude a tumour.
MRI pelvis: Magnetic resonance imaging that maps abscesses and fistula tracts against the sphincters.
MRI pituitary: Magnetic resonance scan focused on the pituitary gland and hypothalamus.
MRI small bowel: MRI scan of the small intestine used to map the extent of Crohn's disease.
MRI spine: Magnetic resonance scan of the spine, the gold standard for suspected cord compression.
