Palpable pulse: A pulse that can be felt with the fingers.
Palpable thrill: A vibration felt with the hand over a loud murmur.
Palpitations: An unpleasant awareness of one's own heartbeat.
Palsy: Paralysis or weakness of a muscle or group of muscles.
Pan-systolic murmur: A heart murmur heard through the whole of systole.
Pancoast tumour: Lung cancer at the apex that invades the sympathetic chain, brachial plexus or recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Pancreatic cancer: Cancer of the pancreas, which can present as new diabetes with weight loss in older people.
Pancreatic dysfunction: The pancreas failing to make enough enzymes or insulin.
Pancreatitis: Inflammation of the pancreas with severe upper abdominal pain; a GLP-1 mimetic side effect.
Pancytopenia: Low red cells, white cells and platelets together.
Panic attacks: Sudden episodes of intense fear with fast breathing and palpitations.
Pannus: Thickened, invasive inflamed synovium that erodes cartilage and bone in RA.
Pansystolic murmur: A murmur lasting the whole of systole, as in mitral or tricuspid regurgitation.
Papillary muscle: Muscle in the ventricle that anchors the mitral leaflets via chordae.
Papillary muscle rupture: Tear of a papillary muscle after MI, causing sudden severe mitral regurgitation.
Papilloedema: Swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure.
Pappenheimer bodies: Iron-containing granules in red cells, seen in sideroblastic anaemia.
Papular: Made of small raised spots (papules) under 1 cm.
Papules: Small raised solid skin bumps under 1 cm.
Paracentesis: Putting a needle or drain into the peritoneal cavity to sample or remove ascitic fluid.
Paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunc: Circulatory collapse and renal impairment after large-volume drainage without albumin cover.
Paracetamol: A simple analgesic; first line for tension-type headache.
Paracetamol level: Blood concentration of paracetamol, used to judge overdose risk and need for NAC.
Paradoxical: Moving the opposite way to normal, as when chest and abdomen move out of sync.
Paradoxical embolus: A venous clot that crosses to the arterial side through a hole in the heart, such as a PFO.
Paradoxically: In the opposite way to what you would expect.
Paraesthesia: Pins and needles or numbness, here from ischaemic nerves.
Parakeratosis: Retained nuclei in the outer skin layer from incomplete maturation; gives psoriatic scale.
Paralysis: Loss of movement; in limb ischaemia it means muscle is dying.
Paramyxovirus: Virus family including mumps, a cause of viral meningitis.
Paranasal sinuses: Air-filled spaces in the facial bones (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid) that drain into the nose.
Paraneoplastic: Caused by the immune response to a tumour rather than by the tumour itself.
Paraparesis: Weakness of both legs, here from spinal cord ischaemia.
Paraplegia: Paralysis of both legs, usually from a spinal cord lesion.
Parapneumonic effusion: A collection of fluid in the pleural space next to a pneumonia.
Paraprotein: An abnormal antibody made by a single clone of plasma cells, seen in myeloma.
Parasites: Organisms that live in or on a host and harm it, such as amoebae.
Parasternal heave: Lifting felt at the left sternal edge from an enlarged right ventricle.
Parasympathetic: The rest-and-digest part of the autonomic nervous system, carried largely by the vagus nerve.
Parasympathetic fibres: Nerve fibres running on the outside of CN III that constrict the pupil; squashed first, so the pupil dilates.
Parathyroid: Four small glands behind the thyroid that make PTH to control calcium.
Parathyroid glands: Four small glands behind the thyroid that release PTH when calcium falls.
Paravalvular abscess: A pocket of pus in the tissue around a heart valve.
Parenchyma: The functional tissue of an organ; in the brain, the neurons and glia rather than the coverings.
Parenteral: Given by a route other than the gut, such as injection.
Parenterally: Given by a route other than the gut, such as IV or IM injection.
Parietal cells: Stomach lining cells that make acid and intrinsic factor.
Parietal pericardium: The outer layer of the pericardium, lining the fibrous sac.
Parietal peritoneum: The peritoneal layer lining the abdominal wall; it has somatic nerves, so pain is sharp and well localised.
Parkinson's: Neurodegenerative disease that slows movement and also slows gut transit.
Parkinson's disease: Degenerative dopamine-deficient disorder causing tremor, rigidity and slow movement.
Parkinson's disease dementia: Dementia developing in someone who has had Parkinson's disease for over a year.
Parkinsonian crisis: Sudden severe worsening of rigidity and immobility, often after missed medication.
Parkinsonism: Slowness, rigidity and tremor, as seen in Parkinson's disease.
Parotid: The large salivary gland in front of the ear.
Parotid gland: The large salivary gland in front of the ear, which swells in mumps.
Parous: Having given birth at least once.
Paroxysmal: Coming and going in sudden episodes.
Partial gastrectomy: Surgical removal of part of the stomach.
Partial respiratory compensation: Breathing changes that move pH back towards normal but not fully.
Partial reversibility: FEV1 improves significantly after a bronchodilator, but obstruction remains.
Partial thrombosis: A clot that narrows but does not completely block the artery.
Particulates: Tiny solid particles in the air that can be breathed deep into the lung.
Parvovirus B19: Virus causing 'slapped cheek' rash that can temporarily stop red cell production.
Passive movement: Movement of a joint by the examiner without the patient's effort.
Passively: Moving without energy use, following a concentration gradient.
Pasteurella multocida: Bacterium from cat and dog mouths that infects bite wounds; covered by co-amoxiclav.
Patch test: Allergens taped on the back for 48 hours to detect delayed contact allergy.
Pathognomonic: So characteristic that it strongly points to one diagnosis.
Pathological: Caused by or relating to disease.
Pathological fracture: A fracture through bone weakened by disease, caused by trauma that would not break normal bone.
Pathology: Disease, or the study of disease processes in tissues.
Pathophysiology: The abnormal processes in the body that cause a disease.
Paxlovid: Oral nirmatrelvir plus ritonavir for early Covid-19 in high-risk patients.
Peak flow: Peak expiratory flow: the fastest rate of breathing out, in L/min.
Peak flow variability: How much peak flow readings change over the day or between days; high variability suggests asthma.
Peak gradient: The maximum pressure difference across the valve on echo; above 40 mmHg is severe AS.
Peak jet velocity: Fastest blood speed through the valve on echo; higher means more severe stenosis.
Peaked P waves: Tall, pointed P waves on ECG showing an enlarged right atrium.
Pear drops: Sweet, fruity breath smell caused by exhaled acetone in ketoacidosis.
Peau d'orange: Orange-peel pitting of breast skin from blocked dermal lymphatics.
Pelger-Huët: Neutrophils with hyposegmented or bilobed nuclei; a classic film finding in MDS.
Pelger-Huët anomaly: Neutrophils with hyposegmented or bilobed nuclei, a classic film finding in MDS.
Pelvic autonomic fibres: Autonomic nerves supplying the bladder and genitals.
Pelvic floor: Sheet of muscles supporting the bladder, uterus and bowel and helping close the urethra.
Pelvic floor muscle training: Supervised exercises for at least 3 months; first-line for stress incontinence.
Pelvic lymph node dissection: Removal of pelvic nodes during cystectomy for staging and control.
Pelvic mass: A lump felt in the lower abdomen or on pelvic examination.
Pemberton's test: Raising both arms over the head; facial plethora or stridor suggests thoracic inlet obstruction.
Penetrating injury: A wound where an object pierces through the skin into deeper tissue.
Penetration: How well a drug reaches into a tissue.
Penicillamine: Copper chelator used in Wilson's disease, not haemochromatosis.
Penicillin: A beta-lactam antibiotic and one of the commonest drug causes of anaphylaxis.
Penicillin V: Phenoxymethylpenicillin: the oral daily prophylaxis after splenectomy.
Penicillin allergic: Having an allergic reaction to penicillin-type antibiotics, so flucloxacillin must be avoided.
Penicillin allergy: True immune reaction to penicillin: rash, angioedema or anaphylaxis, not diarrhoea or nausea.
Penicillin-binding protein: Bacterial enzyme that builds the cell wall; the target of beta-lactam antibiotics.
Penicillins: A family of beta-lactam antibiotics including amoxicillin.
Pentad: A group of five classic features.
Pentose phosphate pathway: A side branch of glucose metabolism that makes NADPH; G6PD is its first enzyme.
Peptic bleed: Bleeding from an ulcer in the stomach or duodenum.
Peptic ulcer: A break in the stomach or duodenal lining, often from NSAIDs or H. pylori.
Peptic ulcer disease: Sores in the lining of the stomach or duodenum, made worse by NSAIDs.
Peptic ulceration: Open sores in the stomach or duodenal lining.
Percussion: Tapping the chest to hear whether the area beneath is air-filled, solid or fluid.
Percutaneous: Done through the skin with a needle or catheter rather than open surgery.
Percutaneous colostomy tube: A tube placed through the abdominal wall into the colon to decompress and anchor it.
Percutaneous nephrolithotomy: Keyhole removal of a large stone through a track made directly into the kidney.
Percutaneous transhepatic biliary draina: Draining the bile ducts through the skin and liver under imaging guidance.
Percutaneous transluminal angioplasty: Inflating a balloon inside a narrowed artery via a needle puncture to widen it.
Perforating artery: A small deep artery supplying the internal capsule, thalamus or basal ganglia; blocked in lacunar stroke.
Perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the wall of a hollow organ.
Performance status: A score of how well a patient functions day to day, used to decide if they can tolerate treatment.
Perfusion: Blood flow delivering oxygen to a tissue or organ.
Perfusion scan: Nuclear scan showing areas of reduced blood flow to the myocardium under stress.
Peri-lesional oedema: Swelling of brain tissue immediately around a lesion.
Perianal abscess: An acute collection of pus in the tissues around the anus.
Perianal sepsis: Infection around the anus, such as an abscess, which can spread or become systemic.
Perianal skin: The skin around the anal opening.
Periarticular: Around a joint rather than inside it.
Periarticular osteopenia: Reduced bone density around a joint; the earliest X-ray sign of RA.
Pericardial effusion: Fluid collecting in the pericardial sac.
Pericardial friction rub: Scratching sound heard when inflamed pericardial layers rub together.
Pericardial knock: An early diastolic sound in constrictive pericarditis as filling stops abruptly.
Pericardial sac: The fibrous bag that surrounds the heart.
Pericardiectomy: Surgical removal of the pericardium for constrictive pericarditis.
Pericardiocentesis: Draining pericardial fluid with a needle, ideally sub-xiphoid under ultrasound.
Pericarditis: Inflammation of the pericardium causing pleuritic chest pain and saddle ST elevation.
Pericardium: The fibrous two-layered sac around the heart.
Pericranial: Around the skull: the scalp, temple, neck and shoulder muscles.
Perihilar: Around the hila, where the main bronchi and vessels enter each lung.
Perimenopausal: The years around the menopause when periods become irregular.
Perimenopause: The years around the menopause when hormone levels swing most.
Perineum: The area between the genitals and the anus.
Perioperative: Around the time of surgery: before, during and after an operation.
Perioperative mortality: Risk of death around the time of an operation.
Periorbital cellulitis: Infection of the eyelid skin in front of the orbital septum, with normal eye movements.
Periorbital puffiness: Swelling of the soft tissue around the eyes.
Periosteal elevation: Lifting of the periosteum by pus or oedema, seen early on MRI.
Periosteal reaction: New bone laid down by lifted periosteum, seen on X-ray as a later sign.
Periosteum: The tough membrane covering the outer surface of bone.
Peripheral: Towards the edges of the body, such as the hands and feet.
Peripheral arterial disease: Narrowing of the leg arteries by atherosclerosis, reducing blood flow and slowing healing.
Peripheral arteries: Arteries outside the heart and brain, mainly those of the legs.
Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor: Stops levodopa turning into dopamine outside the brain, reducing nausea and letting more reach the brain.
Peripheral field loss: Loss of the outer parts of the visual field.
Peripheral lesion: A problem in the inner ear or vestibular nerve rather than in the brain.
Peripheral nerves: Nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, very sensitive to ischaemia.
Peripheral neuropathy: Damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, causing numbness, pain or weakness.
Peripheral oedema: Swelling of the legs or ankles from fluid in the tissues.
Peripheral vascular disease: Narrowed leg arteries giving poor blood flow to the limbs.
Peripheral vascular resistance: The resistance to blood flow from the small arteries; when it rises, BP rises.
Peripheral vasoconstriction: Narrowing of blood vessels in the limbs and skin, pushing blood to the core organs.
Peripheral vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels in the skin and limbs, which drops blood pressure.
Peripheral vertigo: Vertigo from the inner ear or vestibular nerve rather than the brain.
Peripheral vestibular disorder: A balance problem arising in the inner ear or vestibular nerve, not the brain.
Peristalsis: Waves of muscle contraction that push urine down the ureter.
Peristaltic: Wave-like muscle contractions that push contents along a tube.
Peritoneal carcinomatosis: Cancer spread across the peritoneum, causing low-SAAG malignant ascites.
Peritoneal cavity: The space between the two layers of peritoneum lining the abdomen and covering the gut.
Peritoneal dialysis: Dialysis using the lining of the abdomen as the filter, with fluid exchanged through a catheter.
Peritoneum: The thin membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the abdominal organs.
Peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound tenderness and rigidity.
Peritonitic: Showing peritonitis: a rigid, very tender abdomen from inflamed peritoneum.
Peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, the membrane lining the abdominal cavity and covering the organs.
Peritonsillar abscess: Pus between the tonsil capsule and the pharyngeal muscles, causing trismus and a hot potato voice.
Peritonsillar mass: A swelling beside the tonsil, usually pus in quinsy.
Peritonsillar space: The tissue space between the tonsil capsule and the throat muscles.
Peritubular fibroblasts: Cells around the kidney tubules that make erythropoietin.
Periureteric fat stranding: Hazy fat around the ureter on CT, showing recent stone passage or inflammation.
Periurethral: Around the opening of the urethra.
Perivalvular abscess: An abscess in the tissue around an infected valve.
Periventricular: Next to the brain's ventricles; the classic site of MS plaques.
Permanent pacemaker: An implanted device that sends electrical impulses to keep the heart beating at a safe rate.
Permeability: How easily fluid and protein leak through vessel walls.
Permeability factor: A circulating substance that makes the glomerular filter leaky.
Permissive hypotension: Accepting a lower blood pressure in bleeding patients to avoid worsening the haemorrhage.
Pernicious anaemia: Autoimmune B12 deficiency from antibodies against intrinsic factor or gastric parietal cells.
Persistent airflow limitation: Narrowing of the airways that does not fully reverse with a bronchodilator.
Persistent cough: A cough that goes on for weeks.
Personality change: A shift in behaviour or character, often from frontal lobe involvement.
Personality traits: Lasting patterns of thinking, feeling and behaving that make up a person's character.
Pessary: A medicated tablet inserted into the vagina.
Petechiae: Pinpoint red spots from capillary bleeding, typical of low platelets.
Petechial: Tiny pinpoint bleeding spots in the skin that do not blanch.
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome: Autosomal dominant hamartomatous GI polyps with dark freckles on lips, palms and soles.
Peyer's patches: Clusters of lymphoid tissue in the distal ileum, targeted by typhoid.
Phaeochromocytoma: Catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla causing episodic headache, sweating and palpitations.
Phagocytosis: Engulfing and destroying microbes by white cells such as macrophages.
Phalen's: Holding the wrists flexed for a minute reproduces carpal tunnel symptoms.
Pharyngeal: Relating to the pharynx, the throat behind the nose and mouth.
Pharyngeal dilator muscles: Throat muscles, such as genioglossus, that hold the pharynx open; their tone falls during sleep.
Pharyngeal muscles: The constrictor muscles of the throat wall.
Pharyngitis: Sore throat from inflammation of the pharynx.
Pharynx: The throat behind the nose and mouth, the part of the airway that collapses in OSA.
Phase 0 depolarisation: The rapid upstroke of the cardiac action potential, driven by sodium entering the cell.
Phenobarbital: A barbiturate anti-epileptic that induces liver CYP450 enzymes.
Phenotype: The observable type of a disease in a patient, such as eosinophilic asthma.
Phenoxymethylpenicillin: Penicillin V, oral daily antibiotic prophylaxis against pneumococcus.
Phenylephrine: Alpha-agonist eye drop that constricts superficial vessels; blanches episcleritis but not scleritis.
Phenytoin: A sodium channel blocking AED given IV as second line in status epilepticus.
Philadelphia chromosome: Shortened chromosome 22 from t(9;22), carrying the BCR-ABL fusion gene.
Phlebotomy: Drawing blood from a vein; therapeutic phlebotomy is venesection.
Phosphate: A mineral that combines with calcium to form bone crystal.
Phosphate binder: A drug taken with meals to bind dietary phosphate in the gut.
Phosphate reabsorption: The kidney taking phosphate back into the blood.
Photic stimulation: Flashing lights, used as a seizure trigger in some epilepsies and during EEG.
Photochemotherapy: Light treatment combined with a light-sensitising drug, as in PUVA.
Photocoagulation: Using a laser to burn and seal retinal tissue.
Photophobia: Pain or discomfort on exposure to light.
Photosensitive: Made worse by sunlight or ultraviolet light exposure.
Phototherapy: Treatment of skin disease with ultraviolet light.
Phyllodes tumour: A rare, fast-growing fibroepithelial tumour that can be benign or malignant.
Physiological: Normal for the body's state, not caused by disease.
Physiological stress: Illness, injury or surgery that raises the body's need for cortisol.
Physiological tremor: A tiny normal tremor everyone has, increased by adrenaline, anxiety, caffeine or fatigue.
Physiotherapy: Therapy using exercise and movement to keep function and prevent contractures.
Pill-rolling: Resting tremor where thumb and fingers rub as if rolling a pill.
Pillars: The four core principles of medical ethics: autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice.
Pilonidal abscess: An abscess in the natal cleft from infected hair follicles, not related to the anus.
Pimecrolimus: A topical calcineurin inhibitor, like tacrolimus, used in eczema.
Pinch point: Where the diaphragm squeezes the herniated stomach, causing friction and erosions.
Pink frothy sputum: Blood-tinged foamy phlegm coughed up in severe pulmonary oedema.
Pinnae: The visible outer parts of the ears.
Pinpoint pupils: Very small, constricted pupils, typical of opioid or cholinergic toxicity.
Piperacillin with tazobactam: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic used first-line in neutropenic sepsis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam: Broad-spectrum anti-Pseudomonal penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor, for severe HAP.
Pirfenidone: Oral antifibrotic drug that slows IPF progression.
Pitting: The spleen's removal of inclusions such as nuclear remnants from red cells.
Pitting oedema: Swelling that keeps a dent after pressing, from fluid in the tissues.
Pituitary: Small gland under the brain that releases ACTH and other control hormones.
Pituitary MRI: Magnetic resonance scan of the pituitary to find an ACTH-secreting adenoma.
Pituitary adenoma: A benign tumour of the pituitary gland.
Pituitary feedback: The loop where high thyroid hormone tells the pituitary to make less TSH.
Pituitary tumour: A growth of the pituitary gland at the base of the brain; usually benign.
Pivmecillinam: Penicillin-type antibiotic used second-line for lower UTI.
Placenta: The organ linking mother and fetus that passes oxygen and nutrients; some viruses can cross it.
Plantar fascia: The thick band of tissue running along the sole from the heel to the toes.
Plantar fasciitis: Inflammation of the plantar fascia insertion at the heel, causing heel pain.
Plantar flexion: Pointing the foot downwards, as when standing on tiptoe.
Plantar responses: Foot reflex from stroking the sole; toes normally go down, upgoing toes mean a UMN lesion.
Plaque: A focal area of demyelination seen on MRI as a bright T2 lesion.
Plaque erosion: Loss of the lining cells over a plaque, which can trigger a clot without a full rupture.
Plaque psoriasis: The commonest type: well-demarcated red plaques with silvery scale on extensors.
Plaque rupture: Breakdown of a plaque's cap, exposing material that triggers clotting.
Plaques: Raised, flat-topped patches on skin or mucosa.
Plasma: The liquid part of blood, carrying proteins, salts and water.
Plasma ACTH: Blood level of ACTH, used to tell ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent causes.
Plasma concentration: The level of a drug in the blood.
Plasma exchange: Removing the patient's plasma and replacing it with donor plasma; treatment for TTP.
Plasma free metanephrines: Blood test for breakdown products of adrenaline and noradrenaline; the first test for phaeochromocytoma.
Plasma levels: Concentration of a drug in the blood.
Plasma proteins: Proteins carried in the blood, such as albumin and clotting factors.
Plasmapheresis: Removing plasma from the blood to clear harmful antibodies.
Plasmodium: The protozoan parasite that causes malaria.
Platelet: A small blood cell fragment that clumps together to plug bleeding vessels.
Platelet aggregation: Platelets sticking together to form a plug.
Platelet consumption: Using up platelets faster than they are made, as they are used in clots.
Platelet count: The number of platelets in the blood, normal in haemophilia.
Platelet disorders: Conditions with too few or poorly working platelets, causing skin and mucosal bleeding.
Platelet transfusion: Giving donated platelets intravenously to prevent or stop bleeding.
Platelet-fibrin thrombus: A small clot of platelets and fibrin that forms on damaged endocardium.
Platelets: Small cell fragments that help blood clot.
Pleura: The thin membranes lining the lungs and inner chest wall.
Pleural aspirate: Fluid drawn from the pleural space with a needle so it can be tested for pH, glucose and organisms.
Pleural biopsy: A tissue sample taken from the lining of the lung.
Pleural effusion: Fluid collecting between the two layers of the pleura.
Pleural fluid: Fluid collecting between the lung and chest wall.
Pleural plaques: Benign, often calcified patches of pleural thickening that mark past asbestos exposure.
Pleural rub: Creaking sound on auscultation as inflamed pleural layers rub together.
Pleural thickening: Fibrous thickening of the pleura; diffuse or nodular thickening may suggest mesothelioma.
Pleuritic: Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in or coughing, from inflamed pleura.
Pleuritic chest pain: Sharp chest pain that is worse on breathing in.
Pleuritis: Inflammation of the pleura, causing sharp chest pain on breathing in and sometimes an effusion or rub.
Pleurodesis: Sealing the pleural space (e.g. with talc) to stop an effusion recurring.
Plummer's disease: Another name for toxic multinodular goitre.
Plummer-Vinson syndrome: Iron deficiency anaemia with a post-cricoid web causing dysphagia.
Pluripotent: Able to become many different cell types.
Pneumococcal sepsis: Sepsis caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, the classic OPSI organism.
Pneumococcal vaccination: A vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae, a common cause of pneumonia.
Pneumococcal vaccine: Vaccine against Streptococcus pneumoniae, given 2 weeks before elective splenectomy and boosted every 5 years.
Pneumoconiosis: Lung disease from inhaled mineral dust (coal, silica, asbestos).
Pneumocystis jirovecii: Fungus causing pneumonia in people with CD4 below 200.
Pneumoperitoneum: Free gas in the peritoneal cavity, usually from a perforated hollow organ.
Pneumothorax: Air in the space around the lung, causing it to collapse.
Podiatry: Specialist foot care, including nail and callus care and footwear advice.
Podocyte: Specialised cell wrapping glomerular capillaries whose foot processes stop protein leaking.
Point mutation: A change in a single DNA base.
Point mutations: Changes in single letters of a gene's code.
Point-of-care test: Rapid finger-prick antibody test giving a result in minutes; 90-day window period.
Polarised light microscopy: Microscopy with polarised light, used on joint fluid to identify crystals by shape and birefringence.
Poliovirus: Enterovirus that can cause meningitis and paralytic poliomyelitis; rare where vaccination is routine.
Polyarthralgia: Pain in many joints without obvious swelling.
Polyarthritis: Arthritis affecting five or more joints.
Polychromasia: Bluish-tinged young red cells on a film, reflecting high reticulocyte output.
Polyclonal B-cell proliferation: Many different B-cell families multiplying at once, rather than one clone.
Polycystic kidney disease: An inherited disorder where many fluid-filled cysts grow in both kidneys and slowly destroy them.
Polycythaemia: Raised haemoglobin and red cell mass, here from chronic hypoxia.
Polymerisation: Joining small units into a long chain, as tubulin forms microtubules.
Polymerise: Link together into long chains; deoxygenated HbS does this inside red cells.
Polymicrobial: Caused by more than one species of organism together.
Polymorphic: Changing in shape from beat to beat.
Polymorphonuclear: Neutrophils; the white cells that dominate CSF in bacterial meningitis.
Polymyalgia rheumatica: Inflammatory condition of older adults causing proximal pain and morning stiffness with a raised ESR.
Polymyositis: Inflammatory myopathy with proximal weakness and a markedly raised CK.
Polyneuropathy: Damage to many peripheral nerves, usually symmetrical and starting in the feet.
Polyol pathway: Route by which excess glucose is turned into sorbitol and fructose, stressing nerve cells.
Polyps: Small growths projecting from the bowel lining.
Polysomnography: Overnight sleep study recording airflow, chest effort, oxygen saturation, EEG and heart rate; the gold standard for OSA.
Pons: Part of the brainstem where the trigeminal nerve enters.
Poor perfusion: Too little blood reaching the tissues, seen as cold, pale, mottled skin and confusion.
Poor posture: Holding the body in a strained position, which tightens neck and scalp muscles.
Poorly demarcated: With a blurred edge that merges into normal skin.
Popliteal artery: Continuation of the femoral artery behind the knee.
Popliteal fossa: The hollow at the back of the knee.
Portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal vein, usually from a scarred cirrhotic liver resisting blood flow.
Portal of entry: The route by which organisms get into the body.
Portal venous drainage: Blood from the gut drains via the portal vein to the liver, so cancer spreads there first.
Portosystemic collaterals: Veins linking portal and systemic circulations that open up in portal hypertension.
Portosystemic shunt: A channel connecting the portal vein to the systemic veins, bypassing the liver.
Positional headache: Headache that changes with posture, such as lying down or standing.
Positive airway pressure: Air pressure kept above atmospheric pressure inside the airway.
Positive energy balance: Energy intake persistently exceeding energy expenditure, so fat stores grow.
Post-ROSC care: Oxygen, treating the cause and ICU support after circulation returns.
Post-coital prophylaxis: A single antibiotic dose after sex to prevent UTI.
Post-enteric: Following a bowel infection, typically one causing diarrhoea.
Post-germinal centre B cells: B cells that have matured in a lymph node germinal centre, the stage from which plasma cells arise.
Post-herpetic neuralgia: Persistent burning nerve pain after shingles.
Post-ictal: The period of confusion, drowsiness and headache after a seizure; absent after a faint.
Post-infectious: Starting after an infection has cleared, usually by an immune reaction.
Post-renal: AKI caused by obstruction to urine flow after the kidneys, such as BPH or stones.
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis: Kidney inflammation 1-3 weeks after strep infection, causing haematuria, oedema and hypertension.
Post-surgical bleeding: Bleeding that continues or restarts after an operation.
Post-thyroiditis: Hypothyroidism following thyroid inflammation, such as after viral or postpartum thyroiditis.
Post-viral: Coming on after a viral infection.
Post-void residual: Urine left in the bladder after voiding, measured by ultrasound.
Posterior MI: Infarction of the back wall of the heart, seen as ST depression in V1-V3 and elevation in V7-V9.
Posterior acoustic enhancement: Bright area behind a fluid-filled lesion on ultrasound.
Posterior canal: The most dependent semicircular canal; affected in most BPPV.
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm: A ballooned artery near the third nerve that presses on it, causing a painful palsy with a dilated pupil.
Posterior cortex: The back part of the brain's outer layer, including parietal and occipital lobes.
Posterior dislocation: The ball of the hip slipping out backwards; the leg looks short and turned in.
Posterior lesions: Abnormalities at the back of the heart, better seen from the oesophagus on TOE.
Postero-lateral: Towards the back and side; the usual direction a disc bulges, hitting the nerve root.
Posteromedial papillary muscle: Mitral papillary muscle usually supplied only by the RCA, so it ruptures after inferior MI.
Postictal: The recovery period after a seizure, often with confusion and drowsiness.
Postmenopausal: After the menopause, when ovarian oestrogen production has stopped.
Postoperative pneumonia: Chest infection after surgery, common after oesophagectomy.
Postpartum thyroiditis: Thyroid inflammation after childbirth, often with a thyrotoxic then hypothyroid phase.
Postsynaptic: On the receiving side of a synapse, here the muscle membrane.
Postsynaptic membrane: The muscle membrane under the nerve ending, packed with acetylcholine receptors.
Postural drainage: Positioning so gravity drains sputum from affected lung segments.
Postural headache: Headache that changes with position, e.g. worse lying down with raised ICP.
Postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness.
Postural instability: Poor balance and tendency to fall, especially when turning or pushed.
Posturing: Abnormal rigid limb positions (flexion or extension) in severe brain injury, a sign of deep coma.
Potassium: Salt mainly inside cells; abnormal levels can cause heart rhythm problems.
Potassium chloride: Potassium salt added to IV fluids to replace potassium lost and driven into cells during treatment.
Potassium citrate: Urine alkaliniser used to prevent calcium stones.
Potassium iodide: Iodine given in thyroid storm to block release of thyroid hormone.
Potency: How strong a topical steroid is: mild, moderate, potent or very potent.
Potent: A strong grade of topical steroid, such as betamethasone.
Potentiate: To increase the effect of something.
Pott's disease: Tuberculosis of the spine, causing back pain and vertebral collapse.
Prader-Willi syndrome: Genetic syndrome with neonatal hypotonia, then hyperphagia, obesity and learning difficulty.
Pramipexole: Oral dopamine agonist used in Parkinson's.
Pre-auricular lymph node: Lymph node just in front of the ear; enlarged in viral conjunctivitis.
Pre-diabetes: Glucose above normal but below the diabetes cut-off (HbA1c 42 to 47 mmol/mol).
Pre-eclampsia: Pregnancy disorder after 20 weeks with high blood pressure and proteinuria; seizures mean eclampsia.
Pre-formed: Already present before the transfusion, so the reaction is immediate.
Pre-malignant: Not yet cancer but able to become cancer.
Pre-proliferative: The stage before new vessel growth, similar to severe NPDR.
Pre-renal: AKI caused by reduced blood flow to otherwise healthy kidneys.
Precipitant: A trigger that brings on a condition.
Precipitants: Things that trigger or tip a patient into a condition.
Precipitate: Come out of solution and clump inside the cell.
Precipitation: Crystals coming out of solution when a substance is too concentrated.
Preclinical phase: The period when disease exists but has not yet produced symptoms.
Precursor: A larger molecule that is cut up to make smaller active molecules.
Precursors: Inactive forms of a molecule that need modifying before they work.
Prediabetes: Blood glucose higher than normal but below the diabetes threshold.
Predictive values: PPV and NPV: the chance a positive or negative result is correct.
Predisposition: A tendency to develop a condition.
Prednisolone: Oral corticosteroid used in severe alcoholic hepatitis when Maddrey's DF is 32 or more.
Pregabalin: An anticonvulsant related to gabapentin, used for neuropathic pain.
Pregnancy: Raises pelvic venous pressure and causes constipation, so haemorrhoids are common.
Pregnancy test: A urine or blood hCG test, done to exclude ectopic pregnancy in women with abdominal pain.
Prehn's sign: Pain relieved by lifting the testis; supports epididymitis rather than torsion.
Preload: The stretch on the ventricle at the end of filling, set by venous return.
Premalignant: Not cancer, but able to turn into cancer.
Premature haemolysis: Red cells destroyed before their normal 120-day lifespan.
Premenopausal: Still having periods, before the menopause.
Premenstrual: Before periods have started, meaning girls before puberty in this context.
Pressing: A steady pressure or squeezing pain rather than throbbing.
Pressure gradient: A difference in pressure between two spaces that pushes contents from high to low.
Presumption of capacity: The Mental Capacity Act starting point that every adult has capacity unless shown otherwise.
Presynaptic: On the nerve cell that releases the neurotransmitter.
Presyncope: Feeling about to faint without actually losing consciousness.
Pretest probability: How likely a disease is before the test result is known.
Pretibial myxoedema: Raised, waxy plaques on the shins in Graves' disease.
Prevalence: The proportion of a population who have a condition at a given time.
Previously expressed wishes: What the patient said they wanted before losing capacity, which guides best-interests decisions.
Priapism: Prolonged painful erection; can occur from leukostasis in leukaemia.
Primaquine: Antimalarial drug that can trigger haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.
Primary: The original tumour from which secondary deposits spread.
Primary CNS lymphoma: EBV-driven brain lymphoma in advanced HIV, usually a single lesion.
Primary PCI: Emergency PCI as the first reperfusion treatment for STEMI, within 120 minutes.
Primary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure from disease of the adrenal gland itself; ACTH is high.
Primary anastomosis: Joining the bowel ends back together in the same operation.
Primary ciliary dyskinesia: Inherited defect of cilia causing poor mucus clearance, sinusitis, subfertility and sometimes dextrocardia.
Primary headache: A headache disorder that is not caused by another condition, such as migraine or cluster headache.
Primary hyperaldosteronism: The adrenal glands make too much aldosterone on their own, causing hypertension and low potassium.
Primary hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism caused by failure of the thyroid gland itself, so TSH is high.
Primary infection: The first-ever infection with HSV, with no existing antibodies; usually the most severe.
Primary open-angle glaucoma: Chronic raised eye pressure damaging the optic nerve; listed in the notes as a contraindication to amitriptyline.
Primary prevention: Treatment to prevent a first cardiovascular event in someone without CVD.
Primary progressive: MS that worsens steadily from onset with no discrete relapses.
Primary psychotic disorder: A condition such as schizophrenia where psychosis is the main problem, not secondary to mood.
Primary syphilis: Treponema pallidum infection causing a single painless genital ulcer (chancre).
Primary tumour: The original site where a cancer began.
Primordial germ cells: The earliest precursor cells that later become sperm or eggs.
Probability: How likely something is, as a percentage.
Probe to bone: Bedside test: a sterile probe touching bone through an ulcer strongly suggests osteomyelitis.
Procainamide: An antiarrhythmic drug known to cause drug-induced lupus.
Prochlorperazine: A dopamine antagonist used short-term for nausea and vertigo; it does not treat BPPV.
Proctoscopy: Looking inside the rectum and anus through a short tube.
Prodrome: Early warning symptoms, such as tingling or burning, before lesions appear.
Productive cough: A cough that brings up sputum.
Progenitor cell: An early cell committed to becoming a particular blood cell line.
Progesterone: Hormone of the luteal phase that also acts on breast tissue.
Progestogen-only: Contraception without oestrogen, such as the progestogen-only pill, implant or hormonal coil.
Prognosis: The likely course and outcome of a disease.
Prognostic: Telling you about the likely outcome.
Prognostic benefit: A drug effect that improves survival rather than just symptoms.
Prognostic factor: Something that predicts how a disease is likely to turn out.
Prognostic marker: A finding that predicts how a patient will do.
Progressive dysphagia: Swallowing difficulty that steadily worsens, typically solids first, then liquids.
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopat: A brain infection by JC virus that destroys myelin in several areas, seen with severe immunosuppression.
Proliferative glomerulonephritis: Glomerulonephritis with an increased number of cells in the glomeruli.
Prolonged QT: A long QT interval on ECG, which raises the risk of dangerous arrhythmias; macrolides can lengthen it.
Prolonged expiration: Breathing out taking longer than normal because air leaves narrowed airways slowly.
Prolonged expiratory phase: Breathing out taking longer than normal because air leaves narrowed airways slowly.
Prolonged exposure: Being exposed to something over a long time.
Promethazine: Sedating antihistamine with strong anticholinergic effects.
Promyelocyte: Myeloid precursor between myeloblast and myelocyte; accumulates in APML.
Pronator drift: When an arm held out palm-up drifts down and turns inwards, a sign of subtle upper motor neurone weakness.
Propagate: To grow and extend along the vessel.
Propagation: Extension of a tear or clot further along a vessel.
Prophylactic: Given to prevent a problem rather than treat it.
Prophylactic antibiotics: Antibiotics given before infection occurs, usually at induction of anaesthesia, to reduce SSI risk.
Prophylactic factor replacement: Regular scheduled factor infusions to prevent bleeds, mainly in severe haemophilia.
Prophylactic-dose: A lower dose given to prevent clots rather than treat one.
Prophylactically: Given in advance to prevent a problem rather than treat it.
Prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent disease in someone exposed.
Propranolol: Non-selective beta-blocker used to prevent variceal bleeding in cirrhosis.
Proprioception: The sense of where the joints are in space, without looking.
Proptosis: Forward bulging of the eye out of the orbit.
Propylene glycol: A solvent in some IV drugs that can build up and cause acidosis.
Propylthiouracil: Antithyroid drug inhibiting thyroperoxidase; first-line in the first trimester and in storm.
Prostacyclin analogue: Drug mimicking prostacyclin, a natural vasodilator, used in PAH (e.g. epoprostenol).
Prostaglandins: Lipid mediators released in anaphylaxis that add to vasodilation and bronchospasm.
Prostate cancer: Malignant tumour of the prostate, usually in the peripheral zone.
Prostatitis: Inflammation or infection of the prostate.
Prosthetic heart valve: An artificial heart valve; mechanical ones can shear red cells.
Prosthetic joint: An artificial joint replacement, such as a hip or knee.
Prosthetic valves: Artificial heart valves, mechanical or tissue.
Protease inhibitor: Drug such as atazanavir that stops viral proteins maturing.
Proteases: Enzymes, for example neutrophil elastase, that break down proteins in tissue.
Protective sensation: Enough feeling in the feet to notice pain from injury before damage occurs.
Protein denaturation: Heat unfolding proteins so they stop working, killing cells.
Protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins; detects the paraprotein of myeloma, a PMR mimic.
Protein synthesis: The process by which cells build proteins; chloramphenicol blocks it in bacteria.
Proteinuria: Protein in the urine; a marker of kidney damage and worse prognosis.
Proteolytic enzymes: Enzymes that break down proteins, here destroying cartilage.
Proteus: Gram-negative urease-producing bacterium linked to UTIs and struvite stones.
Proteus mirabilis: Urease-producing Gram-negative bacterium that causes struvite stones.
Prothrombin complex concentrate: A concentrate of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X used to reverse warfarin fast.
Prothrombin time: Time for blood to clot via the extrinsic pathway; prolonged in liver synthetic failure.
Proton pump inhibitor: A drug that blocks the stomach's acid pump to cut acid production.
Protrudes: Pushes out beyond its normal position.
Provoked: Caused by a clear temporary trigger such as surgery or immobility.
Proximal: Nearer the trunk; for muscles, the shoulder and hip girdles.
Proximal humerus: The top end of the upper arm bone, near the shoulder.
Proximal leg vein: Deep veins above the knee, such as the popliteal and femoral veins.
Proximal muscle weakness: Weakness of the shoulder and hip muscles, making it hard to stand from sitting.
Proximal myopathy: Weakness of the muscles near the trunk, such as the hips and shoulders.
Proximal renal tubule: The first part of the kidney tubule, where most glucose is reabsorbed.
Proximal tibia: The top end of the shin bone, just below the knee.
Proximal urethra: The part of the urethra nearest the bladder, running through the prostate.
Proximally: Towards the centre of the body, e.g. from calf up to thigh.
Pseudo-obstruction: Massive colonic dilatation without a mechanical blockage, also seen in frail elderly patients.
Pseudodementia: Depression that looks like dementia; the MMSE is typically normal.
Pseudogout: Acute arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, usually in the knee or wrist of older people.
Pseudohyphae: Chains of elongated yeast cells, typical of Candida on microscopy.
Pseudomembranous colitis: Severe C. difficile colitis with yellow plaques on the colon lining.
Pseudomonas: Gram-negative rod that causes hospital and ventilator infections and resists many antibiotics.
Pseudomonas aeruginosa: Gram-negative rod that chronically colonises damaged airways; marks more severe disease.
Psittacosis: Pneumonia caused by Chlamydia psittaci, caught from infected birds such as parrots.
Psoriasis: Chronic immune-mediated skin disease with thick, scaly plaques from fast keratinocyte turnover.
Psoriatic: Caused by or relating to psoriasis.
Psoriatic arthritis: Inflammatory, usually seronegative arthritis linked to psoriasis, classically affecting DIP joints.
Psychic aura: Strange feelings such as deja vu, fear or unreality at the start of a seizure.
Psychoeducation: Teaching patients and carers about the illness and how to cope.
Psychoeducational groups: Group sessions teaching people about their condition and coping skills.
Psychological distress: Emotional suffering such as worry, low mood or fear that affects daily life.
Psychological stress: Mental strain that can trigger or worsen IBS via the gut-brain axis.
Psychomotor slowing: Slowed thinking and movement, typical of severe depression.
Psychosis: Loss of contact with reality, with hallucinations, delusions or disordered thinking.
Psychosocial: Relating to psychological and social factors such as stress and relationships.
Pterygoid muscles: Jaw muscles near the tonsil; their spasm causes trismus in quinsy.
Public Health England: The former name of the national public health agency, replaced by UKHSA in 2021.
Public health authorities: Organisations responsible for protecting the health of the whole population, such as UKHSA.
Public interest: Disclosure to protect others from serious harm, which can outweigh confidentiality.
Puerperal: Occurring in the weeks after childbirth.
Pulmonary TB: Tuberculosis of the lungs, the infectious form.
Pulmonary area: The second left intercostal space beside the sternum, where pulmonary valve sounds are best heard.
Pulmonary arterial pressure: Blood pressure inside the pulmonary arteries that carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
Pulmonary arteries: The arteries carrying blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
Pulmonary capillary filter: The fine lung capillary network that normally traps emboli before blood reaches the systemic arteries.
Pulmonary congestion: Fluid and blood backing up in the lungs.
Pulmonary emboli: Blood clots that have travelled to and lodged in the lung arteries.
Pulmonary embolism: A blood clot that has travelled to and blocked an artery in the lungs.
Pulmonary fibrosis: Scarring of the lungs that stiffens them and reduces gas exchange.
Pulmonary filtration: The lung capillaries acting as a sieve that trap clots and bacteria from venous blood.
Pulmonary function testing: Breathing tests including spirometry, lung volumes and gas transfer.
Pulmonary function tests: Breathing tests measuring lung volumes, airflow and gas transfer.
Pulmonary hypertension: Raised pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
Pulmonary infiltrates: Abnormal shadowing in the lung on X-ray from cells or fluid.
Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung air spaces from high pulmonary venous pressure.
Pulmonary pressures: Pressures measured in the pulmonary artery and right heart, key to confirming pulmonary hypertension.
Pulmonary regurgitation: Backflow through the pulmonary valve, often because the dilated artery stretches the valve ring.
Pulmonary rehabilitation: A supervised exercise and education programme that improves breathlessness and exercise tolerance.
Pulmonary stenosis: Narrowed pulmonary valve obstructing right ventricular outflow; usually congenital.
Pulmonary valve: The valve between the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery to the lungs.
Pulmonary vascular remodelling: Thickening and narrowing of the lung blood vessel walls.
Pulmonary vascular resistance: How hard it is for blood to flow through the lung vessels.
Pulmonary vasculature: The network of arteries, capillaries and veins within the lungs.
Pulmonary vasoconstriction: Narrowing of the lung blood vessels, which raises pressure in the pulmonary arteries.
Pulmonary vasodilators: Drugs that relax lung artery smooth muscle to lower pulmonary pressure, used in PAH.
Pulmonary venous pressure: The pressure in the veins draining the lungs into the left atrium.
Pulsatile: Pumping in rhythm with the heartbeat.
Pulsatile abdominal mass: A lump in the abdomen that throbs with each heartbeat, suggesting an aortic aneurysm.
Pulsatile hepatomegaly: An enlarged liver that pulses with each heartbeat, typical of severe TR.
Pulsatile mass: A swelling that throbs with each heartbeat.
Pulsating: Throbbing, beating in time with the pulse.
Pulse deficit: A pulse that is weaker, delayed or absent compared with the same pulse on the other side.
Pulse pressure: Systolic minus diastolic blood pressure: narrow in AS, wide in AR.
Pulsed: Given as short courses of high doses, usually intravenously.
Pulseless: No palpable pulse distal to a blockage.
Pulseless VT: Ventricular tachycardia without a pulse; shockable.
Pulselessness: No palpable pulse distal to a blockage.
Pulsus alternans: A regular pulse that alternates between strong and weak beats; a sign of severe LV impairment.
Pulsus paradoxus: An exaggerated fall in systolic BP on inspiration, seen in cardiac tamponade and severe asthma.
Pulsus parvus et tardus: A small-volume, slow-rising pulse typical of severe aortic stenosis.
Punched-out erosions: Sharply defined bone erosions near joints on X-ray, seen in recurrent gout.
Punched-out lesions: Sharp-edged holes in bone on X-ray where bone has been destroyed.
Pupil: The black hole in the centre of the iris that lets light in.
Pupils: The black central openings of the irises; normal in conjunctivitis.
Purine: A building block of DNA and RNA; its breakdown produces uric acid.
Purine turnover: The rate at which cells break down and remake purines; high in rapid cell death.
Purple striae: Wide purple stretch marks on the abdomen, thighs or arms from thin, fragile skin.
Purpuric: Larger non-blanching purple patches from bleeding into the skin.
Purulent: Containing pus; green or yellow sputum.
Purulent nasal discharge: Thick, coloured (yellow or green) mucus containing pus from the nose.
Purulent sputum: Yellow or green sputum containing pus, suggesting infection.
Pus: Thick fluid of dead white cells, bacteria and tissue debris collecting at a site of infection.
Pustules: Small raised spots filled with pus.
Pyelonephritis: Infection of the kidney, causing fever, loin pain and rigors.
Pyrazinamide: An anti-tuberculosis drug that raises serum urate.
Pyridostigmine: Long-acting acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; first-line symptomatic treatment for myasthenia.
Pyridoxal-5-phosphate: Active vitamin B6; needed more for ALT than AST synthesis, so its deficiency lowers ALT.
Pyridoxine: Vitamin B6, needed for the first step of haem synthesis.
Pyrimethamine: Antiparasitic used with sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis.
Q fever: Infection with Coxiella burnetii from farm animals.
QFracture: UK fracture risk calculator, an alternative to FRAX.
QIV-HD: High-dose quadrivalent influenza vaccine, covering four flu strains.
QIVr: Recombinant quadrivalent influenza vaccine, covering four strains.
QRISK3: NICE-recommended score estimating 10-year risk of heart attack or stroke.
QRS: ECG complex showing ventricular depolarisation; widens in severe hyperkalaemia.
QRS complex: The ECG wave produced by ventricular depolarisation.
QRisk: Score estimating 10-year cardiovascular risk; above 10% means offer a statin.
QT: The ECG interval from the start of the QRS to the end of the T wave; prolonged in hypothermia.
QT interval: ECG time from start of QRS to end of T wave; short in hypercalcaemia.
QTc: QT interval corrected for heart rate.
Quadruple therapy: Four drugs taken together; here the RIPE regimen.
Quality of life: A person's overall wellbeing and ability to enjoy daily life.
Quantiferon: Interferon-gamma release blood test for latent tuberculosis.
Queen Anne's sign: Another name for Hertoghe sign: loss of the lateral third of the eyebrows.
Quetiapine: Atypical antipsychotic used first line for hallucinations in Parkinson's.
Quincke's sign: Visible pulsation of the nail bed capillaries in aortic regurgitation.
Quinolones: Antibiotic class including ciprofloxacin that can lower the seizure threshold.
Quinsy: Peritonsillar abscess: a collection of pus beside the tonsil.
R/S transition: The chest lead where the R wave becomes bigger than the S wave, normally around V3 to V4.
R0: Complete resection with microscopically clear margins.
R3A: Active proliferative retinopathy on screening; needs urgent referral.
RA: Rheumatoid arthritis: chronic autoimmune symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints.
RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system: hormones that retain salt and water when kidney perfusion falls.
RANK: A receptor on osteoclast precursors; when RANKL binds it, osteoclasts form and resorb bone.
RANKL: Signal molecule that drives osteoclast formation and activation.
RANKL inhibitor: A drug blocking RANKL, the signal that switches on osteoclasts.
RAPD: Relative afferent pupillary defect: the pupil dilates when light swings to the eye with the damaged optic nerve.
RARA: Retinoic acid receptor alpha gene on chromosome 17, needed for myeloid cells to mature.
RBBB: Right bundle branch block: RSR' in V1–3 and slurred S in lateral leads.
RBC: Red blood cell: carries oxygen using haemoglobin.
RCA: Right coronary artery, supplying the inferior wall and usually the SA and AV nodes.
RCOG: Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists, which writes UK pregnancy guidelines.
RDW: Red cell distribution width: a high value means red cells vary widely in size.
REM sleep behaviour disorder: Acting out dreams (shouting, kicking) because normal REM paralysis is lost.
REM sleep disorder: Acting out dreams (shouting, kicking) because normal REM sleep paralysis is lost.
RF-positive: Having rheumatoid factor antibodies in the blood, seen in rheumatoid arthritis.
RFA: Radiofrequency ablation, using heat from radio waves to close a vein.
RIF: Right iliac fossa: the lower right area of the abdomen.
RIPE: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol: the first-line TB regimen.
RNA polymerase: The enzyme that copies DNA into RNA.
RNA virus: Virus whose genetic material is RNA, such as norovirus and rotavirus.
ROSC: Return of spontaneous circulation: a pulse returns.
ROSIER: Recognition of Stroke in the Emergency Room scale, separating stroke from mimics.
RRMS: Relapsing-remitting MS: attacks followed by recovery, the most common course.
RRT: Renal replacement therapy: dialysis or transplant.
RSR': A QRS with two upward peaks (M shape) in V1, typical of RBBB.
RSV: Respiratory syncytial virus; a common respiratory virus, worst in infants and the elderly.
RUQ: Right upper quadrant of the abdomen, where the liver and gallbladder lie.
RV: Right ventricle, which pumps blood into the pulmonary arteries.
RV afterload: The resistance the right ventricle pumps against, set mainly by pulmonary vascular resistance.
RV hypertrophy: Thickening of the right ventricular wall from pumping against high pressure.
RV strain: ECG pattern of ST depression and T inversion in V1-V3 from right ventricular overload.
Radial artery: The wrist artery, the preferred access route for PCI.
Radial deviation: Bending the wrist towards the thumb side.
Radial head: The top end of the radius at the elbow.
Radial nerve: Nerve that straightens the elbow, wrist and fingers and supplies the back of the hand.
Radiating: Spreading out from one place along the path of a nerve.
Radiation: Pain spreading from where it starts to another area, such as arm or jaw.
Radiation exposure: Contact with ionising radiation, which damages DNA.
Radical cystectomy: Surgical removal of the whole bladder, with urinary diversion.
Radicular pain: Pain shooting along the territory of a nerve root.
Radiculopathy: Damage or compression of a spinal nerve root causing pain, numbness or weakness along its path.
Radio-femoral delay: The femoral pulse arriving after the radial; seen in type B dissection and coarctation.
Radio-radial delay: One radial pulse arriving later than the other; points to type A dissection.
Radioactive iodine: Radioiodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; can worsen eye disease.
Radioactive iodine ablation: Destroying thyroid tissue with oral radioactive iodine to treat hyperthyroidism.
Radiofrequency ablation: Catheter heat destroys the tissue causing an arrhythmia.
Radioiodine: Radioactive iodine treatment that destroys thyroid tissue; often leads to hypothyroidism.
Radiological: Relating to imaging such as ultrasound or X-ray.
Radiosurgery: Not surgery with a knife: many precisely aimed radiation beams meet on a small target.
Radiotherapy: Treatment with ionising radiation to kill cancer cells, used for painful bone metastases.
Raised ICP: Pressure inside the skull above normal, causing headache, vomiting, papilloedema and drowsiness.
Raised JVP: A higher than normal jugular venous pressure in the neck, showing high right-sided filling pressure.
Ramipril: ACE inhibitor used first-line for diabetic nephropathy with ACR 3 mg/mmol or more.
Ramsay Hunt syndrome: Facial nerve palsy from VZV reactivation, with severe ear pain and vesicles in or around the ear.
Random plasma glucose: Blood glucose measured at any time regardless of meals.
Range of movement: How far a joint can move in each direction.
Ranolazine: Antianginal add-on drug used when other agents are insufficient.
Ranson's criteria: An older pancreatitis severity score using admission and 48-hour values.
Rapid Rhino: An inflatable anterior nasal pack for bleeds not stopped by simple pressure.
Rapid correction: Bringing glucose or osmolality down too fast.
Rapid tranquillisation: Urgent use of medication to calm a dangerously agitated patient.
Rasagiline: MAO-B inhibitor that slows dopamine breakdown in the brain.
Rasburicase: Recombinant urate oxidase that breaks down uric acid; prevents and treats tumour lysis.
Rate control: Slowing the ventricular rate in AF without trying to restore sinus rhythm.
Rate-limiting CCB: Calcium channel blocker that slows the heart (verapamil, diltiazem).
Rate-limiting enzyme: The slowest step in a pathway, which sets how fast the whole pathway runs.
Raw shellfish: Uncooked seafood that can carry Vibrio vulnificus, which thrives in iron overload.
Raynaud's: Fingers and toes turning white then blue with cold, from vessel spasm; worsened by beta-blockers.
Raynaud's phenomenon: Fingers turning white, blue then red in the cold from blood vessel spasm.
Re-entry: An impulse circling a loop of tissue and repeatedly re-exciting it.
Re-intervention: A further procedure needed to fix or maintain a previous repair.
Re-orientation: Helping a patient know where they are and what time it is, using clocks, calendars and family.
Re-sedation: Return of opioid toxicity once short-acting naloxone wears off.
Re-suturing: Stitching a wound closed again after it has opened.
Reabsorption: Taking substances back from urine into the blood in the kidney.
Reactivation: Latent virus becoming active again and causing a recurrence.
Reactive: Enlarged in response to nearby infection rather than from disease within the node.
Reactive arthritis: Sterile inflammatory arthritis starting 1 to 4 weeks after a GU or GI infection.
Reactive oxygen species: Unstable oxygen molecules that damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA.
Reassurance: Explaining the illness is usually mild and self-limiting.
Rebleeding: Fresh bleeding into an existing collection.
Rebound: A worsening of symptoms caused by the treatment itself, here headache from frequent painkillers.
Rebound tenderness: Pain felt when pressure on the abdomen is suddenly released, from parietal peritoneal irritation.
Rebound vasodilation: Vessels widen more than before once a constricting drug wears off, worsening congestion.
Rebreathing mask: A mask that lets the patient breathe back exhaled CO2 to correct overbreathing.
Recall: Inviting a person back for their next routine screening test.
Recent trauma: A recent injury, such as a fall or blow to the head.
Receptor: A protein on a cell surface that a molecule or virus binds to.
Receptor adaptation: Gradual change in receptor number or sensitivity after a lasting rise in neurotransmitter.
Receptor clustering: Gathering of acetylcholine receptors into dense patches opposite the nerve ending.
Receptor density: How many receptors are packed into an area of membrane.
Receptor downregulation: Cells reduce the number of receptors after constant stimulation, so a drug works less well.
Reciprocal change: ST depression in leads facing the opposite wall to an ST elevation.
Recombinant: Made in the lab using genetically engineered cells rather than from donated blood.
Recombinant factor VIII: Factor VIII made by genetic engineering, given IV to treat or prevent bleeds.
Recovery position: Lying an unconscious, breathing patient on their side to keep the airway clear.
Recreational: Drug use for pleasure rather than medical need.
Rectal biopsy: A small sample of rectal wall taken to look at under the microscope.
Rectal bleeding: Blood passed from the back passage.
Rectal mass: A lump felt in the rectum on DRE, which may be cancer.
Recurrence: The cyst or condition coming back after treatment.
Recurrent VTE: A new clot after a previous one.
Recurrent episode: Return of infection after it had resolved.
Recurrent herpes: Repeat outbreaks after the first infection, due to reactivation of latent virus.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Branch of the vagus nerve that supplies the vocal cords.
Recurrent vaginal candidiasis: Four or more episodes of vaginal thrush in a year.
Red cell mass: The total volume of red blood cells in the body.
Red flag: A feature that suggests a serious underlying cause needing urgent action.
Red flags: Features suggesting cancer: skin changes, hard irregular mass, lymphadenopathy.
Redcurrant jelly: Thick, dark red, blood-stained sputum typical of Klebsiella pneumonia.
Redeployment: Moving a worker to a different role away from the harmful exposure.
Reduced breath sounds: Quieter sounds heard through the stethoscope, as with over-inflated lungs or poor air entry.
Reduced chest expansion: The chest moves less than normal on breathing in, as in stiff fibrotic lungs.
Reduced consciousness: Drowsiness or unresponsiveness, measured with the GCS.
Reduced tone: Floppy muscles that offer less resistance than normal to passive movement.
Redundant: Describes bowel that is longer than normal and forms extra floppy loops.
Reed-Sternberg cells: Large cells with bilobed nuclei and prominent eosinophilic nucleoli; diagnostic of Hodgkin lymphoma.
Reference population: Healthy young adults whose average bone density the T score is compared with.
Referral: Sending a patient to a specialist team.
Referred: Of pain: felt away from its source because the two areas share a nerve supply.
Reflex: An automatic, involuntary nervous system response to a stimulus.
Reflex arc: The nerve loop from a sensory receptor to the spinal cord and back to a muscle.
Reflex syncope: Fainting caused by an inappropriate autonomic reflex; vasovagal is the commonest type.
Reflex tachycardia: A rise in heart rate when a vasodilator lowers BP; why beta-blockade comes first.
Reflux: Backward flow of stomach contents up into the oesophagus.
Refractory anaphylaxis: Breathing or circulation problems that persist despite two doses of IM adrenaline.
Refractory ascites: Ascites that does not respond to, or recurs despite, diuretics.
Refractory hypotension: Low blood pressure that does not respond to fluids.
Refractory period: Time after depolarisation when a cell cannot fire again.
Regenerative nodules: Clumps of regrowing liver cells surrounded by scar tissue in cirrhosis.
Regimen: A planned schedule of drugs, doses and timing.
Regional lymph nodes: The nearby lymph nodes that drain an area, e.g. groin nodes for the leg.
Regional wall motion abnormality: A segment of heart muscle that moves poorly, showing ischaemia or scar.
Regurgitant jet: The stream of blood flowing backwards through a leaky valve.
Regurgitation: Stomach contents coming back up into the mouth without vomiting.
Rehabilitation: Treatment to help regain function and independence.
Reinfarction: A further MI after a recent one.
Reintroduction: Bringing the food back after elimination; symptoms returning confirms the allergy.
Reiter's syndrome: Older name for reactive arthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis.
Relapse: A return or worsening of symptoms after a period of improvement.
Relapse prevention: Strategies to stop weight being regained after it is lost.
Relapse rate: How often relapses occur, usually counted per year.
Relapsing-remitting: MS course with attacks followed by partial or full recovery; the commonest form.
Relative afferent pupillary defect: Abnormal swinging light test showing reduced signal from one optic nerve.
Relative hypovolaemia: Normal blood volume but too little filling the widened vessels, acting like blood loss.
Relative insulin deficiency: Some insulin is made but not enough to overcome resistance, as in Type 2.
Relative risk: How many times more likely an outcome is in one group than another.
Remission: A period where the disease is controlled and blood tests normalise.
Remodelling: Permanent structural airway change: thickened walls, fibrosis, muscle hypertrophy.
Remodels: Bone is broken down and rebuilt in a new shape in response to load.
Renal angle: Same as the costovertebral angle; tender in pyelonephritis.
Renal artery stenosis: Narrowing of the artery to a kidney; creatinine jumps when an ACE inhibitor is started.
Renal biopsy: Taking a core of kidney tissue to examine the glomeruli; gold standard.
Renal blood flow: The blood supply reaching the kidneys.
Renal bruit: A whooshing sound heard over the abdomen or flank from turbulent flow in a narrowed renal artery.
Renal calcium reabsorption: The kidney taking calcium back into the blood instead of losing it in urine.
Renal colic: Severe loin-to-groin pain from a kidney stone; a classic misdiagnosis for ruptured AAA.
Renal compensation: The kidneys keeping more bicarbonate to bring a low pH back towards normal over days.
Renal failure: Loss of the kidneys' ability to filter blood and make urine.
Renal function: How well the kidneys are filtering the blood, usually judged by creatinine and eGFR.
Renal haematuria: Blood in the urine coming from the kidney itself rather than the lower urinary tract.
Renal parenchyma: The functional tissue of the kidney itself.
Renal pelvis: The funnel-shaped part of the kidney that collects urine and drains into the ureter.
Renal perfusion pressure: The pressure driving blood through the kidneys.
Renal regulation: Control by the kidneys, here over vitamin D activation.
Renal replacement therapy: Dialysis or haemofiltration used to take over kidney function.
Renal screen: Blood tests for glomerular causes: ANCA, anti-GBM, ANA, dsDNA, C3, C4, immunoglobulins and protein electrophoresis.
Renal transplant: Surgery to place a donor kidney in a patient with kidney failure.
Renal tubules: The small tubes in the kidney that modify filtered fluid into urine.
Renal ultrasound: A scan of the kidneys showing their size, shape and any blockage.
Renal vein: The vein draining blood from the kidney into the inferior vena cava.
Renal vein thrombosis: Clot in the renal vein causing flank pain and haematuria; classic in membranous nephropathy.
Renally safe: Safe in kidney disease because it is not cleared by the kidneys.
Renin: Kidney enzyme that drives the angiotensin-aldosterone system; high when aldosterone is low.
Renin:aldosterone ratio: Blood test screening for primary hyperaldosteronism: high aldosterone with suppressed renin.
Renoprotection: Protecting the kidneys from further damage.
Reperfusion: Restoring blood flow, which can release potassium and acid from damaged muscle.
Reperfusion injury: Tissue damage caused when blood returns to ischaemic tissue, releasing oxidative and inflammatory products.
Repetitive nerve stimulation: EMG test firing a nerve repeatedly; myasthenia shows a falling (decremental) response.
Repetitive strain: Injury from repeating the same movement many times, such as typing.
Repolarisation: Heart cells resetting their electrical charge after each beat.
Repositioning manoeuvres: Head-position sequences, such as Epley, that move otoconia back into the utricle.
Reproductive years: The years between puberty and menopause.
Rescue antibiotic: An antibiotic used only if symptoms do not improve after a set time.
Rescue medication: A reliever inhaler, usually salbutamol, used to ease symptoms during an attack.
Rescue pack: Prednisolone and antibiotics kept at home to start at the onset of an exacerbation.
Resection: Surgical removal of part of an organ.
Residual margins: Cancer cells left at the cut edge of removed tissue.
Residual mass: A lump still present after a cyst has been drained; needs biopsy.
Residual urine: Urine left in the bladder after passing urine.
Resistance: Bacteria no longer killed or stopped by an antibiotic.
Resistant depression: Depression that has not responded to adequate trials of treatment.
Resistant hypertension: Blood pressure not controlled despite three drugs, including a diuretic.
Resolution: Recovery from DKA, defined as pH >7.3, ketones <0.6 mmol/L and bicarbonate >15 mmol/L.
Resorption: Reabsorption of fluid back into the body.
Respirations: Breaths; slow respirations means a low breathing rate.
Respiratory: Here, an acid-base change driven by CO2 and breathing.
Respiratory acidosis: Low pH caused by CO2 retention from inadequate ventilation.
Respiratory alkalosis: High blood pH from blowing off too much CO2 by overbreathing.
Respiratory arrest: Breathing has stopped or is ineffective while the heart may still be beating.
Respiratory centre: The area in the brainstem that controls the rate and depth of breathing.
Respiratory compensation: Changing breathing to correct a pH problem; in metabolic acidosis, breathing deeper to blow off CO2.
Respiratory cycle: One full breath in and out.
Respiratory depression: Slow, shallow breathing that fails to clear carbon dioxide.
Respiratory distress: Visible hard work of breathing: fast rate, recession, nasal flaring, use of accessory muscles.
Respiratory droplets: Small drops from coughs and sneezes that carry virus a short distance.
Respiratory epithelial cells: The cells lining the airways and alveoli.
Respiratory epithelium: The cell lining of the airways, with cilia and mucus to trap and clear germs.
Respiratory failure: Failure of the lungs to keep blood oxygen up and/or carbon dioxide down, defined by PaO2 below 8 kPa.
Respiratory infection: An infection of the airways or lungs.
Respiratory rate: The number of breaths per minute.
Rest pain: Ischaemic pain in the foot at rest, often at night, when flow is inadequate even without exercise.
Resting tremor: Tremor present when the limb is relaxed and supported, easing with movement.
Restlessness: Inability to stay still or relax, often with fidgeting.
Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Stiff heart muscle that cannot fill properly.
Restrictive myopathy: Stiff, swollen muscle that cannot stretch, so the eye cannot move fully.
Restrictive pattern: Low FEV1 and FVC with a normal or high FEV1/FVC ratio, as in fibrosis.
Restrictive spirometry: Both FEV1 and FVC reduced with a normal or high ratio, as in stiff lungs.
Resus: The resuscitation area or team for critically unwell patients.
Resuscitation: Urgent treatment to restore circulation, such as fast IV fluids.
Resuscitation Council UK: UK body that publishes the anaphylaxis treatment algorithm.
Retain: Hold information in mind long enough to make the decision; it need not be remembered long-term.
Reticular activating system: Brainstem network that keeps us awake; CO2 retention depresses it, causing drowsiness.
Reticular shadowing: A net-like pattern of lines on X-ray from thickened interstitium.
Reticulocyte: A young red cell; a low count means the marrow is not responding.
Reticulocytes: Young red cells released from the marrow; raised when the marrow is compensating.
Reticulocytosis: Raised reticulocyte count, showing the marrow is making red cells faster.
Reticulonodular shadowing: A net-like pattern with small nodules on chest X-ray, seen in interstitial disease.
Retina: The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.
Retinal detachment: Separation of the retina from the underlying layer; an emergency.
Retinal infarction: Death of a small area of retina from blocked blood supply, seen as cotton wool spots.
Retinoid: A vitamin A derivative; acitretin is an oral retinoid that is highly teratogenic.
Retinopathy: Diabetic damage to retinal vessels; its presence supports diabetic nephropathy as the cause of proteinuria.
Retrobulbar neuritis: Optic neuritis behind the eye, so the disc looks normal at first.
Retrograde: Moving backwards, against the normal direction.
Retrograde spread: Travel of a virus backwards along a nerve axon, from the nerve ending towards the brain.
Retroperitoneal: Behind the peritoneum; most AAA ruptures bleed here at first.
Retrospective: Looking back afterwards; tryptase confirms anaphylaxis after the event.
Retrovirus: RNA virus that copies itself into DNA and inserts it into the host genome.
Revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to an ischaemic limb.
Reversal: Undoing the effect of a drug, here restoring normal clotting.
Reverse cholesterol transport: HDL carrying cholesterol from tissues back to the liver for removal.
Reverse tick: Downsloping ST depression typical of digoxin effect.
Reverse transcriptase: Viral enzyme that copies RNA into DNA.
Reversibility: Improvement in FEV1 after a bronchodilator; 12% or more supports asthma.
Reversible causes: Treatable problems that mimic dementia, such as low B12, hypothyroidism or depression.
Reversible obstruction: Narrowing of the airways that improves, either by itself or with a bronchodilator.
Revision: A repeat operation to replace or fix a failed joint replacement.
Reye's syndrome: Rare, serious liver and brain injury in children linked to aspirin.
Reynold's pentad: Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion: severe cholangitis with sepsis.
Rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin and CK, which can cause AKI; seen after long lies or crush injury.
Rheumatic disease: Heart valve damage after rheumatic fever, an immune reaction to strep throat.
Rheumatic fever: Autoimmune illness after group A streptococcal throat infection that can scar heart valves.
Rheumatic heart disease: Valve scarring years after rheumatic fever; a common cause of AR worldwide.
Rheumatoid arthritis: Autoimmune inflammatory arthritis of small joints; the commonest cause of scleritis.
Rheumatoid factor: Autoantibody against IgG Fc, positive in many with RA and negative in spondyloarthropathies.
Rheumatoid nodules: Firm lumps under the skin over pressure points in rheumatoid arthritis.
Rheumatology: The medical specialty that manages joint, muscle and autoimmune inflammatory diseases.
Rhinitis medicamentosa: Rebound nasal congestion caused by overuse of decongestant sprays.
Rhinosinusitis: Inflammation of the nasal lining and the paranasal sinuses together.
Rhinovirus: The commonest cause of the common cold.
Rhomboid: A slanted box shape, like a squashed rectangle.
Rhonchi: Low-pitched, snoring sounds from secretions in larger airways.
Rhythm control: Trying to restore and keep normal sinus rhythm, with drugs or cardioversion.
Richter's hernia: Only part of the bowel wall is trapped, so it can strangulate without causing obstruction.
Richter's transformation: CLL turning into an aggressive high-grade lymphoma.
Rifampicin: Antibiotic added for prosthetic valves because it penetrates biofilm.
Rifamycins: The antibiotic family that includes rifampicin and rifabutin.
Rifaximin: Poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria in hepatic encephalopathy.
Right HF: Right-sided heart failure: fluid backs up into the body, causing raised JVP, oedema and liver swelling.
Right atrium: The heart chamber that receives blood from the body before passing it to the right ventricle.
Right axis deviation: QRS axis beyond +90 degrees, often from right ventricular hypertrophy.
Right heart: The right atrium and ventricle, which pump blood to the lungs.
Right heart catheterisation: A catheter passed into the right heart and pulmonary artery to measure pressures directly; the gold standard.
Right heart failure: Failure of the right ventricle causing raised JVP, oedema, ascites and hepatomegaly.
Right heart strain: The right ventricle under excess pressure load, often from pulmonary hypertension.
Right hemicolectomy: Removal of the caecum, ascending colon and terminal ileum, joining ileum to colon.
Right main bronchus: The airway to the right lung; wider and more vertical than the left.
Right upper sternal edge: The aortic area: 2nd intercostal space just right of the sternum.
Right ventricular hypertrophy: Thickening of the right ventricle wall from pumping against high lung pressures.
Right-sided failure: Failure of the right ventricle, causing raised JVP, liver swelling and leg oedema.
Right-to-left shunt: Blood passing from the right heart to the left without going through the lungs.
Rigid abdomen: A board-like abdomen from muscle spasm over inflamed peritoneum.
Rigid sigmoidoscopy: Examination of the rectum and sigmoid with a straight rigid scope; used to untwist sigmoid volvulus.
Rigidity: Constant, involuntary board-like tension of the abdominal wall, typical of generalised peritonitis.
Rigler sign: Gas seen on both sides of the bowel wall on X-ray; a sign of perforation.
Rigler's sign: Gas outlining both sides of the bowel wall on abdominal X-ray, indicating perforation.
Rigors: Uncontrollable shaking with fever, suggesting bacteraemia.
Rimegepant: An oral CGRP receptor antagonist (gepant) for acute treatment or prevention of migraine.
Ring sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron trapped in a ring around the nucleus; diagnostic of sideroblastic anaemia.
Ring-enhancing lesion: A lesion whose rim lights up with contrast on CT or MRI while the centre stays dark.
Ringed sideroblasts: Red cell precursors with iron-loaded mitochondria ringing the nucleus, seen on marrow iron stain in MDS.
Ringer's lactate: A balanced crystalloid fluid, very similar to Hartmann's solution.
Rinne: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction.
Rinne's test: Tuning fork test comparing air and bone conduction in one ear; positive (air louder) is normal or sensorineural.
Risedronate: Oral bisphosphonate, an alternative first-line option.
Risk factors: Things that make a disease more likely or more severe.
Risk stratification: Sorting patients by how likely they are to have a bad outcome, to guide treatment.
Risk-stratified: Sorting patients by their risk to decide who needs admission and who can go home.
Risk-stratify: Sort patients by how likely they are to have a bad outcome, to guide treatment.
Ritonavir: A protease inhibitor used in low doses to boost levels of other protease inhibitors.
Rituximab: Antibody drug that depletes B cells; used in warm AIHA.
Rivastigmine: An acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, available as a patch, used in Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia.
Romberg: A test where the patient sways or falls with eyes shut, showing loss of position sense.
Romberg test: Standing with eyes shut to test position sense and balance.
Romberg's: Unsteadiness with eyes closed, showing loss of position sense.
Rome criteria: Symptom-based diagnostic criteria for IBS centred on pain linked to defecation.
Root entry zone: The point where a cranial nerve enters the brainstem; vulnerable to compression and demyelination.
Ropinirole: Oral dopamine agonist for Parkinson's and restless legs.
Rotation: Turning around an axis; in torsion, the testis spins on its cord.
Rotational: Spinning; the sensation that you or the room is turning.
Roth spots: Retinal haemorrhages with pale centres, seen on fundoscopy in endocarditis.
Rotigotine: Dopamine agonist given as a skin patch; used when patients are nil by mouth.
Roux-en-Y gastric bypass: Bariatric operation creating a small stomach pouch joined directly to the small bowel.
