Trigeminovascular system: Trigeminal nerve fibres supplying meningeal blood vessels; their activation drives migraine pain.
Trigger-directed workup: Tests chosen to look for the specific cause the history suggests.
Triggers: Factors that set off an attack, such as poor sleep or stress.
Triglyceride: The main storage form of fat: glycerol plus three fatty acids.
Triglycerides: Blood fats from diet and the liver; very high levels risk pancreatitis.
Trimester: One of three roughly 13-week periods of pregnancy.
Trimethoprim: An antibiotic that raises creatinine and potassium by blocking tubular secretion.
Triple assessment: Clinical examination, imaging and core needle biopsy of a breast lump.
Triple therapy: ICS + LABA + LAMA, usually in one inhaler.
Triple-negative: Tumour negative for ER, PR and HER2, so no targeted hormone or HER2 drug works.
Triptan: A 5-HT1B/1D agonist used to treat acute migraine attacks.
Triptans: Serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists, such as sumatriptan, used to treat acute migraine.
Trismus: Difficulty opening the mouth because of jaw muscle spasm.
Troisier's sign: Finding a palpable Virchow's node on examination.
Trophic changes: Shiny skin, hair loss and thick nails from long-term poor blood supply.
Troponin: Heart muscle protein released into blood when myocytes die; raised in MI.
Trousseau's sign: Carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated above systolic pressure.
Trousseau's syndrome: Migratory thrombophlebitis linked to pancreatic cancer, not myeloma.
Truelove and Witts: Criteria grading UC flare severity by stool count and systemic markers.
Tryptase: Mast cell enzyme measured in blood to confirm anaphylaxis.
Tuberculin skin test: Another name for the Mantoux test: tuberculin injected into the skin and induration measured.
Tubular epithelial cells: The cells lining the kidney tubules that reabsorb salt and water.
Tubular flow: The rate of fluid moving through the kidney tubules.
Tubuloglomerular feedback: The kidney's reflex in which sodium delivery to the distal tubule adjusts afferent arteriole tone.
Tumour: An abnormal growth of cells; here a cancer.
Tumour burden: The total amount of cancer in the body.
Tumour infiltration: Cancer cells growing into and replacing normal tissue.
Tumour localisation: Imaging to find exactly where a tumour sits once blood tests suggest it is there.
Tumour lysis syndrome: Rapid tumour cell death releasing potassium, phosphate and urate, with low calcium, risking AKI and arrhythmia.
Tumour marker: A blood substance made by a cancer, used to track response and recurrence.
Tumour markers: Substances in the blood, such as AFP and hCG, made by some cancers.
Tumour suppressor gene: A gene that normally stops cells dividing out of control.
Tumour suppressor genes: Genes that normally stop cells growing out of control; loss of both copies allows cancer.
Tuning fork: A metal fork that vibrates when struck, placed on bony points to test vibration sense.
Tunnel vision: Loss of peripheral vision so only the centre remains, a common pre-faint symptom.
Turbid: Cloudy, as CSF looks when full of white cells.
Turbulent flow: Disorganised blood flow that damages the valve lining.
Turner syndrome: Chromosomal condition (45,X) in girls with one X, so an X-linked recessive gene can be expressed.
Turnover: The time taken for new skin cells to replace old ones.
Tympanic: Drum-like, hollow note on percussion, caused by gas-filled bowel.
Tympanic membrane: The eardrum; red and bulging in acute otitis media.
Type 1: Respiratory failure with low oxygen but normal or low carbon dioxide: an oxygenation problem.
Type 1 diabetes: Autoimmune destruction of insulin-making cells in the pancreas.
Type 2: Respiratory failure with low oxygen and carbon dioxide above 6 kPa: a ventilation problem.
Type 2 diabetes: Diabetes from insulin resistance, which raises infection risk.
Type 2 respiratory failure: Low pO2 with a raised pCO2 (above 6.0 kPa).
Type 7: Entirely liquid stool on the Bristol stool chart.
Type A: The influenza type that infects humans and animals and can undergo antigenic shift.
Type B: The influenza type found mainly in humans; causes seasonal outbreaks but not pandemics.
Type I hypersensitivity: Immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction within minutes, e.g. hay fever, urticaria, anaphylaxis.
Type II hypersensitivity: Antibodies binding a fixed cell-surface antigen, causing damage or blocking function.
Type II respiratory failure: Low oxygen with a raised carbon dioxide from inadequate ventilation.
Type III hypersensitivity: Immune-complex-mediated reaction, causing inflammation where complexes deposit.
Type IV hypersensitivity: Delayed, T-cell-mediated reaction taking 2 to 3 days, e.g. allergic contact dermatitis.
Tyrosine kinase: Enzyme that switches on cell signalling; overactive in CML.
Tyrosine kinase inhibitor: A drug that blocks a growth-signalling enzyme; imatinib is one.
U score: British Thyroid Association ultrasound grade from U1 (benign) to U5 (malignant).
U&E: Urea and electrolytes: a blood test of kidney function and salts.
U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: the routine kidney blood test (sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine).
UAS7: Urticaria activity score over 7 days (0 to 42), tracking wheals and itch.
UC: Ulcerative colitis: continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon starting at the rectum.
UIP: Usual interstitial pneumonia: the basal, peripheral honeycombing CT pattern typical of IPF.
UKHCDO: UK Haemophilia Centre Doctors' Organisation, which writes UK haemophilia guidelines.
UKHSA: UK Health Security Agency, the public health body that receives notifications and runs contact tracing.
UKMEC: UK criteria grading how safe each contraceptive is for a given condition; 4 means unacceptable risk.
ULN: Upper limit of normal for a lab test.
UMN: Upper motor neurone: from cortex to brainstem; a facial UMN lesion spares the forehead.
UMN signs: Signs of damage above the anterior horn cell: brisk reflexes, spasticity, weakness, upgoing plantars.
URTI: Upper respiratory tract infection, such as a cold or sore throat.
USS KUB: Ultrasound of the kidneys, ureters and bladder, used to look for obstruction.
UV exposure: Sunlight, a common trigger for cold sore reactivation.
Uhthoff's phenomenon: Temporary worsening of MS symptoms with heat, such as a hot bath or exercise.
Ulceration: Formation of an open sore that breaks through the skin.
Ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease with continuous mucosal inflammation of the colon, rarely causing fistulas.
Ulcers: Breaks in the skin or mucosa exposing the tissue underneath.
Ulnar: On the little finger side of the forearm or hand.
Ulnar deviation: Drift of the fingers towards the little finger side at the MCP joints.
Ulnar nerve: Nerve supplying most small hand muscles and feeling to the little finger side of the hand.
Ultrasound abdomen: Sound-wave imaging of the abdomen, very sensitive for free fluid.
Ultrasound bladder: Bladder scan measuring the post-void residual volume.
Ultrasound-guided: Using ultrasound to place the needle accurately.
Ultrasound-guided aspiration: Drawing pus out through a needle while watching on ultrasound.
Umbrella term: A general name covering several related conditions.
Uncomplicated: Without any added problems or high-risk features.
Unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; rises when red cells break down.
Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation: Mitochondria burn fuel without making ATP, producing heat and lactic acid.
Underlying cause: The disease or problem that led to the dehydration.
Underlying precipitant: The trigger that started the DKA, such as infection or missed insulin, which must also be treated.
Undescended testis: A testis that has not moved down into the scrotum by birth or infancy.
Unequal pupils: Pupils of different sizes; a late sign of brain compression on one side.
Unfractionated heparin: An IV anticoagulant that stops clots growing and can be quickly reversed.
Units of blood: Standard bags of donated red cells, each raising Hb by about 10 g/L.
Universal donor: Group O red cells, which lack A and B antigens.
Unmyelinated fibres: Small nerve fibres without a myelin sheath, including autonomic fibres; vulnerable in diabetes.
Unopposed oestrogen: Oestrogen action without the balancing effect of progesterone.
Unpaired chains: Excess alpha or beta chains with no partner, which clump and damage red cell precursors.
Unpasteurised: Not heat-treated to kill bacteria, so may carry Listeria.
Unprotected intercourse: Sex without a condom, the main risk for sexually transmitted infection.
Unprovoked: Occurring without an immediate trigger such as low glucose, alcohol withdrawal or head injury.
Unresectable: A cancer that cannot be removed surgically.
Unresponsive: Not reacting to voice or pain.
Unstable angina: Chest pain at rest or worsening, from plaque rupture without infarction; troponin normal.
Unsynchronised shock: A shock given at any point in the cycle, used in VF and pulseless VT.
Unvaccinated: Not having received a vaccine, here the MMR.
Unwise decision: A choice others disagree with; under the MCA it is not evidence of lacking capacity.
Upgoing plantar: Big toe extends upwards when the sole is stroked; an upper motor neuron sign.
Upper GI endoscopy: A camera passed through the mouth to view the oesophagus, stomach and duodenum.
Upper airway: The nose, mouth, pharynx and larynx, above the trachea.
Upper airway obstruction: Narrowing or blockage of the nose, throat or larynx that hampers breathing in.
Upper airway surgery: Operations to widen the throat, such as removing tonsils or palate tissue; third-line and rarely used.
Upper lobe diversion: Prominent upper lobe vessels on CXR from raised pulmonary venous pressure.
Upper lobe emphysema: Emphysema mainly in the top of the lungs, typical of smoking and suitable for volume reduction surgery.
Upper motor neurone: The nerve cell running from the brain down the spinal cord to the anterior horn.
Upper outer quadrant: The part of the breast towards the armpit; holds most breast tissue.
Upper reference limit: The top of the normal range for a lab test.
Upper third: The top part of the oesophagus, in the neck and upper chest.
Upper urinary tract: The kidneys, renal pelvis and ureters.
Upper zones: The top third of each lung field on a chest X-ray.
Upregulate: Increase the number or activity of something, such as receptors on a cell.
Uraemia: Build-up of waste products in the blood, causing nausea, confusion, pericarditis and a grey-brown skin tinge.
Uraemic: Caused by a build-up of urea and waste in the blood from kidney failure.
Uraemic pericarditis: Pericardial inflammation from uraemia; chest pain relieved by sitting forward and a dialysis indication.
Uraemic tinge: A brown-grey or sallow skin colour from retained waste products in kidney failure.
Urate oxidase: An enzyme that converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin.
Urate-lowering therapy: Long-term drugs (allopurinol, febuxostat) that lower serum urate to prevent gout attacks.
Urea: A waste product of protein breakdown cleared by the kidneys; rises disproportionately in pre-renal AKI.
Urease: Bacterial enzyme that splits urea into ammonia, making urine alkaline.
Ureteric: Relating to the ureter, the tube from kidney to bladder.
Ureteric dilation: Widening of the ureters, which slows urine flow.
Ureteroscopy: Camera passed up the ureter to remove or fragment a stone.
Ureters: The tubes carrying urine from each kidney to the bladder.
Urethra: The tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.
Urethral closure pressure: The pressure the urethra and pelvic floor hold against to keep urine in.
Urethral instrumentation: Passing any device up the urethra, such as a catheter or cystoscope.
Urethral swab: A sample taken from inside the urethra to test for infection.
Urethritis: Inflammation of the urethra causing dysuria and discharge.
Urge incontinence: Leakage after a sudden strong urge to pass urine, caused by detrusor overactivity.
Urgency: Sudden strong need to pass urine.
Urgent referral: Referral to be seen quickly, usually within two weeks, when cancer is suspected.
Uric acid: The end product of purine breakdown in humans; urate is its salt form.
Urinalysis: Testing urine, usually with a dipstick, for blood, protein, glucose and infection.
Urinary alkalinisation: IV sodium bicarbonate to make urine alkaline, trapping salicylate in the urine to speed excretion.
Urinary antigen: A urine test detecting bacterial proteins, used for Legionella and Strep pneumoniae.
Urinary calcium: The amount of calcium lost in urine.
Urinary catheter: A tube passed into the bladder to drain and accurately measure urine output.
Urinary pathogens: Bacteria that usually cause urinary tract infection, chiefly E. coli.
Urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder fully.
Urinary sodium: The concentration of sodium in the urine; low when the kidney is holding on to salt.
Urinary tract: The kidneys, ureters, bladder and urethra.
Urine culture: Growing bacteria from urine to identify them and their antibiotic sensitivities.
Urine cytology: Microscopy of urine for cancer cells; insensitive for low-grade tumours.
Urine dipstick: A test strip dipped in urine to detect blood, protein, glucose, leucocytes and nitrites.
Urine ketones: Ketones detected on a urine dipstick, graded from + to ++++.
Urine microscopy: Looking at urine under a microscope for red cells, white cells, casts and organisms.
Urine osmolality: How concentrated the urine is; above 500 mOsm/kg suggests pre-renal AKI.
Urine output: Volume of urine produced; falls in shock and AKI.
Urine protein:creatinine ratio: A spot urine test that estimates daily protein loss without a 24 hour collection.
Urodynamic studies: Bladder pressure tests that show detrusor overactivity or stress leakage.
Urodynamics: Pressure studies of bladder filling and voiding, used when the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery.
Urological: Relating to the urinary tract and male genital organs.
Uropathogen: An organism that commonly causes urinary infection.
Urothelial carcinoma: Another name for transitional cell carcinoma.
Urothelium: Transitional epithelium lining the renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and urethra.
Urticaria: Itchy, raised red wheals (hives) caused by histamine release in the skin.
Urticarial vasculitis: Inflamed vessels causing wheal-like lesions that last over 24 hours and leave bruising.
Ustekinumab: Monoclonal antibody against the p40 subunit of IL-12 and IL-23.
Utricle: An inner ear sac whose macula holds the otoconia.
Utricular macula: The sensory patch in the utricle where otoconia normally sit, detecting linear movement and gravity.
Uveitis: Inflammation of the uvea, causing pain, photophobia and blurred vision.
Uvula: The small fleshy tag hanging from the soft palate; pushed away from a quinsy.
V wave: JVP wave from right atrial filling in systole; giant in tricuspid regurgitation.
V/Q mismatch: Air reaching lung units that get no blood flow, so oxygen is not picked up.
V/Q ratio: Ventilation to perfusion ratio; falls when collapsed lung is still perfused.
V/Q scan: Ventilation/perfusion scan; shows lung areas that are ventilated but not perfused.
V1: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve: forehead, eye and upper nose.
V1-V3: Chest ECG leads overlying the right ventricle and septum.
V2: Maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve: cheek, upper lip and upper teeth.
V2 receptor: ADH receptor in the collecting duct that triggers aquaporin-2 insertion.
V3: Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve: jaw, lower lip, chin and chewing muscles.
VAP: Ventilator-associated pneumonia: pneumonia arising 48 hours or more after intubation.
VBG: Venous blood gas: gives pH and bicarbonate reliably, but not oxygen.
VCA IgM: Antibody to the EBV viral capsid antigen showing recent infection.
VEGF: Vascular endothelial growth factor: signal released by ischaemic tissue that drives new vessel growth.
VEGF inhibitors: Drugs that block vascular endothelial growth factor, stopping leaky new vessel growth.
VEP: Visual evoked potentials: measures conduction time along the visual pathway; delayed in demyelination.
VF: Ventricular fibrillation: chaotic ventricular activity with no cardiac output.
VFR: Visiting friends and relatives: travellers at high risk because they often skip prophylaxis.
VGCC: Voltage-gated calcium channel at the nerve terminal; targeted by antibodies in LEMS.
VOC: Vaso-occlusive crisis: painful sickling episode from blocked small vessels.
VP shunt: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt: a tube draining CSF from the brain's ventricles to the abdomen.
VSD: Ventricular septal defect: a hole in the septum; after MI it is septal rupture.
VT: Ventricular tachycardia: a fast, broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles.
VTE risk: Higher chance of developing a blood clot in a vein.
VZV: Varicella zoster virus, the chickenpox and shingles virus; it causes Ramsay Hunt syndrome.
Vaccination: Giving a vaccine to prevent infections such as flu and pneumococcus.
Vagal: Relating to the vagus nerve, which controls gut movement and slows the heart.
Vagal manoeuvres: Valsalva or carotid sinus massage, which slow AV node conduction.
Vagal reflex: Reflex through the vagus nerve that slows the heart and lowers blood pressure.
Vagal tone: The background activity of the vagus nerve, which drives gut movement.
Vaginal candidiasis: Thrush; a common side effect of SGLT2 inhibitors due to glucose in the urine.
Vaginal delivery: Birth through the birth canal, exposing the baby to genital secretions.
Vaginal swab: A sample taken from the vagina with a swab for microscopy or culture.
Vagus nerve: Tenth cranial nerve; carries parasympathetic signals that slow the heart.
Valaciclovir: Prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption, so fewer daily doses.
Valgus: Deformity with the knee pointing inwards, giving a knock-kneed look.
Valid consent: Consent given voluntarily by an informed person with capacity.
Validate: Acknowledge to the patient that their symptoms are real and taken seriously.
Valsalva: Forced expiration against a closed airway to increase vagal tone.
Valve area: The opening area of the aortic valve; normal is 3-4 cm².
Valve incompetence: Vein valves that no longer close, letting blood flow backwards.
Valve pockets: Small spaces behind vein valves where blood flows slowly and clots start.
Valve repair: Surgery that fixes the patient's own valve rather than replacing it.
Valve replacement: Surgery that removes a diseased valve and fits a mechanical or tissue valve.
Valvular disease: Disease of the heart valves, such as stenosis or regurgitation.
Valvuloplasty: Widening a narrowed valve, usually with a balloon passed through a vein.
Vancomycin: IV glycopeptide antibiotic used for MRSA.
Varenicline: A partial nicotinic agonist used to help people stop smoking.
Variceal bleeding: Bleeding from ruptured varices, usually presenting as haematemesis.
Variceal haemorrhage: Bleeding from dilated veins (varices) in the oesophagus or stomach caused by portal hypertension.
Varices: Dilated collateral veins, usually in the oesophagus, that can bleed catastrophically.
Varus: Deformity with the knee pointing outwards, giving a bow-legged look.
Vasa nervorum: The tiny blood vessels supplying peripheral nerves.
Vascular calcification: Calcium deposits in artery walls, raising cardiovascular risk in CKD.
Vascular catheter: A tube placed into a large vein, for example for dialysis.
Vascular compartment: The space inside the blood vessels.
Vascular dementia: Dementia from cumulative ischaemic brain damage, causing stepwise decline.
Vascular exam: Examination of pulses, colour, temperature and capillary refill.
Vascular pedicle: The stalk carrying the blood supply to an organ, here the spermatic cord.
Vascular permeability: How leaky blood vessel walls are; when raised, fluid escapes into tissues and causes swelling.
Vascular phenomena: Duke minor criteria from emboli, such as Janeway lesions or infarcts.
Vascular plexus: A network of interconnecting blood vessels.
Vascular remodelling: Thickening of blood vessel walls over time, making the narrowing permanent.
Vascular risk factors: Things that raise heart attack and stroke risk, such as smoking, diabetes and hypertension.
Vascular smooth muscle: Muscle in blood vessel walls that contracts to narrow the vessel and relaxes to widen it.
Vascular supply: The blood vessels feeding a tissue.
Vascular surgeon: Surgeon who treats diseases of arteries and veins.
Vascular surgery: Surgical specialty treating diseases of the arteries and veins.
Vascular tone: The degree of tightening of blood vessel walls, which maintains blood pressure.
Vasculitic: Caused by vasculitis, inflammation of blood vessel walls.
Vasculopathy: Disease of the blood vessel walls.
Vaso-occlusion: Blockage of small vessels by sickled red cells, causing infarction and pain.
Vaso-occlusive crisis: Painful episode where sickled cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia, often in bone.
Vasoactive: Able to widen or narrow blood vessels.
Vasoactive mediators: Chemicals released from the clot and platelets, such as serotonin, that narrow vessels and airways.
Vasoconstriction: Narrowing of blood vessels, reducing blood flow and swelling.
Vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, lowering blood pressure.
Vasogenic oedema: Brain swelling from fluid leaking out of damaged blood vessels into the surrounding tissue.
Vasomotor: Controlling the narrowing and widening of blood vessels.
Vasopressin: Hormone used as a second vasopressor when noradrenaline alone is not enough.
Vasopressor: Drug that constricts blood vessels to raise blood pressure, e.g. noradrenaline.
Vasovagal: Involving the vagus nerve and blood vessels: slowing of the heart plus vessel dilation.
Vasovagal syncope: A faint from a reflex drop in heart rate and BP, with pallor and no rash.
Vastus lateralis: Muscle of the outer thigh, the site for IM adrenaline.
Vegan: A diet with no animal products, so it lacks natural vitamin B12.
Vegetation: An infected clump of platelets, fibrin and bacteria stuck to a heart valve.
Velcro crackles: Fine, end-inspiratory crackles like pulling apart velcro; typical of pulmonary fibrosis.
Venepuncture: Taking blood from a vein, a classic vasovagal trigger.
Venesection: Therapeutic removal of blood (usually 450 to 500 mL) to remove iron.
Venodilation: Widening of veins, which pools blood and reduces preload.
Venography: Imaging of veins; MR or CT venography shows the cerebral venous sinuses.
Venous: From a vein: lower pressure, so blood collects slowly.
Venous congestion: Pooling of blood in the veins, causing swelling and pain.
Venous eczema: Itchy, scaly skin on the lower legs from chronic venous hypertension, often bilateral.
Venous hypertension: Persistently high pressure in the leg veins.
Venous looping: Veins that loop back on themselves, a sign of retinal ischaemia.
Venous obstruction: A blockage to blood flowing back through a vein.
Venous outflow: Blood draining out of an organ through its veins.
Venous outflow obstruction: A blockage to blood draining out of the brain, raising pressure inside the skull.
Venous pooling: Blood collecting in the leg veins on standing, reducing return to the heart.
Venous return: Blood flow back to the heart; raising the legs increases it.
Venous sinus thrombosis: A clot in the brain's draining venous sinuses, which can raise ICP and mimic IIH.
Venous stasis: Slow or pooled blood flow in the veins.
Venous thrombosis: A clot in a vein, such as a DVT.
Ventilation: Mechanical breathing support from a machine.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia: Pneumonia arising in a patient on a ventilator, often from Pseudomonas.
Ventilatory drive: The brain's signal to breathe, set mainly by carbon dioxide levels.
Ventilatory response: The body breathing harder in response to a rise in carbon dioxide.
Ventricle: One of the two lower pumping chambers of the heart.
Ventricular tachycardia: Fast broad-complex rhythm from the ventricles; can cause collapse or sudden death.
Ventriculoperitoneal shunt: A tube draining excess brain fluid from a ventricle into the abdomen.
Venturi mask: A mask that delivers a fixed, controlled oxygen percentage.
Verapamil: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that slows the AV node.
Verbal de-escalation: Calm, non-confrontational talking to reduce agitation without drugs.
Vertebrae: The bones that make up the spine.
Vertebral body: The thick, weight-bearing front block of each vertebra.
Vertebral collapse: Compression fracture of a vertebral body, causing back pain and height loss.
Vertebral osteomyelitis: Infection of the bones of the spine.
Vertebral wedge fracture: Collapse of the front of a vertebral body, typical of osteoporosis.
Vertical transmission: Passing an infection from mother to baby during pregnancy or birth.
Vertigo: A false sense that you or the room is spinning.
Vesicle fluid: Clear fluid inside a blister; in VZV it is full of virus and can be swabbed for PCR.
Vesicles: Small fluid-filled blisters under 5 mm across.
Vesicovaginal fistula: An abnormal opening between bladder and vagina causing constant leakage, often after obstructed labour.
Vessel calibre: The width of a blood vessel's channel.
Vessel integrity: How strong and intact a blood vessel wall is.
Vestibular: Relating to the inner-ear balance system.
Vestibular apparatus: The semicircular canals, utricle and saccule that sense balance.
Vestibular nerve: The nerve carrying balance signals from the inner ear to the brainstem.
Vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: continuous vertigo for days, hearing normal.
Vestibular organs: The parts of the inner ear that detect head movement and gravity.
Vestibular rehabilitation: Exercise therapy that helps the brain compensate for vestibular problems.
Vestibular sedatives: Drugs such as prochlorperazine and cinnarizine that dampen vertigo but slow recovery if used long-term.
Vestibular system: The inner ear balance organs that sense head movement and position.
Vibration sense: Feeling a vibrating 128 Hz tuning fork on a bony point; lost early in neuropathy.
Vicious cycle: A loop where each step makes the next worse, so the problem keeps itself going.
Villi: Finger-like projections of the small bowel lining that absorb nutrients.
Viraemic: Having virus circulating in the blood; usually the most infectious phase.
Viral PCR: A test that detects viral genetic material to identify the exact virus.
Viral RNA replication: The virus copying its RNA genetic material to make new viruses.
Viral hepatitis: Liver inflammation caused by hepatitis viruses A to E.
Viral hepatitis screen: Panel of blood tests for hepatitis A to E antibodies, antigens and viral genetic material.
Viral illness: An infection caused by a virus, such as a cold or flu.
Viral load: Amount of HIV RNA in blood, measured by PCR, showing disease activity.
Viral pneumonia: Infection of the lung tissue itself caused by a virus.
Viral prodrome: The early flu-like symptoms of a viral infection before the main illness.
Viral reactivation: A dormant virus in nerve cells becoming active again.
Viral screen: Blood tests for hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, E) to exclude viral causes.
Viral serology: Blood tests for antibodies or antigens to identify viral infection.
Virchow's node: Enlarged left supraclavicular lymph node from abdominal cancer spread.
Virchow's triad: The three causes of thrombosis: venous stasis, endothelial injury and hypercoagulability.
Virion: A complete virus particle outside a cell.
Virulence factors: Molecules a microbe uses to infect and damage the host.
Viruses: Tiny infectious agents that multiply only inside cells; antibiotics do not work on them.
Visceral adiposity: Fat stored around the abdominal organs, the most metabolically harmful type.
Visceral pain: Dull, poorly localised pain from internal organs.
Visceral pericardium: The inner layer of the pericardium stuck to the heart's surface.
Visceral peritoneum: The peritoneal layer covering the organs; autonomic nerves make its pain dull and poorly localised.
Viscosity: Thickness or stickiness of a fluid, here blood.
Viscus: A hollow internal organ such as the stomach, duodenum or colon.
Visible haematuria: Blood that can be seen in the urine; also called macroscopic or frank haematuria.
Visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart (6/6 is normal).
Visual agnosia: Seeing objects but being unable to recognise them.
Visual field defects: Loss of parts of the visual field, often from a pituitary mass pressing on the optic chiasm.
Visual field deficit: Loss of part of the field of vision, such as a homonymous hemianopia.
Visual hallucinations: Seeing things that are not there.
Vital capacity: The most air that can be breathed out after a full breath in.
Vital signs: Basic observations: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, consciousness.
Vitamin B1: Thiamine, needed for energy production in nerves and brain.
Vitamin B12: Cobalamin, a water-soluble vitamin from animal foods, needed for DNA synthesis and nerve myelin.
Vitamin B6: Pyridoxine, a vitamin needed to make aminotransferase enzymes such as ALT.
Vitamin C: Ascorbic acid; it boosts iron absorption from the gut.
Vitamin D: A vitamin that raises calcium absorption from the gut.
Vitamin D analogue: Topical drug like calcipotriol that reduces keratinocyte proliferation.
Vitamin D loading: Giving high doses of vitamin D over a few weeks to quickly replace body stores.
Vitamin D receptors: Proteins inside cells, including muscle, that respond to active vitamin D.
Vitamin K: A vitamin the liver needs to make clotting factors; warfarin blocks its action.
Vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment in patches; associated with Addison's.
Vitrectomy: Surgery to remove the vitreous gel, blood or scar tissue.
Vitreous haemorrhage: Bleeding into the vitreous gel, causing floaters or sudden vision loss.
Vmax: Peak velocity of blood through the aortic valve on echo.
Voice tremor: A shaky, wavering voice caused by tremor of the laryngeal muscles.
Volatile acid: An acid that can be breathed out as a gas; carbonic acid leaves as CO2.
Voltage-gated sodium channels: Membrane channels that open with depolarisation to let sodium in and fire action potentials.
Volume depletion: Loss of fluid from the body's circulation.
Volume overload: A heart chamber having to handle more blood than normal, which stretches it over time.
Volume-depleted: Having too little fluid in the circulation.
Voluntary movement: Movement the person chooses to make, such as reaching for a cup.
Volvulus: Twisting of a segment of bowel around its own mesentery, causing obstruction and possible ischaemia.
Von Graefe's sign: The upper eyelid lags behind the eye when looking down.
Von Hippel-Lindau: Inherited tumour syndrome associated with phaeochromocytoma and renal cancers.
Vulval: Relating to the vulva, the external female genitalia.
WBC: White blood cells; the count rises with infection or inflammation.
WBCs: White blood cells, which fight infection.
WBRT: Whole-brain radiotherapy: radiation to the entire brain for multiple metastases.
WPW: Wolff-Parkinson-White: an accessory pathway causing delta waves and re-entrant tachycardias.
Waddling gait: A side-to-side walk caused by weak hip muscles.
Waist circumference: Measure of central fat; above 94 cm in men or 80 cm in women means raised CV risk.
Waldenström macroglobulinaemia: A lymphoma producing an IgM paraprotein.
Waldeyer's ring: The ring of lymphoid tissue (adenoids, palatine and lingual tonsils) guarding the throat.
Walking pneumonia: A mild atypical pneumonia, usually Mycoplasma, where the patient feels unwell but stays up and about.
Wall stress: Force per unit area acting on a vessel wall.
Wall tension: The stretching force within a vessel wall; rises with pressure and radius.
Walled-off: Surrounded by a fibrous capsule, separating the pus from surrounding tissue.
Wallenberg's: Lateral medullary syndrome from a PICA infarct, with crossed sensory loss and Horner's.
Warfarin: A vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant; the only oral anticoagulant for mechanical valves.
Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia: Antibodies against red cells active at body temperature; associated with CLL.
Warmed IV fluids: Fluids heated to about body temperature and given into a vein to rewarm and support circulation.
Washout: Surgical flushing of an infected joint to remove pus and bacteria.
Washout period: Time allowed after stopping a drug for it to leave the body before, for example, conception.
Wasting: Visible loss of muscle bulk, a lower motor neuron sign.
Watch and wait: Monitoring without treatment until disease causes symptoms; used in early CLL.
Watch-and-wait: Monitoring without treatment, starting only if things change.
Watchful waiting: Monitoring without treatment until the disease progresses or causes symptoms.
Water bottle sign: A large, globular heart shadow on chest X-ray from a big pericardial effusion.
Water hammer pulse: Another name for the collapsing pulse of aortic regurgitation.
Water-soluble vitamin: A vitamin that dissolves in water rather than fat, such as B vitamins and vitamin C.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia, causing acute adrenal failure.
Watering: Excess tears running from the eye.
Waterlow: Pressure ulcer risk score: 10 at risk, 15 high risk, 20 very high risk.
Waterlow score: Tool that scores pressure-sore risk, not malnutrition.
Weak stream: Reduced force of the urine flow.
Weakness: Reduced muscle power, a sign of neurological damage.
Wean: Reduce a drug dose gradually rather than stopping it suddenly.
Wearing-off: Return of Parkinson's symptoms before the next levodopa dose is due.
Weber: Tuning fork test placed on the forehead to lateralise hearing loss.
Weber's syndrome: Midbrain stroke: ipsilateral oculomotor palsy with contralateral hemiparesis.
Weber's test: Tuning fork on the forehead; it lateralises to the good ear in sensorineural loss and the bad ear in conductive loss.
Weibel-Palade bodies: Storage granules in endothelial cells that hold von Willebrand factor.
Weigh up: Use the information, balancing risks and benefits, to reach a decision.
Weight loss: The most important lifestyle measure in OSA, reducing fat around the pharynx.
Weight-bear: Put weight through a leg when standing or walking.
Weight-bearing exercise: Exercise on your feet, such as walking, which loads bone and helps keep it strong.
Weight-bearing joints: Joints that carry body weight, such as hips, knees and spine.
Well-demarcated: With a sharp, clear edge between affected and normal skin.
Wellens syndrome: Rest chest pain with deep or biphasic T waves in V2–V3, signalling critical proximal LAD stenosis.
Wells score: A clinical score of DVT probability; 2 or more means DVT likely.
Wenckebach: Mobitz I block: PR lengthens until a beat is dropped.
Wernicke's: Receptive aphasia from a superior temporal gyrus lesion: fluent speech with poor comprehension.
Wernicke's encephalopathy: Acute brain dysfunction from thiamine deficiency: confusion, ataxia and eye movement problems.
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Wernicke's encephalopathy progressing to Korsakoff's permanent memory loss with confabulation.
Wet wrapping: Damp bandages over emollient or steroid to boost absorption in severe childhood eczema.
Wheal: A raised, pale or red, itchy swelling of the skin that fades within 24 hours.
Wheal-and-flare: A raised swelling with surrounding redness, the immediate IgE skin reaction.
Wheeze: Whistling expiratory sound from narrowed lower airways (bronchospasm).
Wheezing: A high-pitched whistling sound on breathing out caused by narrowed airways.
Whipple procedure: Pancreaticoduodenectomy: removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, bile duct and gallbladder.
Whipple's triad: Hypoglycaemic symptoms, a low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is given.
White blood cells: Immune cells in the blood: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils.
White cell count (WCC): The number of white blood cells in a sample; high counts suggest inflammation or infection.
White ethnicity: People of European descent, who have a higher risk of osteoporosis.
Whole blood PCR: A blood test that detects meningococcal DNA when LP cannot be done.
Whole-brain irradiation: Radiotherapy given to the whole brain.
Whole-brain radiotherapy: Radiation to the whole brain, used for numerous metastases, at a cost to memory and cognition.
Wide-bore cannula: A large-diameter plastic tube inserted through the skin.
Widened mediastinum: A broadened central shadow on chest X-ray, here from a dilated dissected aorta.
Wilson and Jungner: The WHO criteria a disease and test must meet to justify population screening.
Wilson's disease: Autosomal recessive copper overload with liver and neuropsychiatric disease.
Window period: Time after infection when a test can still be negative.
Withdraw gradually: Reduce the dose step by step to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
Withdrawal: Unpleasant symptoms when a drug the body has adapted to is stopped.
Withhold: Temporarily not give a dose of a drug.
Witnessed apnoeas: Pauses in breathing during sleep seen by a bed partner, often ending in a snort or gasp.
Wolff-Chaikoff effect: Iodine excess temporarily shutting down thyroid hormone synthesis, causing hypothyroidism.
Work-up: The set of tests used to investigate a symptom.
Wound breakdown: Separation or failure of a healing wound, often due to infection.
Wound dehiscence: Separation of the edges of a closed surgical wound.
Wound healing: The body's repair of damaged tissue, slowed by diabetes, steroids and poor blood supply.
Wound swab: Sample of wound discharge sent for culture and antibiotic sensitivities.
Wrist flexors: Forearm muscles that bend the wrist forwards.
X-linked recessive: Inheritance via a faulty gene on the X chromosome: males affected, females usually carriers.
X-ray: Plain radiograph; in gas gangrene it can show gas in the soft tissues.
Xanthelasma: Soft yellow cholesterol plaques on the eyelids.
Xanthine: Purine breakdown product that can form radiolucent stones.
Xanthine oxidase: Enzyme that converts hypoxanthine and xanthine into uric acid.
Xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from broken-down blood, typical of subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Xiphoid: The small pointed bottom tip of the breastbone.
Xylometazoline: A decongestant nasal spray; causes rebound congestion if used for more than a week.
Y descent: The fall in the JVP waveform as the tricuspid valve opens; absent in tamponade.
Yeast: A single-celled fungus; Candida grows as yeast that reproduces by budding.
Yersinia: A genus of Gram-negative bacteria; Yersinia enterocolitica is the classic trigger of mesenteric adenitis.
Yersinia enterocolitica: A Gram-negative bacterium spread by contaminated food that can cause mesenteric adenitis and 'pseudoappendicitis'.
Z score: Bone density compared with people of the same age and sex.
Z-thumb: Thumb deformity with flexed MCP and hyperextended IP joint.
Ziehl-Neelsen: A stain that shows acid-fast bacilli as red rods on a blue background.
Zoledronic acid: Yearly intravenous bisphosphonate used by specialists.
Zollinger–Ellison syndrome: Severe peptic ulcers, reflux and diarrhoea from a gastrinoma.
Zona fasciculata: Middle cortical layer that makes cortisol.
Zona glomerulosa: Outer cortical layer that makes aldosterone.
aTIV: Adjuvanted trivalent influenza vaccine, offered to people aged 65 and over.
abdominal X-ray: A plain X-ray film of the abdomen, also called an AXR.
abdominal angina: Pain after eating caused by gut arteries too narrow to meet digestive demand.
abdominal distension: Swelling or bloating of the abdomen from gas, fluid or bowel dilation.
abdominal ultrasound: Imaging of the abdomen with sound waves; first choice for the gallbladder.
abdominal wall: The layers of skin, fat, muscle and fascia that enclose the abdomen.
abdomino-perineal resection: Removal of rectum, anal canal and anus, leaving a permanent end colostomy.
absent pulses: No palpable pulse, suggesting blocked arteries upstream.
absorptive surface area: The total area of gut lining available to take up nutrients, increased by villi.
acetylates: Adds an acetyl group to a protein; aspirin does this to COX-1, permanently switching it off.
achalasia: Failure of the LOS to relax with loss of peristalsis, causing dysphagia to solids and liquids.
acid-fast: Retains stain after acid washing because of a waxy mycolic acid cell wall.
acid-peptic digestion: Damage to the gut wall by stomach acid and the enzyme pepsin.
acidosis: A process lowering blood pH below 7.35.
acinar cells: The pancreatic cells that make digestive enzymes.
acoustic neuroma: Benign tumour of the vestibulocochlear nerve causing hearing loss, tinnitus and imbalance.
acromegaly: Excess growth hormone in adults, causing soft tissue and bone overgrowth.
action potential: The electrical cycle of a heart cell; hypercalcaemia shortens it.
action tremor: Tremor during voluntary movement, such as pouring or writing.
activated charcoal: Oral adsorbent that binds drugs in the gut; best within an hour of ingestion.
active movement: Movement the patient makes by themselves, limited in PMR by pain.
active rewarming: Adding heat with warmed IV fluids, forced-air blankets or internal methods.
active surveillance: Monitoring low-risk cancer with PSA, MRI and biopsy, treating only if it progresses.
active vitamin D: Calcitriol, the form made by the kidney that acts on the gut and bone.
acute abdomen: Sudden severe abdominal pain that may need urgent surgery.
acute adrenal insufficiency: Sudden lack of cortisol causing shock, low sodium and collapse; an adrenal crisis.
acute angle-closure glaucoma: Sudden rise in eye pressure causing a red, painful eye, haloes and vomiting.
acute bronchitis: Short-lived, usually viral, inflammation of the bronchi causing cough, without lung consolidation.
acute chest syndrome: Fever, chest pain, hypoxia and a new lung infiltrate in sickle cell disease; a medical emergency.
acute cholangitis: Infection of an obstructed bile duct: fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
acute disease effect: MUST item scoring patients so unwell they are likely to have no intake for over 5 days.
acute exacerbation: A sudden worsening of a long-term condition.
acute fatty liver of pregnancy: Third-trimester fat infiltration of the liver causing acute liver failure.
acute mesenteric ischaemia: Sudden loss of bowel blood supply, usually from an embolus or thrombosis.
acute pancreatitis: Sudden inflammation of the pancreas caused by its own enzymes being switched on too early.
acute promyelocytic leukaemia: A subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia classically complicated by DIC.
acute retention: Sudden, painful inability to pass urine.
acute urinary retention: Sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a distended bladder.
acute-on-chronic: Sudden decompensation of an already cirrhotic liver after an acute insult.
adenocarcinoma: Cancer arising from glandular epithelium, here of the small bowel.
adenoma: A benign tumour of glandular tissue.
adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence: Stepwise mutations turning a benign adenomatous polyp into invasive cancer over years.
adenomatous polyp: A benign, pre-malignant growth of colonic glandular tissue.
adenovirus: Virus family; serotypes 40 and 41 cause mild childhood gastroenteritis.
adhesions: Bands of scar tissue inside the abdomen, usually after surgery, that can kink or trap bowel.
adjusted calcium: Total calcium corrected for the albumin level; the value used to make decisions.
adjuvant chemotherapy: Chemotherapy given after surgery to reduce the risk of recurrence.
admission: Being kept in hospital for treatment.
adrenal adenoma: Benign tumour of the adrenal cortex; the commonest endogenous cause of Cushing's.
adrenal crisis: Life-threatening cortisol deficiency with shock, vomiting and low sodium.
adrenalectomy: Surgical removal of an adrenal gland.
adrenaline: A stress hormone from the adrenal glands that raises glucose and triggers sweating, tremor and palpitations.
aerosols: Tiny airborne particles that can carry virus over longer distances than droplets.
affect: The outward expression of emotion seen by the examiner.
afferent: Carrying signals towards the brain; the optic nerve is the afferent limb of the pupil reflex.
affinity: How tightly a drug binds its target.
afterload: The resistance a ventricle must pump against.
aganglionic: Lacking the nerve cell bodies (ganglia) that let the bowel wall relax.
agonist: A drug that binds to a receptor and activates it, copying the natural hormone.
air entry: How well air can be heard moving into the lung on listening with a stethoscope.
air leak: Continued escape of air from the lung into the pleural space.
air-bone gap: Difference between air and bone thresholds; a gap means conductive loss.
air-fluid level: A flat line on X-ray where gas sits above fluid inside a cavity.
air-fluid levels: Flat lines on an erect X-ray where gas sits on top of fluid in dilated bowel.
airway resistance: How hard it is for air to flow through the airways; raised when they narrow.
albumin: Main blood protein; low in malnutrition and malabsorption.
alcohol misuse: Drinking at a level that harms health; also causes poor diet and vitamin loss.
alcoholic hepatitis: Acute inflammation of the liver from heavy drinking, often after a binge.
alcoholic ketoacidosis: Ketoacidosis after heavy drinking and starvation, with a normal or low glucose.
aldosterone: Adrenal hormone that makes the kidney retain sodium and water and lose potassium.
alfacalcidol: Active vitamin D analogue that works without PTH or renal activation.
alfuzosin: An alpha-1 antagonist used like tamsulosin in BPH.
alkalosis: A process raising blood pH above 7.45.
allopurinol: A gout drug that blocks breakdown of azathioprine, so together they can cause dangerous bone marrow suppression.
allosteric: Binding at a site other than the main one to change how a receptor responds.
alpha-1 antagonist: Drug that blocks alpha-1 receptors, relaxing smooth muscle; first-line in BPH.
alpha-toxin: Lecithinase made by Clostridium perfringens that destroys cell membranes.
alteplase: A recombinant tissue plasminogen activator that converts plasminogen to plasmin to dissolve clot.
altered mental state: Any change in alertness, behaviour or thinking.
alveoli: Tiny air sacs where gas exchange happens.
amaurosis fugax: Painless, temporary, curtain-like loss of vision in one eye from retinal artery ischaemia.
ambulatory device: A small portable drain with a valve that lets the patient go home with it in place.
aminosalicylates: 5-ASA drugs such as mesalazine and sulfasalazine.
amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for sleep and pain.
amlodipine: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for hypertension; a drug cause of constipation.
ammonia: A toxic by-product of protein breakdown normally cleared by the liver's urea cycle.
amoxicillin: A penicillin antibiotic; causes a rash in EBV infection.
ampicillin: A penicillin antibiotic closely related to amoxicillin.
ampulla of Vater: Where the common bile duct and pancreatic duct open into the duodenum.
amputation: Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb.
amygdala: Brain region that detects threat and drives fear responses.
amylase: A pancreatic enzyme that digests starch; 3x the upper limit supports pancreatitis.
anabolic steroids: Testosterone-like drugs used in bodybuilding; they raise red cell production.
anaemia: A low haemoglobin level, causing tiredness, breathlessness and pallor.
anaemic: Having a low haemoglobin, so blood carries less oxygen.
anaerobes: Bacteria that grow without oxygen, common in the mouth and dental plaque.
anaerobic glycolysis: Breaking down glucose without oxygen, producing lactate.
anaerobic metabolism: Making energy without oxygen, which produces lactate.
anal cancer: Usually squamous cell carcinoma of the anus; can mimic a fissure off the midline.
anal fissure: A linear tear in the lining of the anal canal.
anal tone: Resting tightness of the anal sphincter, checked on rectal examination.
anal verge: The outer edge of the anal canal where it meets perianal skin.
anaplastic carcinoma: Rare, very aggressive thyroid cancer in the elderly.
anastomosis: A surgical join between two ends of bowel.
anastomotic leak: Leakage of bowel contents from a surgical join, typically days 5 to 7.
anatomical barriers: Skin and mucous membranes that normally keep bacteria out.
andexanet alfa: Decoy factor Xa protein that reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban.
androgen deprivation therapy: Treatment that removes or blocks testosterone to slow prostate cancer.
angioplasty: Widening a narrowed artery from inside with a balloon, sometimes with a stent.
anhedonia: Loss of interest or pleasure in activities that used to be enjoyable.
anhidrosis: Loss of sweating on one side of the face.
anion gap: (Na + K) − (HCO3- + Cl); a raised value means unmeasured acid such as ketones or lactate.
ankle-brachial pressure index: Ratio of ankle to arm systolic blood pressure; low values mean arterial disease.
ankylosing spondylitis: Chronic inflammatory arthritis of the spine and sacroiliac joints that causes back stiffness.
annulus fibrosus: The tough outer ring of an intervertebral disc.
anoderm: The thin, sensitive skin lining the lower anal canal.
anorectal manometry: A test that measures pressures in the anal sphincters and rectum.
anorexia nervosa: Eating disorder with deliberate restriction of intake and very low body weight.
anosmia: Loss of the sense of smell; a distinctive Covid-19 symptom.
antacids: Alkaline medicines that neutralise stomach acid for quick relief.
anterior axillary line: A vertical line down from the front fold of the armpit.
anterior chamber: Fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
anterior epistaxis: Bleeding from the front of the nose, usually Little's area; typically mild.
anterior ethmoidal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery (internal carotid) supplying the upper anterior nose.
anterior horn cells: Lower motor neuron cell bodies in the spinal cord.
anterior pituitary: Front lobe of the pituitary, making prolactin, GH, ACTH, TSH, LH and FSH.
anterior resection: Removal of the upper rectum with anastomosis, often protected by a loop ileostomy.
anterior rhinoscopy: Examination of the front of the nasal cavity with a headlight and speculum.
anterior uveitis: Inflammation of the iris and ciliary body: photophobia, small pupil, ciliary flush.
anterograde amnesia: Inability to form new memories after the brain injury.
anti-GAD: Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase; positive in autoimmune type 1 diabetes.
anti-HBc: Antibody to hepatitis B core antigen; shows natural infection (IgM recent, IgG past or chronic).
anti-HBs: Antibody to hepatitis B surface antigen; means immunity from vaccine or recovery.
anti-HCV: Antibody to hepatitis C; shows exposure but not whether infection is still active.
anti-LKM: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibody, the marker of type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.
anti-TNF: Biologic drugs neutralising tumour necrosis factor alpha.
anti-TTG: Anti-tissue transglutaminase antibody; blood test for coeliac disease.
anti-VEGF: Drugs injected into the eye that block VEGF, reducing leakage and new vessels.
anti-androgen: Drug that blocks androgen receptors, e.g. bicalutamide, flutamide, cyproterone.
anti-emetics: Drugs that stop nausea and vomiting.
anti-endomysial antibodies: IgA antibodies against the connective tissue around smooth muscle; highly specific for coeliac disease.
anti-factor Xa: Blood test measuring LMWH activity, used when monitoring is needed.
anti-tTG: Antibodies against tissue transglutaminase; IgA anti-tTG is the first-line coeliac test.
anti-tTG IgA: Antibody blood test used to screen for coeliac disease.
antibodies: Immune proteins that bind specific targets; in NMO they attack aquaporin-4.
anticholinergic side effects: Dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, retention and confusion from blocking acetylcholine.
anticholinergics: Drugs blocking acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, slowing the gut.
anticoagulant: Drug that reduces the blood's ability to form clots.
anticoagulants: Drugs that reduce clotting, such as warfarin or apixaban.
anticoagulated: Taking a drug that reduces blood clotting, such as warfarin or a DOAC.
anticonvulsants: Anti-seizure drugs; some speed up vitamin D breakdown.
antiemetics: Drugs that reduce vomiting, such as ondansetron.
antigenic drift: Gradual point mutations in H and N causing seasonal epidemics and annual vaccine updates.
antigenic shift: Reassortment between strains creating a novel subtype with pandemic potential.
antimicrobial: A drug that kills or stops microorganisms, such as antibiotics or antivirals.
antimicrobial stewardship: Using antibiotics only when needed to limit resistance and side effects.
antimuscarinic: Drug that blocks muscarinic receptors, calming an overactive bladder; can cause retention.
antiphospholipid syndrome: An autoimmune thrombophilia causing venous and arterial clots and miscarriages.
antiplatelet: Drug that stops platelets clumping, reducing arterial clots.
antispasmodic: A drug that relaxes gut smooth muscle to relieve cramps.
antithrombin: A natural anticoagulant protein that heparins enhance.
antithrombin III: Natural anticoagulant protein; heparin boosts its action.
antrum: The lower part of the stomach before the pylorus.
aorta: Main artery leaving the heart, often affected by atherosclerosis upstream of leg arteries.
aortic dissection: A tear in the inner wall of the aorta letting blood split its layers.
aphasia: Loss of language ability from a brain lesion.
apical: At the top (apex) of the lung.
apical node: The highest lymph node at the vascular tie; its involvement makes Duke's C2.
apixaban: DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa.
aplastic crisis: Sudden stop in red cell production, usually from parvovirus B19, with a low reticulocyte count.
appendicitis: Inflammation of the appendix, usually from blockage of its lumen.
appendicular abscess: A pus collection around the appendix, often after perforation, causing swinging fever.
appendix mass: An inflamed appendix walled off by omentum and bowel, felt as a tender RIF lump.
aquagenic pruritus: Itching after contact with water, especially a hot bath; characteristic of PV.
aquaporin: A channel protein that lets water move across cell membranes.
aquaporin-2: Water channel inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
aquaporin-4: Water channel on astrocytes; antibodies against it cause neuromyelitis optica.
aquaporins: Water channels inserted into collecting duct cells by ADH.
aqueous humour: Clear fluid that fills the front of the eye.
arabinogalactan: A cell wall polysaccharide in mycobacteria, target of ethambutol.
arachnoid granulations: Protrusions of arachnoid into the venous sinuses where CSF is reabsorbed.
arachnoid mater: The thin middle meningeal layer, beneath the dura.
arcuate fasciculus: White matter tract linking Wernicke's and Broca's areas.
argatroban: A direct thrombin inhibitor used instead of heparin in HIT.
artemisinin: Fast-acting antimalarial drug class from sweet wormwood.
arterial compromise: Reduced arterial blood supply to the limb.
arterial disease: Narrowing or blockage of arteries, usually from atherosclerosis.
arterial embolus: A clot or debris that travels in the blood and lodges in an artery.
arterial insufficiency: Arterial blood supply too low to meet the tissue's needs.
arterial occlusion: Blockage of an artery so blood cannot reach the tissue.
arterial phase CT: A CT taken just as contrast fills the arteries, to show blockages.
arterial supply: Blood flowing into a tissue through the arteries.
arterial territories: The areas of tissue each artery supplies.
arterial thrombosis: Clot forming within an artery, suddenly cutting off blood supply.
arterial ulcer: A skin ulcer caused by poor arterial blood supply, usually from peripheral arterial disease.
arterioles: Small arteries that control blood flow into capillaries.
artesunate: Artemisinin drug given IV as first-line treatment for severe falciparum malaria.
arthralgia: Joint pain without swelling or inflammation.
asbestos: Fibrous mineral once used in insulation; causes mesothelioma and raises lung cancer risk.
ascending cholangitis: Infection of the bile ducts from obstruction, with fever, jaundice and RUQ pain.
ascitic fluid culture: Growing the ascitic fluid in the lab to identify the bacteria.
aspart: A rapid-acting insulin given with meals.
aspiration: Inhaling blood or fluid into the airway.
aspiration pneumonia: Lung infection from inhaling food, fluid or stomach contents.
aspirin: Antiplatelet that irreversibly blocks COX-1, stopping thromboxane A2 production.
aspirin-sensitive asthma: Asthma worsened by aspirin and NSAIDs, often with nasal polyps.
asterixis: A coarse flapping tremor of outstretched, dorsiflexed hands; sign of hepatic encephalopathy.
astrocytes: Brain support cells that take up ammonia and swell when it accumulates.
ataxia: Lack of coordination, here a broad-based unsteady gait.
atheroma: The fatty plaque inside an artery wall in atherosclerosis.
atherosclerosis: Build-up of fatty plaque in artery walls, narrowing them.
atherosclerotic: Describing fatty, fibrous plaques that build up in artery walls and narrow them.
atherosclerotic plaque: Fatty, fibrous deposit in an artery wall that narrows it and can rupture.
atonic: Lacking muscle tone, so it cannot contract properly.
atorvastatin: A statin given at 80mg after ACS to lower cholesterol and stabilise plaques.
atrial fibrillation: An irregularly irregular heart rhythm; a major source of emboli.
atrial septal defect: A hole between the two atria that can allow right-to-left passage of clot.
atrophic: Wasted or thinned from loss of cells.
atrophic gastritis: Chronic inflammation that thins the stomach lining and loses acid-producing glands.
atrophy: Shrinking of an organ, here a testis after ischaemic damage.
atropine: Long-acting cycloplegic and mydriatic eye drop.
atypical cover: Antibiotics, such as a macrolide, that also treat Mycoplasma, Chlamydia and Legionella.
atypical lymphocytes: Large reactive CD8+ T cells seen on the blood film in EBV.
atypical organisms: Bacteria such as Mycoplasma and Legionella not covered by penicillins; covered by macrolides.
audiogram: The chart produced by pure tone audiometry.
audiometry: Hearing test plotting the quietest sounds heard at each frequency.
aural fullness: A feeling of pressure or blockage in the ear.
auramine: A fluorescent stain for acid-fast bacilli; the fastest smear method.
autoantibody: An antibody that attacks the body's own tissues.
autodigestion: The pancreas being digested by its own activated enzymes.
autoimmune: When the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.
autoimmune screen: Blood tests for autoantibodies such as RF, anti-CCP, ANA and ANCA.
autologous stem cell transplant: High-dose chemotherapy then return of the patient's own stored stem cells.
autonomic: Symptoms from the sympathetic nervous system: sweating, tremor, palpitations and anxiety.
autonomic dysfunction: Faulty control of automatic functions such as heart rate and blood pressure.
autonomic innervation: Nerve supply from the automatic nervous system, which gives vague, poorly localised gut pain.
autonomic nervous system: Nerves controlling involuntary functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and sweating.
autonomic neuropathy: Damage to autonomic nerves, which can blunt the warning response to hypoglycaemia.
autonomous: Working on its own, no longer controlled by normal feedback.
autonomous function: Making thyroid hormone without TSH control.
autosomal dominant: Inheritance where one copy of the gene causes the condition; each child has a 50% risk.
autosomal recessive: Inheritance needing two faulty copies of a gene; two carrier parents have a 1 in 4 chance of an affected child.
autosplenectomy: Shrinking and loss of the spleen through repeated infarction in sickle cell disease.
avascular necrosis: Bone death from lost blood supply, often of the femoral head; MRI finds it early.
axillary nerve: Supplies deltoid and skin over the lower lateral deltoid.
axis: The line around which the bowel twists.
axonotmesis: Axon disrupted but its connective tissue sheath intact, so it can regrow.
azathioprine: A thiopurine immunosuppressant used as a steroid-sparing drug.
back pain: Pain in the back; with new retention it may signal cauda equina compression.
bacterial contamination: Bacteria entering a normally sterile space.
bacterial overgrowth: Too many bacteria multiplying in a blocked space.
bacterial peritonitis: Peritoneal inflammation caused by bacterial infection.
barium swallow: X-ray after swallowing barium contrast; most sensitive test for hiatus hernia.
basal cisterns: CSF spaces around the base of the brain, where SAH blood collects on CT.
basal ganglia: Deep brain nuclei controlling movement initiation, damaged in Parkinson's disease.
basal plasmacytosis: Plasma cells crowded at the base of the mucosa; a sign of chronic colitis.
basal-bolus: Insulin regimen of a long-acting daily dose plus rapid-acting doses with meals.
bedbound: Unable to get out of bed.
bendroflumethiazide: A thiazide diuretic that increases salt and water loss.
benign: Not cancerous; does not invade or spread.
benzodiazepines: Sedative drugs such as diazepam that enhance GABA; avoided long-term because of dependence.
berry aneurysm: A small saccular outpouching at an arterial bifurcation, usually on the Circle of Willis.
beryllium: Metal whose dust can cause lung disease and raises lung cancer risk.
beta cells: Insulin-producing cells in the pancreatic islets of Langerhans.
beta-3 agonist: A drug that stimulates beta-3 receptors in the bladder wall, relaxing the detrusor.
beta-adrenergic: Relating to beta receptors stimulated by adrenaline and noradrenaline.
beta-blockers: Drugs such as propranolol that block adrenaline's effect on the heart and muscles.
beta-hCG: Pregnancy hormone; measured to exclude ectopic pregnancy.
betahistine: Histamine analogue used to reduce the frequency of Ménière's attacks.
bicalutamide: An anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors.
bicarbonate buffer: The CO2, carbonic acid and bicarbonate system that resists changes in pH.
biconvex: Bulging outwards on both sides, like a lens or lemon.
bilateral cortical innervation: Both hemispheres supply the upper face, so a one-sided cortical lesion spares the forehead.
bilateral infiltrates: Shadowing in both lungs on imaging, typical of Covid-19 pneumonia.
bile: Fluid made by the liver that helps digest fat.
bile acid malabsorption: Unabsorbed bile acids reach the colon and cause watery diarrhoea.
bile acids: Detergent-like molecules from the liver that form micelles to absorb fat.
bile duct: Tube that carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
bile leak: Bile escaping after gallbladder surgery, e.g. from a slipped cystic duct clip.
bile salt: Detergent-like molecule in bile that keeps cholesterol dissolved and helps absorb fat.
bile salt pool: The total amount of bile salts the body recycles between the liver and gut.
bile salts: Detergent molecules in bile that keep cholesterol dissolved; reabsorbed in the terminal ileum.
bile stasis: Bile sitting still instead of flowing, which encourages infection and stones.
biliary colic: Pain from a stone temporarily blocking the cystic duct, without infection.
biliary stent: A tube placed in the bile duct, usually at ERCP, to relieve obstruction.
bilious: Containing bile, so green or yellow.
bilious vomiting: Green vomit containing bile, suggesting obstruction beyond the ampulla.
bilirubin: A yellow pigment made when haemoglobin is broken down; build-up causes jaundice.
biochemical: Based on blood or urine chemistry tests.
biochemistry: Blood chemistry results such as calcium and PTH levels.
biologics: Antibody or protein drugs that block specific immune molecules.
biopsy: Taking a tissue sample for histology.
bipolar disorder: Mood disorder with episodes of depression and mania or hypomania.
bisacodyl: Stimulant laxative available as tablets or suppository.
bisoprolol: A cardioselective beta-blocker that slows the heart and lowers oxygen demand after MI.
bisphosphonate: Drug that binds bone and kills osteoclasts, reducing bone resorption.
bisphosphonates: Drugs that inhibit osteoclasts, used for bone metastases (e.g. zoledronic acid).
bitemporal hemianopia: Loss of both outer visual fields, from a chiasm lesion such as a pituitary tumour.
bladder dysfunction: Problems controlling or emptying the bladder, from spinal cord damage in NMO.
bladder outlet obstruction: Blockage at the bladder neck or urethra that stops the bladder emptying.
bladder scan: A bedside ultrasound measuring how much urine is in the bladder.
blanch: To turn pale when pressed, as normal skin does.
blanching: Whitening of a red area when its vessels constrict or are pressed.
blasts: Immature blood cells; many in the blood suggest acute leukaemia.
bleb: A small air-filled blister under the visceral pleura, usually at the lung apex.
bleeding disorder: Condition such as haemophilia where the blood does not clot normally.
bleomycin: A chemotherapy drug in BEP; can cause lung fibrosis.
bloating: A feeling of abdominal fullness or swelling.
blood culture: Blood placed in bottles to grow any bacteria present; the test for typhoid.
blood cultures: Blood samples incubated to grow bacteria and identify the organism and its sensitivities.
blood smear: A drop of blood spread on a slide, stained and examined under the microscope.
blood-aqueous barrier: Tight junctions in iris and ciliary vessels that keep protein and cells out of the aqueous.
blood-retinal barrier: Tight junctions in retinal vessels that stop fluid and protein leaking into the retina.
blood-stage: The part of the life cycle when the parasite lives inside red blood cells.
bloodstream infection: Bacteria growing in the blood (bacteraemia), often from a line.
board-like: Describes a rigid abdomen with involuntary muscle spasm from peritonitis.
bolus: A set volume of fluid given quickly through a drip.
bone marrow biopsy: Sample of marrow, usually from the pelvis, to count plasma cells.
bone profile: Blood panel of calcium, phosphate, albumin and ALP.
bone resorption: Breakdown of bone by osteoclasts, releasing calcium into the blood.
bone scan: Isotope scan showing areas of high bone turnover, such as metastases.
bone tenderness: Pain when pressing over a bone.
bony prominence: An area where bone lies close under the skin, such as the sacrum or heel.
boom-bust: Doing too much on good days and then crashing for days afterwards.
bortezomib: A proteasome inhibitor used to treat myeloma.
botulinum toxin: A nerve toxin injected to temporarily paralyse the internal anal sphincter.
bowel compromise: Bowel whose blood supply is failing, so it may be dying.
bowel habit: A person's usual pattern of passing stool.
bowel ischaemia: Lack of blood supply to the bowel.
bowel obstruction: Blockage stopping bowel contents passing through.
bowel sounds: Gurgling noises of gut movement heard with a stethoscope; reduced when the bowel stops moving.
bowel wall oedema: Swelling of the bowel wall with fluid.
brachial: Relating to the upper arm; brachial pressure is measured at the arm.
brachial neuropathy: Damage to the nerves of the brachial plexus causing arm pain, weakness or numbness.
brachial plexus: The network of nerves from the neck that supplies the arm.
brachioradialis reflex: Supinator reflex at the wrist, C5/C6.
brachytherapy: Radiotherapy given by implanting radioactive seeds in the prostate.
bradykinesia: Slowness of movement with decreasing amplitude on repetition.
brain atrophy: Shrinkage of brain tissue with age or alcohol, stretching bridging veins.
brain fog: Difficulty thinking, concentrating and finding words.
breath sounds: The sounds of air moving in the lungs heard through a stethoscope.
bridging veins: Veins crossing from the brain surface to the dural sinuses; tear in subdural haemorrhage.
broad-spectrum: Active against a wide range of bacteria.
broad-spectrum IV antibiotics: Antibiotics covering many bacteria, given through a vein.
broad-spectrum antibiotics: Antibiotics that kill a wide range of bacteria, including normal gut flora.
bromocriptine: Older dopamine agonist used for prolactinoma.
bronchi: The large airways branching from the trachea into each lung.
bronchial breath sounds: Harsh, hollow breath sounds with a gap between inspiration and expiration, heard over consolidated lung.
bronchial breathing: Harsh, hollow breath sounds heard over consolidated lung.
bronchial epithelium: The layer of cells lining the airways (bronchi).
bronchoalveolar lavage: Washing a lung segment with saline at bronchoscopy to collect a sample.
bronchodilator: A drug that widens the airways, such as salbutamol.
bronchoscopy: Camera passed into the airways to see and biopsy a tumour; the confirmatory test.
bronchospasm: Narrowing of the airways; a risk of non-selective beta-blockers in asthma.
bruising: Bleeding under the skin from damaged small vessels, seen as a purple or blue mark.
brush border: Microvilli on enterocytes, carrying digestive enzymes.
bubble echocardiogram: Echo with agitated saline to show right-to-left shunting across a PFO.
bubbling: Air bubbles in the water seal, showing an ongoing air leak.
buccal: Given inside the cheek, absorbed through the lining of the mouth.
buccal mucosa: The lining of the inside of the cheeks.
budesonide: Steroid with high first-pass liver metabolism, used for Crohn's induction.
buffalo hump: Fat pad over the upper back and base of the neck.
bulbar: Relating to the brainstem cranial nerves controlling speech and swallowing.
bulbar injection: Redness of the conjunctiva over the eyeball itself, rather than inside the lids.
bulk-forming: Laxatives that absorb water to increase stool mass, such as ispaghula husk.
bulla: An air space larger than 1 cm within the lung, common in emphysema.
burr hole: A small hole drilled in the skull to drain a clot in an emergency.
burr hole craniostomy: Drilling a small hole in the skull to drain liquefied chronic subdural blood.
bypass: Surgery that routes blood around a blocked artery using a vein or graft.
cAMP: Cyclic AMP: a second messenger that relaxes smooth muscle when raised by beta-2 agonists.
cART: Combination antiretroviral therapy: usually three drugs from at least two classes.
cabergoline: Long-acting dopamine agonist; first-line for prolactinoma.
cachexia: Wasting of muscle and fat from chronic disease such as cancer.
caecum: The first pouch of the large bowel, where the appendix attaches.
caffeine: A stimulant in coffee and tea that irritates the bladder and increases urine output.
calamine lotion: Soothing pink lotion used to ease chickenpox itch.
calcified vessels: Arteries stiffened by calcium, common in diabetes and CKD, giving falsely high ABPI.
calcimimetic: A drug that mimics calcium at its sensing receptor, switching off PTH release.
calcineurin inhibitors: Ciclosporin and tacrolimus; block T-cell activation.
calcitonin: Hormone that rapidly but briefly lowers calcium; used with steroids in severe cases.
calcitriol: 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, the active form; increases gut calcium absorption.
calcium: A mineral needed for bones, absorbed in the duodenum with the help of vitamin D.
calcium channel blockers: Drugs that block calcium entry into smooth muscle, causing relaxation.
calcium gluconate: IV calcium preparation used for acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia.
calcium-sensing receptor: Receptor on parathyroid cells that detects calcium and reduces PTH when calcium is high.
calf claudication: Cramping calf pain on walking that eases with rest, from inadequate arterial supply.
calf muscle pump: Calf muscles squeezing deep veins during walking to push blood back to the heart.
canalicular: Spread along natural channels such as bile ducts, airways or the urinary tract.
cannabis: A recreational drug; smoking it raises the risk of pneumothorax.
cannonball metastases: Multiple large round lung metastases, classically from renal cell carcinoma.
capillaries: The tiniest blood vessels, where oxygen passes to the tissues.
capillary: The tiniest blood vessels, where oxygen passes to the tissues.
capillary bed: A network of tiny vessels where blood exchanges substances with tissue; circulating cancer cells get trapped there.
capillary blood glucose: Finger-prick glucose reading at the bedside.
capillary closing pressure: The external pressure that collapses capillaries and stops blood flow (about 32 mmHg).
capillary glucose: Finger-prick blood glucose measured at the bedside.
capillary leak: Inflamed capillaries letting fluid escape into tissues and body spaces.
capillary permeability: How easily fluid leaks out through the walls of the smallest blood vessels.
capillary refill: Time for colour to return after pressing the skin; over 2 seconds suggests poor perfusion.
capillary refill time: Seconds for skin colour to return after pressing; over 2 to 3 seconds suggests shock.
capsular invasion: Tumour breaking through its capsule; defines follicular carcinoma.
carbohydrate metabolism: The chemical breakdown of sugars and starch to release energy.
carbon-13 urea breath test: Breath test detecting H. pylori, which splits labelled urea into labelled CO2.
carboplatin: A platinum chemotherapy drug used for seminoma.
carcinogen: A substance that can cause cancer.
carcinoid: Neuroendocrine tumour that can secrete hormones including ACTH.
carcinoma: A cancer arising from epithelial cells.
cardiac preload: The filling of the heart with blood before it contracts; falls when great veins are compressed.
cardinal signs: The key features that define a condition.
cardiogenic shock: Low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion because the heart is failing as a pump.
cardiomyopathy: Disease of the heart muscle that weakens or stiffens it.
cardiothoracic surgery: The surgical specialty operating on the heart, lungs and chest.
cardiovascular disease: Disease of the heart and blood vessels, such as angina, MI, stroke and peripheral arterial disease.
cardiovascular events: Heart attacks, strokes and similar arterial events.
care homes: Residential homes for older people, a classic closed setting for norovirus outbreaks.
carotid Doppler: Ultrasound measuring carotid narrowing and blood flow.
carotid arteries: The main arteries in the neck supplying the head and brain.
carotid atherosclerosis: Fatty plaque build-up in the carotid arteries in the neck.
carotid bruit: A whooshing sound over the carotid from turbulent flow through a stenosis.
carotid endarterectomy: Surgery to remove atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery.
carotid stenosis: Narrowing of the carotid artery, usually by atherosclerosis.
carpal spasm: Cramping of the hand with the wrist and fingers flexed, a sign of low calcium.
carpal tunnel: Median nerve compression at the wrist, causing tingling in the fingers.
carpal tunnel syndrome: Median nerve compression at the wrist under the flexor retinaculum.
carpopedal spasm: Spasm of the hands and feet, fingers flexed at the knuckles.
caseating necrosis: Cheese-like dead tissue at the centre of a TB granuloma.
cast nephropathy: Tubular blockage by protein casts made of light chains.
catabolic: Breaking down tissue, for example muscle protein.
catabolism: Breaking down body tissues (fat, muscle) for energy.
cataracts: Clouding of the eye's lens; a chronic hypocalcaemia complication.
catheter: A tube placed into the body, often into the bladder to drain urine.
catheterisation: Passing a tube into the bladder to drain urine.
cauda equina: Bundle of lumbosacral nerve roots below the end of the spinal cord.
cauda equina syndrome: Compression of the cauda equina causing saddle anaesthesia, sphincter disturbance and bilateral leg signs.
causative organism: The microbe responsible for the infection.
cautery: Sealing a bleeding vessel with heat or chemicals.
cavernous sinus: Venous channel beside the pituitary containing CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI and the carotid artery.
cavernous sinus thrombosis: Infected clot in the venous sinus beside the pituitary, causing bilateral eye signs and cranial nerve palsies.
cavitating: Forming air-filled holes within lung consolidation.
cavitating lesion: A lesion whose centre has died and broken down, leaving an air-filled hole.
cavitation: Formation of an air-filled hole in the lung where necrotic tissue has drained away.
cefotaxime: IV third-generation cephalosporin used for orbital cellulitis.
ceftriaxone: A third-generation cephalosporin given IM to treat gonorrhoea.
cefuroxime: A second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used with metronidazole in penicillin allergy.
cell-mediated immunity: T cell immunity; when it falls, VZV can reactivate.
cells and flare: Slit-lamp signs of inflammatory cells and protein in the anterior chamber.
cells/µl: Cells per microlitre, the unit for counting cells in a fluid sample.
cellulitis: Bacterial skin infection with fever and spreading, well-demarcated redness.
central DI: Another name for cranial DI: too little ADH is made or released by the brain.
central lines: Catheters placed in a large central vein for drugs, fluids or monitoring.
central obesity: Fat gain around the abdomen and trunk with relatively thin limbs.
central retinal artery: Branch of the ophthalmic artery supplying the inner retina.
central scotoma: A blind or dim spot in the centre of the visual field.
central sulcus: The groove between the two prostate lobes; lost when cancer spreads across the gland.
centrilobular: Around the central vein of the liver lobule (zone 3), where paracetamol damage is worst.
cephalosporins: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as ceftriaxone; a major C. difficile risk.
cerebello-thalamo-cortical circuit: Loop from cerebellum through thalamus to motor cortex, thought to generate essential tremor.
cerebral amyloid angiopathy: Amyloid deposits in cortical vessel walls causing lobar haemorrhages in the elderly.
cerebral malaria: Severe falciparum malaria with reduced consciousness, confusion or seizures.
cerebral oedema: Swelling of the brain from excess water, causing drowsiness and seizures.
cervical lymph nodes: Lymph nodes in the neck; often enlarged after a sore throat.
cervical myelopathy: Spinal cord compression in the neck causing UMN signs and sensory loss.
cervical sympathetic plexus: The network of sympathetic nerves in the neck that supplies the eye and face.
chemical irritation: Inflammation caused by acid or bile rather than bacteria.
chemical peritonitis: Peritoneal inflammation caused by acid or bile rather than bacteria.
chemotherapy: Drug treatment that kills rapidly dividing cancer cells.
chest drain: A tube inserted into the pleural space, connected to an underwater seal, to let air or fluid out.
chest expansion: How much the chest widens on a deep breath; reduced when the rib joints stiffen.
chiasmal compression: Pressure on the optic chiasm, usually from a mass in or above the pituitary fossa.
chickenpox: Itchy, feverish childhood illness with spots at different stages at once.
chlordiazepoxide: Long-acting benzodiazepine used to manage alcohol withdrawal.
chloroquine: Antimalarial for non-resistant vivax and ovale; falciparum is often resistant.
chlorphenamine: Sedating oral antihistamine used for itch.
chlortalidone: A thiazide-like diuretic that can cause metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia.
chlorthiazide: A thiazide diuretic (also spelt chlorothiazide) used in nephrogenic DI.
cholangiocarcinoma: Cancer of the bile ducts; tumour marker CA 19-9.
