retrograde spread: Infection travelling backwards up a duct, here from urethra to epididymis.
retrograde venous flow: Blood flowing back down a vein through incompetent valves; also called reflux.
retroperitoneal: Lying behind the peritoneum, at the back of the abdomen.
reuptake: Return of a released neurotransmitter into the nerve ending that released it.
revascularisation: Restoring blood flow to a limb by angioplasty or bypass surgery.
reversal: Undoing a drug's effect on clotting, for warfarin by giving vitamin K.
rewarming shock: A fall in blood pressure during rewarming as vessels dilate before cardiac output rises.
rhabdomyolysis: Muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin, potassium and CK; can cause AKI.
rhinoscopy: Looking inside the nose with a light and speculum.
rhinovirus: The common cold virus; the most common cause of acute bronchitis.
rhonchi: Low-pitched rattling sounds from mucus in large airways, often clearing after a cough.
ribavirin: An antiviral sometimes added to hepatitis C treatment.
ribonucleotide reductase: The enzyme that makes DNA building blocks; blocked by hydroxycarbamide.
rickets: Defective mineralisation in children before the growth plates fuse.
rifabutin: A rifamycin with fewer drug interactions, used in place of rifampicin.
rifampicin: TB drug that inhibits RNA polymerase; turns urine orange and induces liver enzymes.
rifaximin: A poorly absorbed antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing gut bacteria.
right heart strain: Overload of the right ventricle from a sudden rise in pulmonary pressure.
right hemicolectomy: Removal of caecum, ascending and proximal transverse colon.
right iliac fossa: The right lower part of the abdomen (RIF).
right lower quadrant: The right lower quarter of the abdomen, overlapping the RIF.
rigid abdomen: A board-like hard abdomen, a sign of peritonitis.
rigidity: A board-like abdomen from constant muscle spasm; suggests generalised peritonitis.
rigors: Violent shaking with a feeling of cold as the temperature rises.
riluzole: Antiglutamatergic drug that modestly slows MND progression.
ring-shaped inclusions: Ring forms inside red cells on a film; typical of P. falciparum.
risk factor modification: Reducing risks such as smoking, cholesterol and blood pressure.
risperidone: An atypical antipsychotic that blocks dopamine and so can raise prolactin.
ritonavir: Booster that inhibits nirmatrelvir's metabolism (CYP3A4) to raise its levels.
rivaroxaban: DOAC that directly inhibits factor Xa.
rolling hernia: Para-oesophageal hernia: fundus rolls up beside the oesophagus, GOJ stays below the diaphragm.
rose spots: Faint pink macules on the trunk in typhoid fever.
roseola infantum: HHV-6 infection in infants: high fever for 3 days, then rash as fever settles.
rotavirus: Virus causing severe gastroenteritis in under 5s; prevented by a UK routine vaccine.
rotavirus vaccine: Oral vaccine in the UK infant schedule preventing severe rotavirus.
rouleaux: Red cells stacked like coins on a blood film, caused by excess protein.
rubber band ligation: A tight band placed at the base of an internal haemorrhoid so it dies and falls off.
rubella: German measles: a mild viral rash illness, dangerous to the fetus in pregnancy.
rupture: A tear or burst through a structure.
sacral: Relating to the sacrum at the base of the spine.
sacroiliitis: Inflammation of the sacroiliac joints causing low back pain.
sacrum: The triangular bone at the base of the spine, the commonest pressure ulcer site.
saddle anaesthesia: Numbness of the perineum, buttocks and inner thighs.
safety-net: Clear advice on which changes mean coming back urgently.
safety-netting: Telling a patient which warning signs should prompt them to return.
salbutamol: Short-acting beta-2 agonist inhaler that opens narrowed airways.
salicylate: Aspirin and related drugs; overdose causes respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis.
salivary cortisol: Late-night saliva cortisol; raised in Cushing's because the night-time dip is lost.
salvage: Saving the testis so it can be kept rather than removed.
sanitation: Clean water supply and safe disposal of sewage.
saphena varix: A swelling of the great saphenous vein at the groin with a cough impulse.
saphenofemoral junction: Where the great saphenous vein joins the femoral vein in the groin.
saponification: Fatty acids from fat necrosis combining with calcium, lowering serum calcium.
sarcoidosis: Inflammatory disease with granulomas that can infiltrate the pituitary and hypothalamus.
saturations: Percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen, measured by pulse oximetry.
scalloping: A notched, saw-tooth look to the duodenal folds at endoscopy, seen in coeliac disease.
scapular winging: Medial border of the scapula lifting off the chest wall.
scarlet fever: Group A Strep infection with a sandpaper rash and strawberry tongue.
schistocytes: Fragmented red cells on a blood film, seen in microangiopathic haemolysis such as TTP.
schizogony: Asexual multiplication of the parasite, first in the liver then in red cells.
sciatic nerve stretch test: Straight leg raise test for L5/S1 root irritation.
sciatica: Pain radiating down the back of the leg from a lumbar or sacral nerve root, usually a disc prolapse.
sclera: The tough white outer wall of the eyeball.
scleritis: Painful inflammation of the white of the eye that can threaten sight.
scleromalacia perforans: Painless necrotising scleritis without inflammation, classically in long-standing rheumatoid arthritis.
sclerotherapy: Injection of a sclerosant to scar and shrink a haemorrhoid.
sclerotic: Dense, white-looking bone lesions on X-ray from extra bone formation.
scotoma: An area of lost or reduced vision within the visual field.
screening: Testing people without symptoms to find disease or risk early.
scrotal: Relating to the scrotum, the skin sac holding the testes.
scrotal ultrasound: Imaging of the scrotum; Doppler shows testicular blood flow to exclude torsion.
secondary bacterial pneumonia: Bacterial lung infection that follows a viral illness such as flu.
secondary hyperparathyroidism: Appropriate PTH rise in response to low calcium, e.g. vitamin D deficiency or CKD.
secondary polycythaemia: Raised red cells driven by raised EPO, from hypoxia or an EPO-producing tumour.
secondary prevention: Finding disease early, before symptoms, such as cancer screening.
secondary spontaneous pneumothorax: Pneumothorax caused by underlying lung disease such as COPD.
secondary tumour: A tumour formed by cancer cells that have spread from the original (primary) site.
secretory diarrhoea: Watery diarrhoea from active secretion of fluid by the gut lining.
segmented RNA genome: A viral genome split into separate RNA pieces, which can swap between strains.
seizures: Bursts of abnormal electrical brain activity causing fits or altered awareness.
self-limiting: Gets better on its own without specific treatment.
self-peptides: Small fragments of the body's own proteins.
self-tolerance: The immune system's normal ability not to attack the body's own tissues.
sella: Sella turcica: the bony pocket in the skull base holding the pituitary.
semaglutide: A GLP-1 receptor agonist used when BMI is 37 or more.
seminiferous tubules: Tubules in the testis where sperm are made.
seminoma: A slow-growing, radiosensitive germ cell tumour; about half of testicular cancers.
senna: Stimulant laxative, usually taken at night.
sensitivity: The proportion of people with the disease who test positive: TP/(TP+FN).
sensorineural hearing loss: Hearing loss from the cochlea or auditory nerve rather than the outer or middle ear.
sensory level: A level on the trunk below which sensation is reduced; points to a cord lesion.
sentinel pile: Another name for the sentinel skin tag of a chronic fissure.
sentinel skin tag: A small tag of skin at the outer end of a chronic fissure.
sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
septic: Having sepsis: a life-threatening body-wide response to infection causing organ dysfunction.
septic shock: Sepsis with low blood pressure needing vasopressors and a raised lactate despite fluids.
sequestration: Infected red cells trapped in small vessels of the brain, kidney and other organs.
serial CT: Repeated CT scans to watch whether a bleed grows.
serology: Blood tests that detect antibodies (e.g. IgM, IgG) to an infection.
seronegative: An arthritis with negative rheumatoid factor in the blood.
serosal: Relating to the outer surface layer of the bowel.
serosal surface: The smooth outer lining of organs inside a body cavity.
serotonin: Neurotransmitter (5-HT) involved in mood and anxiety; raised by SSRIs.
serotonin syndrome: Excess serotonin activity causing hyperthermia, agitation, tremor, clonus and dilated pupils.
serotypes: Strains of a microbe distinguished by their surface antigens.
sertraline: SSRI antidepressant; first-line drug for GAD.
serum: The fluid part of blood left after clotting, used for many lab tests.
serum osmolality: Measured particle concentration of serum; above 320 mOsm/kg in HHS.
serum protein electrophoresis: Blood test separating proteins to show a monoclonal paraprotein band.
sestamibi: Technetium-99m sestamibi scan; nuclear imaging that lights up an overactive parathyroid gland.
seton: A loose thread placed through a fistula to keep it draining.
severe hypoglycaemia: A hypo where the person needs help from someone else to treat it.
severe malaria: Malaria with organ dysfunction, e.g. glucose below 2.2, reduced GCS, AKI, acidosis or severe anaemia.
sex hormones: Oestrogen, progesterone or testosterone, replaced when gonadotrophins fail.
shear: Force when skin stays still while deeper tissue slides, tearing small vessels.
shifting dullness: Dullness to percussion that moves when the patient rolls; a sign of ascites.
shingles: Painful, one-sided, dermatomal blistering rash from reactivated varicella zoster virus.
shiny skin: Thin, smooth, tight skin from chronic ischaemia.
shivering: Involuntary muscle contractions that generate heat; stops in severe hypothermia.
shock: Inadequate tissue perfusion: prolonged capillary refill, tachycardia, cold peripheries, low BP.
short bowel syndrome: Malabsorption after removal of a large length of small bowel.
short saphenous vein: Superficial vein of the back of the calf that drains into the popliteal vein.
shoulder dystocia: Baby's shoulder stuck behind the pelvis during delivery; can stretch the brachial plexus.
shrivelled: Shrunken and wrinkled from drying out.
shunt: A tube that drains CSF from the ventricles to relieve hydrocephalus.
sialic acid: Sugar on host cell surfaces that influenza haemagglutinin binds.
sick day rules: Advice for illness: keep insulin going, check glucose often, drink fluids, pause metformin and SGLT2 inhibitors.
sick-day rules: Advice to double steroid replacement during illness to avoid adrenal crisis.
sickle cell disease: An inherited haemoglobin disorder causing chronic haemolysis and vaso-occlusive crises.
sickle cell trait: Carrying one sickle gene (HbAS); usually no symptoms.
sickle solubility test: Quick screening test for HbS; positive in both trait and disease.
side room: A single isolation room, ideally with its own toilet, to stop spread on the ward.
sigmoid: The S-shaped last part of the colon before the rectum.
sigmoid colon: The S-shaped last part of the colon before the rectum, in the left iliac fossa.
sigmoidoscope: Camera tube passed into the rectum and sigmoid colon.
sigmoidoscopy: Camera examination of the rectum and sigmoid colon.
signet ring cell: Cancer cell full of mucin that pushes the nucleus to one side, like a signet ring.
silent MI: A myocardial infarction without typical chest pain, more common in diabetics, women and the elderly.
silent hypoxia: Low oxygen saturation in a patient who does not feel very breathless.
silver nitrate cautery: Chemical cautery stick applied to a visible bleeding vessel to seal it.
simple transfusion: Giving donor red cells without removing any of the patient's blood.
sitagliptin: A DPP-4 inhibitor; rarely causes pancreatitis.
sitophobia: Fear of eating because food brings on pain.
skin tags: Small soft flaps of skin, here around the anus.
skin turgor: How quickly pinched skin springs back; slow return suggests dehydration.
skin ulcer: A break in the skin that fails to heal.
skip lesions: Patches of inflamed bowel separated by normal bowel, typical of Crohn's.
slapped cheek: Bright red cheeks of parvovirus B19 infection.
slapping gait: Foot slaps the floor on each step because of weak dorsiflexion.
sleep apnoea: Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, often with loud snoring.
sliding hiatus hernia: Commonest type: the GOJ and upper stomach slide up into the chest, causing reflux.
slipped clips: Surgical clips that have come off the cystic duct stump, letting bile leak.
slit lamp: A microscope with a bright light used to examine the eye in detail.
slough: Soft, yellow dead tissue in a wound bed.
slurred speech: Unclear, poorly articulated speech from impaired brain function.
small bowel: The small intestine: duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
small bowel mucosa: The inner lining of the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed.
small bowel obstruction: Blockage of the small intestine causing vomiting, distension and colicky pain.
small cell lung cancer: Aggressive lung cancer linked to smoking; the commonest source of ectopic ACTH.
small saphenous vein: Another name for the short saphenous vein.
smear-positive: Acid-fast bacilli seen on sputum microscopy; the patient is highly infectious.
smoking cessation: Stopping smoking, the single most important risk factor change in PAD.
sodium bicarbonate: IV alkali used in salicylate poisoning to alkalinise urine and speed excretion.
sodium tetradecyl sulfate: A sclerosant drug used to make foam for sclerotherapy.
sodium valproate: An antiepileptic drug that can cause acute pancreatitis.
sofosbuvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks the NS5B polymerase.
somatic: Relating to the body: physical symptoms such as palpitations or tremor.
somatic innervation: Nerve supply that senses sharp pain and touch precisely.
somatic pain: Sharp, well-localised pain from the body wall or parietal peritoneum.
somatostatin analogue: Drug such as octreotide that inhibits GH release.
spasm: Sudden involuntary contraction of a muscle wall.
spasticity: Velocity-dependent increase in tone from UMN damage.
specific: A specific test rarely gives a positive result in people who don't have the disease.
specificity: The proportion of people without the disease who test negative: TN/(TN+FP).
spectrophotometry: Laboratory measurement of CSF bilirubin and oxyhaemoglobin to detect xanthochromia.
spent phase: Late PV when the marrow scars and counts fall, progressing to myelofibrosis.
sperm banking: Freezing sperm before treatment that may affect fertility.
spermatic cord: The bundle carrying the vas deferens, testicular vessels and nerves.
sphenopalatine artery: Terminal branch of the maxillary artery supplying the posterior nasal cavity.
sphenopalatine artery ligation: Endoscopic surgical tying or clipping of the sphenopalatine artery for refractory epistaxis.
sphincter: A ring of muscle that closes an opening, here the urethra.
sphincterotomy: Cutting the sphincter of Oddi during ERCP to let stones pass.
spider naevi: Small red skin lesions with radiating vessels, seen in chronic liver disease.
spike protein: Surface protein of SARS-CoV-2 that binds ACE2.
spinal cord compression: Pressure on the cord causing back pain, leg weakness, a sensory level and retention.
spinal cord disease: Damage to the spinal cord, disrupting nerve control of the bladder.
spinal cord injury: Damage to the spinal cord causing loss of movement and sensation below the level.
spinal metastasis: Cancer that has spread to the vertebrae, risking spinal cord compression.
spinal mobility: How well the spine bends forwards, backwards and sideways.
spiral groove: Groove on the back of the humerus where the radial nerve runs.
spironolactone: An aldosterone antagonist diuretic, the mainstay for ascites.
splenic flexure: The bend of the colon near the spleen; a watershed between SMA and IMA.
splenic rupture: Tearing of the spleen causing internal bleeding; a surgical emergency.
splenic sequestration: Red cells pool in the spleen, which enlarges fast, causing acute anaemia and shock in children.
spongiform: Sponge-like ultrasound appearance with many small cysts; a benign feature.
spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: Infection of ascitic fluid with no perforation or surgical cause, seen in cirrhosis.
spores: Tough dormant bacterial forms that survive heat, drying and alcohol.
sporozoites: Infective stage injected by the mosquito; travels to the liver.
sputum culture: Growing organisms from coughed-up phlegm to identify a chest infection.
squamous cell carcinoma: Cancer of squamous epithelium; central, smoking-linked, cavitates and secretes PTHrP.
squamous cell lung cancer: Central lung cancer strongly linked to smoking and known for PTHrP secretion.
stable angina: Predictable chest pain on exertion relieved by rest or GTN, caused by fixed narrowing without thrombus.
stacked coins: AXR look of dilated small bowel with valvulae conniventes, like a pile of coins.
staggered overdose: Overdose taken over more than an hour, so the treatment nomogram cannot be used.
staging: Working out how far a cancer has spread to plan treatment.
stalk effect: Mild prolactin rise when a tumour compresses the pituitary stalk and blocks dopamine.
stapedius: Tiny middle-ear muscle, supplied by CN VII, that damps loud sounds.
stapled haemorrhoidopexy: Stapling procedure that lifts prolapsed haemorrhoids back into place.
stat: Given immediately, as a single dose.
statin: Cholesterol-lowering drug that inhibits HMG-CoA reductase.
statutory duty: A legal obligation set out in law; it does not depend on the patient's consent.
steatorrhoea: Pale, bulky, offensive, greasy stools that float, from fat malabsorption.
stem cell transplant: Replacing the marrow with donor stem cells; the only curative option in PMF.
stent thrombosis: Clot forming inside a coronary stent, causing MI; the danger of stopping antiplatelets early.
stepped care: Starting with the least intensive effective treatment and stepping up if it fails.
stepwise fever: A fever that rises a little higher each day, typical of typhoid.
sterile saline: Germ-free salt water used to clean wounds.
steroid tapering: Slowly reducing the steroid dose over months to avoid relapse and adrenal crisis.
steroid-sparing: A drug added so that the steroid dose can be reduced or stopped.
steroids: Anti-inflammatory hormones, here used to reduce swelling around brain tumours.
stimulant laxative: Laxatives such as senna or bisacodyl that increase colonic motility via enteric nerves.
stony dull: Very dull percussion note typical of pleural fluid.
stool antigen test: Detects H. pylori proteins in faeces; shows active infection.
stool burden: The amount of stool felt in the abdomen or seen on imaging.
stool culture: Growing bacteria from a faecal sample in the lab to identify the organism.
stool microscopy: Looking at stool under a microscope for parasites, cysts and cells.
stool sample: A sample of faeces sent to the lab to look for the cause of infection.
stooped posture: A forward-bent, hunched posture, the 'question mark' spine of late AS.
straight leg raise: Raising the straight leg stretches the L5/S1 roots; leg pain between 30° and 70° is positive.
strangulated: A hernia whose blood supply is cut off, causing ischaemia; a surgical emergency.
strangulation: Cut-off blood supply to prolapsed tissue; an emergency.
strawberry tongue: Bright red tongue with prominent papillae in scarlet fever.
streptokinase: A streptococcal enzyme that breaks down clots, helping bacteria spread.
striae: Stretch marks; in Cushing's they are wide and purple.
stricture: An abnormal narrowing of a tube such as the bowel, often from scarring.
stridor: High-pitched noisy breathing from upper airway narrowing.
stroke: Sudden loss of brain function from a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain.
sub-Saharan Africa: Africa south of the Sahara; where most falciparum malaria is caught.
subacute: Developing over days, not seconds or months.
subarachnoid space: The CSF-filled space between the arachnoid mater and pia mater.
subchondral erosions: Areas where bone just under the joint cartilage has been eaten away.
subcutaneous emphysema: Gas or air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling.
subcutaneous tissue: The fatty layer beneath the dermis.
subdural: The space between the dura mater and the arachnoid mater.
subdural haematoma: Blood collecting between the dura and brain, often after a fall.
subdural haemorrhage: Bleeding beneath the dura from torn bridging veins, crescent-shaped on CT.
subendocardial: The inner layer of heart muscle, the first to become ischaemic when blood supply falls.
submucosa: Layer of connective tissue and vessels just beneath the mucosa.
submucosal fibrosis: Scarring in the layer under the bowel lining.
subperiosteal abscess: Collection of pus between the orbital bone and its periosteum, usually next to the ethmoid sinus.
succussion splash: Sloshing sound over the stomach when shaken, from retained fluid in outlet obstruction.
suicide risk assessment: Structured questions on thoughts, plans, intent, means, protective factors and previous attempts.
sulcal effacement: Loss of visible sulci on CT from brain compression.
sulfasalazine: An anti-inflammatory used in IBD and arthritis; can cause pancreatitis.
sulfonamide: A class of antibiotics containing a sulfa group, such as co-trimoxazole.
sulfonylureas: Drugs such as gliclazide that stimulate insulin release; cause hypoglycaemia and weight gain.
sulphonylurea: Oral diabetes drug class, such as gliclazide, that makes the pancreas release insulin.
superficial femoral artery: The main thigh artery, a common site of PAD occlusion.
superficial thrombophlebitis: Clot and inflammation in a superficial vein: a hard, tender, red cord.
superficial veins: Veins just under the skin, above the deep fascia.
superimposed infection: Infection that develops on top of an existing problem, here in dead tissue.
superinfection: A second, often bacterial, infection on top of a first, often viral, one.
superior labial artery: Facial artery branch supplying the upper lip and anterior septum.
superior mesenteric artery: The artery supplying the small bowel and right colon; the usual site of embolus.
superior quadrantanopia: Loss of an upper quarter of the field; from a temporal lobe lesion.
superior vena cava: The large vein returning blood from the head, neck and arms to the heart.
superomedial thigh: Upper inner part of the thigh.
supersaturated: Holding more of a substance in solution than it can stably dissolve, so it crystallises.
supervised exercise programme: Structured walking exercise that improves claudication by building collateral circulation.
supinator reflex: Another name for the brachioradialis reflex (C5/C6).
supportive care: Fluids, rest and monitoring while the body recovers.
supportive mattress: A pressure-relieving mattress that spreads weight to prevent and treat pressure sores.
suppository: A solid medicine inserted into the rectum, where it dissolves.
suprasellar: Above the sella turcica, where the pituitary sits.
suprasellar extension: Growth of a pituitary tumour upward out of the sella towards the optic chiasm.
supratentorial: Above the tentorium cerebelli, so involving the cerebral hemispheres.
surgical clipping: Open surgery placing a metal clip across the aneurysm neck.
surgical decompression: An operation to relieve pressure, here on the optic chiasm.
surgical drain: A tube left in after surgery to let fluid escape.
surgical drainage: An operation to release pus from an abscess.
surgical emergency: A problem needing an operation without delay.
surgical emphysema: Air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling (crepitus).
surgical exploration: Opening the scrotum in theatre to look at, untwist and assess the testis.
surveillance: Repeating scans over time to watch for change rather than treating straight away.
susceptibility: How likely someone is to be affected.
suture lines: Fibrous joints between skull bones where the dura is firmly attached.
swelling: Enlargement of a body part, often from fluid (oedema).
swinging: Drain fluid moving up and down with breathing, showing the drain is patent.
swinging fever: A temperature that rises and falls repeatedly, typical of an abscess.
swinging fevers: Temperature that rises and falls sharply, typical of a collection of pus.
swinging light test: Moving a torch between the eyes to compare each optic nerve's pupil response.
swinging pyrexia: A fever that rises and falls repeatedly through the day, typical of a collection of pus.
sympathetic: The fight-or-flight part of the autonomic nervous system.
sympathetic chain: A string of nerve ganglia running beside the spine carrying sympathetic nerves.
syncope: Brief loss of consciousness from reduced blood flow to the brain.
synovium: The lining of a joint that makes joint fluid; inflamed in rheumatoid arthritis.
systemic: Affecting the whole body rather than one area.
systemic illness: Being generally unwell, for example fever, lethargy or sepsis, not just a local problem.
systemic inflammatory response: Body-wide inflammation, with fever, fast heart rate and leaky vessels, triggered by severe injury or infection.
systemic symptoms: Whole-body symptoms such as weight loss, fatigue and fever.
systemic therapy: Treatment that travels through the whole body, such as chemotherapy.
systemic toxicity: Signs of whole-body illness such as fever, fast pulse and low blood pressure.
systemically unwell: Ill throughout the body, such as fever, fast pulse or low blood pressure.
systolic BP: The peak blood pressure when the heart contracts.
systolic pressure: The higher blood pressure reading, during heart contraction.
tTG: Tissue transglutaminase: the enzyme that deamidates gliadin and the target of coeliac antibodies.
tachycardia: Heart rate above 100 beats per minute.
tacrolimus: Calcineurin inhibitor immunosuppressant used after transplant.
tamponade: Stopping bleeding by direct pressure on the vessel.
tamsulosin: An alpha-1 antagonist that relaxes prostate and bladder neck muscle to improve flow.
tapered: A dose reduced gradually rather than stopped suddenly.
target saturations: The oxygen saturation range you aim to keep a patient in, adjusting oxygen to stay there.
targeted therapy: Drugs aimed at a specific mutation or protein in the cancer, such as EGFR.
tear film: The thin fluid layer that keeps the cornea moist.
teardrop cells: Red cells deformed into a teardrop shape squeezing through a scarred marrow.
telangiectasia: Small dilated blood vessels visible on skin or mucosa.
temporal artery: The artery running over the temple at the side of the head, biopsied to diagnose GCA.
temporal bone: Skull bone at the side of the head around the ear and temple.
temporal lobe: The part of the brain at the side, under the temple, involved in hearing and memory.
temporal visual field: The outer half of what each eye sees, towards the side of the head.
tenderness: Pain when an area is pressed on examination.
tendon: Tough cord joining muscle to bone.
tenecteplase: A clot-busting tissue plasminogen activator given as a single bolus.
tenesmus: A constant feeling of needing to open the bowels even when the rectum is empty.
tenofovir: A nucleotide analogue antiviral, first-line for chronic hepatitis B.
tension pneumothorax: Life-threatening pneumothorax where trapped air builds pressure, shifts the mediastinum and causes shock.
tentorial notch: The gap in the tentorium through which the brainstem passes.
tentorium: Fold of dura separating the cerebrum from the cerebellum.
teratogenic: Able to cause abnormalities in a developing baby.
teratoma: A germ cell tumour containing several tissue types; grows and spreads faster than seminoma.
terminal ileum: The last part of the small bowel, where bile salts and vitamin B12 are absorbed.
tertiary hyperparathyroidism: Autonomous PTH secretion after long-standing secondary disease, with a high calcium.
tertiary prevention: Reducing complications of established disease, such as rehabilitation.
test and treat: Testing for H. pylori and treating it before endoscopy in patients without red flags.
test of cure: HPV test and cytology 6 months after CIN treatment to confirm clearance.
testicular torsion: Twisting of the spermatic cord cutting off the testis's blood supply; a surgical emergency.
tetany: Involuntary sustained muscle spasm from irritable nerves.
thalamus: Central brain relay station; medial thalamic damage contributes to Korsakoff's amnesia.
thalidomide: An immunomodulatory drug used in myeloma.
thenar: The muscle bulge at the base of the thumb.
thermoregulation: The body's control of temperature, run by the hypothalamus.
thiamine: Vitamin B1; given before glucose in alcohol-related illness to prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy.
thiazide: Diuretic acting on the distal tubule; paradoxically reduces urine in nephrogenic DI.
thiazide diuretic: Drug acting on the distal tubule that increases sodium and water loss in urine.
thiazides: Diuretics acting on the distal tubule; cause hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis.
thick film: Blood film that concentrates cells to detect parasites and count the burden.
thienopyridines: Class of P2Y12 blockers including clopidogrel and ticlopidine.
thin film: Blood film spread in a single layer to identify the Plasmodium species.
third space: Fluid lost into body cavities or tissues (gut, pleura, peritoneum) rather than the circulation.
third spacing: Fluid shifting out of the blood into the bowel lumen and wall, where it cannot be used.
thoracic duct: Main lymph vessel draining most of the body into the left subclavian vein.
thoracostomy: Making an opening into the chest cavity to let air or fluid out.
threshold: The level a cell must reach before it fires.
thrombin: Enzyme (factor IIa) that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
thrombolysis: Drug treatment that dissolves a clot, such as alteplase.
thrombophilia: An inherited or acquired tendency to form clots, such as factor V Leiden.
thrombophlebitis: Inflammation and clot in a superficial vein, felt as a tender red cord.
thrombosed external haemorrhoid: A clotted haemorrhoid below the dentate line causing a tender purple lump.
thrombosed haemorrhoid: A haemorrhoid with clotted blood inside; purple, tense and very painful.
thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot inside a vessel.
thrombotic: Caused by a clot forming at the site of blockage.
thromboxane A2: Platelet-made signal that causes platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction.
thrombus: A blood clot formed inside a vessel.
thumb-printing: Thickened, oedematous colonic wall folds seen on imaging in severe colitis.
thumbprinting: Rounded indentations of the bowel wall on X-ray caused by mucosal oedema.
thunderclap headache: A severe headache reaching maximum intensity within seconds to a minute.
thyroglobulin: Protein made by thyroid cells; used to monitor differentiated thyroid cancer after surgery.
thyroglossal cyst: Midline neck cyst from the embryonic thyroid tract; rises on tongue protrusion.
thyroid cancer: Malignant tumour arising from thyroid cells.
thyroid eye disease: Autoimmune orbital inflammation in Graves' disease causing proptosis and lid retraction.
thyroid function tests: Blood tests of TSH and thyroid hormones (T4, T3).
thyroid nodule: A discrete lump within the thyroid gland; most are benign.
thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of the thyroid gland.
thyroxine: Thyroid hormone (T4), given as levothyroxine for replacement.
ticagrelor: A P2Y12 antiplatelet used with aspirin in ACS, given with caution over 75 because of bleeding risk.
ticlopidine: An older thienopyridine antiplatelet drug, now rarely used, also linked to TTP.
tinkling bowel sounds: High-pitched bowel sounds of fluid and gas forced past a mechanical blockage.
tinnitus: Ringing in the ears; an early sign of salicylate toxicity.
tirzepatide: Dual GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist used for early-onset type 2 diabetes and weight loss.
tissue death: Death of cells in an area of tissue, also called necrosis.
tissue factor: Protein from damaged tissue that starts the extrinsic pathway.
tissue planes: Natural layers between muscles and fascia along which gas and infection spread.
tissue transglutaminase: Enzyme that modifies gliadin, making it more immunogenic; the antigen in the coeliac blood test.
tissue viability: Whether tissue is still alive and can recover.
titubation: Rhythmic nodding ('yes-yes') or shaking ('no-no') tremor of the head.
tocilizumab: Antibody against the IL-6 receptor, used in ventilated Covid-19 patients.
toes: The most distal part of the foot, first to lose blood supply in PAD.
toileting: Getting to and using the toilet.
tolerance: Needing a higher dose for the same effect.
tolterodine: An antimuscarinic for bladder storage symptoms.
tolvaptan: V2 receptor antagonist that blocks ADH; used for SIADH, not DI.
tongue protrusion: Sticking the tongue out; a thyroglossal cyst rises when this is done.
topical: Applied directly to the skin or affected area.
topiramate: Anticonvulsant used as a further option for essential tremor.
torsion: Twisting of an organ on its blood supply; here the testis rotating on its spermatic cord.
total parathyroidectomy: Surgical removal of all the parathyroid glands.
total thyroidectomy: Removal of the whole thyroid gland.
toxic megacolon: Acute, non-obstructive dilatation of the colon with systemic toxicity; risks perforation.
toxin: A harmful substance made by a microorganism.
toxin A: C. difficile enterotoxin that damages the colonic lining.
toxin B: C. difficile cytotoxin, the main cause of colonic cell damage.
toxins: Poisons made by bacteria that damage tissue.
toxins A and B: The two toxins made by C. difficile that damage the colon lining.
tracer: A radioactive substance taken up by active thyroid tissue on a scan.
tracheal deviation: The trachea pushed off the midline; away from the side of a tension pneumothorax.
tracheobronchial: Relating to the trachea and bronchi together.
trafficking: Movement of proteins such as aquaporin-2 to their working place in the cell membrane.
tranexamic acid: Drug that blocks fibrinolysis; generally avoided in DIC.
trans-sphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
transcoelomic: Spread across a body cavity such as the peritoneum or pleura, e.g. ovarian cancer.
transcoelomic spread: Spread of cancer cells across a body cavity such as the peritoneum.
transcranial Doppler: Ultrasound through the skull measuring cerebral artery blood flow velocity, raised in vasospasm.
transformation zone: The area of the cervix where cells change type, where most CIN arises.
transfusion: Giving donated blood or blood products into a vein.
transient outward potassium current: Early repolarising potassium current in heart cells; cold changes it, producing the J wave.
transilluminate: Light passing through a swelling, showing it contains fluid.
transilluminates: Lets light shine through, as fluid-filled swellings do.
transition point: The point on CT where dilated bowel changes to collapsed bowel; the site of obstruction.
transition zone: The part of the prostate surrounding the urethra, where BPH arises.
transketolase: Thiamine-dependent enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway.
transmissibility: How easily an infection spreads from person to person.
transmural: Affecting the full thickness of the heart wall, from endocardium to epicardium.
transperineal biopsy: Prostate biopsy through the skin between scrotum and anus, with lower infection risk.
transsphenoidal surgery: Pituitary surgery performed through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
transverse colon: The part of the colon running across the upper abdomen.
trauma: Physical injury, even a minor cut.
traumatic tap: Blood in CSF from the needle itself; red cells fall across successive tubes.
treatment-resistant depression: Depression that has not responded to adequate trials of treatment.
tremor: Involuntary shaking, here caused by adrenaline release.
trephine: A core biopsy of bone marrow, used when the aspirate is a dry tap.
tricyclic antidepressants: Older antidepressant class; low doses help pain and sleep.
tricyclics: Older antidepressants, such as amitriptyline, that can raise prolactin.
trigeminal nerve: Cranial nerve V; its ophthalmic branch is the classic site of facial shingles.
triple therapy: PPI plus two antibiotics for 7 days to eradicate H. pylori.
triple vessel disease: Significant narrowing in all three main coronary arteries, often better treated by CABG than PCI.
tropism: The preference of a virus for particular cells or tissues.
troponin: A heart muscle protein released into the blood when cardiomyocytes die; the key blood test for myocardial infarction.
truss: A support belt that holds a reducible hernia in place.
trypsin: A protein-digesting enzyme that activates the other pancreatic enzymes.
trypsinogen: The inactive form of trypsin, normally activated only in the duodenum.
tumour: An abnormal growth of tissue, benign or malignant.
tumour flare: Temporary worsening of cancer from the testosterone surge when a GnRH agonist starts.
tumour marker: A blood substance that rises with a tumour and helps diagnose or monitor it.
tumour markers: Features of a tumour, such as mutations or proteins, that predict response to specific drugs.
tunica vaginalis: Double layer of membrane surrounding the front and sides of the testis.
two-week wait: Urgent cancer referral: the patient is seen by a specialist within two weeks.
tympanic: Measured in the ear canal; unreliable at extremes of temperature.
tympanometry: Test of middle ear pressure and eardrum movement.
type 1 respiratory failure: Low oxygen (pO2 below 8 kPa) with a normal or low carbon dioxide.
type 2 respiratory failure: Low oxygen with high carbon dioxide from hypoventilation.
typhoid: Enteric fever caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread by contaminated food and water.
ulcer: A break in the skin or mucosa that fails to heal.
ulcerative colitis: Inflammatory bowel disease of the colon; classically associated with episcleritis.
ultrasound: Imaging using sound waves; good for gallstones and the biliary tree.
umbilical hernia: A hernia at the umbilicus; common in babies and usually closes by 12 months.
uncal herniation: The uncus pushes through the tentorial notch, compressing CN III and the brainstem.
uncomplicated grief: A normal, time-limited reaction to loss with waves of sadness.
unconjugated bilirubin: Bilirubin not yet processed by the liver; raised in haemolysis.
unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia: Raised bilirubin that the liver has not yet processed, typical of haemolysis.
uncus: The innermost part of the temporal lobe; herniates first when ICP rises.
underlying cause: The disease driving the malnutrition, such as cancer or malabsorption.
underwater seal: Drain bottle where the tube sits under water so air escapes but cannot return.
undetectable: Too low to be measured by the test.
unfractionated heparin: An anticoagulant given IV that boosts antithrombin; preferred when immediate PCI is planned as it is quickly reversible.
ungradable: A pressure ulcer whose depth cannot be judged because eschar or slough covers it.
unheralded: Happening without any warning symptoms beforehand.
unmeasured anions: Negative ions not included in routine tests, such as lactate, ketones and toxin acids.
unpasteurised: Not heat-treated to kill bacteria, so raw milk or cheese can carry infection.
unplanned weight loss: Weight lost without trying, a key warning sign of illness or malnutrition.
unprovoked DVT: A DVT with no clear trigger; prompts a look for cancer or thrombophilia.
unrefreshing sleep: Sleep that does not restore energy despite adequate hours.
unstable angina: Ischaemic chest pain at rest or worsening, with normal troponin, so there is no infarction.
uraemia: Build-up of urea and other waste products from kidney failure.
urate: A breakdown product of DNA; raised with high cell turnover.
urea: Waste product of protein breakdown; the most sensitive U&E marker of dehydration.
urea breath test: Swallowed labelled urea is split by H. pylori; labelled CO2 in breath shows active infection.
urea cycle: Liver pathway that converts ammonia into urea for excretion.
urea:creatinine ratio: Urea divided by creatinine; a high ratio suggests a pre-renal, volume-depleted state.
urease: Enzyme that splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide.
urethral obstruction: A blockage of the urethra, such as a stricture or enlarged prostate.
urethral sphincter: The muscle ring around the urethra that keeps urine in.
urgency: A sudden, hard-to-delay need to open the bowels.
urinalysis: Testing urine for blood, protein, glucose, leucocytes and nitrites.
urinary calcium: The amount of calcium lost in the urine.
urinary dye studies: Tests putting coloured dye in the bladder to see whether it leaks into the vagina.
urinary free cortisol: Cortisol measured in a 24-hour urine collection; raised in Cushing's.
urinary retention: Inability to empty the bladder; often painless in cauda equina.
urine culture: Growing bacteria from a urine sample to identify a UTI and its sensitivities.
urine dip: A dipstick test of urine for blood, protein, leucocytes and nitrites.
urine dipstick: A quick strip test for leucocytes, nitrites, blood and protein in urine.
urine osmolality: Concentration of dissolved particles in urine; low means dilute urine.
urine output: How much urine is passed; falls as the kidneys are poorly perfused.
uroflowmetry: A test measuring how fast urine flows; low peak flow suggests obstruction.
ursodeoxycholic acid: A bile acid used to treat primary biliary cholangitis.
uvea: The pigmented middle layer of the eye: iris, ciliary body and choroid.
uveitis: Inflammation of the iris, ciliary body or choroid, causing a red, photophobic eye.
valaciclovir: Oral prodrug of aciclovir with better absorption.
valve incompetence: Failure of vein valves to close, letting blood flow backwards.
valveless veins: Orbital veins with no valves, so blood and infection can flow back to the cavernous sinus.
valvulae conniventes: Mucosal folds of the small bowel that cross its full width on X-ray.
valvular incompetence: Failure of vein valves to close, letting blood flow backwards.
valvular lesions: Diseased heart valves, which can shed clots.
vancomycin: Glycopeptide antibiotic; given orally it stays in the gut to treat C. difficile.
varicella: Chickenpox, the primary infection with varicella zoster virus.
varicocele: Dilated veins of the spermatic cord; feels like a 'bag of worms'.
varicose veins: Dilated, twisted superficial veins caused by leaky valves.
vas deferens: The duct carrying sperm from the epididymis to the urethra.
vasa recta: Small straight arteries that pierce the colonic muscle to supply the mucosa.
vascular cushions: Normal pads of blood vessels and connective tissue that help seal the anus.
vascular invasion: Tumour cells growing into blood vessels.
vascular markings: Blood vessels normally visible through the bowel lining at endoscopy.
vascular surgery: Surgical specialty treating arteries and veins.
vasculitis: Inflammation of blood vessel walls, causing narrowing, ischaemia or bleeding.
vasculopathic: Having diseased blood vessels, for example from smoking, diabetes or atherosclerosis.
vaso-occlusive crisis: Sickled cells block small vessels, causing ischaemia and severe pain; the commonest presentation.
vasoconstriction: Narrowing of blood vessels to keep heat in the core.
vasoconstrictor: A drug that narrows blood vessels.
vasodilation: Widening of blood vessels, which releases heat and lowers blood pressure.
vasospasm: Sudden tightening of a coronary artery causing ischaemia, classically triggered by cocaine.
velpatasvir: A hepatitis C DAA that blocks NS5A.
venesection: Removing blood from a vein to lower the red cell mass.
venlafaxine: SNRI used if an SSRI fails or is not tolerated in GAD.
venoarterial ECMO: ECMO that supports both heart and lungs by returning blood to an artery.
venous beading: Sausage-like irregular dilation of retinal veins; a sign of ischaemia.
venous congestion: Blood pooling because outflow is blocked; causes swelling in early torsion.
venous drainage: Blood flowing out of a tissue through the veins.
venous eczema: Itchy, scaly inflamed skin of the lower leg from venous hypertension.
venous hypertension: Raised pressure in the leg veins from reflux or obstruction.
venous reflux: Backward flow of blood in a vein because the valves leak.
venous return: The flow of blood back to the heart through the veins.
venous stasis: Slow or pooled blood flow in the veins.
venous thrombosis: A clot in a vein, here the mesenteric veins, blocking blood outflow.
venous ulcer: Shallow, irregular ulcer over the medial malleolus caused by chronic venous hypertension.
ventilation: Moving air in and out of the lungs, which clears carbon dioxide.
ventilator: A machine that breathes for a patient through a tube in the airway.
ventricular fibrillation: Chaotic ventricular electrical activity with no output, the commonest cause of death early in ACS.
ventricular septal rupture: A tear in the wall between the ventricles days after MI, causing a new pansystolic murmur and heart failure.
vertical transmission: Spread of infection from mother to baby around birth.
vertigo: A false sense of movement, usually spinning, from vestibular disease.
vesicles: Small fluid-filled blisters under 5 mm across.
vestibular compensation: The brain's adaptation to a vestibular lesion; slowed by long-term sedatives.
vestibular neuritis: Viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve: days of vertigo without hearing loss.
vestibular schwannoma: Correct name for an acoustic neuroma.
vestibular suppressant: A drug that dampens vestibular signalling to reduce acute vertigo.
vestibulo-ocular reflex: Reflex keeping the eyes still in space when the head moves.
viable: Still alive and able to recover once the blood supply returns.
villi: Finger-like projections of the small bowel lining that absorb nutrients.
villous adenoma: A colonic polyp that can secrete large amounts of fluid and potassium.
villous atrophy: Flattening of the finger-like villi of the small bowel, cutting absorptive surface area.
villous tips: Ends of the villi, where mature absorptive enterocytes sit.
virions: Complete virus particles that can infect other cells.
visceral hypersensitivity: A lowered pain threshold to normal stretching of the gut.
visceral innervation: Autonomic nerve supply that senses stretch, not cutting or pinching.
visceral pain: Dull, poorly localised pain from stretched or inflamed organs, felt in the midline.
visceral pleura: The membrane covering the lung surface.
viscosity: How thick and sticky the blood is; higher viscosity slows flow and causes clots.
visible peristalsis: Waves of bowel contraction seen through a thin abdominal wall in obstruction.
visual acuity: Sharpness of vision, measured on a Snellen chart.
visual cortex: The area of the occipital lobe that receives and interprets signals from the eyes.
visual field: The whole area a person can see while looking straight ahead.
visual field defect: An area of lost vision within the visual field.
visual field testing: Formal mapping of the visual field (perimetry).
visual loss: Reduction or loss of sight in one or both eyes.
visual pathway: The route from retina through optic nerve, chiasm and tracts to the visual cortex.
visual symptoms: Problems with sight, such as blurring, double vision or loss of vision.
vitamin A: A fat-soluble vitamin needed for vision in dim light and healthy skin.
vitamin B12 deficiency: Lack of vitamin B12, absorbed in the terminal ileum, causing anaemia and nerve damage.
vitamin D: Vitamin that, once activated by the kidney, increases calcium absorption from the gut.
vitamin D deficiency: Too little vitamin D, so less calcium is absorbed from the gut.
vitamin K: Vitamin needed to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX and X; reverses warfarin.
vitamin K epoxide reductase: Enzyme that recycles vitamin K; blocked by warfarin.
vitamin supplementation: Giving extra vitamins by mouth or injection to correct deficiencies.
vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment, giving white patches.
vitreous: Clear gel filling the back of the eye.
vocal cord paralysis: Loss of movement of a vocal cord, often from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion.
vocal resonance: How clearly speech is heard through the chest wall; increased over consolidation, reduced over fluid.
volume depletion: Loss of circulating fluid, causing low BP and fast pulse.
volvulus: Twisting of a loop of bowel on its mesentery, causing closed-loop obstruction.
vomiting: Forceful bringing up of stomach contents.
von Hippel-Lindau: Inherited syndrome causing tumours such as haemangioblastomas, kidney cancer and phaeochromocytoma.
von Willebrand factor: Protein that helps platelets stick and carries and protects factor VIII in blood.
waddling gait: Side-to-side walk from weak hip muscles.
waiter's tip: Arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, wrist flexed: Erb's palsy.
wall off: When the body surrounds infection, often with omentum, to stop it spreading.
warfarin: Oral vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant monitored with the INR.
washout: Rinsing the abdominal cavity during surgery to remove contamination.
watchful waiting: Monitoring without surgery, with advice on symptoms that need urgent review.
water deprivation test: Withholds fluid, then gives desmopressin, to confirm DI and its type.
water reabsorption: Taking water back from the urine into the blood as it passes through the kidney.
water seal chamber: The part of a chest drain bottle under water that lets air out but not back in.
watershed: Tissue at the far end of an arterial territory, most vulnerable to low flow.
watershed area: A region at the edge of two blood supplies with relatively poor perfusion.
weight-bearing pain: Pain on standing or walking on the affected limb.
wet AMD: Neovascular age-related macular degeneration, also treated with anti-VEGF.
wet beriberi: Thiamine deficiency causing high-output heart failure and oedema.
wet gangrene: Gangrene with infection: moist, swollen, painful, foul-smelling, no clear edge.
wheeze: High-pitched whistling from narrowed airways, usually on breathing out.
whole-body low-dose CT: CT of the whole skeleton at low radiation dose to find lytic lesions.
whooping cough: Pertussis: Bordetella pertussis infection with bouts of coughing and an inspiratory whoop.
wound discharge: Fluid or pus leaking from a surgical or other wound.
wound healing: The process of repairing damaged tissue.
wound swab: A sample from a wound sent to find the infecting organism.
wrist drop: Inability to extend the wrist, from radial nerve injury.
xanthochromia: Yellow CSF from bilirubin produced as red cells break down, proving an older bleed.
yolk sac tumour: A non-seminomatous germ cell tumour that produces AFP.
zanamivir: Inhaled (or IV) neuraminidase inhibitor; can cause bronchospasm in asthma or COPD.
zoledronic acid: Potent IV bisphosphonate used after rehydration in hypercalcaemia of malignancy.
zygomatic: The cheekbone, which forms the outer wall and floor of the orbit.
γGT: Gamma-glutamyl transferase, a liver enzyme raised with ALP in cholestasis.
